a-century-of-robotics-ep01: 机器人百年史ep01：1920s-1960s 从科幻照进现实 从恰佩克的戏剧、阿西莫夫的三定律，到unimate与stanford arm：工业界和ai实验室的两条道路，如何汇合为现代机器人。 机器人百年史 在美国硅谷，有一个现代信息技术的时光穿梭机：computer history museum；在chm，有一个ai机器人展区，我前段时间在这里待了几个小时，在几十年前被创造出来的各种机器人的包围下，眼前的一切让我无比震惊：近百年的机器人研究历史长河里，相似形态的机器人在不同的时间节点留下足迹，原来，人类在同样的机器人形态下有过那么多轮的尝试。 这些机器人的外壳，像是一次次轮回在这个地球上的我们，不同时代的科学家和梦想家一次次的试图给它们注入“灵魂”。在robot这个词汇被创造出来的105年后，我们似乎来到了人与机器人故事的”临界点“：机器人的躯体和灵魂似乎在这一轮的尝试终于可以和我们共生在地球上。 a century of robotics系列，启发自chm：今天的盛况是否在历史上也存在过？当下的机器人供应链体系是怎么形成的？历史上产业界和学术界在这个方向上的探索都有哪些？哪些落地了？哪些没落地？ai发展的今天为什么会刺激大家对通用机器人的探索？历史不会告诉我们未来的答案，却能帮助我们分辨，什么是真正改变范式的突破，什么只是被时代重新包装的旧命题。 让我们一起来回顾历史，展望未来。 第一部分：科幻和戏剧承载了人类对未来的想象 1921年：捷克剧作家创造了"robot" 1921年，捷克剧作家卡雷尔·恰佩克在戏剧《罗素姆万能机器人》（rossum’s universal robots，r.u.r.）》中，第一次让“robot”这个词走进大众视野。 robot来自捷克语robota，原意是“苦役、劳作”。在恰佩克的故事里，人类在工厂中制造出一种人工生命，让它们承担繁重的劳动——机器人从诞生之初，就是被创造出来替人类干活的。但故事的结局并不美好：这些原本任劳任怨的“工人”最终发动反抗，并毁灭了人类。 chm（computer history museum）robot一次来源的照片 有意思的是，机器人历史的起点并不是一项技术，而是一个关于机器与人的故事。但年轻的俄罗斯裔美国科幻作家isaac asimov（艾萨克·阿西莫夫）并不喜欢这个故事。 1942年：小说家asimov立下的机器人三原则 1939年，19岁的asimov写下自己的第一篇机器人小说《robbie》，并于1940年发表。在他的故事里，机器人robbie并不是一个等待觉醒的怪物，而是一个陪伴小女孩成长、忠诚而可靠的伙伴。asimov第一次开始认真想象：如果机器人是由人类设计和制造的，我们为什么不能从一开始，就把保护和服从人类写进它的规则里？ 这个想法最终变成了著名的“机器人三定律”。1942年，在小说《runaround》中，asimov第一次完整写下这三条规则：机器人不得伤害人类；必须服从人类；在不违反前两条的情况下保护自己。此后几十年，他不断围绕这些看似简单的规则构造新的故事——当规则彼此冲突怎么办？当机器面对模糊的人类命令怎么办？当一个足够聪明的机器人开始理解社会乃至整个人类的利益，又该怎么办？ 1950年，这些早期故事被收入《i, robot》。此后，asimov又把机器人的故事不断向未来延伸，最终甚至将机器人系列与自己的《foundation》系列连接起来。 asimov在机器人历史上的意义，并不只是提出了“三定律”。在真正的机器人还没有走进工厂之前，他已经把问题从“机器人会不会毁灭人类”，推进到了一个更现代的问题——人类究竟应该如何设计一种比普通机器更聪明、能够自主行动的机器？ 而历史很快就从小说走进了现实。 第二部分：总有一些人将人类的想象落到现实 1954年：美国发明家devol让机器人从科幻照进现实 1954年，美国发明家george devol提出了一种“可编程机械臂”——这成为现代机器人的真正起点之一。他设想的机器不再只是按照固定机械结构重复运动，而是可以把一系列动作记录下来，再按照程序自动执行。 1956年，在一次鸡尾酒会上，george devol和joseph engelberger偶然相识。两个人都是科幻迷，很快聊到了isaac asimov笔下的机器人。但这场关于科幻的闲聊，很快变成了一次真正改变机器人历史的讨论。 世界上第一个机器人创业公司unimation两位创始人和他们的送酒机器人unimate devol刚为他的机械臂申请了一项专利，他有技术和想法，但需要资金和商业伙伴；而engelberger恰好是一名工程师，一直在思考如何用更灵活的机器实现工厂自动化。一个想造机器，一个想改造工厂，两个人一拍即合。现代工业机器人的故事由此开始。两人的相遇，最终催生了后来被称为世界第一台工业机器人的unimate，意为universal working mate。 世界上第一个机械臂unimate（1954年） 当时几乎没有现成的机器人零部件可用：早期unimate甚至使用真空管进行数字控制，后来才换成晶体管；编码器、存储器等也不够成熟，因此团队不得不自己设计和制造大量核心部件，包括一套特殊的磁鼓存储系统来记录机器人的动作程序。 虽然最初的unimate已经可以“编程”，但它还没有真正的编程语言。当时采用的是一种非常直观的示教方式：操作人员把机械臂移动到指定位置，机器记录这个位置；再移动到下一个位置，继续记录。完成一系列动作后，unimate就可以按照记录的顺序不断重复执行。 unimate诞生的初衷很简单：把人从那些肮脏、重复而危险的工作中解放出来 1961年：第一台进入工厂的机器人unimate 1961年，通用汽车（gm）以1.8万美元买下了第一台unimate。第一台unimate被安装到通用汽车位于新泽西的工厂。它的第一份工作很简单，却非常适合机器人——从压铸机里取出滚烫的金属零件，再整齐地堆放起来。随后，机器人又开始承担点焊等危险、重复的工作。 但这其实是一笔“赔本买卖”：当时制造一台unimate的成本高达6.5万美元（售价1.8万美元）。engelberger之所以愿意低价出售，是因为他知道，让gm成为第一个客户，本身就是最好的广告，而且他相信更多订单很快就会到来。unimate很快引起汽车行业的注意，chrysler、ford、fiat等汽车公司陆续开始采购机器人。工业机器人也由此从一项发明，真正变成了一门产业。 到1970年代初，unimate的售价已经提高到3.5万美元。但即便如此，unimation直到1975年才第一次实现盈利——距离公司成立已经过去了19年。 第一台unimate，成本6.5万美元，却只卖了1.8万美元。工业机器人从诞生到真正成为一门赚钱的生意，花了近20年。 1970年：机器人进入工厂的第一次冲突 最初，gm工人并不排斥unimate。毕竟，从压铸机中搬运滚烫的金属，是一份危险又没人愿意做的工作。1967年，gm又在俄亥俄州norwood工厂部署了两台点焊机器人，同样没有引起太大争议。 1970年的lordstown工厂，gm一次部署了28台点焊机器人，同时开始大幅提高生产效率。为了生产雪佛兰vega，工厂裁减了至少700名员工，又取消了300—500个被认为“过于简单、不需要人来做”的岗位，并将生产线速度从每小时60辆提高到101辆，提升了67%。 更快的流水线伴随着更长的工作时间。工人被要求每天工作11—12小时，甚至周末加班。矛盾很快爆发：工人提交了超过1.6万起申诉，随后开始罢工。1972年3月，一场罢工让整个工厂停产了22天。 lordstown后来成为“自动化冲击工人”的经典案例。机器人第一次不再只是替人完成危险工作，也开始与裁员、生产提速和劳动强度联系在一起。 这场冲突也在一定程度上影响了unimation在美国的形象。工业机器人虽然诞生于美国，却迟迟没有在自己的故乡真正打开市场。 1970s：unimation点燃了日本工业机器人的浪潮 相比美国，unimate在日本找到了更大的舞台。 1966年，engelberger来到日本，与数百位日本工业界人士进行了数小时交流，希望寻找一家合作伙伴，在日本本土生产机器人。日本企业表现出了极大的兴趣，其中川崎航空（后来的川崎重工）最为积极，最终拿下了unimation的技术授权。1968年，川崎专门成立工业机器人国产化部门，川崎随后派工程师前往美国学习，并将样机带回日本，在此基础上继续研发和国产化。 1969年，第一台日本国产的kawasaki-unimate 2000诞生，它是一个十足的庞然大物：重达1.6吨，体积约1.6×1.2×1.3米，却只能搬运12公斤的物体。售价更是高达约9万美元，相当于今天约59.5万美元。而当时日本大学毕业生的平均起薪，每月只有200多美元。 川崎重工在日本生产的unimate机器人 一个诞生于美国的机器人，由此漂洋过海，在日本开启了另一场更大规模的工业机器人革命。到1980年代中期，日本已经成为“机器人王国”，拥有全球近70%的工业机器人。 第三部分：定义ai的人创造了第一批机器人实验室 1961年：在mit，ai第一次“伸出一只手” 1950年代末，当devol和engelberger正在尝试把unimate送进工厂时，在mit的实验室里，另一群人也开始对“机械手”产生兴趣。但他们想的不是自动化生产，而是一个更像ai的问题：如果计算机真的能够拥有智能，它能不能自己控制一只手，与真实世界发生交互？ 1956年的dartmouth会议刚刚为“artificial intelligence”这个新领域命名。几年后，会议的核心人物开始汇聚mit：1958年john mccarthy（后来的stanford sail创办人）从dartmouth来到mit，1959年marvin minsky（后来的mit csail创办人）加入，而信息论之父claude shannon原本就在这里。最早研究机械臂的这批人，本身就是最早定义“artificial intelligence”的那群人。 1961年，在claude shannon和marvin minsky的指导下，mit博士生heinrich ernstt以《mh-1, a computer-operated mechanical hand》完成博士论文，mh-1也成为最早由计算机直接控制的manipulator之一。 但mh-1真正重要的地方，并不是“计算机终于能让机械臂动起来”。ernst更想知道的是：机械手能不能通过传感器获得外界的信息，再由计算机决定下一步应该怎么动？换句话说，他已经开始尝试建立一个后来贯穿整个机器人研究的闭环：感知世界→计算与判断→控制身体→改变世界。 mh-1 而几年之后，john mccarthy离开mit前往stanford。这群研究“机器如何思考”的人，也将把同一个问题带到美国西海岸——在那里，bernard roth、donald pieper和victor scheinman会进一步追问：如果计算机要控制一只手，我们是不是应该从一开始，就造一只专门为计算机而设计的手？ 1962—1963：john mccarthy来到stanford—ai开始寻找“身体” 1962年，john mccarthy离开mit回到stanford。随后他建立了stanford artificial intelligence laboratory，也就是著名的sail。stanford官方将sail的创立追溯到1963年前后；到1965年，随着计算机系成立和资金、设备完善，sail成为美国最重要的ai实验室之一。 mccarthy到了stanford以后，也想继续做机器人。但问题来了：ai lab里都是搞计算机和数学的人，谁来造机器人的身体？ 于是stanford校方把机械工程系年轻教授bernard roth介绍给了mccarthy。roth是stanford机械工程教授，他的学术背景不是ai，而是经典的mechanism与kinematics——机构学和运动学。恰恰是这套背景，让他成为现代机器人学非常重要的奠基人物之一。因为计算机想控制机械臂，首先必须回答一个看似简单的问题：如果我要让机械臂末端到达空间中的某一个位置，每个关节到底应该转多少度？这就是后来机器人学最基本的问题之一：inverse kinematics，逆运动学。 roth后来回忆，stanford当时担心mccarthy虽然是伟大的数学家，但未必适合负责机械系统，因此希望roth来补上这一块。roth随后承担了sail中机械臂相关的工作。roth在1962年加入stanford机械工程系之前，他曾在columbia跟随ferdinand freudenstein攻读博士，研究的是机构学、连杆和运动学。这批研究者当时正在做的一件事情，就是把过去依靠几何作图解决的机械机构问题，变成可以由数字计算机计算的数学问题。 mccarthy和roth的结合：ai研究者想让计算机控制机器；机械工程研究者开始把机器的运动变成计算机可以理解的数学。 而机器人学恰好诞生在两者的交界处。1962年，sail作为机器人学习的先锋组织，让ai和robotics交汇，在这个ai+robotics的摇篮里，逐步培养了这个交叉领域的早期探索者：scheinman，donald pieper等为机器人学习奠定基础的早期探索者。 1963年：rancho arm—stanford先拿来了一只现成的手 stanford最早并不是自己从零开始造机械臂。他们获得了一只rancho arm。这只机械臂最初并不是为ai设计的，而是为残障人士开发的辅助机械臂。stanford把它接到计算机上，希望用它研究计算机控制。这时候，年轻的victor scheinman进入了bernard roth的团队。 victor scheinman很早就展现出工程天赋，15岁进入mit，1963年获得航空航天工程学位。毕业后，他曾在boeing参与月球重力模拟器，也在apollo项目中参与过指令舱隔热罩和saturn火箭涡轮泵相关工作。后来他进入stanford继续深造，并从航空航天转向机械工程。 真正改变他人生的是加入stanford ai lab。在那里，他成为bernard roth的研究助理，任务是研究如何“为计算机制造手和手臂”。实验室当时已经有一只rancho arm，但这只原本为残障人士设计的机械臂精度不高，逆运动学也很难计算。scheinman随后尝试了蛇形的orm arm和力量巨大的液压机械臂，但都不好控制。这些失败反而让他逐渐意识到：与其造好一只机械臂，再想办法让计算机控制，不如从一开始就造一只“为计算机而生”的手。 1968年：donald pieper—先解决机械臂的“数学” 这个问题首先被bernard roth的学生donald pieper向前推进了一大步。1968年，pieper完成博士论文：《the kinematics of manipulators under computer control》他系统研究机械臂的运动学，并证明：如果机械臂采用某些特殊的关节布局，复杂的逆运动学问题可以得到简化。其中后来影响非常深远的一个思想，就是让腕部的多个旋转轴交于一点。 今天计算机算逆运动学并不是什么大事，但在1960年代完全不同。当时计算机的算力非常有限，所以最聪明的办法不是造一只复杂的机械臂，再用更强的计算机解决它，而是重新设计机械臂，让数学问题本身变简单。这其实奠定了后来很多工业六轴机械臂的设计思想。 1969年：victor scheinman—造一只“为计算机而生的手” pieper解决了数学问题之后，victor scheinman开始把这种思想真正变成一只机械臂。 1969年，他设计出了著名的：stanford arm。stanford arm：全电驱、六自由度，并让腕部三个旋转轴交于一点，使当时算力有限的计算机也能够计算和控制机械臂的空间运动。stanford后来制造了gold arm和blue arm，并将机械臂与视觉结合，研究手眼协调和双臂协作。 1969年的stanford arm（全电驱、六自由度，并让腕部三个旋转轴交于一点） stanford arm最大的意义因此不是“又出现了一只机械臂”。而是机器人设计思想发生了变化：以前是先把机器造出来，再想办法让计算机控制它。stanford arm则是机械结构、运动学和控制系统第一次开始被放在一起设计。换成2026年我们最熟悉的说法，就是软硬件系统协同设计—co-design。 1972年前后，scheinman又应老一代ai先驱marvin minsky邀请回到mit，设计了一只更紧凑的mit arm。它进一步采用全旋转关节，把线路藏进机械臂内部，并通过专门设计的齿轮降低回程间隙。此时，它的形态已经越来越接近后来我们熟悉的工业六轴机械臂。 1972年的mit arm 1973：scheinman创办vicarm—学术机器人开始走出实验室 1973年，scheinman决定把stanford积累的研究真正变成产品，于是创办了vicarm。stanford arm原本是一台科研设备，而vicarm开始把它变成：机械臂 + 伺服系统 + 控制器 + 编程语言。一套完整的机器人系统。包括后来非常重要的机器人编程语言val。机器人开始从“实验室里的机械臂”，逐渐变成一种真正可以编程的计算机外设。 有趣的是，scheinman和unimation的缘分其实很早就开始了。他在stanford读书时曾获得unimate发明人george devol资助的fellowship，还跟随devol和joseph engelberger参观unimation及其客户，因此亲眼看到早期unimate如何搬运、上下料和焊接。他也看到了它的局限：这些液压机器人主要靠记录一个个位置重复动作，很难真正控制机械臂连续沿着一条轨迹运动。 后来scheinman把一台vicarm直接搬到了engelberger的办公室，放在他的桌子上，演示unimate当时做不到的连续轨迹控制。在一次机器人展会上，vicarm甚至因为太小而被主办方认为只是“玩具”，scheinman干脆把它摆在展馆门口，用延长线接上电源演示，反而吸引了一群真正懂机器人的研究者。 最终看中这只“小机械臂”的是gm。gm希望把它放大，用于汽车装配，但又担心vicarm这样的小公司没有大规模供货能力，于是鼓励scheinman寻找一家更大的合作伙伴。这个合作伙伴最终就是unimation。 第四部分：学术路线和工业路线终于汇合 1977年，机器人历史上两条走了近二十年的道路，终于交汇到了一起。 在1961这一年，unimate进入gm工厂。它代表工业界对机器人的理解：把人的动作教给机器，让机器不知疲倦地重复。几乎与此同时，mit的mh-1代表了另一种完全不同的想象：不是告诉机器每一步怎么做，而是让计算机感知环境，再决定自己的手应该怎么动。 同样起始于1961年的两条路，在之后的几十年里却有着不同的命运：一条路线通向了工业机器人，没有”想法“的机器”奴隶“替代了大量的人工在工业制造领域完成了商业闭环，并催生了工业自动化产业链的繁荣；另一条路线则开始通向ai与机器人学，人类想让机器拥有眼睛、大脑和自己的判断，让它真正完成从感知到行动的闭环。六十多年过去，我们依然在路上。 我们很早就学会了制造机器人的身体，却依然没有真正赋予它智慧。这大概也是机器人百年历史最耐人寻味的悖论：机器迟迟没有获得智慧，是人类的不幸，或许也是人类的幸运。1921年，čapek已经写下机器人觉醒并反抗人类的结局；1942年，asimov又急着用三条定律约束一个尚不存在的智能生命。而到了2026年，我们终于投入前所未有的资本、算力和智慧，试图完成那个六十多年没有完成的梦想。我们如此渴望机器人拥有智慧，却也许只有在它真正拥有智慧的那一天，才会明白为什么一百年前的人类，已经开始害怕它。未完待续 1920s–1960s from čapek’s theater and asimov’s three laws to unimate and the stanford arm: how industry and ai laboratories converged to shape modern robotics. a century of robotics in silicon valley, there is a time machine for modern information technology: the computer history museum. inside the museum is an exhibition on artificial intelligence and robotics. i spent several hours there recently, surrounded by robots created decades ago. what i saw astonished me. across nearly a century of robotics research, robots with similar physical forms have appeared at different moments in history. humanity has made so many attempts with the same kinds of robot bodies. the shells of these robots reminded me of ourselves, returning to this world again and again. scientists and dreamers in different eras have repeatedly tried to breathe a “soul” into them. now, 105 years after the word “robot” was coined, we seem to have reached a tipping point in the story of humans and robots. in this latest attempt, it seems that robotic bodies and souls may finally be ready to share the earth with us. the series a century of robotics was inspired by the museum. has the excitement we see today appeared before? how did today's robotics supply chain take shape? what have industry and academia explored in this field? which ideas made it into the real world, and which did not? why is today's progress in ai encouraging people to pursue general-purpose robots? history cannot tell us what the future holds, but it can help us distinguish breakthroughs that truly change a paradigm from old questions repackaged for a new era. let us look back at history, and forward to the future. part i: science fiction and theater carried humanity's imagination of the future 1921: a czech playwright introduces “robot” in 1921, czech playwright karel čapek brought the word “robot” into public view in his play rossum's universal robots, or r.u.r. “robot” comes from the czech word robota, meaning forced labor or drudgery. in čapek's story, humans manufacture an artificial form of life in factories to perform arduous work. from the very beginning, robots were created to work on humanity's behalf. but the story does not end well: these initially tireless, obedient “workers” eventually rebel and destroy humanity. a photograph at the computer history museum documenting the origin of the word “robot.” interestingly, the history of robots begins with a story about machines and people, rather than a piece of technology. but the young russian-born american science fiction writer isaac asimov did not like that story. 1942: asimov lays down the three laws of robotics in 1939, at the age of 19, asimov wrote his first robot story, “robbie,” which was published in 1940. in his story, robbie is not a monster waiting to awaken, but a loyal and dependable companion to a little girl as she grows up. asimov began to seriously consider a question: if robots are designed and manufactured by humans, why could we not build the protection of, and obedience to, humans into their rules from the very start? this idea eventually became the famous three laws of robotics. in his 1942 story “runaround,” asimov first set out all three rules together: a robot must not harm a human; it must obey humans; and it must protect itself as long as doing so does not violate the first two laws. over the following decades, he kept constructing new stories around these seemingly simple rules. what happens when the rules conflict? what happens when a machine receives an ambiguous human command? what happens when a sufficiently intelligent robot begins to understand the interests of society, or even humanity as a whole? in 1950, these early stories were collected in i, robot. asimov went on to extend his robot stories further into the future, eventually even connecting the robot series with his foundation series. asimov's importance in robotics history goes beyond proposing the three laws. before real robots had even entered factories, he had already moved the discussion from “will robots destroy humanity?” to a more modern question: how should humans design a machine that is smarter than an ordinary machine and capable of acting autonomously? history would soon step out of fiction and into reality. part ii: there are always people who turn imagination into reality 1954: american inventor devol brings robots from science fiction into reality in 1954, american inventor george devol proposed a “programmable mechanical arm,” which became one of the true starting points of modern robotics. he envisioned a machine that would no longer merely repeat movements dictated by a fixed mechanical structure. instead, it could record a sequence of actions and then execute them automatically according to a program. in 1956, george devol and joseph engelberger met by chance at a cocktail party. both were science fiction fans, and they soon began talking about the robots in isaac asimov's stories. that casual conversation about science fiction quickly turned into a discussion that would genuinely change the history of robotics. the two founders of unimation, the world's first robotics startup, with their drink-serving robot, unimate. devol had recently applied for a patent for his mechanical arm. he had the technology and the idea, but needed capital and a business partner. engelberger happened to be an engineer who had been thinking about how more flexible machines could automate factories. one wanted to build machines; the other wanted to transform factories. they immediately hit it off. the story of modern industrial robotics began there. their meeting ultimately led to unimate, later known as the world's first industrial robot, its name meaning “universal working mate.” a unimate-family robotic arm. the original caption gives 1954, the year of devol’s patent application; that date should not be read as the manufacturing date of the pictured unit. at the time, almost no off-the-shelf robot components were available. early unimate systems even used vacuum tubes for digital control before later switching to transistors. encoders and memory devices were also immature, so the team had to design and manufacture many of the core components themselves, including a special magnetic drum memory system to record the robot's motion programs. although the original unimate could already be “programmed,” it did not yet have a proper programming language. it used a very intuitive teaching method: an operator moved the arm to a specified position, and the machine recorded it; the operator then moved it to the next position, which was recorded in turn. once a sequence of movements had been taught, unimate could repeat them in the recorded order over and over again. unimate began with a simple purpose: to free people from dirty, repetitive, and dangerous work. 1961: unimate becomes the first robot to enter a factory in 1961, general motors bought the first unimate for $18,000 and installed it at its plant in new jersey. its first job was simple, but particularly well suited to a robot: removing hot metal parts from a die-casting machine and stacking them neatly. robots subsequently began taking on other dangerous and repetitive jobs, including spot welding. it was, however, a loss-making sale: manufacturing one unimate cost as much as $65,000, against a selling price of $18,000. engelberger was willing to sell it so cheaply because he knew that having gm as the first customer was the best possible advertisement. he also believed that more orders would soon follow. unimate quickly attracted the attention of the automotive industry, and companies including chrysler, ford, and fiat began purchasing robots. industrial robotics grew from an invention into an industry. by the early 1970s, unimate's selling price had risen to $35,000. even so, unimation did not turn its first profit until 1975—19 years after the company was founded. the first unimate cost $65,000 to build and sold for just $18,000. it took industrial robotics nearly 20 years to go from its birth to a genuinely profitable business. 1970: the first conflict over robots in factories initially, gm workers did not object to unimate. moving scorching metal out of a die-casting machine was, after all, dangerous work that nobody wanted to do. in 1967, gm installed two spot-welding robots at its norwood plant in ohio, again without much controversy. at the lordstown plant in 1970, gm deployed 28 spot-welding robots at once and began sharply increasing production efficiency. to produce the chevrolet vega, the plant laid off at least 700 employees and eliminated another 300–500 jobs deemed “too simple to require a person.” the production line accelerated from 60 to 101 cars per hour, an increase of 67%. the faster assembly line came with longer working hours. workers were required to work 11–12 hours a day, sometimes with weekend overtime. tensions quickly erupted. workers filed more than 16,000 grievances and then went on strike. in march 1972, a strike shut the entire plant down for 22 days. lordstown later became a classic case of automation's impact on workers. for the first time, robots were associated not just with doing dangerous work on people's behalf, but also with layoffs, faster production, and greater work intensity. to some extent, the conflict also affected unimation's image in the united states. although industrial robots were born in america, they struggled to gain a real foothold in their home market. the 1970s: unimation ignites japan's industrial robotics boom compared with the united states, japan offered unimate a bigger stage. in 1966, engelberger visited japan and spent several hours speaking with hundreds of people from japanese industry, hoping to find a partner to manufacture robots locally. japanese companies showed tremendous interest. kawasaki aircraft, later part of kawasaki heavy industries, was particularly enthusiastic and ultimately secured a technology license from unimation. in 1968, kawasaki established a dedicated department to localize industrial robot production. it then sent engineers to the united states for training and brought a prototype back to japan as the basis for further development and domestic manufacturing. in objects weighing just 12 kilograms. its price was about $90,000, equivalent to roughly $595,000 in the original article’s present-day comparison. at the time, the average starting salary for a japanese university graduate was only a little over $200 per month. the inflation comparison and contemporary graduate salary are estimates quoted by the original article, rather than newly calculated values. a unimate robot manufactured in japan by kawasaki heavy industries. a robot born in america had crossed the pacific and set off another, larger industrial robotics revolution in japan. by the mid-1980s, japan had become the “kingdom of robots,” with nearly 70% of the world's industrial robots. part iii: the people who defined ai created the first robotics laboratories 1961: at mit, ai reaches out a hand for the first time in the late 1950s, as devol and engelberger were trying to bring unimate into factories, another group of people in mit's laboratories began taking an interest in mechanical hands. their concern was not automated production. it was a question more closely associated with ai: if a computer could truly possess intelligence, could it control a hand of its own and interact with the physical world? the 1956 dartmouth conference had only recently given the new field of “artificial intelligence” its name. a few years later, key figures from that conference began gathering at mit. john mccarthy, who would later found stanford's sail, arrived from dartmouth in 1958. marvin minsky, who would later be a founding figure in the lineage of mit's csail, joined in [historical note: minsky joined mit’s faculty in 1958; the ai laboratory was founded the following year. the original conflates those dates.] in 1961, under the guidance of claude shannon and marvin minsky, mit doctoral student heinrich ernst completed his dissertation, mh-1, a computer-operated mechanical hand. mh-1 became one of the earliest manipulators directly controlled by a computer. but the real significance of mh-1 was not simply that “a computer could finally make a mechanical arm move.” ernst wanted to know whether a mechanical hand could obtain information about the outside world through sensors, and whether a computer could then decide what movement to make next. in other words, he was already trying to establish a loop that would run through the entire history of robotics research: perceive the world → compute and decide → control the body → change the world. mh-1. a few years later, john mccarthy left mit for stanford. this group of people studying how machines could think would carry the same question to the american west coast. there, bernard roth, donald pieper, and victor scheinman would take it a step further: if a computer is going to control a hand, should we design a hand specifically for the computer from the outset? 1962–1963: john mccarthy arrives at stanford, and ai begins looking for a body in 1962, john mccarthy left mit and returned to stanford. he subsequently established the stanford artificial intelligence laboratory, the renowned sail. stanford officially traces sail's founding to around 1963. by 1965, with the establishment of the computer science department and improvements in funding and equipment, sail had become one of america's most important ai laboratories. after arriving at stanford, mccarthy wanted to continue working on robots. but there was a problem: the ai lab was full of computer scientists and mathematicians. who was going to build the robot's body? stanford introduced mccarthy to bernard roth, a young professor in the mechanical engineering department. roth's academic background was not in ai, but in classical mechanism theory and kinematics. that background was precisely what made him an important founding figure in modern robotics. before a computer could control a robotic arm, it needed to answer a seemingly simple question: if the end of the arm must reach a certain position in space, how far should each joint rotate? this became one of the fundamental problems in robotics: inverse kinematics. roth later recalled that stanford was concerned that, although mccarthy was a great mathematician, he might not be the right person to take responsibility for mechanical systems. the university hoped roth would fill that gap. roth subsequently took on sail's work on robotic arms. before joining stanford's mechanical engineering department in 1962, he had studied for his doctorate under ferdinand freudenstein at columbia, working on mechanisms, linkages, and kinematics. one of the things this group of researchers was doing was turning mechanical problems previously solved through geometric constructions into mathematical problems that digital computers could calculate. the combination of mccarthy and roth brought together ai researchers who wanted computers to control machines and mechanical engineers who were beginning to translate machine motion into mathematics that computers could understand. robotics emerged precisely at the intersection of the two. in 1962, sail, a pioneering organization in robot learning, brought ai and robotics together. this cradle of ai and robotics gradually nurtured early explorers of the intersection, including scheinman and donald pieper, who helped lay the foundations for robot learning. [the original’s 1962 date refers to mccarthy’s arrival; stanford’s archives date sail’s founding to 1963, as noted above.] 1963: the rancho arm—stanford starts with an existing hand stanford did not initially build its own robotic arm from scratch. it acquired a rancho arm. this arm had originally been developed as an assistive device for people with disabilities, rather than for ai. stanford connected it to a computer to study computer control. around this time, the young victor scheinman joined bernard roth's team. scheinman showed engineering talent early. he entered mit at 15 and earned a degree in aeronautics and astronautics in 1963. after graduation, he worked at boeing on a lunar gravity simulator and also participated in work related to the apollo command module's heat shield and saturn rocket turbopumps. he later went to stanford for further study, moving from aerospace into mechanical engineering. joining the stanford ai lab truly changed his life. there, as bernard roth's research assistant, he was tasked with studying how to “build hands and arms for computers.” the laboratory already had a rancho arm, but this arm, originally designed for people with disabilities, lacked precision and had difficult inverse kinematics. scheinman subsequently tried a snake-like orm arm and a powerful hydraulic arm, but neither was easy to control. these failures donald pieper first solves the arm's mathematics bernard roth's student donald pieper made the first major advance on this problem. in 1968, pieper completed his dissertation, the kinematics of manipulators under computer control. he systematically studied manipulator kinematics and demonstrated that certain special joint configurations could simplify the complex problem of inverse kinematics. one idea with a particularly lasting influence was to make several of the wrist's rotational axes intersect at a single point. today, calculating inverse kinematics is no great challenge for a computer. in the 1960s, the situation was entirely different. computing power was extremely limited. the smartest approach was therefore not to build a complicated arm and use a more powerful computer to handle it, but to redesign the arm so that the mathematics itself became simpler. this helped establish the design philosophy behind many subsequent six-axis industrial robotic arms. 1969: victor scheinman builds a hand “born for the computer” after pieper addressed the mathematical problem, victor scheinman began turning the idea into a real mechanical arm. in 1969, he designed the famous stanford arm. it was fully electric, had six degrees of freedom, and placed the wrist's three rotational axes so that they intersected at one point. this allowed even the limited computers of the time to calculate and control the arm's movement in space. stanford later built the gold arm and the blue arm, combining the arms with vision to study hand–eye coordination and cooperation between two arms. the 1969 stanford arm: fully electric, with six degrees of freedom and three wrist axes intersecting at one point. the stanford arm's greatest significance was therefore not that “another robotic arm had appeared.” the philosophy of robot design had changed. previously, people built a machine and then tried to figure out how a computer could control it. with the stanford arm, mechanical structure, kinematics, and control systems began to be designed together. in the language most familiar to us in 2026, this was hardware–software system co-design. around 1972, at the partner turned out to be unimation. part iv: the academic and industrial paths finally converge in 1977, two paths in robotics history that had developed for nearly two decades finally came together. one came from industry. since devol and engelberger created unimate, the focus had been on a practical problem: how to get robots into factories to work on people's behalf. the other came from the laboratories of mit and stanford. from mccarthy and minsky to bernard roth, donald pieper, and victor scheinman, these researchers were concerned with a different question: how could a computer truly understand and control a mechanical hand, moving it along a calculated trajectory? in 1977, unimation acquired victor scheinman's vicarm, and the two paths truly joined for the first time. with encouragement from gm, the technology that had originated in stanford's laboratories continued to develop, eventually producing the famous puma arm: the programmable universal machine for assembly. in 1980, scheinman left unimation and joined automatix, where he continued developing new robot systems. among them was the modular robot world, which was later acquired by yaskawa. starting in an ai laboratory, scheinman spent nearly a decade thinking about how to build a genuinely useful hand for a computer. starting in factories, devol and engelberger thought about how to make robots genuinely work on people's behalf. after nearly two decades, the paths converged. the laboratory's “hand” was fitted to the industrial robot's “body,” and puma was born. a puma robotic arm. if unimate represented the first commercialization of industrial robots, puma's greater significance was that it brought computer control, kinematics, and electrically driven arms developed in stanford's laboratories into the industrial world. from the stanford arm to puma, the basic form of the modern industrial arm was becoming increasingly clear. from this moment onward, laboratory robots and factory robots were no longer two entirely different species. in 1983, unimation was sold to westinghouse electric for $107 million. engelberger subsequently shifted his attention to medical and domestic service robots, while devol gradually left the robotics field. the two later became known as the “father” and “grandfather” of industrial robotics, respectively. [the original names western electric; the acquiring company was westinghouse.] a chance encounter at a cocktail party in 1956 ultimately ignited a robotics revolution that swept through manufacturing around the world. a century of robotics, episode one: closing thoughts in 1961, unimate entered a gm factory. it represented industry's understanding of a robot: teach a machine human movements and have it repeat them without fatigue. at almost the same time, mit's mh-1 represented a very different vision: instead of telling a machine exactly what to do at every step, let a computer perceive its environment and decide how its hand should move. these two paths, both starting in 1961, would follow different destinies in the decades that followed. one led to industrial robotics. machine “slaves” without “thoughts” replaced large amounts of human labor, achieved commercial viability in manufacturing, and helped a flourishing industrial automation supply chain emerge. the other led toward ai and robotics research. humans wanted to give machines eyes, brains, and judgment of their own, allowing them to truly complete the loop from perception to action. more than six decades later, we are still on that journey. we learned to build robotic bodies long ago, yet we have still not truly given them intelligence. this may be the most thought-provoking paradox in a century of robotics: the fact that machines have been so slow to acquire intelligence may be humanity's misfortune—or perhaps its good fortune. in 1921, čapek had already written an ending in which robots awaken and rebel against humanity. in 1942, asimov was already eager to constrain an intelligent life form that did not yet exist with three laws. now, in 2026, we are finally investing unprecedented amounts of capital, computing power, and intellect in an attempt to fulfill a dream that has remained unfinished for more than six decades. we are so eager for robots to possess intelligence. yet perhaps only on the day they truly acquire it will we understand why, a hundred years ago, humans had already begun to fear them. to be continued. references unimation puma video: vla 第一部分 关于世界模型 郭彦江：我印象比较深的是2024年初sora刚发布的时候，大家都很震撼，因为它第一次比较好地建模了物理世界的变化过程。当时我已经在研究基于vlm的vla通用策略，看到sora的视频后，我意识到这种视频模型对机器人决策会很有用。 如果我们从第一性原理出发，去判断两件事的难度：是“生成一段机器人操作的视频”更容易，还是“训练一个能完成操作的机器人策略”更容易？哪个更成熟？前者显然更接近当前技术能力。一方面物理世界的操作本身就是一个更难的问题，另一方面大规模预训练的视频模型已经具备很强的泛化能力。如果连“生成通用机器人操作的视频”的问题都无法解决，我很难想象“机器人通用策略”的问题可以被解决。 由于当时的机器人数据规模其实非常有限，我们自己训练的vla的通用策略感觉没有很好的泛化能力，基本是“给什么学什么”，面对新场景/新任务vla往往会卡着不动或者漫无目的，很难做出“合理的”动作。最近随着数据质量和规模的提升，vla也涌现出新任务的泛化能力，例如最近pi发布的pi0.7的工作，这也让我有了一些新的思考。 但在当时的语境下，视频的泛化能力确实深深吸引了我，只要给定当前观测和指令，视频模型就可以向后预测过程。所以我当时的想法是：既然我直接练不出一个有泛化能力的机器人策略，我能不能退一步，先练一个有泛化能力的视频模型，再以此为基础尝试策略的泛化。 胡钰承：从定义上看，world model的核心是：基于当前和历史的状态观测，去预测未来的状态。 虽然现在大家提到world model，更多是指视频预测或视频生成（尤其是video prediction），但从更广义的角度看，像vla或vlm这类方法，其实也可以被视为一种world model——因为它们本质上也是在预测状态，只是没有显式输出图像。 在实际工作中，我们通常会把图像（或视频）和动作一起纳入预测，因为图像中包含了大量有效信息，有助于更好地建模环境。 从当前的发展来看，world model大致可以分为三类： 第一类是基于图像/视频+action的预测，例如vpp、rt-1、openvla等。这类方法通过当前观测来预测未来状态或辅助生成action，目前也可以归为world action model这一类，比较流行。 第二类是基于3d表征的建模，例如李飞飞团队提出的“空间智能”，通过预测或构建3d表示来理解和建模世界。 第三类是基于隐式表征的方法，例如jepa。这类方法不直接预测像素级图像，而是预测压缩后的特征或latent representation，用于表示未来状态。 整体来看，这三类方法在“预测什么样的未来状态”这一点上有所不同：分别对应显式的图像/视频、3d结构，以及隐式特征表征。 胡钰承：可以打个比方来理解我们（以vpp为代表的world action model）和李飞飞他们思路的区别。3d world model，更强调的是rendering质量，也就是未来观测需要尽可能真实地还原世界。这类方法的核心目标，是构建一个高保真的环境模型，因此更适用于simulation、virtual reality等场景。 而vpp这类方法，并不过分强调像素级预测的精确性。我们更关注的是利用视频建模来服务action生成。可以把它理解为一种“action decoder”：通过视频建模，把大量不带动作标注的跨本体数据耦合进来，起到一个桥梁的作用，在vla框架中连接感知和动作。 当然，这种方法也有缺点。像素级预测虽然包含了丰富信息，但同时也带来了冗余，尤其是背景等与任务无关的部分，也会被一并建模和预测。因此，这类方法的一个缺点是，需要消耗较多算力去重建像素中的冗余信息，尤其是与任务无关的背景部分。但从另一个角度看，它的优势在于保留了完整的信息。虽然存在冗余，但像素中那些真正有效的信息也被一并保留下来了。 相比之下，像jepa这类方法会对信息进行压缩，虽然更高效，但可能会带来信息损失。而我们这种基于像素的方式，可以看作是一种“近似无损”的信息保留方式。从某种角度看，我们和jepa其实是有相似之处的——在最终用于action生成时，并不一定直接使用完整的像素。 但关键区别在于训练方式。我们在训练阶段，仍然是在像素空间做完整的重建，也就是显式地预测未来图像或视频；而jepa更多是在特征或latent空间进行预测，并不直接生成像素。 在使用阶段，我们也不会把完整的视频预测结果作为condition输入到action模块中，而是使用其中的中间表征。所以可以理解为：训练时，我们走的是像素空间的建模路径；但在使用时，更接近于利用隐式表征来辅助action生成。 胡钰承：首先，我们认为当前以wan等为代表的视频模型，仍然存在一定局限性，尤其是在高层语义理解能力上相对较弱。相比之下，vlm（视觉语言模型）由于经过大量视觉-语言数据训练，在语义理解方面更强。 因此，第一个方向是训练一个视觉语言模型与world model耦合的unified model，这也是我们当前正在探索的重点之一。 第二个方向是数据规模。目前vpp以及相关工作的后训练数据量仍然不够，未来需要引入更多机器人数据，进一步训练更强的world model。 第三个方向是引入更多模态。未来可能会加入触觉等模态，不仅作为condition输入，也作为预测目标之一。不过目前触觉相关的硬件还不够成熟，因此这部分可能会在后续逐步推进。 郭彦江：我觉得基于视频的世界模型最大的优势在于它的scalability。因此一个很重要的发展方向是scale到更大的 manipulation数据集。随着数据规模的提升，很可能会涌现出新的能力。 还有一点我觉得是要学习机器人自己的预训练video model。目前大多数world model工作还是基于video community训练的video foundation model。 但video generation研究人员的训练目标，其实和robot domain并不一致。video模型更关注生成的美学效果，这与机器人操作任务的目标是有差异的。现在的做法，是在这些video foundation model上进行微调，适配机器人任务。 因此，从长远来看，更理想的方向是robot community能够训练自己的foundation model——专门面向manipulation的world model，其优化目标直接服务于操作任务，而不是生成“更好看”的视频。 第二部分 关于vpp 郭彦江：当时对我影响最大的是yilun du教授的unipi工作（专访yilun du：基于ebm和视频生成的具身智能研究路线）。这篇工作其实非常超前，因为当时甚至还没有“video foundation model”这个概念，视频模型整体能力也比较弱。但unipi已经提出可以利用视频预测来实现机器人决策。作为开创性工作，它也存在一些小缺陷，最关键的一点是他采用了open-loop control：由于视频生成速度太慢，unipi先预测完整的视频，再用inverse dynamics model从中提取整条trajectory的action来执行。在看完这篇工作后，我开始思考如何将这种方法改进为closed-loop policy，就开始了vpp的工作。 在具体实现上，我们的一个核心目标就是替换成当时开源的视频基础模型，以及最重要的是大幅加速。我们很直观地分析，视频模型慢的主要原因在于需要多步去噪，一般是10步到50步不等。 我们仔细观察了视频预测去噪的过程，其实大尺度的动态信息在去噪的前几步就已经完成，后期去噪往往是修补细节。因此我们就极限压缩这个过程，直接用一步denoising。如果只用一步，模型推理其实就不慢了。本质上它只是一个几b参数的transformer，推理速度和同规模language model是一个数量级的。 实验中我们发现一步denoising虽然细节不准确，生成结果中已经包含了大量整体的motion信息，比如机器人应该往哪个方向移动、如何接近目标物体。基于这个观察，我们直接使用视频模型中间的latent表征。因为一步denoising本质上可以看作对输入进行了一次前向编码，这使得视频模型可以被视为一个强大的视觉表征编码器。 郭彦江：vpp训练可以分成两个阶段。在第一阶段，我们基于一个通用视频模型，在大量机器人操作数据上继续进行continue trianing。整体训练流程与原始视频模型保持一致，变化主要体现在数据分布上：我们显著增加机器人操作相关数据，同时去除与机器人无关或动态模式差异较大的内容，例如自然风景、山水、人脸等。这样做的目标，是让模型更加聚焦于操作相关的动态建模能力。当时我们是在2024年中开始做这个方向的。那个阶段可用的视频基础模型还不多，不像现在这么丰富。我们当时使用的是一个相对比较早期、但应用较广的模型stable video diffusion，内部是基于transformer u-net的结构。 第二阶段训练隐式的inverse dynamics model，即 implicit idm。它的核心思想是：输入并不是两帧都清晰可见的图像，而是由清晰的当前观测和带有一定模糊性的未来预测表征共同构成。这里的模糊性来源于我们只进行了一步前向预测，因此未来细节并不完整。也正因如此，这里的 action prediction 并不等同于严格意义上、完全依赖两帧图像差异进行反推动作的传统 idm；更准确地说，它是利用视频模型提供的未来信息来辅助动作推断，因此我们将这一机制称为 implicit idm。 郭彦江：关于vpp，我们当时还有一个很重要的观察：视频预测质量与最终决策效果是强正相关的。这一点在我们的paper中被重点阐述。这个观察后来也被后续工作反复验证，几乎所有world action model相关工作都会提到这一点。 在此之前，大多数vla或相关方法基本都是黑盒系统，很难理解模型内部在做什么。而基于视频模型的vpp，让我们有机会“打开黑盒”，通过预测的视频去间接观察模型的决策过程。这也是我喜欢的地方。 胡钰承：我觉得尽量保留vlm（或原有foundation model）的能力，对机器人是非常有价值的。在做完vpp之后，我们也逐渐发现了它的一些问题。与此同时，大约在2025年，尤其是年底，多模态领域开始出现一类“理解-生成一体化”的unified model，并且能力在快速提升。我们发现，这类模型与机器人所需要的能力是非常契合的。在机器人场景中，world model不仅需要做预测，本质上也是对视频数据的一种编码；但与此同时，机器人还需要具备“理解”能力。 因此，我们希望构建一个统一模型，同时具备理解能力和预测能力，并利用理解能力来提升预测效果。在这个思路下，我们开始探索用unified model作为新一代的vla框架。在具体实践上，2025年初我们基于一个较早的生成-理解一体化模型提出了upvla。虽然当时模型还比较初期，但已经具备一定能力。 到了2025年6月，字节跳动推出了bagel，这是一类更成熟的生成-理解一体化多模态模型。我们看到它在多模态理解和编辑方面的潜力，因此以它为基础，进一步发展出了bagelvla。这一类方法的核心优势在于：能够结合视觉语言模型的高层语义理解能力，与world model的时序预测能力，从而在统一框架下同时提升理解与决策能力。 这种unified model的优势在于，可以同时耦合不同能力模块。在我们的框架中，不只是简单地融合预测和理解，还进一步把文本推理、未来状态预测以及动作预测统一在一个模型中进行耦合。也就是说，它是一个同时具备理解、推理和预测能力的一体化框架。希望通过unified框架来利用更大规模的数据，学习更丰富的能力。 unified model的另一个代表是世界模型ep04：motus，bagelvla和motus一个重要区别在于，他们的视觉语言模型是完全冻结的，只作为一个encoder使用，本质上更像是特征提取模块；而我们的做法是将视觉语言模型与world model进行强耦合，以mot的方式融合在一起，更接近一个一体化结构。 因此，他们的视觉语言模型不参与推理，也不具备文本reasoning能力；而我们的视觉语言模型是可以进行文本reasoning的，可以同时支持自回归（autoregressive）和diffusion两种模式。 相比之下，他们主要只在做diffusion，用于视频预测；而我们是在一个统一框架中，同时建模理解、推理和预测，这是两者在架构上的一个核心差异。 胡钰承：简单来说，pi的结构是将vlm和一个action expert，通过mixture of transformer（mot）的方式组合在一起。它的核心思路是，在融合action能力的同时，尽可能保留原有vlm的能力。因为在以往的一些方法（比如groot、motus）中，如果不对vlm进行冻结或特殊处理，它的能力在联合训练中容易被破坏。 pi通过mot的结构，让不同模块在一定程度上保持相对独立，从而在学习action的同时，也能保留vlm本身的能力，这是它的一个主要优势。 基于这个思路，我们在bagel或bagel vla中，也采用了类似的mixture of transformer框架。目标是构建一个unified模型，同时保留三种能力：视觉语言模型的理解能力、world model的未来预测能力，以及action expert的动作生成能力。 胡钰承：我们的训练是分阶段进行的。第一阶段不会引入带动作标注的数据，而是先训练一个生成-理解一体化的基础模型，然后在后续阶段再学习action expert。 在第一阶段中，主要使用了几类数据：首先是vqa数据，包括object365等视觉语言数据，用于保留vlm的理解能力。其次是机器人领域的planning数据，主要是任务拆解和规划相关的数据，这部分数据是我们自行处理和构建的。此外，还加入了视频数据、人手操作数据，以及一些开源的机器人数据。对于这些数据，我们也做了进一步处理，比如对任务过程进行切分，标注中间的subtask，用于理解任务结构，同时结合goal image进行预测训练。在预训练阶段，主要使用的就是这些数据。 其中，vqa数据本质上就是视觉语言模型常用的数据形式：给定图像和文本输入，让模型生成对应的文本输出。其实，在训练中引入vqa数据并不是我们独有的做法，很多相关工作也都采用了类似策略。例如pi-0.5，以及chatvla等方法，都使用了vqa数据来保留vlm的能力。 我们的不同之处在于，在vqa数据基础上，还加入了机器人领域的planning数据，也就是任务拆解和规划相关的数据。整体上，可以理解为我们结合了开源的通用vqa数据，以及自建的、与机器人任务相关的vqa数据，一起用于训练这个统一的模型，从而同时增强其理解能力和任务规划能力。 胡钰承：在第一阶段的pre-training中，除了训练vlm相关能力，我们也同时训练了world model部分。因为生成模块本身需要具备预测未来观测的能力，无论是预测未来图像还是视频，所以需要引入world model数据来进行训练。 因此，这一阶段实际上是同时在训练两个能力：一方面是基于vqa数据的理解能力（vlm），另一方面是基于视频数据的未来预测能力（world model）。可以理解为，这一阶段已经在训练“生成专家”，也就是具备未来状态预测能力的模块。 在这个框架中，vlm会先对当前任务进行“理解”和“思考”，然后将这些信息传递给world model，用于未来预测。 这些信息主要有两类：第一类是显式的信息，比如对指令的理解和分解。vlm会对原始指令进行任务拆解，相当于预测“下一步应该做什么”，这些高层语义信息会作为condition输入给world model。第二类是隐式的信息。这些信息不是以文本形式存在，而是存在于vlm中间层的表征中。这些中间表示包含了丰富的高层语义和状态信息。 在mot（mixture of transformer）结构下，world model可以直接从vlm的中间表示中获取这些信息，而不是通过显式的文本传递。也就是说，在attention过程中，这些隐式表征会被自然地传递过去。 因此，vlm传递给world model的输入，本质上包括两部分：一是显式的任务理解（指令分解），二是隐式的高层语义表征。 胡钰承：首先，生成-理解一体化模型在图像编辑和预测能力上，显著强于没有引入理解模块（vlm）的模型。从复杂任务的预测效果来看，如果缺少中间的“思考过程”，也就是文本层面的reasoning，模型很难做出高质量的预测。 这一点可以类比当前的语言模型：如果没有中间的thinking或reasoning步骤，模型往往难以一步得到正确答案。因此，我们的目标是构建一种“文本-图像的思维链”，通过引入中间的推理过程，来提升模型在长时序、复杂任务中的预测能力。 胡钰承：在bagelvla中，我们在图像预测上有一个重要区别：预测的不是完整视频，而是keyframe。 具体来说，在数据处理阶段，我们会先对视频进行标注，找到每个subtask对应的keyframe。也就是说，每个子任务都会对应一个关键帧。 在训练时，模型预测的目标就是这些subtask对应的keyframe，而不是连续的视频序列。因此，整个框架中包含两个核心能力：一是linguistic planning，用于生成subtask；二是video forecasting，用于预测对应的keyframe。在这两个能力的基础上，再进行action generation，整体效果会更好。 首先，这一设计的有效性也体现在我们的实验结果中，包括仿真和真机实验。从直觉上来说，这也是比较合理的：最有用的预测其实是不完整图片的预测，而不是完整的去噪。 同时，引入subtask相当于把一个长任务拆解成多个更简单的子任务，这有助于world model进行更准确的预测。因为world model的数据量（尤其是机器人数据）相对有限，它在简单任务上的预测能力通常更强，而对于复杂长指令的直接预测能力相对较弱。 通过“subtask + keyframe”的方式，相当于降低了预测难度，使模型可以逐步完成复杂任务。 可以参考我们论文中figure 4的结果，我们在其中展示了subtask和keyframe的预测效果。 可以看到，在处理稍微长一些的任务时，引入中间的“文本+图像”的思考过程，会显著降低学习难度。相比直接端到端预测，加入subtask（文本层面的分解）和keyframe（视觉层面的关键状态），能够帮助vla更容易学习到长时序任务的结构，从而提升整体效果。 胡钰承：我们的一个核心思路，其实是围绕“最大化数据利用”来做模型迭代。 之所以从vla转向world action model（比如vpp），最初的出发点就是：视频生成是一种自监督训练方式，可以利用大量不带动作标注的数据。这一点非常关键，因为机器人领域本质上是一个“数据永远不够”的工程问题。 因此，除了不断扩充数据规模，更重要的是如何充分利用已有数据，包括跨本体的数据。这也是我们转向world action model的原因，它能够利用这部分无标注数据，从而缓解vla中数据不足的问题。 但world model本身也有局限——即使是目前最好的视频生成模型也无法产生llm类似的强大推理能力。 因此，我们进一步提出unified框架，希望同时利用视频数据、机器人数据以及视觉语言数据，把不同来源的数据统一纳入训练，从而最大化数据利用效率。这就是我们整体的工作思路。 其实像motus也可以看作一种unified框架，但它的问题在于，motus并没有真正做到让理解帮助生成。更具体来说，motus中的vlm往往是冻结的，更多是作为一个固定的特征提取器，给生成模型传递的依然是原始的粗颗粒度指令。 从模型结构上看，可以理解为有三个“专家”：理解专家（vlm），负责文本输出和任务理解（subtask）；生成专家（world model），负责keyframe预测；动作专家（action expert），负责action生成。这三个专家是同时存在的，并且共享attention计算，但各自有独立参数。也就是说，它们在同一个计算图里交互信息，但功能分工不同。 在输入上，会有不同类型的token：比如text token、visual token（vlm相关）、vae token（生成模块相关）等，这些token一起参与attention计算，实现信息融合。 在输出上：vlm产生subtask（语言层面的任务拆解），world model产生keyframe（视觉层面的关键状态），两者共同作为condition，输入到action expert，生成最终动作。整体可以理解为一个“统一的大模型”，能够同时吸收多模态信息，并在内部完成理解、预测和决策。 从直觉上看，这种结构既在形式上更统一，也更符合scale的方向：可以持续吸收不同来源的数据，并在同一个模型中进行学习。 第四部分 ctrl-world 13. ctrl-world和vpp的区别（或者基于video的世界模型分类） 郭彦江：我们可以先将基于video的world model分成两类：第一大类是video world model as policy，也就是直接将视频模型当错策略使用。本质上是利用视频模型的预测能力来生成optimal的轨迹，辅助生成action。 在world model as policy中，又可以进一步分成几种范式：第一类是两阶段方法，比如unipi、vpp、mimic video、large video planner等。这类方法先做视频预测，再从预测的结果或者表征中提取action。两阶段方法的优势在于能够最大程度保留视频预训练模型的泛化能力。它的缺点是有累积误差：一旦视频预测出错，后续的action基本也会跟着出错。第二类是联合建模预测action和video，例如我之前做的pad，以及现在的dreamzero，cosmos policy等等。这类方法共享模型参数，优势在于即使video预测出错，action仍然可能是正确的。该类方法的缺点是引入action模态后，会打破原有video模型的预训练。 第二大类是video world model as simulator，即将视频模型作为环境模拟器来使用。在这类方法里，world simulator根据当前观测加上机器人的action，去预测未来的观测，包括成功和失败的未来。这个过程本质上就和simulation是一样的，也就是在建模“执行一个action之后会发生什么”，对应真实世界的dynamics。 在做ctrl-world之前，我已经做了vpp，所以我会想尝试一些不一样的东西。我已经做过world model as policy，就很想看看world model as simulator到底能做到什么程度，后来是在stanford chelsea finn组和lucy shi合作完成了这部分工作。 所以我当时的直觉是，world model as simulator一定更难，因为它需要覆盖的分布更大。world model as policy本质上只需要建模相对“最优”的轨迹，它关注的是接近成功的那部分未来；但world model as simulator需要对所有可能结果进行建模，不管action和观测是什么，都要尽量真实地还原结果。 郭彦江：关于数据集选取：world model simulator的质量和数据集关系很大。我最终选择使用droid数据集，第一点是这个数据集非常diverse。droid数据集是chelsea等很多团队用了两年时间基于franka机械臂收集的，因为当时没有“数据工厂”这种体系，在北美各个学校的实验室里，由很多博士生，本科生等推着franka机器人一条一条采集出来的，所以数据分布非常丰富。第二点，这个数据集还包含了相当一部分失败数据，这对于world model as simulator是很重要的。现在像roboarena等一些评测平台，其实也在使用这个数据集。 关于模型架构：在训练过程中，需要对video model做一些调整。因为在world model as simulator中，会引入新的机器人action模态，同时也需要预测多视角，和现在最好的vla policy能够匹配，从而两者能够交互。让模型学习在“观测+action”的条件下预测未来观测。输出形式本身没有变化，还是预测未来的视频或图像序列。 最终的效果是，你可以随意搭建一个新的droid平台上，模型就可以泛化到这个新的场景/相机视角，虽然仍然存在不少失败案例。 和世界模型ep02：interactive world simulator的工作对比 这两个工作有不同的侧重点，分别关注的是准确性和泛化性。interactive world simulator主要是针对大约5到6个task，收集了非常大量的数据，在这些特定task上做了非常充分的拟合，因此在这6个任务上的准确性很高，policy evaluation更加准确。而ctrl-world当时使用的是droid数据集，diversity要高得多，覆盖的是更广泛的分布，所以训练出来的这个control-world，在整个droid平台上是具备不错的泛化能力，但缺点是在具体单一任务上的精细程度不够高。 这也涉及到world model simulator非常大的挑战：它对数据量的需求非常大，不仅需要成功轨迹，还需要大量失败轨迹，要覆盖的整个state-action的分布。 但从另一个角度，world model simulator它可以吸收和利用失败数据，这似乎又是一个很好的有点。因为vla或world model as policy，通常只能在optimal数据上训练，我们很难使用失败或者suboptimal的数据。world model as simulator给利用失败的数据提供了一种途径。 郭彦江：当前world model policy和world simulator两种用途区别：world model policy类方法可以直接输出action，用于决策执行。world model simulator一方面可以作为evaluation工具，用来评估policy的效果；另一方面也可以用于online planning， world model可以模拟不同的未来trajectory，生成多个candidate sequence，然后从中选择最优的一个执行。因此，这两类model在实际系统中可以有不同分工，同时也可以融合到同一个决策框架中。整体来看，这些方向都很有价值，也都值得进一步探索。 除了基于video的model，还有一些其他路线： 比如一类是基于3d的方法，代表工作是先做3d reconstruction，再通过rendering，在构建出的3d世界中进行交互和建模。我觉得3d路线的一个核心问题还是数据不足。不像2d视频，几乎整个互联网都是可用数据，而3d数据相对来说非常稀缺。也有一些工作发现，用纯视频做预测，再从中进行3d reconstruction，效果甚至可以超过直接基于3d数据训练的模型。这很大程度上得益于视频数据规模更大、更加scalable。 另一类是lecun提出的jepa（joint embedding predictive architecture）这类方法。它的出发点是认为pixel-level reconstruction过于低效，更关注学习高层的、内在的表征信息。优点是思路非常优雅，缺点是这种表征监督信号比较薄弱，好坏也比较难衡量——不像2d或3d reconstruction，有明确的的监督目标。 此外，还有一些基于graph，particle或dynamics的建模方法，比如yunzhu li等人的工作，可以很好利用一些inductive bias，在机器人数据有限的场景会很有用。 整体来看，我个人感觉video这一路线目前是最scalable的，也最容易承载大规模数据，因此最近会相对更受关注。 第五部分. 关于world model和vla的一些思考 郭彦江：虽然现在world model很火，但它不一定就比基于vlm的vla更好。我很早就开始做world model的研究，但我也一直进行着vla的研究。 很多人因为之前做了比较久的vla，发现其中有不少问题没有解决，这时候看到world model，就容易把它当成一个“更优解”甚至“救星”。但从我自己的经验来看，并不一定是这样。我观察到在有些任务上， world action model表现更好；但在另一些任务上，vla反而更有优势。我目前的感觉是，world action model在新任务上的泛化能力，通常会比vla略好一些，这主要得益于它更好地保留了视频预训练带来的能力。但在一些对精度要求最高、最细致的操作任务，往往还是由vla方法完成得更好。看了pi0.7的论文之后，我觉得可能数据足够之后可能两者都可以work，在数据少的时候可能各有优势。 所以我觉得，world model并不是一个“唯一正确”的方向，而是和vla并行存在的两类modeling方式。在达到足够的数据规模之前，我们很难知道什么才是机器人领域正确的学习目标，到底哪一个监督方式才是机器人领域的“next token prediction”。world model和vla路线争论的最后，我们可能还是先回到了所有人都在说的数据问题。在我看来，如何构建最有信息熵的数据集，才是今天的通用策略训练的真正门槛所在。 reference： 郭彦江主页： https://robert-gyj.github.io/ 胡钰承主页： https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=wamdptwaaaaj&hl=zh-cn one: on world models yanjiang guo: i vividly remember sora's release in early 2024. everyone was amazed because, for the first time, it modeled changes in the physical world quite well. i was already researching general-purpose vla policies based on vlms. after watching sora's videos, i realized that this kind of video model could be very useful for robot decision-making. if we start from first principles and compare two problems, which is easier: generating a video of a robot performing a manipulation task, or training a robot policy that can perform that task? which is more mature? the former is clearly closer to what current technology can achieve. physical manipulation is itself a harder problem, and large-scale pretrained video models already have strong generalization capabilities. if we cannot even solve the problem of generating videos of general-purpose robot manipulation, i find it hard to imagine solving the problem of general-purpose robot policies. robot datasets were actually very limited at the time. the general-purpose vla policies we trained did not seem to generalize well: they basically learned only what we gave them. in new scenes or tasks, vlas would often freeze or behave aimlessly, struggling to produce “reasonable” actions. more recently, improvements in data quality and scale have also led vlas to show generalization to new tasks—for example, pi's recent π0.7 work. that has prompted some new thoughts for me as well. but in that earlier context, video's generalization capabilities really drew me in. given the current observation and an instruction, a video model could predict what would happen next. so my thinking was: if i cannot directly train a robot policy that generalizes, could i take a step back, first train a video model that generalizes, and then use it as a foundation for exploring policy generalization? yucheng hu: at its core, a world model predicts future states based on current and historical state observations. today, when people mention world models, they usually mean video prediction or video generation, especially video prediction. in a broader sense, however, methods such as vlas and vlms can also be viewed as world models: they too are essentially predicting states, even if they do not explicitly output images. in practice, we usually predict images or videos together with actions, because images contain a great deal of useful information that helps us model the environment better. looking at current developments, world models can broadly be divided into three categories: the first predicts images or videos together with actions, as in vpp, rt-1, and openvla. these methods use current observations to predict future states or help generate actions. they can currently also be grouped under the increasingly popular world action model category. [this is the interviewee’s broad taxonomy. rt-1 and openvla are action-prediction policies; they do not inherently predict future images or qualify as video world models in the narrower sense.] the second models the world using 3d representations—for example, the “spatial intelligence” proposed by fei-fei li's team, which understands and models the world by predicting or constructing 3d representations. the third uses implicit representations, as in jepa. these methods do not directly predict pixel-level images. instead, they predict compressed features or latent representations of future states. overall, these three approaches differ in the kind of future state they predict: explicit images or videos, 3d structures, or implicit feature representations. yucheng hu: an analogy may help explain the difference between our approach—world action models such as vpp—and fei-fei li's. a 3d world model places more emphasis on rendering quality: future observations should reproduce the world as realistically as possible. its core objective is to build a high-fidelity environmental model, making it more suitable for simulation, virtual reality, and similar applications. methods such as vpp do not place excessive emphasis on the precision of pixel-level prediction. we are more interested in using video modeling to support action generation. you can think of it as an “action decoder”: video modeling brings in large amounts of cross-embodiment data without action labels and acts as a bridge between perception and action within a vla framework. of course, this approach has drawbacks. pixel-level prediction contains rich information but also redundancy, especially backgrounds and other task-irrelevant content, which are modeled and predicted as well. one disadvantage is therefore the substantial computation needed to reconstruct redundant pixel information, particularly irrelevant backgrounds. on the other hand, its strength is that it preserves all the information. despite the redundancy, genuinely useful pixel information is retained too. by contrast, methods such as jepa compress information. this is more efficient but may lose information. our pixel-based approach can be viewed as preserving information in a “nearly lossless” way. in some respects, we are actually similar to jepa: when generating actions, we do not necessarily use all the pixels directly. the key difference lies in training. during training, we still perform complete reconstruction in pixel space, explicitly predicting future images or videos. jepa instead mainly predicts in feature or latent space and does not directly generate pixels. at inference time, we do not feed the complete predicted video into the action module as a condition. we use its intermediate representations. so you could say that we follow a pixel-space modeling approach during training, while at inference time we are closer to using implicit representations to assist action generation. yucheng hu: first, we think current video models such as wan still have limitations, particularly relatively weak high-level semantic understanding. vlms, by contrast, have stronger semantic understanding because they have been trained on large amounts of vision-language data. the first direction is therefore to train a unified model coupling a vision-language model with a world model. this is one of our main current areas of exploration. the second direction is data scale. vpp and related work still have insufficient post-training data. we need to incorporate more robot data to train stronger world models. the third direction is to introduce more modalities. we may add touch and other modalities, both as conditioning inputs and as prediction targets. however, tactile hardware is not yet sufficiently mature, so this may be pursued gradually in subsequent work. yanjiang guo: i think the biggest advantage of video-based world models is scalability. an important direction is therefore to scale to larger manipulation datasets. new capabilities are likely to emerge as data scale increases. another point is that we should learn pretrained video models specifically for robots. most world-model research currently relies on video foundation models trained by the video research community. but video-generation researchers' training objectives differ from those in robotics. video models pay more attention to aesthetic quality, which is different from the goals of robot manipulation. our current practice is to fine-tune those video foundation models for robot tasks. in the long run, a more desirable direction is for the robotics community to train its own foundation models: world models designed specifically for manipulation, with optimization objectives that directly serve manipulation tasks rather than generating “better-looking” videos. part two: on vpp yanjiang guo: professor yilun du's unipi work had the greatest influence on me at the time (see “interview with yilun du: embodied ai research based on ebms and video generation”). it was far ahead of its time: the concept of a “video foundation model” did not even exist yet, and video models were generally quite weak. yet unipi had already proposed using video prediction for robot decision-making. as a pioneering work, it also had some limitations. the main one was open-loop control: because video generation was too slow, unipi first predicted a complete video, then used an inverse dynamics model to extract actions for the entire trajectory and execute them. after reading it, i began thinking about how to turn this into a closed-loop policy, which led me to start vpp. [control-loop clarification: this is the interviewee’s comparison of expensive video-plan generation with vpp’s fast feedback policy. unipi’s authors also describe closed-loop execution of inferred actions, so “open-loop” here should not imply that every control layer lacked feedback.] in implementation, one core objective was to replace the video model with an open-source video foundation model available at the time, and, most importantly, to make it substantially faster. our straightforward analysis was that video models were slow mainly because they required multiple denoising steps, usually between 10 and 50. we examined the video-prediction denoising process carefully. large-scale dynamics were already captured in the first few steps; later steps mostly refined details. we therefore compressed the process as much as possible, using only one denoising step. with a single step, inference is actually not slow. the model is essentially just a transformer with a few billion parameters, with inference speed on the same order as a language model of comparable size. in experiments, we found that although the details from one-step denoising were inaccurate, the result already contained substantial overall motion information—for example, which direction the robot should move and how it should approach the target object. based on this observation, we used the video model's intermediate latent representations directly. since a single denoising step can essentially be viewed as one forward encoding pass over the input, the video model can be treated as a powerful visual representation encoder. yanjiang guo: vpp training can be divided into two stages. in the first, we continue training a general-purpose video model on a large amount of robot manipulation data. the overall procedure remains the same as the original video model's; the main change is the data distribution. we substantially increase robot manipulation data while removing content unrelated to robotics or with very different dynamics, such as natural scenery, landscapes, and faces. the goal is to focus the model on manipulation-related dynamics. we started this direction in mid-2024. there were far fewer video foundation models then than there are now. we used stable video diffusion, a relatively early but widely used model with a transformer u-net architecture. the second stage trains an implicit inverse dynamics model, or implicit idm. the core idea is that its input is not two clearly visible images, but a clear current observation together with a somewhat blurry representation of the predicted future. that uncertainty comes from using only one forward prediction step, so future details are incomplete. for this reason, action prediction here is not the same as a traditional idm that strictly infers actions from the difference between two images. more precisely, it uses future information supplied by the video model to assist action inference, which is why we call this mechanism an implicit idm. yanjiang guo: we made another important observation in vpp: video-prediction quality is strongly positively correlated with final decision-making performance. we emphasized this in our paper. subsequent work has repeatedly confirmed it, and almost all world action model research mentions it. before this, most vlas and related methods were essentially black boxes: it was hard to understand what the model was doing internally. video-based vpp gives us a chance to “open the black box” and indirectly observe its decision-making process through predicted videos. that is something i like about it. yucheng hu: i think preserving as much of a vlm's—or an existing foundation model's—capabilities as possible is very valuable for robotics. after vpp, we gradually discovered some of its limitations. around 2025, particularly toward the end of the year, a class of unified models combining understanding and generation began emerging in the multimodal field, and their capabilities were improving rapidly. we found that these models aligned very well with what robots need. in robotics, a world model not only predicts; it also essentially encodes video data. at the same time, a robot needs understanding capabilities. we therefore wanted to build a unified model capable of both understanding and prediction, using understanding to improve prediction. with this in mind, we began exploring unified models as a new generation of vla frameworks. in early 2025, we proposed upvla based on an earlier model combining generation and understanding. although it was still at an early stage, it already had some useful capabilities. in may 2025, bytedance released bagel, a more mature multimodal model combining generation and understanding. we saw its potential in multimodal understanding and editing, and developed bagelvla on that foundation. the core advantage of this approach is that it combines the high-level semantic understanding of vision-language models with the temporal prediction capabilities of world models, improving understanding and decision-making within a unified framework. [the original says june; bagel’s official release was may 20, 2025.] a unified model can couple different capability modules. in our framework, we do not simply combine prediction and understanding; we also couple text reasoning, future-state prediction, and action prediction in one model. it is an integrated framework with understanding, reasoning, and prediction capabilities. through this unified framework, we hope to use larger-scale data to learn richer capabilities. another example of a unified model is covered in world models ep04: motus. an important difference between bagelvla and motus is that their vision-language model is completely frozen and used only as an encoder, effectively a feature extractor. we strongly couple the vision-language model and world model through mot, producing a more integrated architecture. their vision-language model therefore does not participate in reasoning and lacks text-reasoning capabilities. our vision-language model can perform text reasoning and supports both autoregressive and diffusion modes. by comparison, they mainly use diffusion for video prediction. we model understanding, reasoning, and prediction together in a unified framework. this is a core architectural difference between the two approaches. yucheng hu: simply put, pi combines a vlm and an action expert through a mixture of transformers (mot) architecture. the central idea is to incorporate action capabilities while preserving as much of the original vlm's capabilities as possible. in some earlier methods, such as gr00t and motus, joint training can damage vlm capabilities unless the vlm is frozen or handled specially. pi's mot architecture keeps the different modules relatively independent, allowing it to learn actions while preserving the vlm's own capabilities. that is one of its main advantages. following this idea, we also use a similar mixture of transformers framework in bagel or bagelvla. our goal is to build a unified model that preserves three capabilities: the vision-language model's understanding, the world model's future prediction, and the action expert's action generation. yucheng hu: we train in stages. the first stage does not introduce action-labeled data. we first train a foundation model combining generation and understanding, then learn the action expert in later stages. the first stage mainly uses several types of data. first is vqa data, including vision-language data such as objects365, to preserve vlm understanding. second is planning data for robotics, primarily task decomposition and planning data that we process and construct ourselves. we also add video data, human-hand manipulation data, and some open robot datasets. we further process these data—for example, segmenting task sequences and labeling intermediate subtasks to understand task structure, while training prediction together with goal images. these are the main data used during pretraining. vqa data are essentially a common data format for vision-language models: given an image and text as input, the model generates corresponding text. we are not the only ones to use vqa data in training. many related works adopt similar strategies. π0.5 and chatvla, for example, both use vqa data to preserve vlm capabilities. our difference is that, in addition to vqa data, we incorporate robotics planning data—task decomposition and planning. overall, we combine open, general-purpose vqa data with self-built vqa data related to robot tasks to train the unified model, improving both its understanding and its task-planning capabilities. yucheng hu: in the first pretraining stage, we train the world-model component alongside vlm capabilities. the generation module needs to predict future observations, whether images or videos, so world-model data must be included in training. this stage therefore trains two capabilities at once: understanding based on vqa data, through the vlm, and future prediction based on video data, through the world model. you can think of this as already training the “generation expert,” the module capable of predicting future states. in this framework, the vlm first “understands” and “thinks about” the current task, then passes that information to the world model for future prediction. there are two main types of information. the first is explicit, such as understanding and decomposing an instruction. the vlm breaks down the original instruction, effectively predicting “what to do next,” and these high-level semantics condition the world model. the second is implicit. rather than existing as text, it resides in the vlm's intermediate representations, which contain rich high-level semantic and state information. under the mot (mixture of transformers) architecture, the world model can obtain this information directly from the vlm's intermediate representations rather than through explicit text. in other words, the implicit representations are naturally passed through the attention process. the vlm's input to the world model therefore consists of two parts: explicit task understanding, through instruction decomposition, and implicit high-level semantic representations. yucheng hu: first, models combining generation and understanding are significantly stronger at image editing and prediction than models without an understanding module—a vlm. for complex-task prediction, it is difficult to make high-quality predictions without an intermediate “thinking process,” or text-level reasoning. this is analogous to current language models: without intermediate thinking or reasoning steps, they often struggle to reach the correct answer in one step. our goal is therefore to build a “text-image chain of thought,” using intermediate reasoning to improve prediction for complex, long-horizon tasks. yucheng hu: an important distinction in bagelvla's image prediction is that we predict keyframes rather than complete videos. specifically, during data processing, we annotate videos to identify the keyframe corresponding to each subtask. each subtask has an associated keyframe. during training, the prediction target is these subtask keyframes rather than a continuous video sequence. the framework therefore contains two core capabilities: linguistic planning, which generates subtasks, and video forecasting, which predicts the corresponding keyframes. generating actions on top of these two capabilities yields better overall performance. the effectiveness of this design is reflected in our experimental results, including simulation and real-robot experiments. intuitively, it is reasonable too: the most useful prediction is actually an incompletely formed image prediction, rather than a fully denoised image. introducing subtasks also breaks a long task into simpler ones, helping the world model make more accurate predictions. because world-model data—especially robot data—are relatively limited, the model is usually better at predicting simple tasks than directly predicting from complex, long instructions. the “subtask + keyframe” approach reduces prediction difficulty, allowing the model to complete complex tasks step by step. see figure 4 in our paper, where we show the predicted subtasks and keyframes. for somewhat longer tasks, introducing intermediate “text + image” thinking substantially reduces learning difficulty. compared with direct end-to-end prediction, adding subtasks—textual decomposition—and keyframes—key visual states—helps a vla learn the structure of long-horizon tasks more easily and improves overall performance. yucheng hu: one of our core ideas is to iterate on models around “maximizing data utilization.” our original reason for moving from vla to world action models such as vpp was that video generation is self-supervised and can use large amounts of data without action labels. this is crucial, because robotics is fundamentally an engineering problem in which “there is never enough data.” beyond continually increasing data scale, it is even more important to make full use of existing data, including cross-embodiment data. this is why we moved toward world action models: they can exploit these unlabeled data and alleviate the data shortage in vla. but world models also have limitations. even the best current video-generation models cannot produce the strong reasoning capabilities of llms. we therefore proposed a unified framework to use video, robot, and vision-language data together, bringing different data sources into training to maximize utilization. this is the overall thinking behind our work. motus can also be viewed as a unified framework, but its limitation is that understanding does not truly help generation. more specifically, motus's vlm is often frozen and serves mainly as a fixed feature extractor, passing the original, coarse-grained instructions to the generation model. architecturally, you can think of three “experts”: an understanding expert—the vlm—for text output and task understanding through subtasks; a generation expert—the world model—for keyframe prediction; and an action expert for action generation. all three exist simultaneously and share attention computation while retaining independent parameters. they interact within the same computation graph but have different responsibilities. the input contains different token types, such as text tokens, visual tokens associated with the vlm, and vae tokens associated with generation. these tokens participate together in attention computation to fuse information. at the output, the vlm produces subtasks through linguistic task decomposition, while the world model predicts keyframes representing key visual states. both condition the action expert, which generates the final actions. overall, it can be understood as a “unified large model” that absorbs multimodal information and internally performs understanding, prediction, and decision-making. intuitively, this structure is more unified in form and better suited to scaling: it can continually absorb different sources of data and learn from them within a single model. 13. differences between ctrl-world and vpp, or categories of video-based world models yanjiang guo: we can first divide video-based world models into two major categories. the first is video world models as policies, which directly use a video model as a policy. essentially, they use its predictive capabilities to generate optimal trajectories and help produce actions. world models as policies can be further divided into several paradigms. the first is two-stage methods, such as unipi, vpp, mimic video, and large video planner. they first predict video, then extract actions from the predictions or their representations. their advantage is that they preserve pretrained video models' generalization capabilities as much as possible. their disadvantage is accumulated error: once video prediction goes wrong, subsequent actions usually go wrong too. the second jointly models and predicts actions and video, as in my earlier pad work, and current methods such as dreamzero and cosmos policy. these approaches share model parameters. their advantage is that actions may still be correct even when video predictions are wrong. their drawback is that introducing the action modality disrupts the video model's original pretraining. the second major category is video world models as simulators, which use a video model as an environment simulator. given the current observation and a robot action, the world simulator predicts future observations, including both successful and unsuccessful outcomes. this is essentially the same as simulation: modeling “what happens after an action is executed,” corresponding to real-world dynamics. before ctrl-world, i had already done vpp, so i wanted to try something different. having worked on world models as policies, i wanted to see how far world models as simulators could go. i later completed this work with lucy shi in chelsea finn's group at stanford. my intuition was that world models as simulators must be harder because they have to cover a broader distribution. world models as policies essentially need to model relatively “optimal” trajectories, focusing on futures close to success. world models as simulators need to model every possible outcome, reproducing it as faithfully as possible regardless of the action and observation. yanjiang guo: on dataset selection: world-model simulator quality depends heavily on the dataset. i ultimately chose droid for two reasons. first, it is highly diverse. chelsea and many other teams collected droid with franka arms over two years. there was no “data factory” system at the time. across university laboratories in north america, phd students, undergraduates, and others moved franka robots around and collected demonstrations one by one, producing a very rich distribution. second, the dataset contains a substantial amount of failure data, which is important for world models as simulators. evaluation platforms such as roboarena also use this dataset. on model architecture: the video model needs adjustments during training. a world model as simulator introduces a new robot-action modality and must predict multiple views to match the best current vla policies, allowing the two to interact. we train it to predict future observations conditioned on “observation + action.” the output format itself remains unchanged: future video or image sequences. the result is that you can set up a new droid platform, and the model can generalize to the new scene or camera viewpoint, although many failure cases remain. comparison with world models ep02: interactive world simulator these two works emphasize different things: accuracy and generalization. interactive world simulator mainly collected a very large amount of data for around five or six tasks and fitted those specific tasks thoroughly. it therefore achieves high accuracy on those six tasks and more accurate policy evaluation. ctrl-world used droid, which is much more diverse and covers a broader distribution. the resulting model generalizes reasonably well across the droid platform, but it is not sufficiently precise on individual tasks. this illustrates a major challenge for world-model simulators: their enormous data requirements. they need not only successful trajectories but also large amounts of failure trajectories to cover the entire state-action distribution. from another perspective, however, world-model simulators can absorb and use failure data, which seems like a valuable advantage. vlas and world models as policies can usually train only on optimal data; failure or suboptimal data are hard to use. world models as simulators provide a way to exploit them. [this describes common demonstration-only training setups. failure or suboptimal data can also be used in some policy-learning methods; π0.7, for example, conditions on metadata to incorporate such data.] yanjiang guo: the two current uses—world-model policies and world simulators—differ as follows. world-model policies can directly output actions for decision-making and execution. world simulators can serve as evaluation tools to assess policies, and can also support online planning: a world model can simulate different future trajectories, generate multiple candidate sequences, and choose the best one to execute. the two types of models can therefore have different roles in practical systems while also being integrated into the same decision-making framework. overall, these directions are valuable and worth further exploration. beyond video-based models, there are other approaches: one is based on 3d. representative work first performs 3d reconstruction, then uses rendering to interact with and model the reconstructed 3d world. i think a core problem for 3d approaches is still insufficient data. unlike 2d video, for which almost the entire internet offers usable data, 3d data are relatively scarce. some work has also found that predicting with pure video and then performing 3d reconstruction can outperform models trained directly on 3d data. this largely benefits from video's greater data scale and scalability. another approach is lecun's jepa, or joint embedding predictive architecture. its starting point is that pixel-level reconstruction is inefficient, so it focuses on learning high-level, intrinsic representations. the idea is elegant, but the supervision signal for these representations is relatively weak and their quality difficult to measure, unlike 2d or 3d reconstruction, which has explicit supervision targets. there are also graph-, particle-, or dynamics-based modeling methods, such as yunzhu li's work, which can make good use of inductive biases and be useful when robot data are limited. overall, my personal view is that video is currently the most scalable approach and the best suited to large-scale data, which is why it has received relatively more attention recently. part five: thoughts on world models and vla yanjiang guo: although world models are popular now, they are not necessarily better than vlm-based vlas. i began world-model research early, but i have also continued researching vla. many people who have worked on vla for a long time see unresolved problems and then encounter world models, which they may regard as a “better solution” or even a “savior.” my experience suggests that this is not necessarily the case. i have observed that world action models perform better on some tasks, while vlas have advantages on others. my current impression is that world action models usually generalize slightly better to new tasks, mainly because they better preserve capabilities from video pretraining. but vla methods often perform better on the most precise, delicate manipulation tasks. after reading the π0.7 paper, i think both might work once there is enough data, while each may have advantages when data are limited. so i do not think world models are the “one correct” direction. world models and vla are parallel families of modeling approaches. before reaching sufficient data scale, it is hard to know the right learning objective for robotics—what form of supervision will be its “next-token prediction.” at the end of the debate between world models and vla, we may come back to the data issue everyone is discussing. in my view, constructing the dataset with the greatest information entropy is the real barrier to training general-purpose policies today. references 我们在选择哪些数据应该由我们来采集，或者说应该由像我们这样相对纯粹、中立的第三方数据公司来提供的时候，其实我最看重一件事情就是数据的跨本体可迁移性。 跨本体可迁移性决定了这个数据能不能在不同的机器人公司，以及不同机器人公司的不同机器人型号之间复用。从成本的角度来说，这是一件非常划算的事情。如果有某一类数据，能够作为整个行业机器人模型训练的素材，并且可以跨本体复用，那么这一类数据就是一个行业共享的数据基础设施，它的价值不在于服务某一家机器人公司，而在于能够被整个行业反复复用。 大家可以想一想，如果有一份数据，30家机器人公司都可以使用。假设它的生产成本是10块钱，作为数据生产方，我并不需要靠一家客户收回全部成本，而是可以通过服务20家、30家公司来覆盖数据采集、标注、质量控制、持续迭代等成本，并支撑后续研发投入。 这意味着，随着越来越多企业使用同一类数据，数据的边际成本不断下降，而整个行业都能以更低的成本获得高质量训练数据。这正是跨本体数据最大的价值——它能够通过规模化复用，实现全行业的数据成本摊薄。 所以，我认为一个第三方数据供应商最应该做的，就是提供跨本体可用的数据；那些不能跨本体使用的数据，本来就应该由甲方自己去做。比如，使用某种特定本体的甲方，应该负责采集那些只有自家机器人才能使用的数据。比如真机遥操作（teleoperation）数据，比如绑定了特定夹爪能力的umi数据，这些数据天然只能服务于某一种机器人本体（或者夹爪），因此应该由机器人本体（或者夹爪）厂商自己完成，而不是由第三方来做。 modalitynet是我们刚刚上线的数据集（它的网址就是modalitynet.com，直接输入这个域名就可以访问）。目前这个网站上有三类数据，这三类数据都是可以跨本体使用的数据。这三类数据集分别是：mov——多模态大空间交互数据集、om——多模态灵巧操作数据集、itw——多模态野采主观视觉数据集。modalitynet就是我们发布的一个包含上述三种类型数据的公开数据集。
