body、loco-manipulation、whole body vla这些方向来说，这个数据集其实已经可以直接使用了。 mov数据规模示例 （粉色是mov，黄色是lafan，蓝色是amass，绿色是motionx++） 3.om——多模态灵巧操作数据集 modalitynet里面第二类数据，是面向精细操作的，尤其是高精度手部动作捕捉，我们叫om（omni manipulation，广谱灵巧操作）。可以把它理解成mov的一个极度缩小版本。 与mov的大空间采集不同，om将原本100平方米、200平方米甚至300平方米的 tracking space 缩小到桌面尺度，但对采集精度提出了极高要求。 它采集finger pose，要求达到亚毫米级别；同时仍然采集whole body pose；还有第一人称rgb和rgb-d视觉；第三人称、多角度rgb和rgb-d视觉；甚至还有spatial audio，也就是空间音频。 为什么还需要音频？很多时候，一个操作任务并不完全依赖视觉。比如我面对大家讲话，把一个东西放到桌子上。这个桌子的存在，对于我来说只是视觉先验。当我把东西放到桌子上的时候，真正确认任务完成的，其实是声音。所以声音也是一种非常重要的信息。 另外还有触觉。比如刚才我做了一个动作，又把东西拿回来，我的眼睛其实没有参与，而是依赖先验知识、力觉、触觉以及本体感觉完成了整个动作。所以在om这类数据集里面，我们同样会采集这些信息。 hiphi-om数据示例 在om的数采空间里，大家会看到许多小隔间，每个隔间里都密集布置了各种传感器和 camera。它们的目的，就是以超高精度采集人的manipulation过程，包括in-hand manipulation、触觉信息、运控信息等等，将这些信息完整采集下来。这就是 modalitynet 的第二类数据。 首先，我们采用光学与惯性融合的动作捕捉，同时还使用了emf，也就是磁传感等数据源。不过，精细化手部操作最重要的是触觉，我们把触觉模态也加入进来了。 另外，因为所有操作都围绕一个固定工作空间进行，所以我们增加了第一人称视觉、第一人称深度视觉，以及第三人称视觉、多视角第三人称视觉、多视角深度视觉。 还有一些目前还不知道未来有没有用的模态，例如温度、音频，我全部都采集了，因为我担心以后这些信息会变得有价值。 这类数据精度非常高，而且模态比第一类还要更完整。 第一类whole body control的数据，比如我推着一把椅子慢慢往前走，当我已经有了手部位姿和椅子的trajectory之后，其实比较容易推断手和椅子之间的关系。 但是如果我要完成一个精细的in-hand manipulation，仅仅依靠手部位姿和瓶子的状态，其实很难准确估计两者之间非常细微的接触关系。这种接触关系，只有把触觉信息一起采集进来，才能真正描述精细操作过程中人与物体之间的接触状态。 这类数据集要小一些，因为它特别难采，也特别贵。目前我们自己手里大概有几千小时的数据。按照前面说的比例，开源部分大概就是除以20，也就是几百小时，大概就是这个体量。 第一个作用，它可以训练一个操作基模（manipulation foundation model），可以帮助模型全面理解人类是如何完成manipulation的，本质上就是一个操作层面的基模，对标身体级别的动作基模kimodo。 这件事情也是我个人现在非常感兴趣的方向。我目前正在和几位top researcher合作做这个方向。 我预计，今年下半年到明年年初，他们可能都会陆续发表相关工作。这些工作会是类似于manipulation foundation model的研究，也就是面向tabletop manipulation层面的操作基模。这是om数据的第一个作用。 第二个作用，是把这套数据对齐到机器人本体上。因为这些数据本来是从人身上采集的，包括人体位姿、手部位姿、触觉以及物体轨迹。如果我把它完整地对齐到某一个机器人本体，比如unitree的本体配sharpa wave灵巧手，我们把这个过程叫做embodiment alignment，也就是本体对齐。 这个过程其实非常复杂。里面涉及前向动力学、逆向动力学，需要做mapping、retargeting，需要使用强化学习，还需要在仿真环境里面完成大量训练，最后还要完成sim-to-real。当这一整套流程全部完成以后，这份数据本质上就已经非常接近遥操作数据了。因为它已经和机器人本体完全对齐。 但是，它又比遥操作更强。很多动作，其实遥操作根本做不出来。比如玩魔方。再比如一些高度依赖力反馈和触觉反馈的精细操作，遥操作很难完成。还有一些精细的抛接动作，遥操作同样做不了。这些动作，人是可以自然完成的。 因此，我们可以先采集human data，再把这些动作完整地对齐到机器人本体上。完成对齐之后，它不仅和机器人本体完全一致，甚至还能在synthetic space里面直接获得对应的运控信息，进一步生成电机层面的控制数据。 所以，om数据的第二个作用，就是完成机器人与人的本体对齐之后，作为遥操作数据的替代，而且能够覆盖那些遥操作本身做不了的精细操作任务。 om数据使用示例 （mov是高精度人体动捕之于人形机器人；om是高精度手部动捕之于灵巧手吗？） 这样理解对也不对。我认为这两个数据集本质上其实是同一个东西。第一个数据集mov，是把人的大空间交互行为完整数字化；第二个数据集om，则是把人的精细操作行为完整数字化。 所以，它们在设备选型、模态构成，甚至整个数据采集软件上，其实都是同一套体系。区别只是一个工作空间是20米×20米，一个是3米×3米。但是，后者的建设成本其实已经与前者非常接近。 动作捕捉只是其中一个模态，我必须强调这一点。motion或者pose，并不是机器人数据里最重要的模态，我认为最重要的仍然是视觉。如果让我排序，我会把视觉排第一，触觉排第二，pose排第三。这里的pose包括body pose和hand pose。当然，还有object trajectory、terrain等很多其他模态，机器人其实都需要。 但如果让我只能保留一个模态，我一定会保留视觉；如果只能保留两个，我会保留视觉和触觉；第三个，我才会选择whole body pose；第四个，才会选择hand pose。 我是有充分理由这样排序的。因为很多hand pose的信息，其实可以通过视觉估计出来，甚至有一部分触觉信息，也能够从视觉中间接推断。但是反过来，视觉一旦没有，就是彻底没有了；触觉一旦没有，当视觉被遮挡的时候，手和身体位姿信息也没有任何办法可以补回来。 所以，你刚才那个理解既对，也不完全对。对的地方在于，我们确实是沿着human pose和hand pose这条自己最熟悉的技术路线切入的。但如果让我客观评价机器人真正需要哪些模态，我甚至并不认为pose是最重要的那个模态。 5. itw——多模态野采主观视觉数据集 modalitynet里面第三部分的数据，是以ego vision为主的野采数据。我们叫itw，也就是in the wild，指的是野外采集。这里所谓的in the wild，真正的含义是非可控环境。ego vision指的是人类主观视觉。比如我戴一个摄像头，或者把手机固定在头上，这就是获取人类主观视觉。第三类数据，就是戴着头部设备，在这些真实环境里面完成采集的数据。 为什么强调主观视觉？我们在屋檐下、摄影棚或者实验室里面采数据，布置大量outside-in sensor，比如光学动作捕捉摄像头、uwb传感器等等，这些属于in the factory或者in the studio的数据，它们都是在可控环境下采集的。 真正的in the wild，是在非可控的，真实的环境里面获取数据。比如真实的养老院、真实的物流仓库、真实的工厂柔性制造产线。以主观视觉（ego-vision）为主干模态，我们也会努力在里面加入一些位姿与触觉信息。 在最完美的情况下，我们希望在野采环境（in the wild），尽可能还原人类感知外界时涉及的所有模态，同时拥有触觉、位姿、手部信息、主观视觉，还希望有ground truth级别的深度（最好肩膀上再挂一个lidar），最后你会发现，我们在数采实验员身上挂满了各种设备，像一棵圣诞树。 这里的观点和我们之前采访的danfei老师提到的人类数据观点非常类似，关于danfei老师的采访可以参考专访danfei xu：人类数据是伪装成另一种形式的机器人数据 但这样的方案，实际上没有办法真正做到in the wild，也没有办法做到10万小时、100万小时这样的采集规模。而今年整个行业，对于in the wild数据的需求已经达到10万到100万小时。因此，在in the wild的数据采集里面，我们必须做取舍，牺牲一部分模态。 （第三类itw数据，它和前面两类数据有什么区别？另外，它和现在市面上的ego vision data这些数据有什么区别？） itw 数据使用的是我们自行设计的一套设备。这套设备搭载了多枚camera。其中有两个fish-eye camera、一个rgb camera，还有一个可以配置成高精度rgb或rgb-d的camera。另外还有四个灰度相机，这四个灰度相机主要用于vslam、head tracking和hand tracking，也就是头部追踪和手部追踪。另外这个设备的开放性非常好，随时可以拥抱第三方其他模态采集设备的接入。 因此，我们理解的ego vision设备，并不仅仅是在头上戴一个gopro。本质上，如果一个设备已经戴到了头上，那么它就应该尽可能完整地覆盖所有希望采集的模态或者说信息。 这个设备本身具备存储、计算和数据传输能力，续航时间也很长，一次充电基本可以连续采集一天。另外，它的fov（field of view，视场角）几乎完整模拟了人眼的视野。 大家可以估计一下，人眼的fov有多大？如果眼球固定不动，人眼的视野大概只有110到120度，所以现在大部分vr头显的fov都设计在105度左右，也有做到120度的，但120度边缘畸变会比较严重，因此主流还是110度左右。但是，我们fish-eye camera的fov是210度。 为什么比人眼还大？因为人眼本身是可以转动的。如果眼球不动，当我正视前方的时候，手移动到一定位置以后，我就已经看不到了。但是因为眼球能够转动，人实际上可以看到耳朵后面的区域，所以真正的人眼可感知视野实际上超过180度，大约可以达到220度。 机器人没有眼球，这个设备也没有眼球，所以我们只能通过210度的大视场角去模拟人眼在眼球转动情况下的整体视野。 另外，周围配置的灰度相机全部采用全局快门，相比普通rolling shutter，其时间对齐更加准确，单帧图像上也较少有撕裂和变形，而且灰度波段受自然光干扰更小，因此特别适合完成hand tracking和head tracking。这就是一个典型的ego vision设备。 是不是戴上这样一个ego vision设备，数据采集就结束了？答案是yes and no。 在绝大多数需要大规模采集的场景里，比如要做到10万小时以上的数据规模，或者采用众包模式的时候，这样一台设备基本就是唯一能够要求参与者佩戴的设备。因为我也不太可能要求做众包的人，再额外穿戴动作捕捉设备、触觉手套或者其他复杂设备。 但是，在很多可控环境下，比如我们自己的fleet，也就是自己的数据采集团队，他们就可以佩戴更多设备，包括动作捕捉设备、触觉手套等，把更多模态一起采集下来。对应到市场需求，现在一些非常领先的机器人团队，他们真正需要的已经不是单纯的ego vision，而是这样的ego vision plus。 早些时候，只要头顶一个手机或者gopro，就可以采回来一些初级的数据，就已经能够满足很多需求。但是现在，这样的数据已经很难完全满足模型训练需求了。这类数据同质化非常严重，即使有人需要，价格也已经变得很低。 现在印度、加拿大法语区、墨西哥、东南亚，包括国内华东、华中的很多省份，都已经有大量团队在采集这种数据。只要是单目视频或者双目视频，下游基本都会要，只是价格会有所区别。真正有门槛的是ego vision plus这类数据，对采集要求会更高。 从去年到今年，我最大的体感是，下游客户对于数据规模的需求增长速度非常惊人。 去年10月份之前，大家跟我们讨论数据的时候，单位还是"几千小时"，基本都是按千小时来聊。 到了年底，generalist发布了一个工作，公开宣称使用了约27万小时的数据集。虽然它主要是手持夹爪数据，并不是纯ego vision，只有少部分带ego vision，但从那一天开始，所有来找我们交流的客户，起步就是30万小时。 今年年初，又有generalist、sunday等团队，用50万小时甚至上千万条数据去验证scaling law，因此整个行业的需求又迅速跳到了50万小时。50万小时已经成为新的起点。 最近几个月，大家开始讨论100万小时的数据规模。甚至有一家海外公司告诉我们："你们明年要准备迎接1000万小时的数据需求。" 这个数字远远超出了我的预期（虽然我未必信）。 因为到目前为止，自动驾驶行业其实都没有使用过这么大规模的数据。我反而不是担心他们买不起数据，而是担心他们是否真的有足够的算力预算，同时承担数据和训练成本，以及是否真的能“玩得动”这么大体量的数据。 所以目前我认为1000万小时的说法仍有一定夸张成分，但100万小时我认为是真实需求。因此，今年我们扩充产能，也是按照100万小时这个目标去规划的。 如果抽象来看，本质上就是一个问题：下游模型不断变化，到底对我们来说是好事还是坏事？我认为，波动本身一定是好事。在商业竞争里面，最怕的不是变化，而是收敛。 如果下游最后只剩下几家大客户，需求完全固定，价格完全透明，而供应商却越来越多，最终所有人只能不断比价，利润被压到刚刚能够活下来、但赚不到钱的水平，那才是真正危险。 所以，下游不断迭代、不断出现新的技术路线，对数据公司来说反而意味着更多机会。 真正的问题不是如何跟着每一种模型变化，而是退一步思考：这些模型到底在学习什么？我一直特别认可一个观点。这一轮具身智能、人形机器人，包括数据产业的发展，本质上是一场仿生学革命。 机器人本体越来越接近人体结构；模型越来越接近人大脑和小脑的学习方式；数据来源也越来越拟人化，越来越依赖人类真实的交互行为和动作行为。 因此，我们真正应该关注的，不是某一个模型今天需要什么，而是人类完成一个任务时，到底使用了哪些最本源的信息。 我认为，无论模型怎么变化，本质上都在学习两类东西：第一类是规则（rules），第二类是先验知识（human prior）。 所以，我们采集数据时，并不是围绕某一个机器人本体，也不是围绕某一个模型架构，而是围绕人本身。我要保证，人完成一个任务时所依赖的全部物理信息，都能够被数字化，而且精度至少达到人类自身感知系统能够感受到的水平。 举个简单例子。比如我刚才调整了一下自己的坐姿。这是一个非常简单的动作，但实际上我用到了很多不同的信息。 首先是视觉。视觉主要提供的是先验，所以并不需要特别高的精度。我只需要知道大家大概在哪个方向。 其次是本体感觉，也就是我对于自己身体姿态、手部姿态的感知。在人身上，这是小脑完成的；而对于机器人训练数据来说，只能依靠动作捕捉系统去数字化。本体感觉告诉我，我现在是什么姿态，要如何从当前姿态调整到目标姿态。除此之外，还有触觉。臀部、腿部、脚底的触觉，都参与了这个动作。 所以，如果我要把这个能力迁移到机器人身上，我就必须采集这些对应的信息。包括身体位姿、环境信息、地形、椅子的几何模型、工具轨迹、触觉、本体感觉等等。这些模态共同构成了人完成这个动作所依赖的全部信息。 因此，我应对模型范式变化的方法其实很简单。我不管未来是vla、world action model，还是新的模型架构。因为无论采用什么模型，人完成任务时依赖的信息不会变。 我要做的，就是尽可能以合理的成本，把这些真正有价值的人类信息全部数字化。只要这些模态都被完整采集下来，我认为它们不会因为模型范式变化而失去价值。长期来看，这些数据不会被淘汰。 8. 真正重要的数据是重建出人类感知世界的input （danfei xu老师专访danfei xu：人类数据是伪装成另一种形式的机器人数据其实也提到过一个类似的观点。核心问题就是，人到底是如何利用我们的感官完成与世界的交互？机器人又如何复现这些human input？） 对。本质上就是围绕人的交互行为，无论是大空间动作，还是精细操作，把所有真正有价值的模态完整数字化。我认为，这件事情本质上就是在蒸馏physical world，蒸馏人类能力本身。 我再举一个更具体的例子。触觉的感知为什么我们最后选择的是柔性触觉传感器？其实它们并不是精度最高的。原因很简单，因为人的触觉本来就没有那么高的绝对精度。 事实上，人几乎所有的感知都是相对测量，而不是绝对测量。无论是姿态、亮度、疼痛、重量、力量，甚至颜色，我们感知的都是相对变化。比如你一直盯着一块红色屏幕，看久之后再看别的东西，都会觉得偏绿色，因为视觉本身就是相对测量。 因此，当我选择传感器时，如果必须在绝对精度、量程、鲁棒性、稳定性之间做取舍，我往往会优先放弃绝对精度。这一点和很多机器人团队不太一样。 很多人在选择传感器时，首先关注的是精度指标，例如比例因子、交叉耦合误差、rms等各种性能参数。这些我当然也会看。但如果这些指标与分辨率、量程、稳定性、鲁棒性发生冲突，我会优先选择后者。因为人的感知系统本身就没有那么高的绝对精度，却拥有极高的量程、鲁棒性、稳定性，以及自修复能力。我认为，这才是真正值得机器人学习的地方。 关于这个问题，其实我专门写过一篇blog（https://noitomrobotics.com/world-compiler/），大家可以去modalitynet官网看看，目前已经发布了两篇blog。第一篇由我们的首席科学家韩磊博士执笔，第二篇则是我写的，标题叫“world compiler”。 我当时写这篇文章，其实是想写一篇"檄文"。所谓檄文，一方面是写给内部团队看的，另一方面也是写给整个行业看的。互联网是有记录的，我希望把自己的观点提前留在这里。多年以后，即使被证明有些地方不对，我也不怕被打脸。但我希望大家知道，这些观点不是事后总结，而是很多年前我们这群人就已经明确提出过。 刚才我提到，noitom robotics现在做的数据业务，本质上是在蒸馏物理世界的信息，也是在蒸馏人类的能力。而这个蒸馏过程，我认为可以分成两个阶段。 第一阶段，是把世界记录下来，也就是完成数据采集。但采集得到的raw data，本身其实非常缺乏可学习性（learnability）。 因为它本质上是不结构化的信息，只包含最原始的传感器数据和视觉数据。当然，大模型作为一个黑盒，可能会在latent space中自己学会很多能力。 第二阶段，是把采集下来的raw data编译成模型能直接学习的信息。过去这么多年的经验告诉我们，如果能够先对这些原始数据进行一次类似"编译"（compile）的处理，把它转换成更加结构化的信息，再送入模型训练，训练效率会明显更高，投在数据上的roi也会更高。这个结构化与抽象化的“编译”的过程也是一个“压缩”的过程，能把最重要的结构化信息提炼出来，让模型聚焦关注学习。 我之所以把这个过程称为“compile”，其实是借用了软件开发里的概念。我们平时写python、c++等程序，本质上写的都是一种接近自然语言的高级语言。这些代码本身机器并不能直接执行。只有经过编译器（compiler）转换之后，机器才能真正理解并执行。 我认为，数据也是一样的。raw data就像源代码，它本身并不是最适合模型学习的形式。如果能够经过一层“编译”，把它转换成更加结构化、更容易学习的数据，那么整个训练过程就会更加高效。 举个例子。如果我只有一段ego vision视频，它本身只是视觉数据。但如果我进一步从里面估计出hand pose、depth、触觉信息，甚至根据已有的信息进一步推断出全身位姿，那么原本一份比较难学习的数据，就会变成一份更加容易学习的数据。整个过程，其实就是不断提高原始数据的结构化程度，提高它的可学习性（learnability）。 所以我认为，提高raw data的结构化程度、提高数据的可学习性，是未来数据行业一个非常重要的方向。这件事情总归需要有人去做。如果不是我们这些数据公司来做，那最终也一定会由模型公司的数据团队来完成。 不过我对此还是比较有信心，因为很多甲方的数据团队其实只有五六个人，他们很难长期投入大量资源完成这样一套完整的数据编译流程。但我们有一百多人的团队，长期只专注做这一件事情，所以我们能够把这件事情做得更加专业。 因此，我一直认为，提高数据的可学习性，把数据中更多能够被模型学习的信息提取出来，是一件非常有价值的事情。事实上，现在几乎所有客户都提出了类似需求。例如文字标注、语义标注，有的是逐秒、逐帧标注，有的是按场景、按任务进行分段标注。这些工作的本质，其实都是在提升数据的可学习性。 从商业模式来看，如果一家数据公司只是购买大量设备、招聘大量人员，采集完数据之后，原封不动地交付给客户，那么在充分竞争的市场里，它最终能够获得的定价，本质上就是设备折旧加人工成本。 因为市场最终会回归成本定价。你投入什么成本，充分竞争之后，就只能获得与成本相匹配的收益。但数据的可学习性不同。它本质上是一个“黑箱”，也是数据服务商与客户之间真正创造价值的部分。 如果我们能够在这个黑箱里做出更多能力，例如不断提高数据的结构化程度、提炼出更多可学习的信息，那么数据本身就能够形成溢价。这样不仅能够让数据公司建立真正的竞争壁垒，把这门生意做得更好，对模型公司来说，同样能够获得更高质量、更高训练效率的数据，实现双方共赢。 （刚才我们一直在讨论数据的可学习性（learnability）。具体来说，有没有一些例子可以说明，如何提升现有数据的可学习性？例如刚才介绍的诺亦腾三类数据，它们分别是如何提高可学习性的？） 首先，刚才提到的三类数据，它们的可学习性其实完全不同。 前两类数据（mov和om）的可学习性非常高。原因在于，它们本身已经高度结构化，包含了大量ground truth级别的信息，例如ground truth级别的触觉、本体姿态等各种真实模态，因此模型学习起来非常直接。 当然，即便如此，它们仍然需要进一步补充一些可学习信息，例如场景标注、过程标注、语义标注等。现在利用多模态大模型，通过post-training，其实已经能够自动完成质量很高的语义标注。硅谷现在已经有不少团队专门做这件事情。 他们拿到大量ego vision数据之后，收费进行自动语义标注。比如每小时数据额外收取几美元，如果处理10万小时的数据，就是几十万美元的生意。这已经成为一个独立的数据服务市场。 相比之下，第三类数据——也就是纯ego vision数据——可学习性就差很多。因为它本质上只是前两类全模态数据中的一个真子集，只保留了视觉信息，以及少量稀疏的其他模态，因此天然缺失了大量信息。也正因为如此，它的可学习性明显更低。 需要关注的是，我们的三个数据集是可以互相支撑的，在全模态，全维度的数据积累基础上，我可以把第三类数据做远远优于行业的后处理。可能我的深度估计比别人更准确，我的hand pose估计比别人更准确。别人估计hand pose可能只有两厘米左右的误差，我可以做到亚厘米级。甚至别人根本没有拍到腿部，我依然能够把腿部姿态估计出来。这些能力，我认为，才是真正有意思的地方。 （这些数据最终都是给模型学习的，但其实我们并不知道模型究竟是通过哪些信息完成学习的。那么，我们如何判断哪些信息是真正有价值的？我们又如何验证？） 其实我可以把这个问题再往底层推进一步。真正的问题其实是：我们自己，以及我们的客户，如何验证一份数据到底是不是好数据？一种可学习性的提升，到底有没有真正产生价值？这其实是整个数据行业最大的挑战。 大家有没有发现，数据交易对于数据供应商来说，其实是一件非常不公平的事情。因为它是一个典型的后验市场。 举个例子。我卖给客户10万小时数据，每小时200元，总共2000万元。客户把数据拿回去训练模型，四五个月、半年以后，如果模型效果不好，loss降不下来，成功率只有40%，双方一定会开始扯皮。客户会说：“你的数据不行。”我可能会说：“是你的模型团队能力不行。”这种事情几乎不可避免。 而所有后验交易都有一个共同特点，就是利润率不会太高。因为客户控制风险的方法，就是提前压价。客户会认为：“我现在就要付钱，而效果要几个月之后才能知道，所以我一定要把价格压下来。” 因此，数据公司的毛利天然就会受到影响。所以，我认为最好的办法，是在交付之前，就能够在同一条技术路线下证明数据确实有价值。 这也是为什么我们现在八九十位正式员工里面，有二十多位专门做模型研究。很多人会觉得奇怪，一家数据公司为什么需要这么多研究员？其实原因就在这里。 他们的工作主要分为三部分。第一，是做感知交互相关算法。第二，是做数据增广、模态补全以及后处理算法。第三，就是做模型验证。 我们的研究团队会使用和客户相同的技术路线。他们会训练vla，会训练world action model，也会训练动作基础模型和teleoperation基础模型。当然，我们训练的规模会比客户小得多。因为我们不会真正去训练一个可以商业部署的模型，而是去验证数据。 例如，我们会从完整数据集中随机抽取十分之一、百分之一的数据，观察loss是否持续收敛。同时，我们还会验证scaling law。例如，同样抽取百分之一的数据，来自5000小时数据集和5万小时数据集，看看更大的数据规模以及更好的数据分布是否确实能够带来更好 的训练收益。 （所以world compiler这个概念，您真正想表达的是，未来physical ai真正需要的，并不是简单的数据，而是模型真正能够理解、能够学习的数据。数据公司真正要做的，就是把这些“可学习的特质”提炼出来？） 对。如果再把这个观点说得更简单一点，就是：当我们还没有能力把所有模态、所有维度的数据全部采集下来时，我们有没有能力把缺失的模态和维度补全？而这个补全过程，本质上就是一种解释的过程。也正是“world compiler”真正想解决的问题。 编者按 be reused by different robotics companies and across their different robot models. it makes economic sense. data that supplies training material for the whole industry and transfers across embodiments becomes shared data infrastructure. its value lies in repeated use throughout the industry, rather than service to a single company. imagine a dataset that thirty robotics companies can use. suppose producing it costs ten yuan. as its producer, i do not need to recover the entire cost from one customer. serving twenty or thirty companies can cover collection, annotation, quality control, ongoing iteration, and subsequent r&d. as more companies use the same category of data, its marginal cost falls, and the whole industry can obtain high-quality training data more cheaply. that is the greatest value of cross-embodiment data: reuse at scale spreads data costs across the industry. a third-party supplier should therefore primarily provide cross-embodiment data. customers should produce data roughly one-twentieth of what we hold. for example, if we have 200,000 hours, approximately 10,000 hours would be public. barring major changes, we intend to maintain that ratio. the remaining in-the-wild data comes from uncontrolled real environments: actual eldercare facilities, logistics warehouses, or flexible manufacturing lines. egocentric vision is the backbone modality, and we also most current vr headsets are designed around 105 degrees; some reach 120, but edge distortion becomes substantial there, so around 110 remains mainstream. our fisheye camera has a 210-degree fov. [editor's clarification: these are the interview's approximate comparisons; binocular overlap, total peripheral visual field, and a headset's display fov are different quantities.] why wider than human eyes? because eyes can rotate. if i look straight ahead without moving them, a hand moving far enough to the side disappears from view. eye movement extends what we can perceive; i describe the overall accessible field as exceeding 180 degrees and reaching approximately 220, including regions toward the back of the ears. robots and this device have no rotating eyeballs, so we use a 210-degree wide-angle field to simulate the overall view available when human eyes turn. the surrounding grayscale cameras all have global shutters. compared with ordinary rolling shutters, they provide more precise temporal alignment and fewer image distortions or tearing within a frame. we find the grayscale configuration less susceptible to natural-light interference in this application, making it well suited to hand and head tracking. this is a typical egocentric device for us. does wearing that device complete the collection setup? yes and no. in most scenarios requiring very large scale—over 100,000 hours, for example—or crowdsourcing, this is essentially the only equipment we can ask people to wear. it is difficult to require crowdsourced participants to add motion-capture equipment, tactile gloves, or other complicated devices. in more controlled situations, our own collection fleet can wear additional equipment, such as motion-capture devices and tactile gloves, to capture more modalities together. some leading robotics teams now need precisely this “ego vision plus,” rather than egocentric vision alone. previously, wearing a phone or gopro could collect basic data that met many needs. such data now struggles to fully satisfy training requirements. it is heavily commoditized, and even where there is demand, prices have fallen substantially. many teams already collect it in india, french-speaking canada, mexico, southeast asia, and provinces across eastern and central china. downstream customers generally want monocular or stereo video, with different prices. the real barrier lies in ego vision plus, which has more demanding capture requirements. 6. how much embodied data is needed today? my strongest impression from last year to this year is how astonishingly fast customer demand has grown. before october last year, conversations were still in units of a few thousand hours. near the end of the year, generalist released work publicly reporting a dataset of roughly 270,000 hours. it was mainly handheld-gripper data, not pure egocentric vision, with only a small portion including that viewpoint. from that day onward, customers began discussions at 300,000 hours. early this year, teams such as generalist and sunday used scales of 500,000 hours or even tens of millions of data samples to investigate scaling laws. demand rapidly jumped to 500,000 hours, which became the new starting point. in recent months, people have begun discussing a million hours. one overseas company even told us, “prepare for demand for ten million hours next year.” that far exceeded my expectations, though i am not necessarily convinced. in my assessment, even autonomous driving has not used data on that scale so far. my concern is less whether customers can afford the data than whether their compute budgets can support both data and training costs, and whether they can actually handle such a volume. i still think the ten-million-hour figure contains some exaggeration, but i regard a million hours as real demand. we are expanding production capacity this year around that target. 7. how can data companies respond to changing model paradigms? abstractly, the question is whether constant changes in downstream models are good or bad for us. i think volatility is good. in business competition, convergence is more frightening than change. the dangerous outcome would be a handful of big customers, completely fixed requirements, transparent prices, and an ever-growing number of suppliers. everyone would compete only on price, with margins reduced to barely surviving rather than making money. continuing iteration and new technical approaches downstream instead create more opportunities for data companies. the real question is not how to follow every model change, but what these models are learning. i strongly agree with the view that this wave of embodied ai, humanoid robotics, and data-industry development is fundamentally a revolution in biomimetics. robot bodies increasingly resemble human anatomy, models increasingly approach how the human brain and cerebellum learn, and data sources increasingly rely on real human interaction and movement. we should therefore focus less on what a particular model needs today and more on the fundamental information humans use to complete a task. whatever the architecture, i think models are essentially learning two things: rules and human priors. we organize capture around the human, rather than a specific robot or model architecture. i want all the physical information a person relies on during a task to be digitized, at a precision at least matching what human perception can detect. for a simple example, i just adjusted my seated posture. it is a small action, but it uses many different kinds of information. first, vision supplies priors, so it does not need particularly high precision here. i only need to know roughly where the audience is. second, proprioception tells me about my body and hand poses. in the interview's simplified account, the cerebellum performs this role for humans; for robot training data, we digitize it using motion capture. proprioception indicates my current pose and how to adjust toward the target. touch at the buttocks, legs, and soles also participates. [editor's clarification: proprioception involves peripheral receptors and multiple neural circuits, rather than the cerebellum alone.] to transfer this capability to a robot, i must capture the corresponding information: body poses, environmental information, terrain, the chair's geometry, tool trajectories, touch, and proprioception. together these modalities comprise the information humans rely on for this movement. my response to changing model paradigms is therefore simple. whether the future uses vlas, world action models, or another architecture, the information humans rely on to perform tasks remains the same. i want to digitize all that valuable human information at a reasonable cost. if these modalities are captured completely, i believe the data will retain its value as model paradigms change. over the long term, it will not become obsolete. 8. reconstructing the inputs through which humans perceive the world (danfei xu made a similar point in an interview with danfei xu: human data is robot data in disguise. the central question is how humans use their senses to interact with the world, and how robots can reproduce those human inputs.) exactly. we center on human interaction, whether large-space movement or fine manipulation, and completely digitize every genuinely valuable modality. i see this as distilling the physical world and human capabilities themselves. consider a more specific example. why did we ultimately choose flexible tactile sensors? they do not have the highest precision. the reason is simple: human touch itself does not have such high absolute accuracy. in my view, almost all human perception is relative rather than absolute: pose, brightness, pain, weight, force, and even color are perceived through relative changes. stare at a red screen for a long time and other things afterward appear greenish. that illustrates the relative nature of vision. when choosing sensors, if i must trade off absolute accuracy, range, robustness, and stability, i often sacrifice absolute accuracy first. that differs from the approach of many robotics teams. many people first examine precision metrics such as scale factor, cross-coupling error, and rms performance. i examine them too. but when they conflict with resolution, range, stability, or robustness, i prioritize the latter. human perception lacks exceptionally high absolute accuracy yet has tremendous range, robustness, stability, and self-repair capability. i think those are the qualities robots should learn. i wrote a blog specifically about this: https://noitomrobotics.com/world-compiler/. there are two relevant posts available through modalitynet. our chief scientist, dr. lei han, wrote the first; i wrote the second, titled “world compiler.” i intended it as a manifesto, addressed both to our internal team and to the industry. the internet keeps a record, and i wanted to put our views on record in advance. even if some prove wrong years later, i am not afraid of being contradicted. i want people to know that these were not retrospective conclusions: our group explicitly proposed them long before. as i said, noitom robotics' data business essentially distills information from the physical world and human capabilities. i see that distillation as two stages. first, record the world through data collection. the resulting raw data has little learnability by itself: it is unstructured, containing basic sensor and visual signals. of course, a black-box large model may learn many capabilities in latent space on its own. second, compile the raw data into information models can learn directly. our years of experience suggest that first “compiling” it into more structured information makes training significantly more efficient and improves data roi. structuring and abstracting data is also a form of compression: it extracts the most important information and focuses the model's learning. i borrow “compile” from software development. python and c++ programs are written in high-level languages, relatively close to natural language. machines cannot directly execute that source; translation by a compiler or language runtime makes execution possible. [editor's clarification: this is a software analogy; python commonly uses bytecode and an interpreter, whereas c++ is typically compiled to machine code.] raw data is like source code: it is not necessarily in the best form for model learning. a compilation layer can turn it into more structured, learnable data and make training more efficient. for example, an egocentric video initially contains only vision. if we additionally estimate hand poses, depth, tactile information, and perhaps infer whole-body poses from what is available, data that was difficult to learn from becomes easier. the process continually increases structure and learnability. [editor's clarification: inferred modalities are estimates, not automatically equivalent to directly measured ground truth.] improving raw-data structure and learnability is an important future direction for the industry. someone must do it. if data companies do not, the data teams inside model companies eventually will. i am confident about our position because many customers' data teams have only five or six people and cannot continually invest the resources needed for a complete compilation pipeline. we have more than a hundred people focused on this task, allowing us to specialize much more deeply. extracting more learnable information from data is valuable. almost every customer now requests it, including text and semantic annotations: sometimes per second or per frame, sometimes segmented by scene or task. these are all ways to improve learnability. if a data company merely buys equipment, hires people, collects data, and delivers it unchanged, fully competitive pricing ultimately amounts to equipment depreciation plus labor costs. competition drives pricing back toward costs: returns correspond to what you put in. learnability is different. it is a “black box,” and the part in which data suppliers and customers create real value. if we develop more capabilities within it—improving structure and extracting more learnable information—the data can command a premium. that builds a real competitive barrier for the data business while giving model companies higher-quality data and more efficient training. both sides benefit. 10. how can we improve data learnability? (we have discussed learnability throughout. could you give concrete examples of improving existing data? how does each of noitom's three categories increase learnability?) the learnability of the three categories is quite different. mov and om are highly learnable because they are already strongly structured and contain substantial ground-truth-level information: touch, body poses, and other measured modalities. models can learn from them directly. even so, they need additional information such as scene, process, and semantic annotations. post-trained multimodal large models can now automatically produce high-quality semantic annotations. several silicon valley teams specialize in this. they charge to automatically annotate large quantities of egocentric data. an additional few dollars per hour, across 100,000 hours, becomes a business worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. this is already an independent data-services market. the third category, largely egocentric vision, is much less learnable. it is effectively a strict subset of the first two all-modality categories, retaining vision and only sparse other modalities. much information is inherently missing, lowering learnability. the three datasets support one another. our full-modality, multidimensional accumulation lets us postprocess the third category much better than the industry norm. our depth or hand-pose estimates might be more accurate: where others' hand-pose errors are around two centimeters, we can achieve subcentimeter results. we can even estimate leg poses when others have not filmed the legs. these are the capabilities i find truly interesting. 11. how can we validate improved learnability? (the data is ultimately used for model learning, but we do not know exactly which information a model learns from. how do we determine what information is valuable and validate that?) i would push the question deeper: how do we and our customers verify that data is good, or that improving learnability has actually created value? that is the data industry's greatest challenge. have you noticed how unfair data transactions can be to suppliers? this is a market in which value is judged after the fact. suppose i sell 100,000 hours at 200 yuan per hour: twenty million yuan in total. the customer trains a model, and four or five months—or half a year—later it performs poorly, the loss does not fall, and success is only 40%. disputes inevitably follow. the customer says, “your data is bad.” i might reply, “your model team lacks the ability.” these disagreements are almost unavoidable. such transactions share a feature: margins tend not to be very high. customers manage risk by pressing the price down in advance. they reason, “i must pay now, but will not know the outcome for months, so i have to lower the price.” that naturally affects data companies' gross margins. i think the best approach is to prove the data's value along the customer's technical route before delivery. this is why more than twenty of our eighty or ninety full-time employees conduct model research. people find it surprising that a data company needs so many researchers, but that is the reason. their work has three parts: perception and interaction algorithms; data augmentation, modality completion, and postprocessing; and model-based validation. our researchers use the same technical routes as customers. they train vlas, world action models, motion foundation models, and teleoperation foundation models, but at a much smaller scale. we are validating data, not training a commercially deployable model. for example, we randomly sample one-tenth or one-hundredth of the complete dataset and check whether loss continues to converge. we also examine scaling: take one percent of a 5,000-hour dataset and one percent of a 50,000-hour dataset, and see whether greater scale and better distributions yield better training benefits. that is the training return we want to verify. (so what you mean by “world compiler” is that physical ai needs more than raw data: it needs data models can actually understand and learn from. a data company's role is to extract those learnable properties?) yes. put even more simply: while we cannot capture every modality and dimension, can we complete what is missing? that completion is a process of interpretation, and the problem the world compiler really seeks to solve. editor's note “an embodied-data company essentially distills the physical world and human capabilities. its value lies in compiling signals collected by sensors from the physical world, and signals representing human capabilities, into data models can learn from directly.” that is my concise interpretation of our guest's central argument, and the problem this dataset aims to address. references 1. noitom robotics website 2. modalitynet 3. world compiler bones studio

这个方向其实已经被研究了很久。大概从上世纪80年代、90年代开始，随着计算机计算能力逐渐发展起来，研究者们开始思考一个很自然的问题：如何从二维信息恢复三维信息。 因为对于人类来说，我们会觉得自己生活在一个三维世界里，但如果不考虑触觉，仅从获取信息的角度来看，我们主要依赖的是视觉，而视觉本质上接收到的是二维图像或者二维视频流。 所以早期研究者关注的问题就是，如何从这些二维观测中恢复出三维世界的结构。 早期一个比较经典的思路是stereo。很多人可能接触过stereo camera（双目相机）。简单来说，当两个相机同时观测同一个场景，并且两个相机之间存在一个小的基线距离，也就是轻微的位置偏移时，我们就可以通过三角化的方法，根据两个相机中对应的像素位置恢复它们在三维空间中的深度信息。 从某种意义上说，这是三维重建的一个特殊情况，因为stereo相机之间的相对位置是已知且固定的。但研究者更希望处理更一般的场景，比如相机之间的位置关系本身也是未知的。这时问题就进一步扩展成：既要恢复场景中各个点在三维世界中的深度，也要恢复相机在三维世界中的位置和姿态。 大概在1995年到2005年之间，人们逐渐发现，这类问题可以通过一种叫structure from motion（sfm）的流程来解决。机器人领域的同学可能更熟悉slam。某种程度上，slam可以看作structure from motion的一个特殊场景或者子集。 structure from motion的输入是一组大致对应同一场景的图像，通过这些图像恢复相机参数和场景深度。而slam则进一步假设这些图像具有时间顺序，是一个连续的视频流。这样虽然对问题做了一些简化，但通常会更加稳定和可靠。 因此在1995年到2005年这个阶段，三维重建领域主要关注的是如何定义和解决这个问题。 随后从2005年到2014年前后，整个领域更多是在做工程层面的提升。研究者关注的是如何让重建速度更快、规模更大、鲁棒性更强。例如能够处理十万张图像，能够处理八小时、十小时甚至更长时间的视频数据。 再往后，从2014年到2022年，深度神经网络开始进入这个领域。那个时期大家普遍认为，重建问题本身已经有非常成熟的数学建模，例如三角化、基础矩阵分解等都有清晰的数学表达。因此研究重点不是让网络直接完成重建，而是利用深度学习提升传统流程中的某些环节。 比如以orb-slam为例，它的第一步需要找到多张图像之间的对应关系。那个时期大家研究的是，如何通过神经网络获得更好的特征表示，在特征图上找到更准确的对应关系，从而获得更好的重建结果。这基本上是2014年至2022年期间的主流研究方向。 而从2022年至今，整个领域开始主动或者被动地更加全面地拥抱深度学习。 比较有代表性的工作包括dust3r，以及后来的vggt、vggt-ω等。这些工作的核心思想是，不再只是利用神经网络帮助寻找更好的对应关系，而是直接把整个重建问题转化成一个端到端的深度学习问题。 （最左侧vggt重建出的效果，肉眼可见的好于后面两个） 换句话说，它变成了一个完全黑盒的过程。有人喜欢这种方式，有人不喜欢，但我个人其实比较喜欢黑盒这个概念。现在我们只需要输入图片，把它送进一个训练好的transformer模型，模型就可以直接输出我们在三维空间中希望获得的各种信息。 我觉得这也是为什么最近两三年三维重建突然再次受到广泛关注。 第一个原因在于，如果这种方法能够采用和二维视觉、语言模型类似的训练范式，那么它就有机会受益于scaling law。 当计算资源增加、数据规模增加、训练投入增加的时候，模型能够持续稳定地获得性能提升。 对于公司来说，这是一个非常有吸引力的特性。因为企业更愿意投入那些能够稳定获得回报的技术路线。 第二个原因是，相比传统重建方法，这种完全深度化的方法开始能够处理动态场景。 这里有一个重要的观点：任何动态物体都可以被看作无数个小刚体运动的组合。在传统重建框架下，这类问题非常难处理，因为同时存在多个刚体运动，很难恢复其真实结构。但现在这些问题开始可以被解决。 例如在一些最新工作的demo中，我们已经能够恢复运动中的人和周围环境之间的空间关系。这意味着许多过去无法解决的问题开始变得可解。 （vggt-ω的一个demo演示，完美呈现动态重建） 第三点也是我个人觉得最有吸引力的一点。在二维视觉领域，我们已经习惯于把一张图片编码成一个全局表示，然后利用这个表示完成分类或者各种下游任务。但在几何领域，至少在2022年之前，其实并不存在类似的东西。 而现在，我们已经可以把一个输入的视频序列转换成一组几何感知的表示或者token。这些token能够编码整个序列中的主要几何结构和运动信息。 有了这样的表示之后，就能够支持大量新的下游应用，也能够衍生出很多有意思的研究方向。 我认为，这就是从2022年到2026年这一轮全面深度化的三维重建浪潮所带来的主要变化。 我觉得可以说，三维重建是整个三维、四维理解，或者说空间理解（spatial understanding）的基础。用比较老一辈研究者的话来说，它相当于是整个几何领域“皇冠上的明珠”。如果能够把三维重建这个问题解决好，很多后续想要的信息其实都能够直接获得。 这也是为什么这么多年来，大家一直非常重视三维重建。如果去看cvpr或者相关领域这些年的发展脉络，会发现无论技术路线怎么变化，学术界始终都非常关注三维重建，因为它在整个领域里有一种比较特殊的基础性地位。 而且在我看来，到了今天，三维重建的重要性不仅没有下降，反而进一步提升了。 还是拿二维深度学习的发展来做类比。回顾二维视觉的发展历程，最早大家往往会先在imagenet这样的图像分类任务上预训练一个模型，比如resnet。之后再把这个预训练模型迁移到目标检测、图像分割等其他任务上。也就是说，图像分类实际上承担了一个预训练任务的角色，为很多下游任务提供通用特征。 对于三维领域来说，我认为重建正在逐渐扮演类似的角色。一个训练好的重建模型，它学到的特征可以被迁移到很多其他三维任务上。例如我们自己做过一些工作，会利用重建模型的特征去做novel view synthesis；类似的特征也可以用于surface estimation等任务，而且通常都会带来明显的帮助。 从这个角度来看，重建可以成为空间理解领域里的一个proxy task。更重要的是，它还是一个具备良好扩展性的proxy task，因为相关数据相对容易获取，不需要特别昂贵的标注成本。 这也是大家如此重视它的重要原因之一。 如果用二维视觉中的概念来类比的话，可以把三维重建理解成某种程度上结合了图像分类和图像分割特点的基础任务。它既能够学习场景的整体语义信息，也能够学习空间结构信息，因此能够为大量下游任务提供通用能力。 从模型结构上看，现在很多vlm通常会有一个语言分支，也会有一个视觉分支。视觉这一侧，很多模型基本上会用clip或者dino这类方法，把图像转换成一组token。 但这些token通常更偏向语义信息。我的感觉是，如果我们的方法足够幸运，未来也有可能扮演类似的角色：比如在现有模型里再开一个分支，或者作为一组额外的token加入进去。 这样的话，我们的模型就可以为vlm、vla，或者其他类型的模型，提供带有几何感知和空间感知能力的token。 这可能也是我比较希望看到的方向，也就是刚刚您提到的那种“基座”的感觉。 我觉得这个问题可以分成两部分。 刚刚您提到，为什么现在三维能力还没有真正进入机器人领域。我可能有一个稍微不同的看法，我觉得核心原因是目前的需求还没有那么强。 如果看现在机器人领域最热门的方向，很多人关注的还是manipulation task，比如机械臂在桌面上做抓取、分拣这类任务。我的直观感受是，这类任务在概念层面相对简单。当然不是说它容易做，而是说它对三维理解的依赖没有那么强。很多时候，即便只用二维数据，针对特定任务进行优化，也能取得很好的效果。 所以我觉得，现阶段机器人领域的发展还没有到必须依赖三维信息的时候。空间信息当然有帮助，但还不是解决这类任务的必要条件。 我反而觉得，真正需要三维能力，可能还要等两三年。当大家的关注点从简单的manipulation task逐渐转向open-world、general-purpose robotics的时候，三维和空间理解的重要性才会真正体现出来，并成为不可或缺的能力。 现在更多还是一些有意义的早期尝试。大家都在探索如何把不同类型的信息融合进来，但它真正能够大放异彩，可能还需要再等两年左右。因为还是要先把当前这些manipulation task解决得差不多，行业的关注点才会自然转向下一阶段的问题。 我之前和不少同学讨论过这个问题，最近在一些cvpr的分享里也会提到类似的观点。 假设未来有一个“gpt-9.8”这样的模型，我们给它很强的控制能力，再给它任意一种机器人平台，无论是人形机器人、机械臂，还是其他设备。我的预期是，在未来某个时间点，也许并不遥远，这样的模型在拿到一个新的机器人之后，只需要十几秒钟就能根据说明书理解这个设备的结构和控制方式，然后在接下来的一两分钟里，通过和环境的实际交互，快速学会如何操纵它。 比如让机器人往前走两步、摔倒一次、跑起来、滑动或者跳跃。通过这种测试阶段的交互，它可能只需要几分钟时间，就能够零样本学会如何控制一个从未见过的机器人。 而我之所以认为robot model需要空间感知能力，也是基于这样的设想。 我希望未来的机器人模型不再需要大量专门采集的机器人数据，不再依赖各种遥操作设备或者具身数据收集流程。相反，在预训练阶段，它就是一个同时理解图像、文本和三维空间的多模态模型。 这样的话，当我们给它任意一个机器人接口时，它不需要额外训练，甚至不需要专门适配，就能够像一个经验丰富的操作员一样，快速理解并操纵这个机器人。 我觉得这样的时代离我们不会太远。 关于大模型公司和机器人创业公司之间的竞争，我个人认为，最终把通用机器人模型做出来的，大概率还是大模型公司。 当然，中间可能会出现很多机器人创业公司，它们可能在数据、硬件或者具体场景上积累出自己的优势，甚至有可能被大模型公司收购，用来补充数据和硬件能力。但如果说最终谁能够做出我们理想中的那种机器人模型，我还是更看好大模型公司。 因为按照我的设想，未来真正意义上的机器人模型，本质上会是一个超大规模参数的基础模型。它不仅需要理解语言、视觉和空间信息，还需要具备比今天所有模型更强的推理能力。 而我觉得，做这样一件事情是需要特定基因的。目前能够持续训练和迭代这种级别模型的公司，其实还是少数几家头部大模型公司。 反过来看现在很多机器人创业公司，我觉得它们在硬件、系统集成或者具体应用场景上可能很有优势，但暂时还比较难看到能够独立做出这种级别基础模型的能力。 所以我的判断是，未来机器人领域最核心的突破，大概率还是会来自大模型公司，而不是机器人创业公司本身。 vggt基本上就是刚刚提到的那种完全数据驱动、拥抱黑盒的范式。它的输入是几张图片，我们首先把这些图片转换成token，然后通过global attention和frame-wise attention进行信息聚合，从而建模不同视角之间的空间关系。 在vggt里，我们最终做的事情是在聚合后的token上开出多个输出分支。比如输出camera参数，包括rotation、translation等位姿信息；输出depth；输出tracks；以及其他各种几何相关的表征。 当时我们的核心想法是，希望学到一种具有几何感知能力的表征。我们认为最简单的方法，就是尽量保持整体架构简单，同时在输出端提供足够丰富的监督信号。 原因在于，如果只训练模型预测camera，它可能会“偷懒”，学到一些能够完成任务但不具备真正几何意义的特征；如果只预测depth，也会有类似的问题。但如果让模型同时预测camera、depth、track以及其他几何信息，那么这些任务共同约束出来的表征就更有可能是真正几何感知的表征，而不是某种投机取巧的解。 所以vggt本质上是在探索如何学习这样的geometric-aware representation。 另一个很重要的优势是，相比传统重建方法，vggt的速度非常快，可以快100倍甚至200倍。因为它不再依赖那些非常耗时的测试阶段优化过程（test-time optimization）。这也是vggt希望解决的问题：不仅做重建，更重要的是学习可泛化的几何表征。 到了vggt-ω，我们当时在想，接下来还有很多方向可以探索，但哪些问题是值得我们优先去做的。 最后我们选择了两个重点。 第一个是研究scaling。 也就是当我们持续增加训练数据、模型规模和计算资源时，重建模型的能力是否会稳定提升。最终我们发现答案是肯定的，这对我们来说是一个非常积极的信号。 第二个重点是研究如何真正实现scaling。 因为scaling并不是简单地增加数据和算力就可以完成。比如模型规模变大之后，需要解决训练效率、显存占用等问题，否则训练过程根本无法进行。围绕这些问题，我们提出了一系列专门的模型设计和训练策略。 所以vggt omega主要回答了两个问题：第一，重建模型具备scaling能力；第二，真正实现scaling并不容易，需要针对性的模型设计。 除此之外，还有一个我个人特别喜欢的发现。我们发现，这类模型学到的token和feature，确实能够帮助机器人等下游任务。 在论文里，我们做了一个vla实验。虽然实验本身比较简单，因为我并不是机器人方向的专家，所以直接采用了开源的openvla实现。 具体来说，我们在openvla的基础上，额外加入了vggt omega从图像中提取的空间感知token。在这个过程中，vggt omega本身是冻结的，参数完全不更新。换句话说，它充当了一个几何编码器（geometric encoder）的角色。 最终我们发现，仅仅加入这部分空间感知特征，就能够带来明显的性能提升，在libero基准上的表现也有所改善。 我们原本还希望进一步在真实机器人平台上验证这些结果，但后来发现这已经超出了我自己的能力范围，后续可能还是需要机器人方向的同学继续探索。 如果总结一下的话，我觉得最核心的一点是：在保证数据质量的前提下，数据量越大，模型获得的提升就越明显。 但这里面有一个非常重要的前提，就是数据本身不能出错。我们其实在这件事情上吃过很多亏。 比如在vggt omega里，我们专门展示过一些bad case。有些数据集在采集之后会做后处理，比如depth fusion这类方法。而这些后处理有时会引入错误，例如把某个物体的深度错误地融合到其他区域。论文里有一个椅子的例子，本来椅面应该高于地面，但经过fusion之后，椅面的深度被错误地赋值成了地面的深度。 这种脏数据会给模型带来非常差的先验。我们在内部分析模型错误时发现，很多能够稳定复现的问题，最终都能追溯到训练数据里的错误标注。模型会学到这些错误模式，并把它们迁移到测试数据甚至分布外数据上。 所以data quality真的非常重要。以前大家都会说数据质量重要，但直到自己完整经历了一遍训练、分析和迭代的过程之后，我才意识到它的重要程度其实远超我的预期。 第二个观察是，我觉得目前三维数据还是太少了。 我们会发现，模型其实有能力记住某些特定的数据分布。有时候模型在某些特殊场景下表现不够理想，虽然不会完全失败，但效果明显不如其他场景。后来深入分析这些案例时，我们发现，往往是因为训练集中存在一小部分外观非常相似的数据，而这部分数据本身的质量又不够高。 原来我一直有一个比较理想化的假设：当高质量数据足够多的时候，模型学到的规律会自然泛化，并覆盖那些低质量数据带来的影响。但至少在目前的重建模型上，这种现象还没有明显出现。 我的感觉是，根本原因还是数据量不够大。现在的模型仍然有能力把不同来源的数据分成一个个独立的分布区域，然后分别去记忆这些区域里的模式，而不是把它们真正平滑地统一起来。 所以如果要总结的话，我觉得最重要的两点就是：第一，数据质量极其重要；第二，目前三维数据的规模依然不够大。 关于第一个问题，什么样的数据才算高质量，我觉得三维重建领域有一个挺有意思的特点，就是它的数据质量很多时候可以直接通过人工检查判断出来。 先说什么是坏的数据。通常我们会把各个视角的depth和camera参数投影回三维空间。如果结果里出现墙面不平、同一个物体出现多层重影，或者不同视角下本该重合的位置对不上，这些都是非常典型的问题。 那什么是好的数据呢？我觉得一个很直观的标准是，看起来是否符合我们对真实三维世界的认知。 比如对于静态场景，如果从100张图片恢复出来的桌角，在三维空间里能够完全对齐，没有明显偏差，那就说明从二维到三维、再从三维投影回二维的过程中几乎没有误差。这种结果通常会非常漂亮。 对于动态场景也是类似的。比如一个人在匀速向前走，如果恢复出来的三维轨迹同样是平滑且连续的，并且和周围环境保持一致的空间关系，那就是好的结果。相反，如果这个人的轨迹突然发生不合理的跳变，比如毫无原因地往前跳了一大截，那显然就不符合真实世界。 所以如果用一句话概括的话，我觉得高质量的重建数据，就是把重建结果放回三维空间之后，尽可能符合人类对于真实世界的直觉。 （vggt的训练数据里使用合成数据的比例比较高，合成数据对重建模型是好数据还是坏数据？） 这些合成数据基本上都来自公开数据集，主要可以分成几类。 第一类是通过blender、unreal engine（ue）这类图形引擎渲染出来的数据。比如我们先搭建一个场景，里面包含各种三维资产，然后在场景中采样不同的相机轨迹，再渲染得到对应的rgb图像、depth以及camera参数。 第二类是从游戏中采集的数据。比较典型的例子就是很多工作会从gta这类游戏中获取训练数据。因为游戏本身已经构建了一个完整的三维世界，所以能够直接得到大量带有精确几何信息的数据。 关于合成数据会不会影响模型质量，我觉得这里和大语言模型领域有一个比较微妙的区别。 在大语言模型里，大家说的合成数据，很多时候指的是模型自己生成的数据，或者从模型中蒸馏出来的数据。本质上，它仍然来自模型本身的分布，所以会存在分布偏移或者错误累积的问题。 但在三维重建领域，我们所说的合成数据并不是这个概念。 如果我们认为场景里的三维资产本身是准确的，那么这个场景其实就是一个完整且真实定义的小型三维世界。而合成数据，本质上只是对这个三维世界进行观测和采样。 所以在目前的发展阶段，对于三维重建来说，合成数据往往是高质量数据，而不是低质量数据。它不仅不会导致模型退化，反而经常能够帮助模型学习更准确的几何规律，并带动其他数据一起提升效果。 我一直很想验证的一件事情是：如果能够构建一个足够多样化、规模足够大的合成数据集，那么完全有可能训练出一个非常准确、非常漂亮的重建模型，而且我觉得它甚至有机会超过目前很多现有模型。 所以至少在当前阶段，对于三维重建领域来说，一个比较反直觉的结论是：合成数据不是问题，反而是非常重要、非常有价值的数据来源。 （你刚提到现实中的3d数据太少了，可穿戴设备或机器人传感器的普及，会增加这些数据吗？） 这其实就是我之前提到的那类典型脏数据，它们的数据质量通常比较差。 比如iphone采集的depth数据。虽然iphone有激光雷达，可以直接获取深度信息，但在我们看来，它的精度还不足以满足高质量重建的需求，反而属于我们希望过滤掉的数据。 除了iphone之外，很多廉价的rgb-d相机也是类似的情况。在工业场景里常见的一些rgb-d设备，在我们看来噪声都比较大，精度也不够高。 即使是一些室内激光雷达，数据质量往往也达不到理想水平。真正比较准确的是高端室外激光雷达，但这类设备价格昂贵，而且数据比较稀疏。 所以对于高精度三维重建来说，很多大家以为很准确的深度数据，其实并没有想象中那么可靠。 空洞其实不是问题。如果传感器能够明确告诉我哪些区域是不确定的，然后把这些地方直接留空，我觉得是可以接受的。 真正麻烦的是那些错误的深度值。也就是说，它看起来测到了某个点，但测出来的depth其实是错的。这类数据会直接误导模型，问题比空洞大得多。 至于训练数据，输入其实很简单，就是一段图片序列（image stream）。输出主要包括两部分：一是每张图片对应的camera参数，二是每张图片对应的depth。 camera参数可以理解为相机在三维空间中的位置和朝向。比如你拿着相机在室内走一圈，在这个过程中，你的位置一直在变化，朝向也一直在变化。你往左转、往右转，或者向前移动，这些都会反映在camera参数里。 它的作用就是描述当前相机是从什么位置、什么角度在观察这个三维世界。有了这些参数，我们才能知道每张图片对应的是哪个观察视角，并进一步恢复整个场景的三维结构。 在omega里我们确实大幅增加了数据规模。最终用于训练的数据大约是400万个sequences。这里面的数据既可以来自视频，也可以是没有时间顺序的图片集合，这一点和vggt本身是一致的。 其实omega里最重要的经验之一，就是我刚刚提到的数据清洗。 在论文发布之前，我们做了很多内部测试。整体效果其实很好，但总会在一些特别的场景下突然崩掉，出现一些非常奇怪的结果。当时我一边很沮丧，一边也特别困惑，不知道问题到底出在哪里。 后来我和合作者花了很长时间排查。我们先检查训练代码，检查checkpoint，检查inference代码，几乎把所有可能出问题的环节都查了一遍，但始终找不到原因。 最后我们开始重新检查训练数据，才发现问题真的出在数据上。有时候占比可能只有0.01%，甚至更少的一小部分脏数据，就足以让模型学到错误的模式，并在某些特殊场景下暴露出来。 到现在其实还有一些问题没有完全解决。比如在某些场景下，如果一个人穿着全黑的衣服，模型对这个人的预测置信度会明显下降，结果也更容易出现偏差。 后来我们发现，这和训练数据有关。出于隐私保护的原因，一些数据集会把人、水印、商标等区域直接mask成纯黑色。模型在训练过程中学到了这种模式，因此会受到影响。 这个问题目前还没有完全解决，我们在论文里也专门提到了这一点。 我的感受是，各个方向的发展其实是相辅相成的。而对于三维重建来说，目前很大程度上还是被数据问题限制住了。 如果看大语言模型的发展历程，虽然现在很多frontier labs都会构建自己的数据体系，但在某个阶段，大家是能够比较有信心地基于一些公开数据集进行训练和验证的。因为这些数据已经经过了社区长期检验，被很多工作反复使用和验证过。 但在三维领域，我们还缺少这样的数据基础设施。到目前为止，还没有形成被整个社区广泛认可和反复验证的大规模高质量数据集。 其实我觉得机器人领域也面临类似的问题。前段时间我在湾区和不少机器人创业公司聊过，大家也经常提到这一点。 很多时候，不同方法使用的训练数据都不一样，测试数据也不一样。同时，大家也缺少一个能够在真实机器人平台上进行公平比较的统一评测标准。 所以从这个角度来看，我觉得机器人领域也有类似的数据问题，而且某种程度上可能比三维重建还要更严重一些。 如果你的任务本身很依赖空间结构、空间关系或者运动信息，那么可以直接把我们输出的token作为condition，或者作为额外输入加入到你的模型里。 我觉得这可能是我最想分享的一点。 说得再直接一点，其实现在机器人领域和视觉领域一直有一个争论：三维理解到底是不是必要的。 一派观点认为，机器人最终不需要显式的三维表示，这些东西未来可能会被更端到端的方法取代。另一派则认为，机器人能力的发展一定离不开显示的三维表征。 这里说的三维，本质上其实是空间感知能力。而空间感知能力又有不同的实现路径。一种是依赖多传感器，比如rgb-d相机、激光雷达等；另一种是纯视觉路线，也就是仅从图像中学习对三维世界的理解。 如果参考特斯拉的发展路径，很多人会天然倾向于第二种方案。因为它更容易扩展，成本更低，也更符合大规模部署的需求。 所以回到最初的问题，三维能力对其他任务到底有没有帮助，其实目前还没有定论，整个领域仍然处在一个持续讨论的阶段。 但我个人是相信它有价值的。至少对于那些需要理解空间结构、空间关系和物体运动的任务来说，我的观点很明确：三维能力是必须的。 因为无论是人类还是机器人，最终都生活在一个三维世界里，我们也希望机器人能够在这个三维世界中帮我们完成任务。但我不认为显式的三维表示是必须的，比如点云、深度图这些形式未必重要。我更相信隐式的三维理解，也就是让模型通过token和feature具备空间感知能力，而不一定直接输出传统意义上的三维表示。 jianyuan wang on the evolution of 3d reconstruction, geometry-aware foundation models, data quality, and the path from digital to physical intelligence. 3d vision many readers will probably have clicked this headline with real excitement. if you did not, you may not yet be familiar with the progress in 3d vision over the past two years. in this interview, we speak with jianyuan wang, first author of vggt, the cvpr 2025 best paper, and vggt-ω, a cvpr 2026 best paper finalist. at the time of this interview, jianyuan is pursuing a joint phd with oxford's visual geometry group and meta ai. his research asks how a model can perceive the three-dimensional world using images or video alone, without additional sensors. in other words, he wants models to understand and perceive 3d space from visual information alone. this conversation reminded me of a discussion with a founder two years ago. today's embodied models build on an open-source base model: previously a vision-language model (vlm), and now a visual geometry model (vgm). so what determines progress in embodied models: the base model, or the company building on top of it? what would the arrival of a hypothetical future “gpt-9.8” mean for today's embodied ai startups? again, i strongly recommend this interview. every paragraph deserves a careful reading; the insights are in the details. contents part i · 3d very long time. around the 1980s and 1990s, as computing power developed, researchers began asking a natural question: how can we recover three-dimensional information from two-dimensional information? we feel that we live in a three-dimensional world. but if we set touch aside and consider how we obtain information, we mainly rely on vision, which essentially receives two-dimensional images or video streams. the question for early researchers was therefore how to recover the structure of the 3d world from these 2d observations. one classic early approach was stereo vision. many readers will have encountered stereo cameras. put simply, when two cameras observe the same scene at the same time, with a small baseline between them—a slight displacement in position—we can use triangulation to recover the depth of a point from the corresponding pixel positions in the two images. in a sense, this is a special case of 3d reconstruction, because the relative positions of the stereo cameras are known and fixed. researchers wanted to handle more general situations in which the relationships between camera positions were themselves unknown. the problem then becomes recovering both the depths of scene points in 3d space and the cameras' positions and orientations. roughly between 1995 and 2005, researchers increasingly found that they could solve these problems using a pipeline called structure from motion, or sfm. people in robotics may be more familiar with slam. in a certain sense, slam can be viewed as a special setting or subset of sfm. [editor's clarification: this is an analogy to visual slam; slam also includes online localization and mapping, and can use nonvisual sensors.] sfm takes a collection of images depicting approximately the same scene and reconstructs camera parameters and scene depth. in the visual slam setting being discussed here, the images additionally have a temporal order: they form a continuous video stream. this simplifies aspects of the problem and can make the result more stable and reliable. so, during the period from 1995 to 2005, the field's main concern was how to formulate and solve this problem. from about 2005 to 2014, the emphasis shifted toward engineering improvements: making reconstruction faster, larger in scale, and more robust. for example, researchers wanted to process 100,000 images, or eight, ten, or even more hours of video. then, from 2014 to 2022, deep neural networks began entering the field. at that time, the prevailing view was that reconstruction already had mature mathematical formulations: triangulation, fundamental-matrix decomposition, and so on all had clear mathematical expressions. the focus was therefore not on having a network perform reconstruction directly, but on using deep learning to improve individual stages of the traditional pipeline. take orb-slam as an example. an early step is to find correspondences between multiple images. researchers investigated how neural networks could produce better feature representations and identify more accurate correspondences in feature maps, improving the reconstruction. that was broadly the mainstream direction between 2014 and 2022. from 2022 onward, the field began embracing deep learning much more comprehensively, whether by choice or through the direction in which the field was moving. representative work includes dust3r and, later, vggt and vggt-ω. their central idea is to stop using neural networks merely to find better correspondences and instead turn the entire reconstruction problem into an end-to-end deep learning problem. (vggt's reconstruction on the far left looks visibly better than the two comparisons.) in other words, it becomes a fully black-box process. some people like that and some do not, but i personally like the black-box concept. we can now feed images into a trained transformer and have it directly output the various kinds of 3d information we want. i think this is also why 3d reconstruction has suddenly attracted renewed attention over the past two or three years. the first reason is that, if the approach can use a training paradigm similar to those in 2d vision and language models, it has a chance to benefit from scaling laws. as computing resources, data volume, and training investment increase, the model can improve steadily and consistently. that is a very attractive property for companies. businesses are more willing to invest in technical approaches that can deliver dependable returns. the second reason is that, compared with traditional reconstruction methods, these fully learned approaches are beginning to handle dynamic scenes. an important idea here is that a dynamic object can be thought of as a combination of many tiny rigid-body motions. traditional reconstruction frameworks struggle with this because multiple rigid motions occur simultaneously, making it difficult to recover the true structure. but these problems are now beginning to be solvable. for example, demos from some recent projects can already recover the spatial relationships between a moving person and the surrounding environment. many previously intractable problems are becoming tractable. (a vggt-ω demo that beautifully illustrates dynamic reconstruction.) the third point is the one i personally find most compelling. in 2d vision, we are accustomed to encoding an image into a global representation and using it for classification or other downstream tasks. in geometry, at least before 2022, we did not really have an equivalent. now we can turn an input video sequence into a set of geometry-aware representations or tokens. these tokens can encode the sequence's main geometric structure and motion information. such representations support many new downstream applications and open up interesting research directions. i see these as the main changes brought by the wave of fully learned 3d reconstruction from 2022 to 2026. i would say that 3d reconstruction underpins 3d and 4d understanding—what we might call spatial understanding. to borrow an expression from an older generation of researchers, it is the “crown jewel” of geometry. if we can solve reconstruction well, much of the information we want afterward becomes directly available. this is why reconstruction has remained important for so many years. looking at the history of cvpr and related research, academia has consistently paid close attention to reconstruction regardless of changes in technical approach. it occupies a distinctive, foundational position in the field. in my view, its importance has grown rather than diminished today. consider an analogy with the development of 2d deep learning. researchers often first pretrained a model, such as resnet, on an image-classification task like imagenet, then transferred it to object detection, image segmentation, and other tasks. classification served as a pretraining task that supplied general features for many downstream applications. i think reconstruction is gradually assuming a similar role in 3d. the features learned by a trained reconstruction model can transfer to many other 3d tasks. in some of our own work, for example, we have used reconstruction features for novel view synthesis. similar features can also support surface estimation and usually provide substantial benefits. from this perspective, reconstruction can be a proxy task for spatial understanding. more importantly, it is a scalable proxy task: the relevant data is relatively easy to obtain, without especially expensive annotation. that is another important reason for the attention it receives. using concepts from 2d vision, we can think of reconstruction as a foundational task that, to some extent, combines aspects of image classification and segmentation. it learns both global scene semantics and spatial structure, supplying general capabilities for many downstream tasks. architecturally, many vlms today have a language branch and a visual branch. on the visual side, many use something like clip or dino to turn images into a set of tokens. those tokens generally lean more toward semantic information. my feeling is that, if our approach is fortunate enough, it might play a similar role in the future: an additional branch in an existing model, or an extra set of tokens supplied to it. our model could then provide geometry-aware and spatially aware tokens to vlms, vision-language-action models (vlas), and other kinds of models. that is a direction i would particularly like to see—the kind of foundational role you mentioned. i think we can divide this question into two parts. you asked why 3d capabilities have not really entered robotics yet. i have a slightly different view: the main reason is that the demand is not yet strong enough. many people in today's most active areas of robotics are focused on manipulation: a robot arm picking and sorting objects on a table, for example. my intuitive sense is that these tasks are relatively simple conceptually. that does not mean they are easy to accomplish; rather, they do not depend so heavily on 3d understanding. often, optimizing for a particular task using only 2d data can already produce very good results. i do not think robotics has reached the point where 3d information is indispensable. spatial information certainly helps, but it is not yet a necessary condition for solving these tasks. my expectation is that the real need for 3d capabilities may come in another two or three years. as attention shifts from simpler manipulation tasks to open-world, general-purpose robotics, 3d and spatial understanding will reveal their importance and become essential. for now, we are mostly seeing meaningful early explorations. people are investigating ways to fuse different kinds of information, but it may take another couple of years for these capabilities to really shine. the industry first needs to solve today's manipulation tasks reasonably well before its attention naturally moves to the next set of problems. i have discussed this with quite a few students, and have made similar points in recent cvpr talks. imagine a future model—let us call it “gpt-9.8”—with strong control capabilities. give it any robot platform: a humanoid, a robot arm, or some other device. i expect that, at some point in the future, perhaps not far away, such a model could read the manual and understand the device's structure and controls in just over ten seconds, then quickly learn to operate it through one or two minutes of real interaction with the environment. for example, the robot might take two steps, fall once, run, slide, or jump. through these test-time interactions, it might learn to control a robot it has never encountered in only a few minutes, in what i describe as a zero-shot setting. [editor's clarification: this imagined setting includes interaction and adaptation at test time; “zero-shot” here means no prior training specifically for that robot.] that scenario is also why i think robot models need spatial awareness. i hope future robot models will no longer require large amounts of specially collected robot data or depend on teleoperation devices and embodied-data collection pipelines. instead, during pretraining, they would already be multimodal models that understand images, text, and 3d space together. then, given any robot interface, they could rapidly understand and operate the robot like an experienced operator, without additional training or dedicated adaptation. i do not think that era is very far away. regarding competition between large-model companies and robotics startups, i personally think the companies building large models are the most likely to produce the eventual general-purpose robot model. of course, many robotics startups may emerge along the way, developing advantages in data, hardware, or particular applications. they might even be acquired by large-model companies to supplement their data and hardware capabilities. but when it comes to who will ultimately build the robot model we envision, i still favor the large-model companies. in my conception, a truly capable future robot model would essentially be a foundation model with an enormous number of parameters. it would need to understand language, vision, and space, as well as have stronger reasoning capabilities than any of today's models. i think that requires a particular organizational dna. at present, only a handful of leading large-model companies can continually train and iterate on models at that level. many robotics startups may have considerable strengths in hardware, systems integration, or specific applications. for now, though, it is harder to see them independently building a foundation model on that scale. my judgment is therefore that the most important future breakthroughs in robotics will probably come from large-model companies, rather than robotics startups themselves. vggt essentially follows the fully data-driven, black-box paradigm we just discussed. it takes several images, converts them into tokens, and aggregates information through global attention and frame-wise attention to model spatial relationships between views. in vggt, we attach multiple output branches to the aggregated tokens. these predict camera parameters, including pose information such as rotation and translation; depth; tracks; and other geometry-related representations. our central idea was to learn a geometry-aware representation. we thought the simplest way to do that was to keep the overall architecture simple while supplying sufficiently rich supervision at the outputs. if a model is trained only to predict cameras, it may take a shortcut and learn features that solve the task without really encoding geometry. predicting only depth can lead to similar issues. but if it must predict cameras, depth, tracks, and other geometric information together, the representation constrained by these tasks is more likely to be genuinely geometry-aware, rather than a shortcut solution. vggt is therefore fundamentally an exploration of how to learn this kind of geometry-aware representation. another important advantage is speed. compared with traditional reconstruction methods, vggt can be 100 or even 200 times faster in such comparisons, because it no longer depends on extremely time-consuming test-time optimization. this is also the problem vggt aims to address: beyond reconstruction itself, the more important goal is to learn generalizable geometric representations. for vggt-ω, we considered the many directions we could pursue next and asked which questions deserved priority. we ultimately chose two main focuses. the first was to study scaling. would reconstruction capabilities improve consistently as we increased training data, model size, and computing resources? we found that they would, which was a very encouraging signal. the second focus was how to make scaling practical. scaling is not simply a matter of adding data and compute. as models grow, training efficiency and gpu memory consumption become problems; without addressing them, training may not even be feasible. we developed a series of targeted architectural designs and training strategies around these issues. vggt-ω therefore primarily answers two questions: reconstruction models can scale, and making that scaling happen is not easy—it requires deliberate model design. there is also a finding i particularly like: the tokens and features learned by these models really can help downstream tasks, including robotics. we conducted a vla experiment in the paper. it was relatively simple, since i am not a robotics expert, and we used an open-source openvla implementation directly. [editor's clarification: the paper's experiment uses the openvla-oft variant.] specifically, we added spatially aware tokens extracted from images by vggt-ω to openvla. vggt-ω remained frozen throughout, with no parameter updates. in other words, it served as a geometric encoder. we found that simply adding these spatial features produced a clear performance gain, including improved results on the libero benchmark. we had hoped to test the results on real robot platforms as well, but eventually realized that this was beyond my own expertise. researchers specializing in robotics may need to explore that next. to summarize, i think the central point is that, provided data quality is maintained, more data produces more substantial improvements. there is a crucial prerequisite, though: the data must not contain errors. we learned that lesson the hard way many times. in vggt-ω, for example, we show some failure cases. some datasets are postprocessed after collection using methods such as depth fusion. that processing can introduce errors, incorrectly merging an object's depth into another region. the paper includes a chair example: the seat should be above the floor, but after fusion its depth is incorrectly assigned the floor's depth. this corrupted data gives the model very bad priors. in our internal analyses, many reproducible model errors could ultimately be traced back to incorrect training annotations. the model learns those erroneous patterns and transfers them to test data, even out-of-distribution data. data quality really is important. we all used to say that, but only after going through the complete cycle of training, analysis, and iteration did i realize that its importance far exceeded my expectations. my second observation is that we still have too little 3d data. models can memorize particular data distributions. sometimes a model performs less well in a special setting: it does not fail completely, but its results are clearly weaker than elsewhere. when we examined those cases closely, we often found a small amount of visually similar training data whose quality was not very good. i used to have a rather idealized assumption: with enough high-quality data, the rules the model learns would naturally generalize and override the influence of poor-quality data. at least in today's reconstruction models, we have not clearly observed that happening. my feeling is that the underlying reason is insufficient data. today's models can still separate different data sources into independent regions of the distribution and memorize their patterns separately, instead of integrating them smoothly. the two main lessons, then, are that data quality is extremely important, and that the scale of 3d data remains insufficient. an interesting property of 3d reconstruction is that we can often judge data quality directly through manual inspection. start with bad data. we typically back-project each view's depth using its camera parameters into 3d space. nonflat walls, multiple ghosted layers of the same object, or positions that should coincide across views but do not are all typical signs of trouble. what makes good data? an intuitive standard is whether it matches our understanding of the real three-dimensional world. for a static scene, suppose a table corner reconstructed from 100 images aligns perfectly in 3d, with no obvious deviation. that suggests almost no error in the process of going from 2d to 3d and projecting back to 2d. such results are usually beautiful. the same applies to dynamic scenes. if a person walks forward at a constant speed, a good reconstruction gives a smooth, continuous 3d trajectory with consistent spatial relationships to the surroundings. an unreasonable discontinuity—suddenly jumping a long distance forward for no reason, for example—clearly does not fit the real world. in one sentence, high-quality reconstruction data is data whose reconstructed result, when placed back in 3d space, agrees as closely as possible with our human intuitions about the real world. (vggt uses a relatively high proportion of synthetic training data. is synthetic data good or bad for reconstruction models?) the synthetic data mainly comes from public datasets, and can be divided into several categories. one category is rendered using graphics engines such as blender or unreal engine (ue). we construct a scene containing various 3d assets, sample different camera trajectories within it, and render the corresponding rgb images, depth, and camera parameters. another category comes from games. many projects, for example, obtain training data from games such as gta. because a game already contains a complete three-dimensional world, it can supply large amounts of data with precise geometry. there is a subtle difference here from large language models when we ask whether synthetic data harms model quality. in the llm field, synthetic data often means data generated by a model itself or distilled from another model. it still comes from a model's distribution, so distribution shifts or accumulated errors can be concerns. that is not what we mean by synthetic data in 3d reconstruction. if the 3d assets in a scene are accurate, the scene is a small, completely and precisely defined 3d world. synthetic data essentially consists of observations and samples of that world. at the current stage, synthetic data in reconstruction is often high-quality data, rather than poor-quality data. instead of degrading a model, it frequently helps it learn more accurate geometric regularities and improves performance on other data as well. i have long wanted to test whether a sufficiently diverse and large synthetic dataset could produce a very accurate, beautiful reconstruction model. i think it might even outperform many existing models. so, at least at this stage, the somewhat counterintuitive conclusion is that synthetic data is not the problem. it is an extremely important and valuable source of data for 3d reconstruction. quality is often quite poor. consider depth collected by lidar-equipped iphones. although they can directly acquire depth, in our view their precision is insufficient for high-quality reconstruction. approach, many people naturally prefer the second route because it is easier to scale, costs less, and better suits large-scale deployment. so the original question—whether 3d capabilities help other tasks—does not yet have a settled answer. the field is still debating it. personally, i believe they are valuable. at least for tasks that require understanding spatial structure, spatial relationships, and object motion, my view is clear: 3d capabilities are essential. both humans and robots ultimately live in a three-dimensional world, and we want robots to help us perform tasks within that world. but i do not believe explicit forms such as point clouds or depth maps are necessarily required. i have more faith in implicit 3d understanding: giving a model spatial awareness through tokens and features, without necessarily outputting traditional 3d representations directly. my understanding as the author: obtaining 3d information does not necessarily require 3d sensors such as lidar or rgb-d cameras. it can come from multiple monocular viewpoints or a moving monocular camera. as long as we obtain the multiview information needed to recover 3d structure, a reconstruction model such as vggt can recover it. nor must this information exist explicitly as a rendered point cloud, mesh, or other 3d representation. the model is more like an encoder that encodes spatial information into tokens or features, giving it an understanding of spatial relationships and geometric structure. (much of today's robot training data relies on rgb images without depth, or on 2d video streams. “rgb in, action out” appears to be a mainstream approach.) first, i would like to clarify a definition. do you see a conflict between relying on 2d input and what we discussed earlier—introducing vggt or another reconstruction model as an additional geometric encoder? i can understand why people choose this route. the first reason returns to our earlier point. most tasks receiving attention today are relatively simple manipulation tasks, and may not genuinely require strong 3d understanding. with folding clothes, for example, i think sufficient training could enable good performance even without complete 3d information. researchers are not deliberately avoiding 3d; at this stage, these tasks simply do not demand it as strongly. the second reason is cost. rgb is the cheapest and easiest form of data to obtain. adding any modality substantially increases collection and processing costs. from an engineering perspective, the rgb-only route is therefore naturally attractive. the third reason is a personal observation: much of robotics today builds on developments in vision. whether we are talking about vlas or world models, many core capabilities were first demonstrated successfully in vision and then transferred to robotics. the robotics community therefore naturally tends to use mature 2d vision models directly, rather than introducing an additional 3d module. i think there are good reasons to choose “rgb in, action out.” but that does not make 3d capabilities unimportant. the combination of today's task requirements, data costs, and technical trajectory is more likely what drives this choice. i would consider expanding into robotics, but not robotics in its present sense. i believe robotics—or, more precisely, physical intelligence—will be the next major opportunity. systems such as gpt, gemini, and codex are essentially pursuing digital intelligence. i strongly believe that intelligence will develop from the digital toward the physical world. what i am less certain about is whether we should currently devote so much effort to specific robot tasks, such as all the subproblems within manipulation. what really interests me is the scenario we discussed earlier: could a future model like the hypothetical “gpt-9.8,” when given any robot, rapidly understand it, learn to control it, and interact with the real world? i believe that day will come. rather than concentrating on one specific robot task, i am more interested in preparing for that day, moving the field in that direction, and ultimately making that scenario a reality. reconstruction itself is certainly fun and elegant, but i have worked on it for a long time. more than continuing to dig deeper into reconstruction alone, i want to consider how it can become part of the path toward the next generation of intelligent systems. references editor's note after writing this blog for so long,
