following the first installment, human data ep01—mocap: twist, we continue exploring human motion capture data and humanoid whole-body control with gmt: general motion tracking for humanoid whole-body control. gmt is a general motion tracking framework that trains a single policy on large-scale, unstructured human motion data to achieve high-fidelity motion tracking on humanoids. gmt’s co-first authors are zixuan chen and mazeyu ji. our guest is zixuan chen, a phd student in xiaolong wang’s group at uc san diego who earned his bachelor’s degree at fudan university. he is also a co-first author of twist (human data ep01—mocap: twist). this interview contains many illuminating details. let’s take a closer look at the work. contents 1. gmt’s core idea 2. the gmt method 3. understanding motion tracking 4. motion capture datasets 5. motion capture data vs. video data 6. gmt vs. deepmimic 7. mixture of experts 8. comparing whole-body control methods 9. motion retargeting a central question for gmt is how to achieve something genuinely general: a single policy that can produce many different movements and execute them on a robot. many companies demonstrate impressive movements such as dancing, somersaults, and jumping. their usual approach, however, is to train a separate policy for each motion. that works for individual movements, but it is difficult to scale when we want to build a general-purpose controller. gmt’s idea is that if one policy can cover and understand different motions, we can generate arbitrary motion sequences during task execution and have the policy track them, allowing the robot to exhibit different behaviors. it can then serve as a foundational controller for a wide range of tasks. gmt builds on deepmimic, introduced by jason peng in 2018. at its core, it still uses reinforcement learning: we define rewards for completing motion tracking. gmt mainly addresses two categories of problems—those arising from the data and those arising from the model architecture. the first data issue is training data quality. training such a controller requires a large amount of data, typically from large human motion capture datasets such as amass and lafan. these datasets contain considerable noise. some recordings are incomplete; others involve highly dynamic movements that require forces a robot cannot produce. we need to filter these out. we therefore curate the data, removing overly dynamic movements and low-quality recordings to obtain a better training dataset and improve policy performance. the second issue is sampling. some movements, such as walking, are relatively easy; others, such as dancing and jumping, are more complex and nonperiodic. in datasets such as amass or lafan, 60–70% of the recordings involve walking, while the remaining 30% contain more challenging movements. we want the policy to learn both easy and difficult movements, so we use adaptive sampling. specifically, we assign probabilities to different motions, sampling complex movements more often and simple movements less often to balance training. i think this is an important point. as for architecture, many previous approaches, especially in locomotion, use simple multilayer perceptron networks. but we need one policy to handle many different motions over long time horizons, and an mlp often is not sufficient. we therefore switched to a mixture-of-experts architecture with multiple experts, borrowing the idea from language models. we found that moe substantially increased the model’s representational capacity and improved the results. we also made changes to the motion inputs. people anticipate what they are about to do. we may know several seconds in advance which movement comes next, and adjust our bodies accordingly. inspired by this, rather than inputting a single frame, we compress the motion targets for the next two seconds into a vector and feed it into the model. compression, however, loses information and can reduce tracking accuracy. to address this, we explicitly provide the nearest target frame alongside the compressed future vector. combining the two lets the model perceive the most important immediate tracking target while also understanding the future trend. the resulting policy performs better. gmt’s main improvements therefore concern both data and model design. motion tracking is simple to understand: we give the robot a sequence of human motion data, typically based on kinematics, and ask it to reproduce the movement. it can be online, tracking and reproducing a person’s movements in real time, as in twist. or it can be offline, taking a recorded sequence and reproducing the whole movement. for offline motion tracking, we give the robot a prerecorded motion sequence and input the entire recording at once. the main difference is that online tracking collects data in real time, so only the next frame is available to feed into the robot. offline, the whole sequence is provided beforehand, allowing access to motion information at any future time. we can, for example, input a window of future movements, giving the robot a longer temporal horizon and a more comprehensive understanding of the sequence. terminology note: in live teleoperation, the “next frame” is the latest received reference target; an unobserved future human movement is not available in advance. amass is large, with recordings totaling several dozen hours, but it contains many low-quality segments, including feet penetrating the ground or floating above it. optimizing details such as ground contact could improve the overall results. for gmt, however, i think it is more important to filter out motions the robot cannot perform and train only on executable movements. that produces a more substantial improvement. lafan’s movements are generally more dynamic. some are difficult, but overall they are executable. each motion is also relatively high quality. the creators manually adjusted some data during preprocessing, so its overall quality is quite good. among the open datasets available today, amass is the largest. we chose it because it covers a wide range of skills, although its quality may have some shortcomings. the idea we are pursuing is a foundation model at the behavioral level: a model that can execute all kinds of movements, including movements produced by generative models, and track them within the model. achieving this may require a very large training dataset that covers as many kinds of movement as possible. a new, high-quality dataset collected from humans would, i think, substantially improve the overall results. here “the largest” reflects the interviewee’s comparison of the motion-capture datasets under discussion, rather than a ranking of all human-data datasets. i am not particularly inclined to rely exclusively on video data at this stage. with video alone, we need a video-to-motion model to convert it into usable motion data, because robots can directly use only the motion data. this conversion is difficult and imposes demanding requirements on camera angles and other conditions. better camera angles may produce better converted results. in terms of accuracy, however, video data certainly falls short of motion capture. if the ultimate application is robotics, i think motion capture is preferable: it converts directly into data the robot can use and offers higher quality. i think deepmimic’s most important contribution was formally framing motion tracking as a reinforcement learning problem. at each step, it provides a motion target and computes the difference between the robot’s current state and that target. this produces a reward that defines the reinforcement learning task. to me, that is deepmimic’s greatest contribution. almost all current models, including phc, maskedmimic, asap, and the more recent gmt and twist, use the paradigm introduced by deepmimic and build innovations on top of it. another deepmimic innovation is random state initialization, or rsi. when the robot falls while performing a motion during training, we do not always restart from the beginning. instead, we choose an arbitrary frame from the motion as the initial state. the robot can thus learn different stages of a movement without having to master the beginning before learning later parts. this significantly improves training. i think it is one of deepmimic’s most influential innovations. terminology note: deepmimic calls this reference state initialization; the reference frame is sampled randomly. the moe we use is actually a soft moe. we train on all the data together, rather than using what i describe as the traditional moe approach in large language models. in a traditional moe, for example in a language model, the idea is typically to train many different experts, each responsible for a particular skill, and then combine them. technical note: sparse moe language models commonly train their experts and router jointly as well. the separate-training description above is an intuitive comparison in the interview, rather than a defining property of llm moe; the distinction here is the dense weighted combination used by gmt. soft moe takes a different approach by adding a gating network. imagine that we have six experts but do not know in advance what each one will do. the gating network outputs six probabilities representing their weights. we then compute a probability-weighted sum of the six experts’ outputs to obtain the final action. the advantage is that we do not have to manually plan or predefine skills. instead, the model learns for itself, discovering, categorizing, and combining different skills to complete a movement. one intuitive inspiration came from exbody2. its authors found that grouping similar motions for training—for example, putting walking movements in one category and dancing or kicking in another—produced better policies. this suggested that different motion categories need different experts to truly master their respective skills. building on that idea, we ultimately chose soft moe. it preserves end-to-end training while allowing different experts inside the model to automatically divide the work, specialize in different skills, and combine their capabilities to execute complex movements. one feature of soft moe is that even when it emphasizes one skill at a particular moment, it does not drive every other expert’s output to zero. some experts might be better at kicking, while others are better at walking. when the robot kicks, the kicking expert receives a higher weight, but the other experts still contribute. adding moe produced a clear improvement in our experiments. it offers relatively little improvement for simple motions, but substantially improves overall performance on difficult movements. first, it is useful to discuss phc and maskedmimic, which are oriented toward computer graphics. i think graphics and robotics differ fundamentally. graphics relies heavily on global information and uses simpler simulation conditions, without the range of domain randomization used in robotics. as a result, these methods tend to depend on global information and privileged information, such as the robot’s linear velocity. choosing a motion tracking controller for graphics is simpler and less demanding. but the conditions and assumptions in graphics cannot be transferred directly to robots. i see our work as distinct from graphics work. graphics more often validates algorithmic feasibility, while actual robot deployment requires additional engineering and design. among robotics projects, humanplus and omnih2o train on the entire dataset, as both papers report. these were relatively early projects using unitree h1. h1’s body differs substantially from a human body, leading to considerable quality differences after motion retargeting. its configuration is also quite different from a person’s. these projects focus more on teleoperation than on developing a broadly compatible motion tracking controller. that is another difference from our work. exbody tracks the upper body while relying on a locomotion policy for the lower body, so it does not perform complete whole-body tracking. although its policy controls the entire body, it does not actually track the whole body. exbody2 was the first work to support a variety of genuinely whole-body motions, but it uses a smaller dataset. it trains separate policies for different motion categories to achieve good results, rather than covering every motion with one policy. asap demonstrates extreme skills such as jumping and tumbling, but each motion has its own policy, limiting its ability to scale. its dataset is manually curated from internet data and open datasets. gmt, by contrast, centers on a general policy that tracks many different movements. the motion data is curated, and the architecture uses moe. progress in whole-body control has been rapid. recent breakthroughs include dynamic movements we might never have expected robots to perform, such as somersaults or functionality remains insufficiently explored: demonstrating athletic ability does not directly translate into useful capabilities. household or factory tasks require a general policy that supports multiple skills. gmt’s retargeting mainly builds on the method introduced in phc. we focus on key points in the robot’s movements, such as the hands and feet, and have the corresponding robot body parts match those points as closely as possible. solving an optimization problem then maps human motion onto the robot. an important question is how to match a skill. human skills are influenced by factors such as height and weight, so different people perform movements differently. we set coefficients for different joints to transfer a person’s skill onto the robot. this is a crucial part of the process. retargeting quality also depends on the robot’s configuration. open datasets and motion capture recordings are based on people, so in theory, the more humanlike the robot, the better the retargeting should work. we clearly observed this in practice: retargeting works much better on g1 than on h1, because g1 is more humanlike. references

system）。twist是一个基于全身动作模仿的人形机器人遥操作系统。该系统通过将人类动捕数据（mocap）重定向（retargeting）到机器人上，生成参考动作片段，然后结合强化学习与行为克隆训练出一个稳健、自适应且高响应的全身控制器。这篇工作的一作是迮炎杰和陈子玄博士。我们这期采访对象是迮炎杰博士，他目前是斯坦福大学计算机科学系攻读博士学位的二年级学生，由jiajun wu和c. karen liu指导。 对如何利用人体动捕来做人形机器人遥操作感兴趣的朋友，欢迎来了解下炎杰的一些思考。twist作为利用动捕遥操人形的系统目前已经开源，欢迎在文末reference部分查看开源链接。 以下为本文目录 👇 1. twist提出的背景 2. twist和其他动捕数据驱动控制的区别 3. 人体动作数据获取都有哪些方案 4. twist方法介绍 5. 关于retargeting 6. 关于gmr 7. 使用mocap遥操的注意事项 dp3和idp3这两个工作dp3+idp3：如何利用3d输入提升diffusion policy的泛化性主要聚焦在让机器人上半身执行人类类似的动作。在做idp3的过程中，我开始更深入地接触全身运动控制相关的内容。因为只控制上半身时，机器人的工作空间会受到限制。以 idp3 为例，我们当时设计了一个能控制腰部和脖子的系统，让机器人的工作空间比普通双臂机器人更大。它可以弯腰触碰前方物体，也能直立完成近距离操作。 当时算法已经能让机器人在特定环境下执行一些动作，比如在前台、客厅或厨房测试时效果不错。但它还不能自主移动，需要人工推着。后来我意识到，机器人应该像人一样，能自主地从一点移动到另一点，并完成任务。于是我们开始思考如何让机器人具备这种能力——先让它被人操纵，先“像人一样动起来”。这成为我们后续研究的起点。 我们做了一些调研，发现要搭建一个能让整个人形机器人像人一样动起来的系统，之前有尝试过，比如利用外骨骼、基于学习的控制或模型预测控制上进行。我们这个系统（twist）尝试以人体动作捕捉设备作为接口，实时获取高质量的人类动作数据，用这些动捕数据去驱动机器人。这样可以让机器人的全身，包括脚、腰、膝盖、胳膊等部位都与人类动作同步，而不仅仅是上半身或末端执行器。 搭建这个系统之后，我们可以让机器人做真正的人类动作。例如，在厨房里遇到挡路的门，同时手上拿着东西时，机器人可以用脚把门踢开，然后继续走过去。这个例子说明了为什么让人形机器人像人一样动起来非常重要——它是实现机器人执行人类功能的基础。第一步是工业界搭建硬件平台，第二步是我们这些做算法的人去设计系统，使机器人能够真正动起来。 twist利用mocap设备遥操人形机器人 我觉得从整个系统设计的角度来看，它确实与之前的很多工作有相似之处。大概十年前或者五年前，在日本就有一些比较早期的尝试，他们通过全身动作捕捉或者外骨骼驱动获取人类数据，然后去驱动人形机器人。当时他们的数据获取平台和我们的思路可能类似，但驱动机器人的方法非常不同。举个例子，他们获取人类数据后，会通过解算一些优化问题，使得人类动作可以匹配到机器人上，如果不匹配，还会加一层模型，比如模型预测控制（mpc）去做采样。这样当时的机器人确实能像人一样动，但这些系统缺乏基于学习的控制，所以只能在受限环境下完成一些动作，比如慢慢走路或蹲下，并没有达到更广泛的功能能力，因此后来这些工作没有持续发展。 最近几年，这方面取得了进展。首先是控制方法的改进，强化学习（rl）已经基本可以取代传统控制方法，几乎所有机器人控制都可以用 rl 来实现。其次是硬件能力的提升，五年前很多硬件还做不到，现在硬件不再是限制因素，使我们可以尝试算法的极限。这也是为什么近期大家重新开始投入这方面研究的原因。相比五年前，现在各个模块都有了显著提升，从长远角度来看，这是对过往工作的升级。 在最近两年的工作，比如omnih2o和humanplus和twist很相似，但仍有区别。以humanplus为例，它的思路大致分三步：第一，获取全身人类数据；第二，做real time retargeting，将人类数据转换成机器人数据，通过关节映射实现 human-to-robot transfer；第三，使用 rl 将数据真实地放到机器人上执行。 虽然思路类似，但twist的系统在各个环节都做了提升。首先是获取高质量人类数据非常重要，我们使用了世界上最高质量的人体动作捕捉数据，这保证了基础的准确性。其次，如何将人类数据转换为机器人数据也很关键。我们花大量时间调试了实时 retargeting 算法，它可以很好地保留人类动作结构，同时避免出现崩坏或错误的结果。这一步比当时简单的映射方法提升很大。第三，需要一个强大的 rl 控制器，将转换后的数据物理可行地执行出来。因为直接转换的数据并不符合物理规律，例如接触地面、力学平衡等，我们设计了一个两阶段算法：第一阶段使用大量先验信息生成教师数据，第二阶段使用教师-学生蒸馏，同时提出了新的 rl+bc 框架，使控制器能更好地跟踪高质量动作。 总体来说，相比一年前或五年前的工作，twist在四个方面对系统进行了全面提升：获取高质量数据、实时高保真 retargeting、多阶段 rl 控制，以及更强大的硬件支持。正因为如此，twist的系统能够展示非常令人印象深刻的全身运动效果，上下半身可以协调、自由运动，几乎像真正的人一样，这也是与过去工作的主要区别。 获取人体数据大概有三种主要方式。第一种是基于相机的视频或图像，比如互联网视频，或者通过图像进行姿态估计。这种方式最大的优点就是便携、便宜、容易获取，但缺点也很明显，就是精度太差，质量最差。第二种是 vr，它比相机贵一些，普通人也不太会买，但它能提供更高质量的上半身数据，缺陷是没有下半身数据。不过有些研究通过让机器人补偿缺失的部分，或者加一些额外输入，比如遥控器来提供下半身位移，从而部分解决这个问题。第三种就是动捕设备，它的优点是精度最高、质量最好，但缺点就是极其昂贵，不具备便携性。 这里有一个很明显的 trade-off：设备越便携，数据质量就越差；设备越不便携，数据就越好。大家都想要更多更好的数据，因为像大模型成功的秘诀就是 scaling up。但要想规模化，就得依赖便携又便宜的系统，否则几十万甚至上百万的设备没人用得起。 所以我尝试过 vr 和基于单目估计的方法，但实际下来感觉都还不足以提供高质量的全身动捕，尤其是在 root tracking 上问题很大。（root tracking，就是人在世界坐标系里的整体位置和移动，比如从 a 点走到 b 点。）如果只用一两个相机，是很难实时准确地提供全身在空间中的移动轨迹的，最多只能在静止状态下获取上半身的动作。 因此，基于相机的方案几乎可以排除了，只剩 vr 和动捕。近期也有不少工作尝试用 vr 做全身控制，比如 vision pro 的应用就是只给手和头的 tracking 数据，然后让策略去学缺失的下半身动作。结果证明是可行的，但问题是下半身会出现不稳定或持续调整的情况，比如机器人明明走到了目标点，但它的下半身动作还在微调，因为它缺乏真实的下半身输入。 有的研究会额外用遥控器提供 base 的移动输入，有的则通过对齐头部的全局 tracking 来巧妙绕开问题。无论哪种方式，都说明 vr 是可用的，但下半身精细的动作，比如下蹲、跨步、马步等，几乎做不到。 相比之下，我们现在坚持用完整的全身数据来做开发，好处就是一切都能做，但坏处也非常明显，就是只能依赖动捕。动捕既不便携，又昂贵，即使实验室有，使用起来也不如 vr 那么方便。所以我认为未来的关键是如何让这些系统更便携。我也看到一些厂商在尝试，比如欧洲有家公司，他们用一两个相机就能提供高质量的全身 global tracking，如果这种商业化方案越来越成熟，或许未来全身动捕会越来越 portable。 总体来说，我认为不能因为缺乏某些数据就放弃高精度的控制，而是应该尽可能获取更多、更好的数据，把数据做扎实，让整个系统变得更强大。这是我目前的一个核心想法。 在整个方法里，其实可以分成两个阶段。第一个阶段是数据的准备，第二个阶段是控制器的训练。在数据准备这一部分，我们的 training data 主要来自两个成熟的来源：一部分是过往的论文里公开的数据集，另一部分是一个叫amass的数据集，这两个都是比较成熟的全身人体动作数据，被广泛用于 motion tracker 的训练。除此之外，我们还额外采集了一小部分 in-house 的动捕数据。之所以要加这部分，是因为我们研究的目标是 real-time control，也就是实时的 motion tracking。 在这之前，其实已经有不少工作研究过 motion tracking，比如跳舞、模仿动作等等，本质上就是给一个 human motion，让机器人去跟踪。但我们发现，如果完全依赖公开数据，controller 的表现并不好，不太能适应我们的任务。原因可能是 motion 本身的质量，也可能是 real-time control 的特性导致的。我们尝试之后发现，只要加上一小部分自己采的 in-house 数据，效果就会明显提升，而且数据量不需要很多，加一点点就够了，多采其实差别不大。因而，这部分内部数据的主要作用在于缩小训练数据与测试数据之间的分布差异。这是我们在数据筛选与整理阶段总结出的一个关键经验。 第二部分是控制器的训练，包含两个部分：rl 和 bc（behavior cloning），整个流程比较经典，我们基于开源的 eth 框架进行修改，使用 ppo 在模拟环境里进行大量 online interaction，通过收集 reward 来训练策略。与之前做走路的工作相比，主要区别在于 reward 的定义以及如何利用训练数据作为 reference motion。 具体来说，每个 time step 机器人都有一个目标坐标系，需要跟踪对应的 motion。如果左手目标在空间中某个点，机器人左手当前位置与目标之间的误差会被转化为 reward，用于 ppo 更新策略。运动跟踪奖励（motion tracking reward） 的设计非常讲究，可以包括空间位置、旋转，或者局部坐标系下的点和旋转。一个重要结论是，如果缺乏全局信息，就很难实现精确的运动跟踪，控制器的性能也会明显下降。我们将运动跟踪从全局坐标系转换到局部坐标系，这样每一步只关注局部动作，即使上一步偏差了，下一步仍可正常执行，整体效果会好很多。 在这个基础上，我们采用 teacher-student 机制。teacher 可以访问一些 student 无法获得的额外信息，比如全局位置，用于更好地监督 root tracking 和 rotation tracking。student 通过 rl + bc 学习，rl能够基于奖励信号进行监督学习，让 student 根据奖励自主调整行为，bc 则作为辅助监督，帮助 student 模仿 teacher 的动作，但不会强行执行每一步动作，从而避免因行为不一致而导致的不稳定或倒地。 此外，在 teacher 端我们还加入了未来 motion 信息，这部分在 student 端不可用，但可以利用 offline 数据集提供给 teacher，以提升指导效果。整体上，rl + bc 框架能够在 online control 任务中保证策略的适应性和稳健性，即便环境或动作出现意外偏差，机器人也能保持合理行为。 在第三步的操控过程中，其实涉及一些真实世界的小设计。整个推理流程是这样的：首先从动捕系统获取人体数据，然后通过然后通过重定向将人体数据转换为类人机器人的整体运动，再通过控制器将这些指令性动作（command motion）转化为机器人实际的动作。这是整个流程的核心，但在真机操作中，会有一些小细节需要处理。 第一个小设计是如何让机器人安全地站立或处于安全状态。穿动捕服的时候，有时你可能想暂时停止控制，例如去上厕所，这时机器人不能一直处于完全受控状态，因此需要退出机制。最笨的方法是关机或手动挂起机器人，但这样下次使用时需要重新启动，非常不便。 为此，我们加了一些辅助装置，比如“手持手柄”，在穿动捕服的过程中，手上握着手柄作为系统的开始和结束控制。例如，当我想结束或暂停控制，让机器人保持站立时，按下手柄上的按键，机器人会进入默认站立姿势，同时停止接受动捕信号，只输出默认的控制指令。这样机器人就安全地站立，我也可以脱手或去做其他事情。 我觉得这个设计非常重要，因为很多人做机器人控制时，只关注中间动作的控制，而忽略了完整的用户体验，包括开始、暂停、继续和结束的连续过程。在成熟的人形系统中，这类设计很常见。例如像 aloha 的系统，国内一些公司在做类似系统时，也会考虑用户可以随时暂停操作，然后继续时无缝接续数据。 公开的动捕数据集和我自己采集的数据集在做 retarget 的时候会遇到很多问题，比如需要大量标定，不同的人穿动捕服可能还需要重新标定，效果也不一样。做 retarget 的时候精度和映射过程中也会出现各种问题。我在从公开数据集到自己穿的动捕服做 retarget 的过程中，首先方法是这样的：这两部分数据的表示形式基本一致，主要把它们作为 3d 空间中的点来使用，每个点有位置和方向，这种表示方式可以通用地从各种动捕数据中提取出来。人体可以理解为由很多骨头和关节组成，每个部分近似为一个刚体，有空间中的位置和旋转量。通过这些描述，就能近似还原一个人体。无论是我自己的数据还是网上的公开数据，最后都可以统一成这种数据格式。 有了这样的表示之后，接下来说怎么做。一般来说，offline 的流程是先人为地建立一个映射关系，把人和机器人各个 body 对应起来。有了这个映射关系之后，就可以利用机器人的运动学或动力学去满足人的关键点约束，比如胳膊在空间中的位置和旋转。这样做的结果就是机器人会表现出与人类似的动作。这基本上就是 retargeting 的过程：把人体的二三十个 body 做好 mapping，然后用机器人的动力学去实现，得到一个看起来跟人差不多的动作。 offline retargeting 和 online retargeting 的区别主要有三点。第一点是优化目标。offline 通常只优化关键点的空间位置约束，并不直接管旋转，因为当位置约束足够多时，旋转就会间接得到保证。但在 online 的时候，我会使用更多的旋转约束。第二点是 smoothness。offline 可以在 trajectory 层面加平滑约束，比如 100 帧每帧独立算出来会抖动很大，但加了 smoothness 后整体就会很丝滑。而 online 虽然也能用历史帧来做平滑，但会导致反应变慢，比如动作只能跟到 0.7 或 0.8，这样就带来延迟，不是好事，所以我在 online 时没有加这个部分。第三点是方法不同。offline 用的是 fk（forward kinematics），可以不断 sample，用 gradient-based 的方法算，因为不在意速度。而 online 我用的是 ik（inverse kinematics），直接通过 solver 算结果，满足实时性。fk 和 ik 在思路上类似，但一个更适合离线优化，一个更适合实时推理。 整体来说，retargeting 的核心就是统一数据表示、建立人和机器人的映射关系，然后根据 offline 或 online 的需求选择不同的优化目标和方法。 第一点区别主要在于优化目标。在 online 的时候，我们用了更多的旋转约束，而不是像 offline 那样主要关注位置约束。原因是不同人穿动捕服时高度、体型各不相同，每个部分尺寸也不太一样。如果只用位置约束，得到的结果可能会非常奇怪。比如今天一个人穿动捕服做 retarget，按照之前配置好的参数去映射胳膊位置，但第二天换了一个体型或者服装穿法略有不同，结果就会不一样，看起来和印象中的动作差距较大。而使用旋转约束，这个问题就没有那么明显。 旋转相比位置来说更稳定，不容易受到个体差异和配置变化的影响。不过它也有一些问题，比如不容易对齐或者存在其他误差。但总的来说，在 online 时使用旋转约束能减少因为体型和服装差异带来的偏差，因此我们选择在线 retarget 时更多依赖旋转而不是大幅度位置约束。这也解决了不同人穿动捕服时不需要每次都重标定的问题。 至于其他类似的工作是否也使用旋转约束，我了解的不太多。有一篇我们最近做的 cross mission 工作使用了旋转约束(即gmr)，但在其他以前的工作中，大家探索的更多是角色动画的视觉效果如何更逼真，而不太涉及在线满足实时约束的问题。总体来说，核心目标都是让动作达到该到达的位置，只是在线场景会有更多现实世界的噪声需要考虑。 第二点区别主要在于轨迹层面的信息处理。offline 的部分更多是提供一些 trajectory-level 的信息，让整个动作看起来顺滑。可以理解为 offline 更像是用来做一些预处理或预训练，而 online 则是用来实时反应和控制动作。虽然严格来说，offline 并不是传统意义上的预训练，它和 online 是在同一个训练框架下，只是 offline 可以提供一个更平滑的初始动作参考。 在实践中，不同数据源的作用也有所不同。比如amass数据可能更侧重提取某一部分信息，而自己采集的动捕数据可能更侧重另一部分信息。此外，ik 和 fk 是两种实现 retarget 的方式。ik 是通过逆运动学计算机器人应如何移动以达到目标位置，可能需要迭代处理误差；fk 则通过前向运动学采样，并使用可微分 fk 去计算目标状态。这两种方式都是比较常见的解决方案。 retargeting 的本质是处理多个关键点的映射和控制。与机械臂不同，机械臂通常只有一个末端，而人体可以看作有二三十个“末端”，包括所有关节和骨骼。因此算法需要同时考虑所有这些末端的约束。总结来说，retargeting 包含两件事：第一，把要映射的部分映射到目标位置；第二，当映射完成后，计算机器人如何移动才能达到这些目标。 gmr 并不是开源原始数据，而是开源了把人类数据映射到机器人数据的过程。简单来说，就是把 retargeting 的方法开源了。对于整个社区来说，这个开源非常有帮助，比如其他人的机器人可以直接用这套 gmr 流程，实现自己的动作映射。 gmr 是一套比较通用的流程，我们已经把一些市面上常见的机器人加入进去，因为很多人会发邮件问能否支持特定机器人，我都帮他们加进去了。我觉得这算是跨本体智能应用的一个重要进展。做跨本体映射，首先需要有统一的数据表示，这样才能把数据整合好，再应用到不同的机器人上。人体是一个很好的媒介，只要能把人体映射到目标机器人，就能利用人类数据作为数据源，这也是 gmr 最大的意义所在。 在 gmr 中，映射过程也包括了前面提到的第一阶段的 offline 和 online 两部分。它提供了一个完整的算法框架，其他人可以在这个基础上做进一步的工程化，这对更多机器人本体公司来说意义很大。twist的发布可以让大家在自己的机器人上复现，实现 human-like 的全身动作控制，同时也能推动具身智能人形机器人方向的数据应用向前发展。 目前整个领域还没有形成共识，尤其是在 human-robot 的交互和动作控制方面，大量方法和流程都不是标准化的。比如很多人使用 vr 控制机器人，这是很好的尝试，但如何真正摇动控制机器人，还没有统一的方法和共识，仍然是一个探索中的领域。 在操控过程中，作为操作者，你的动作是有一些关键点的，但我们并没有使用操作者的数据来进行自主训练，更多的是展示方法。从操作者的角度来看，你可能会觉得需要放慢动作或者适应机器人的结构，但实际上不需要做过多适应。机器人比想象中更容易操控，因为它的控制方式和人的动作高度一致。 有一个例子可以说明这一点，我们尝试过一套给新手操作的系统。它使用双臂外骨骼和一些按钮来控制机器人的腰、前后移动以及抓手等动作，总共有 5 到 8 个按键。我自己尝试后发现，整体控制比想象中简单得多。当我们把 human data 直接作为接口去控制机器人时，它的自然映射让操作非常直观：你抬腿，机器人也抬腿，这让新手上手很快。 如果使用传统分开的控制器，比如单独控制腰或下半身，你每次做完一个动作都需要切换控制器，或者需要额外的助手配合，这会让动作非常不连贯，而且需要大量练习才能熟练操作。而全身遥操作系统则不同，上手难度低，而且更自然、连贯。 之前在 5 月份，我们还遇到一些问题，当时 retargeting 和数据流传输有延迟，导致操控体验不够顺畅。但这些问题目前已经得到改善，系统现在可以提供更实时的反馈，使操作感觉更加舒适自然。 我觉得到目前为止，主要的 take away 是搭建这套系统不仅仅是为了让机器人动起来。让机器人动起来只是一个简单的目标，下一步是让大家都能高效地采集数据。也就是说，我希望这套系统真正成为一个工具，让用户能够直接使用它，而不是每次都去手动操作。目前我们只是走了第一步，距离最终目标——让系统真正易用、高效的数据采集工具——还有一定距离。 references： twist project page 2025, smart note's interviews have largely focused on whole-body motion control for humanoid robots. this includes three consecutive interviews with researchers in the field—interview with xue bin (jason) peng: exploring a general controller for whole-body humanoid control; interview with zhengyi luo: inside phc, a general humanoid controller; and conversation with zhongyu li: building a legged the data for whole-body humanoid control comes from. data has always been a challenge for learning-based robotics. in 2024, our robot data series covered more than ten representative projects collecting data at different levels of the robot-learning data pyramid. human data will focus on how human data can support robot learning. we plan to interview the authors of eight or nine papers that use human motion-capture data or human video data for humanoid learning and control. for the first episode of human data, we interviewed the team behind twist, the teleoperated whole-body imitation system. twist is a humanoid teleoperation system based on whole-body motion imitation. it retargets human motion-capture data, or mocap, to a robot to generate reference motion sequences, then combines reinforcement learning with behavior cloning to train a robust, adaptive and responsive whole-body controller. yanjie ze and zixuan chen are among the paper's co-first authors. our guest for this interview is yanjie ze, who, at the time of the interview, was a second-year phd student in stanford university's department of computer science, advised by jiajun wu and c. karen liu. if you are interested in using human motion capture to teleoperate humanoid robots, read on for yanjie's thinking. twist has been open-sourced; the repository link appears in the references at the end of practical considerations for mocap teleoperation our two earlier projects, dp3 and idp3—see dp3 and idp3: improving diffusion policy's generalization with 3d inputs—mainly focused on getting a robot's upper body to perform movements resembling human actions. while working on idp3, i began looking more deeply into whole-body motion control. controlling only the upper body limits a robot's workspace. for idp3, for example, we designed a system that could control the waist and neck, giving the robot a larger workspace than a conventional dual-arm robot. it could bend over to touch objects in front of it, or remain upright to perform operations nearby. at that point, our algorithm could already make the robot perform certain actions in a particular environment. it worked quite well in tests at a reception desk, in a living room or in a kitchen. but the robot could not move around autonomously: someone had to push it. i then realized that it should be able to move from one point to another on its own, like a person, and perform tasks. we started thinking about how to give it that ability. as a first step, we would let a person operate it and get it to move like a human. that became the starting point for our subsequent research. we surveyed earlier work and found that people had already attempted to build systems that let an entire humanoid robot move like a person, using exoskeletons, learning-based control or model predictive control. twist uses human motion-capture equipment as its interface. we acquire high-quality human motion data in real time and use it to drive the robot. this synchronizes the robot's whole body—including its feet, waist, knees and arms—with the person's movements, rather than controlling just the upper body or the end effectors. once we had built this system, the robot could perform genuinely human-like actions. imagine it is in a kitchen, carrying something in its hands, with a door blocking its path. it can kick the door open with its foot and continue walking through. this example shows why it matters for a humanoid to move like a human: such movement is the foundation for performing human functions. the first step is for industry to build the hardware platform. the second is for those of us working on algorithms to design systems that allow the robot to actually move. twist uses motion-capture equipment to teleoperate humanoid robots. from the perspective of overall system design, i think twist does share similarities with a lot of earlier work. around five to ten years ago, there were some early attempts in japan to acquire human data through whole-body motion capture or exoskeleton interfaces and use it to drive humanoid robots. their data-acquisition platforms may have been similar in spirit to ours, but their methods for controlling the robot were very different. for example, after acquiring human data, they would solve optimization problems to match the human motion to the robot. if the motion did not match, they would add another model-based layer, such as model predictive control, to sample candidate motions. those robots could indeed move like people, but the systems lacked learning-based control. they could therefore perform only certain actions in restricted environments, such as walking slowly or crouching. they did not achieve a broader range of functional abilities, and those lines of work did not continue developing. there has been progress in recent years. first, control methods have improved. in my view, reinforcement learning has become capable of replacing traditional control methods across much of this work, and almost any robot-control task can be tackled with rl. second, hardware capabilities have improved. many things the hardware could not do five years ago are possible now. hardware is no longer the limiting factor in the same way, so we can start exploring the limits of the algorithms. that is also why people have recently returned to this area. compared with five years ago, every module has improved substantially. over the longer term, i see this as an upgrade of the earlier work. recent work from the past two years, such as omnih2o and humanplus, is similar to twist, but there are still differences. humanplus, for example, roughly follows three steps. first, it acquires whole-body human data. second, it performs real-time retargeting, converting human data into robot data through joint mapping to achieve human-to-robot transfer. third, it uses rl to make the physical robot execute those motions. although the overall idea is similar, twist improves each part of the system. first, acquiring high-quality human data is essential. we used what we consider the highest-quality human motion-capture data available, ensuring accuracy at the foundation. second, the conversion from human data to robot data is crucial. we spent a great deal of time tuning the real-time retargeting algorithm so that it preserves the structure of human motion while avoiding broken or erroneous results. that was a major improvement over the simpler mapping methods available at the time. third, we need a strong rl controller to execute the converted motions in a physically feasible way. directly retargeted data does not necessarily satisfy physical constraints, such as ground contact and mechanical balance. we therefore designed a two-stage algorithm. in the first stage, we use extensive privileged information to generate teacher data. in the second, we perform teacher–student distillation and introduce an rl-plus-bc framework that allows the controller to track high-quality motions more effectively. overall, compared with work from a year ago or five years ago, twist upgrades the system in four respects: high-quality data acquisition, real-time high-fidelity retargeting, multi-stage rl control and stronger hardware support. together, these improvements produce impressive whole-body movements. the upper and lower body can move freely and in coordination, almost like a real person. that is the main difference from the earlier work. there are roughly three main ways to acquire human motion data. the first is camera-based video or images: for example, internet videos or pose estimation from images. its biggest advantages are portability, low cost and accessibility. its drawback is equally clear: accuracy is poor, and it provides the lowest data quality of these options. the second is vr. it costs more than cameras, and most ordinary consumers do not own it, but it provides better upper-body data. the limitation is that it does not capture the lower body. some research partly addresses this by having the robot compensate for the missing information, or by adding other inputs, such as a remote controller that supplies lower-body displacement commands. the third option is motion-capture equipment. it provides the greatest accuracy and highest quality, but it is extremely expensive and lacks portability. this comparison concerns the setups evaluated for the original project; adding body trackers changes the information available from a vr system. there is an obvious trade-off here: greater portability tends to mean lower data quality, while less portable equipment tends to provide better data. everyone wants more and better data, because scaling up is one of the secrets behind the success of large models. but scaling requires portable, inexpensive systems. equipment costing hundreds of thousands or even millions is beyond most people's reach. i tried vr and monocular pose-estimation methods, but in practice i felt neither provided sufficiently high-quality whole-body motion capture. root tracking was a particular problem. root tracking describes a person's overall position and movement in world coordinates—for example, walking from point a to point b. with just one or two cameras, it is difficult to accurately capture the whole body's trajectory through space in real time. at best, in our experiments, we could obtain upper-body movements while the person stayed in place. for our requirements, that largely ruled out camera-based approaches, leaving vr and motion capture. several recent projects have tried using vr for whole-body control. for example, applications using vision pro provide only hand and head tracking and ask the policy to learn the missing lower-body motions. this can work, but the lower body can be unstable or keep adjusting. the robot may already have reached its target, yet its lower body continues making small corrections because it has no actual lower-body input. some projects use an additional remote controller to provide base-motion commands. others work around the problem by aligning global head tracking. either way, vr is usable, but fine-grained lower-body movements—crouching, stepping over something or adopting a wide horse stance—are very difficult to achieve. by contrast, we currently insist on developing with complete whole-body data. the benefit is that we can cover all these movements. the downside is obvious: we depend on motion capture. it is expensive and not portable. even if a lab has the equipment, using it is less convenient than using vr. i think the key question for the future is how to make these systems more portable. i have seen vendors working on this. for instance, one european company can provide high-quality global whole-body tracking with just one or two cameras. if commercial solutions like that continue to mature, whole-body motion capture may become more portable. overall, i do not think we should give up on high-precision control simply because some data is missing. instead, we should acquire as much good data as possible, establish a solid data foundation and make the whole system stronger. that is one of my central ideas at the moment. our method can be divided into two stages: data preparation and controller training. for data preparation, the training data mainly comes from two established sources. one is datasets released in earlier papers; the other is amass. both provide mature whole-body human motion data and are widely used to train motion trackers. we also collected a small amount of in-house motion-capture data. we added this because our target is real-time control—in other words, real-time motion tracking. there had already been many studies of motion tracking, such as dancing or imitating movements. essentially, they provide a human motion and ask the robot to follow it. but we found that a controller trained entirely on public data performed poorly for our task. this could be due to the quality of the motions themselves or to the particular demands of real-time control. in our experiments, adding even a small amount of our own in-house data led to a clear improvement. we did not need much: a little was sufficient, and collecting more made relatively little difference. the main role of this internal data is therefore to narrow the distribution gap between training and testing. that was a key lesson from our data selection and preparation. the second part is controller training, which combines rl and bc, or behavior cloning. the overall process is fairly standard. we modified an open-source framework from eth and used ppo to carry out extensive online interaction in simulation, collecting rewards to train the policy. compared with earlier walking-control work, the main differences are the definition of the reward and how the training data is used as reference motion. at each time step, the robot has a target reference frame and a corresponding motion to track. if, for example, the target for its left hand is a particular point in space, we turn the error between the hand's current position and that target into a reward for the ppo policy update. designing motion-tracking rewards requires care. they can include spatial positions and rotations, or points and rotations expressed in local coordinates. one important finding is that without global information, precise motion tracking is difficult and controller performance drops noticeably. at the same time, expressing motion-tracking targets in a local coordinate system lets each step focus on the local action. even if the preceding step deviates, the next can still execute normally, improving the overall result. on that basis, we use a teacher–student mechanism. the teacher can access extra information unavailable to the student, such as global position, to provide better guidance for root and rotation tracking. the student learns through rl plus bc. rl uses reward signals to let it adjust its behavior, while bc supplies auxiliary supervision that helps it imitate the teacher's actions. it does not force the student to reproduce every action regardless of its own state, thereby avoiding the instability or falls that can arise from mismatched behavior. we also give the teacher information about future motion. the student cannot access that information, but offline datasets can supply it to the teacher and improve its guidance. overall, the rl-plus-bc framework provides adaptability and robustness in online control. even if there is an unexpected deviation in the environment or in the motion, the robot can still behave reasonably. the third step, operating the robot, involves some small real-world design choices. the inference pipeline first acquires human data from the motion-capture system, then retargets it into whole-body humanoid motion, and finally uses the controller to turn the commanded motion into the robot's actual movement. that is the core workflow, but some details need to be handled on the physical robot. the first is how to let the robot stand safely or enter a safe state. when wearing a motion-capture suit, you may want to stop controlling it temporarily—for example, to go to the bathroom. the robot cannot remain in active teleoperation all the time, so it needs an exit mechanism. the crudest option is to shut it down or manually suspend it, but that means restarting it the next time, which is inconvenient. we therefore added an auxiliary device: a handheld controller that the operator holds while wearing the suit, to start and stop the system. if i want to end or pause control and leave the robot standing, i press a button. the robot enters its default standing posture and stops accepting motion-capture signals, receiving only the default control commands. it can then stand safely while i release the controls or do something else. i think this design is very important. many people working on robot control focus only on the motion in the middle of the process and overlook the complete user experience: starting, pausing, resuming and finishing. designs like this are common in mature systems. for example, systems such as aloha, and similar systems being built by companies in china, allow users to pause operation whenever they need to and resume data collection seamlessly. retargeting public motion-capture datasets and my own recordings raises many issues. it can require extensive calibration; different people wearing the suit may need recalibration and produce different results. accuracy and the mapping process can cause problems too. when retargeting both public datasets and data from the suit i wear, my first step is to use essentially the same representation for both. we treat the body as points in 3d space, each with a position and an orientation. this representation can be extracted from different types of motion-capture data. a human body consists of many bones and joints, and each part can be approximated as a rigid body with a spatial position and rotation. together, these descriptions approximately reconstruct a person. whether the data is ours or comes from public sources online, it can ultimately be converted into this common format. once we have that representation, what comes next? in a typical offline workflow, we manually establish correspondences between the human body's parts and the robot's body parts. we then use the robot's kinematics or dynamics to satisfy constraints on human keypoints, such as the position and rotation of an arm in space. the result is a robot movement that resembles the human movement. that is essentially retargeting: map the human body's twenty or thirty segments, then use the robot's model to produce a similar-looking motion. there are three main differences between offline and online retargeting. the first is the optimization objective. offline, we usually optimize spatial position constraints on keypoints without directly constraining rotations, because sufficiently many position constraints also determine rotations indirectly. online, i use more rotation constraints. the second difference is smoothness. offline, we can add smoothness constraints across a trajectory. if we solve one hundred frames independently, the result may jitter badly, but smoothing makes the whole sequence fluid. online, we could smooth using past frames, but that slows the response: the motion may only follow to a level of 0.7 or 0.8, as i put it, introducing undesirable lag. that is why i omit this step online. the third difference is the numerical method. offline, i can repeatedly sample and optimize using gradients through forward kinematics, or fk, because speed is less important. online, i use an inverse-kinematics, or ik, solver to obtain a result fast enough for real-time use. these are related ways of solving the retargeting problem, with different implementations suited to offline optimization and real-time inference. overall, the core of retargeting is to unify the data representation, establish a mapping between human and robot bodies, and then choose optimization objectives and methods that suit either offline or online requirements. the first difference is mainly the optimization objective. online, we use more rotation constraints rather than focusing primarily on position constraints as we do offline. people wearing the suit differ in height, body shape and the dimensions of individual body parts. using only position constraints can produce very strange results. suppose one person wears the suit today and we map their arm positions using an existing configuration. tomorrow, another person has a different build or wears the suit slightly differently, and the resulting motion changes. it may look quite unlike the movement we expected. with rotation constraints, this problem is less pronounced. rotations are more stable than positions and less sensitive to differences between people or changes in configuration. they have their own problems—for example, alignment can be difficult and other errors can arise. on balance, though, rotation constraints reduce online errors caused by body shape and the way the suit is worn. we therefore rely more on rotation constraints and less on strong position constraints for online retargeting. this also addresses the need to recalibrate every time a different person puts on the suit. i do not know enough about other similar work to say whether it also uses rotation constraints. one of our recent projects on cross-embodiment retargeting, gmr, does use them. much of the older work, however, explored how to make character animation look more realistic, rather than how to satisfy real-time constraints online. broadly speaking, the goal is always to make a motion reach its intended target. online scenarios simply introduce more real-world noise that we need to consider. the second difference concerns information at the trajectory level. the offline component supplies trajectory-level information that makes the movement look smooth. you can think of offline processing as a kind of preprocessing or preparation, while the online component responds and controls motion in real time. strictly speaking, the offline part is not pretraining in the conventional sense. it belongs to the same training framework as the online part, but can provide a smoother initial motion reference. in practice, different data sources also play different roles. amass data may be more useful for extracting one kind of information, while our own motion-capture data may emphasize another. ik and fk are also two approaches used in retargeting. ik calculates how the robot should move to reach a target position, potentially iterating to reduce error. an fk-based optimization approach samples configurations and uses differentiable forward kinematics to calculate the resulting state. both are common solutions. retargeting is fundamentally about mapping and controlling multiple keypoints. a robot arm typically has one end effector; a human body can be treated as having twenty or thirty such endpoints, including its joints and bones. the algorithm must account for all their constraints at once. in other words, retargeting involves two things: first, assign the body parts being mapped to their target positions; second, calculate how the robot needs to move to reach those targets. gmr, or general motion retargeting, does not release raw data. it open-sources the process of mapping human data to robot data—in other words, the retargeting method. that is useful to the whole community. other researchers can use the gmr pipeline directly to retarget motions to their own robots. gmr is a fairly general pipeline, and we have added support for several common robots on the market. many people email me to ask whether it can support a particular robot, and i have helped add them. i see this as an important advance for cross-embodiment applications. cross-embodiment mapping first needs a unified data representation, so that data can be integrated and applied to different robots. the human body is a very good intermediary. if we can map a human body to the target robot, we can use human motion as a data source. that is gmr's greatest significance. the mapping process in gmr includes both the offline and online parts of the first stage we discussed earlier. it provides a complete algorithmic framework that others can build on and engineer further. that matters for a wider range of robot-hardware companies. releasing twist lets people reproduce human-like whole-body control on their own robots and helps advance the use of data in embodied intelligence and humanoid robotics. the field has not yet reached a consensus, especially around human–robot interaction and motion control. many methods and workflows remain unstandardized. using vr to control robots, for example, is a worthwhile exploration, but there is still no unified approach or consensus on how to teleoperate them in practice. it remains an area under active exploration. during operation, certain points in the operator's movement matter, but we have not used these operator recordings to train autonomous behavior. our focus is more on demonstrating the method. as an operator, you might expect to need to slow down or adapt to the robot's structure. in practice, you do not need to adjust very much. the robot is easier to operate than you might imagine because its control closely matches human movement. here is one example. we tried a system for beginners that used a dual-arm exoskeleton and buttons to control the robot's waist, forward and backward movement, grippers and other actions. there were five to eight buttons in total. when i tried it myself, i found the overall control much easier than expected. when human data becomes the direct interface for controlling a robot, the natural mapping is intuitive: you lift your leg, and the robot lifts its leg. beginners can learn quickly. with traditional separate controllers—for example, one for the waist and another for the lower body—you need to switch controllers after each action or have an assistant help. that interrupts the movement and requires substantial practice to operate smoothly. whole-body teleoperation is different: it has a lower learning barrier and feels more natural and continuous. earlier, in may 2025, ebm（energy-based models）时的一篇 paper，那篇工作蛮有创新性，因为当时主流都还在研究 gan，而我们是比较早去探索denoising的process来做图像处理的。 后来我们也做了一些 compositional generation的研究，探索如何把不同的energy 组合起来做生成，这方向我也觉得挺有价值。另外，在vision方面，我们也有一些工作，比如说如何利用energy-based model去处理不同风格或内容的图像。 再后来就是我们那篇关于planning with diffusion的工作，以及后续的diffusion policy这个工作。 我们还做了几个和video相关的研究，其中一个是unipi这种video generation，还有一个是video-language planning，尝试把video model、language model和action model 结合在一起，用于做复杂任务的 planning。 此外，我们也做了一篇关于多语言模型协作的工作，叫multi-agent llms，研究如何把多个大语言模型协同起来完成任务。 最后一篇是我们最近做的工作，探索如何用energy-based models 来做reasoning，这也是我博士期间比较后期的研究方向。 总体来说，大概就是这些 paper，它们分别在模型架构创新、效率提升和多模态协作方面做了一些探索。这些工作的核心方法大多数还是围绕 ebm 展开的。虽然也有一些不是，比如我们做 multi-agent llms 的那篇，是在探索如何把不同的语言模型组合成一个multi-agent system，这个就不完全是基于 ebm 的。但整体来看，ebm 的思想贯穿了我博士期间大部分的研究方向。 我的phd thesis题目是learning generalizable systems by learning composable energy landscapes，即通过学习可组合的能量图谱来构建可泛化系统，三个关键词，可泛化，能量图谱，可组合。 我认为机器人学习面临的最大问题就是缺乏足够的大规模数据。比如，如果我想训练一个类似于大型语言模型（llm）那样的模型用于自然语言处理，那么网上已有的大量文本数据都可以拿来训练；但如果我想训练一个机器人，比如教它洗碗、做饭，那我能用的数据就非常有限。即便我可以通过人类演示收集一小部分数据，仍然难以覆盖到各种不同的环境与任务设定。 因此，我在思考的一个核心问题就是：在缺乏大规模数据的情况下，如何设计一个系统，能够在未见过的场景或任务中依然表现出色？这就是我提出的 compositional structured system（css）背后的动机。 css 的核心思想是采用组合式结构（compositional manner）来建模。不是去训练一个超大的单一模型，而是将问题拆分为多个较小的、专注于不同子任务的模型。这些子模型可以在需要时进行重新组合（recombine），从而适配新的任务设定。这种方式使模型具有更强的泛化能力，尤其是在面对从未见过的任务时。 这个思路很像我们写程序的方式：当我们要构建一个复杂系统（比如一个 web server 或搜索引擎）时，不是从头写一个大函数，而是调用和组合许多小的功能模块（functions），让它们协同工作。同样，在机器人系统中，我们也希望构建一套类似的“技能库”或“模块库”，使得不同模块可以被灵活地组合，从而执行各种复杂任务。 如果我们单独训练一个 end-to-end 的巨大策略网络（intent policy），那它对环境变化会极其敏感——比如机器人稍微变小一点、桌子高一点、光照强一点，系统就可能完全失效。相比之下，组合式建模可以将任务分解为许多更稳定、通用的子问题，从而提升系统在新环境下的适应能力。 进一步地，我们选择使用能量模型（energy-based model）作为组合这些模块的方式。原因在于：通过能量函数来组合不同模块，可以以一种更优化驱动（optimization-driven）且连续空间友好的方式进行组合，而不是简单地用一个模型去依赖另一个模型的输出。 具体来说，我们可以将每个子模型看作一个带有约束（constraint）的能量项：第一个模型负责一个约束，第二个模型负责另一个约束，第三个模型再负责第三个约束……最后我们通过优化这些能量函数的联合来得到最终的控制策略。这种方式避免了模块之间必须“串联调用”的结构，提供了更灵活、结构化的组合方式。 在当前生成式 ai 领域快速发展的背景下，比如大家在训练 llm、视频模型、决策模型，我们发现 energy-based 的组合框架还可以帮助我们把各种训练方式不同、功能不同的模型整合在一起。你可以同时拥有一个语言模型、一个视频模型、一个动作模型，而 energy-based formulation 给了你一个机制，把它们都整合到一个系统中。这正是 energy model 的强大之处。 关于 ebm（energy-based model），它其实是一类比较早期的生成模型。其核心思想是：通过构建一个能量函数，把真实数据（比如真实的照片）的能量调低，而将其他不符合数据分布的样本能量调高。换句话说，就是用能量的高低来区分“好”的样本和“差”的样本。 ebm 是一种通过能量函数（energy function）来定义概率分布的模型。在这种模型中，每一个输入（如图像、状态等）都有一个对应的能量值，能量低的表示更“可能”或更“合理”的输入，能量高的表示不太可能的输入。不像生成模型（如gan、vae）显式地产生样本，ebm 的目标是学习一个能区分“好样本”和“坏样本”的能量函数。你可以理解为，它在“评价”一个样本是否符合某种数据分布，而不是直接去生成它。 我们在 2019 年早期就在探索用 ebm 来生成图像，当时还发过一篇 openai 的博客，展示如何利用这种方式生成逼真的图像。这种思路在很多方面其实和后来的 diffusion models 很相似，尤其是在引入dynamics的部分。我们用梯度（gradient）进行图像采样，用的是类似 langevin dynamics 的方法，这种基于动力学的采样机制后来也成为 diffusion model 的基础之一。 langevin dynamics（朗之万动力学） 是一种模拟粒子在热浴（thermal bath）中运动的数学方法，广泛用于统计物理、采样算法（如 mcmc）、生成模型（如 ebm 和 diffusion model）中。它的核心思想是：在势能（或能量）引导下运动的粒子，同时也受到热扰动（噪声）和摩擦力的影响。 实际上，我们后来的 score-based 和 diffusion-based 的生成方法，都可以看作是我们那套基于 ebm 的早期工作的延续或演化。所以从某种意义上说，我们当时做的东西可以看作是 diffusion models 出现前的一个重要前。 能量模型这个概念，其实可以追溯到大约二三十年前的图模型（graphical models）领域。在当时，无论是有向图模型（directed graphical models）还是无向图模型（undirected graphical models），都试图通过多个“因子（factors）”的乘积，来刻画一个复杂系统中不同部分的联合分布。这些因子可以分别建模系统中的局部约束或子结构，然后通过联合建模的方式构造出整个系统的表达。 能量模型（energy-based model）本质上就是这种无向图模型的一种形式（这里关于能量模型，笔者暂时也不能透彻的理解，恕我不能展开科普，等后续接触更多这类工作再深入理解）。在这种建模方式中，每个 component 可以用一个能量函数来表示，系统的整体行为则由这些能量函数共同决定。 我们后来提出将这种能量模型的组合方式（compositionality）引入神经网络体系中，并进一步扩展到 embodied ai（具身智能）领域。也就是说，我们不是简单地学习一个 end-to-end 的大模型，而是将任务分解为多个子模块，每个模块表示一个局部结构或子任务，分别用神经网络形式的能量函数来表示，再通过优化这些函数的总能量来组合成一个完整策略。这就像是把早期 graphical models 的思想“神经网络化”了。 虽然以往没有太多人将这种能量组合的方式系统化地用于神经网络中，我们的研究正是尝试把这一经典思路延续并扩展到现代机器学习，尤其是 embodied intelligence 这个方向上。除了机器人领域，我们也在探索这种方法在其他更广泛的场景中的应用。 其实我很早就开始研究 diffusion model，大概在 2018 年、2019 年的时候我们就在做 energy-based model（ebm）。当时我们发现，ebm和score-based model几乎是一模一样的。 score-based model（也叫 score-based generative model 或 score-based diffusion model）是一类基于估计数据分布的梯度（score function）来生成样本的生成模型。这里的 "score" 指的是数据的对数概率密度的梯度。score-based model 的核心思想是学会数据分布的“上升方向”，然后沿着这个方向，从噪声一步步走向真实数据。 在 ebm 里面，你是去学习一个energy function，然后用基于能量的采样方法，比如 langevin dynamics，来生成图像；而在score-based model里，你并不显式地学习energy，而是直接学习 energy 的梯度（score function）。但无论是哪一种，两者用的都是相同的 langevin 采样过程，所以在机制上其实是一致的。 有很多论文也都提到，其实这两个模型本质上就是一样的，只是表述不同，甚至没有必要专门叫成score-based model，其实可以直接认为是energy-based model的一种形式。从这个角度来看，diffusion model也可以被看作是一种特殊的score-based model，所以 diffusion model 和 ebm 之间的关系其实非常紧密。 energy，就是我有一个能量的landscape，比如说我有些照片是低的energy，有些照片是高的energy。然后我想生成一个sample，我是从一个noise sample 开始，然后在这个energy function上跑优化：我先跑一步gradient descent，在这个energy landscape上往低的方向走，然后我加一点noise，再跑一步gradient descent，再加一点noise——我们就是跑这个 langevin sampling的过程。这样一步步跑下来，最后你就会到达一个低能量的区域，这时候你就得到了一个低 energy 的照片，这个就是你生成出来的样本。 你会发现，这整个 langevin sampling 的过程本质上就是 “gradient + noise”，其实跟 diffusion model的反向过程是完全一样的。所以从这个角度来说，这两个model 是非常相似的。 我早期主要从事能量模型（energy-based model, ebm）的研究，始于2019年左右。我们逐渐发现，diffusion model 与 ebm 在本质上非常相似。因此，我们将之前许多关于 ebm 的论文用 diffusion 的术语重新表述，并撰写了相关工作。 我们曾有一篇名为model-based planning with energy-based models的论文。后来，我们将这篇2019年的论文框架迁移到diffusion model的范畴中，我认为这大概是最早将 diffusion model 应用于机器人领域的尝试之一。 之后，我们与舒然和迟宬尝试将planning with diffusion for flexible behavior synthesis 这篇论文中的方法应用于真实机器人任务，实验结果表明，该方法效果不错，这也是diffusion policydiffusion policy—基于扩散模型的机器人动作生成策略这篇工作的背景。 我觉得这类模型特别有意思。那段时间，生成模型领域特别火爆，尤其是基于编辑（edit）和决策（decision）的方法，我觉得这是我以前从未见过的东西，非常吸引我。那时候我在 openai，有个同事lya sutskever非常喜欢ebm，他经常跟我说，他相信未来十年、二十年生成模型都会基于 ebm，所以他天天跟我讨论这个话题，我也就信了。 而且我刚开始读博士时，发现diffusion model开始火起来了，我自己也挺喜欢 ebm 这种思路。我们那时候写了不少相关论文。虽然当时这类模型还不是特别流行，相关论文也不多，但我觉得它们和后来的 diffusion model 非常相近。 所以我想，既然这样，不如把之前做的工作重新用 diffusion 的术语来写，这样可能更容易被更多人接受和阅读。毕竟之前那些论文关注度不高，因为当时做的人不多，大家也不太了解这些内容。用 diffusion 的表达方式，能让更多人看到这类工作。 假如你有一个能量函数，也就是一个能量地形（energy landscape），那么想把两个模型组合起来其实很简单。你只需要把这两个模型对应的能量函数相加就可以了。举个例子，一个模型定义了它想生成的样本能量，另一个模型也定义了它想生成的样本能量，那么把这两个能量函数相加，最终的模型就是在这两个能量函数的“中间”生成样本。 这就是能量模型的好处——可以非常自然地将多个模型组合成一个整体，而这只是简单的加法操作。这也是为什么用能量的形式来表示模型，是一个非常合适的方式，能够方便地组合不同的模型。 第二个点是为什么特别强调“泛化”。当你把不同的模型组合起来之后，你就能让系统在没见过的任务或环境中表现得很好。因为组合后的系统可以覆盖更多不同的能力和约束，能够应对多样化的未知任务。 我觉得机器人领域永远面临的一个核心问题是：我们没有太多的数据，怎么让机器人在没见过的环境或任务中依然能够完成目标？现在很多 imitation learning 或diffusion policy，都是基于有限的示范数据训练的，模型只能在类似环境下表现好。 但这并不是真正聪明的机器人。比如很多人在做仿真强化学习，他们在仿真环境中反复训练，然后再在真实环境中测试，环境几乎一模一样，这样的泛化能力其实很有限。 如果你真正想打造聪明的机器人，必须让它能够在没见过的环境和任务中，依然能做出良好表现。这才是机器人领域最根本、最重要的挑战。 你可以在不同的层级进行组合。举例来说，你可以把大型语言模型（large language model，llm）作为高层的推理模块，负责告诉你“我想做饭”，它会生成具体的步骤，比如“先切菜”、“去找食材”。 接下来，你可以用第二个层级的模型，比如视频模型（video model），把 llm 输出的高层指令转化为视觉理解任务，理解实际的场景和物体状态。 第三个层级则是动作模型（action model），负责将视觉信息转化为具体的动作执行，比如机器人手臂的运动轨迹。 实际上，有很多不同的方式把多种模型组合起来，组合的对象不必仅限于策略（policy）。例如，你可以同时把视觉模型和动作模型结合起来。 此外，你还可以把不同的约束条件（constraint）组合在一起。比如在抓取任务中，你会有多个约束：机器人手臂的轨迹不能碰撞其它物体，必须能够成功抓取目标物体，放置动作要平滑且连续，不能突然跳跃等。这些约束也可以被建模成不同的能量函数，然后一起组合，形成一个整体的策略或规划。 你也可以把不同的模型组合，比如动力学模型（dynamics model）和策略模型一起联合优化，以实现更优的控制效果。 总之，组合有很多方式，既可以是模型之间的组合，也可以是约束之间的组合。其实这和传统机器人学中使用的各种经典算法有相似之处，我们可以借鉴这些经典算法的思想，把它们转化成现代的组合模型框架。 目前使用这种方法的人还不是特别多。因为大家现在更多想的是：如果我们有大量的数据，用端到端的方式去训练模型，能不能直接学出有效的能力？这是目前大家关注的问题。 我觉得，未来几年我们会发现，即使拥有海量数据，单纯训练大型模型的效果也未必特别理想。到那时，大家会开始思考如何在模型中加入更多结构化的设计。 我相信，随着时间推移，这种基于结构组合的方法会被越来越多地采用。但现在仍处于比较早期的阶段，大家大多还是先尝试用端到端训练大模型，看看效果如何。大致来说，我估计在两三年到三四年之后，这条技术路线会逐渐被更多人认可和采用。 11. 您认为在 embodied ai 路线上还有哪些比较有前景的方向？ 我最近主要在做视频模型（video model），尝试用视频模型直接驱动机器人的策略，或者做端到端学习。 其实，我觉得大型语言模型（llm）虽然强大，但它们对物理世界的理解和低层控制的能力其实有限。相比之下，视频模型在学习物理知识方面更有优势。比如，当视频模型看到开门、抓杯子这些动作时，虽然它的物理理解不算非常精确，但它确实掌握了不少物理相关的信息，也知道如何完成具体的动作。 举个例子，视频模型能够展示切菜的动作到底是什么样子，这在机器人执行具体任务时非常有帮助。而大型语言模型对真实物理过程的理解相对较少，比如当你问它“怎么从一个地方走到另一个地方”或者“怎么做饭”，它的回答往往缺乏物理细节，甚至对现实世界的理解比较浅显。 视频模型能直接利用视觉信息，这让它对现实世界的感知更直观，因此把视频模型和机器人技术结合起来，是一个很有趣且有潜力的方向。虽然现在这个方向的研究越来越多，但相比 llm 或大规模多模态模型来说，关注度还没有那么高。不过我认为它的意义更大，也更符合机器人对环境感知和动作的需求。 12. 目前基于视频的方法有哪些？你们主要采用的技术路线又是什么？ 目前常见的一类做法是：有了视频模型后，先用它去生成一些视频数据，然后再将这些数据喂入 vla（vision-language-action）模型中，希望借此提升下游模型的表现。 而我们的方法不太一样。我们更强调将video model直接作为planner来使用（unipi）。具体来说，我们给定当前的一帧图像，由video model生成一段未来的视觉视频序列。根据这段预测视频，我们就可以推断出当前应该采取的动作。因为如果知道未来每一帧应该处于什么位置，那么规划出当前的动作其实是一个相对简单的问题，只需要通过controller进行解析。 所以我们的流程是：用video model做高层规划（video planning），然后通过一个闭环的控制器（closed-loop controller）执行这些计划，并在执行若干步后重新用video model进行一次新的规划。我们认为这种结构是更合理、更具前景的。 相比之下，目前很多其他工作要么是直接做video-based planning，要么就是让video model 用来生成数据，然后把这些数据作为训练样本提升其他模型的表现。但我们观察到，当前的 vla 模型泛化能力仍然有限，控制策略的质量也不高。而通过video model生成的数据，其逆动力学建模（inverse dynamics modeling）也往往不够准确，因此这种“生成数据再训练”的方式效果并不理想。我们认为，直接把 video model 用作high-level planner是更合理、更有效的一条路径。 用video model去造data，是指利用视频生成模型去合成各种各样的机器人轨迹的图像数据。具体做法是先用video model合成机器人执行不同任务时的视频或图片，然后再用一个idm（inverse dynamics model）去对这些图像进行动作标注，从而获得包含视觉和对应动作的训练数据。这种方式可以扩展已有的数据量，用于训练更强的视觉-动作模型（如 vlm）。 13. 生成模型和机器人的交叉，如何共同服务于你对“智能”的理解？ 我觉得智能或者ai，最终都离不开机器人这个载体。如果我们真的想实现真正的ai，这个ai必须能够在真实环境中完成各种各样的任务。视觉、自然语言处理、机器学习这些其实都是解决不同的小问题，它们都是大问题里的部分。 我认为最大的核心问题是：我们怎么才能打造出类似人类那样的、具备通用能力的 ai，也就是所谓的 agi？这其实和如何造一个通用型的机器人是同一个问题，二者本质上是一致的。 所以我认为，通用机器人其实就是ai需要解决的终极问题。虽然距离真正实现还很远，很多细节和方法还不明确，但我觉得这是ai领域的最终目标。其他很多研究方向，其实都是这个终极问题里的子问题。 我觉得现在语言理解其实也不一定完全解决了。比如说，如果我把模型当作一个 agent，跟它说很多话，模型的表现其实并不是特别理想。它可以回答一句话的问题还不错，但如果我要跟它做多步交互，每一步都需要它做出反应，这时候效果就会明显下降。 视觉方面的模型情况更复杂。稍微复杂一点的文本描述，比如“椅子最右边有个桌子，桌子右上角有一杯水，水杯上面还有个碗”，这种细节丰富的描述，模型往往不太能准确理解。同样，如果我给模型一张照片，问它里面具体有什么，它的表现也不尽如人意。 所以我觉得无论是语言还是视觉，虽然现在有些模型看起来效果不错，但距离真正做到灵活、准确的理解和交互，还有很大的差距。 15. 通用机器人这个agi的终局是否更遥远？ 我觉得现在做通用机器人确实有点早。有时候这种情况有点误导人，大家会觉得只要收集了大量数据，训练模型做某个任务就能成功。但实际上，我们做了很多实验，甚至在 google 期间，我们也尝试过一个gemini robotics 项目，我觉得我们的vla模型比别的确实强很多。 可是当我们在真实环境，效果却远没有预期那么好。这就说明了，虽然模型在某些指标上看起来不错，但距离真正能用的机器人系统还很远。所以我觉得现在很多创业公司去做通用机器人，可能还为时过早。 16. 目前具身的路线选择上，哪些是短期内可以落地的路线？ 从短期来看，我个人觉得如果用 video model 去做规划（planner）这类任务，是比较有潜力的。比如在制造业的工厂里，做一些相对简单的任务：比如用机械手把一个零件放进一个孔里，或者把几块东西组合起来，再把一个东西放到另一个物体上面。我感觉用 video model 在这些场景下效果应该不错。同时，也可以用 imitation learning 来训练决策策略，类似diffusion policy。这两种方式短期内都可能在这些简单任务上取得一些实际成果。 但我觉得像用强化学习（rl）去做这种问题，效果可能不会好。我们以前做过类似的尝试，发现如果你在模拟环境里硬编码了整个环境，那其实不如直接用示范数据（demonstrations）去做一模一样的问题，泛化能力非常有限。至于vla这个方向，我的经验是对实际应用帮助不大，所以我也觉得那条路短期内不太现实。 17. 为什么这么看好用video model做 planner？ 在传统机器人领域，我们有很多运动规划（motion planning）的方法。如果想做更通用、更具泛化能力的机器人，规划能力是非常关键的一环。我也参与了不少关于 diffusion-based planning 的工作，我觉得这是一个非常重要且有前景的方向。 我觉得这个思路挺合理的，但我有个疑问：动作数据和语言数据其实非常不一样。你在训练时把动作数据和语言数据放一起，可能会丢失一些推理和因果关系的信息。我现在还没看到把大语言模型（llm）直接应用到动作学习上有什么明显的帮助。 我认为这种路径其实存在问题。其实有很多不同的研究方向和方法，如果做创业，我觉得尝试其他方式可能会比简单复制vla这种模式效果好很多。因为根据我的经验，这些vla模型实际效果都很差，真的去试一试就知道了。 我觉得主要是因为大家普遍很信任大语言模型（llm）的强大效果。虽然 llm 在视觉方面的表现其实并不算特别好，但因为语言模型本身效果出色，他们认为把视觉能力和语言能力结合起来，应该会非常有用。 他们进一步把动作也加进去，这样模型不仅能理解语言和视觉，还能执行动作，听起来这个故事很完整，很容易让人信服。所以很多团队都选择走这条路线。但我的看法是，实际效果可能并没有那么理想，距离真正可用的系统还有差距。 我觉得强化学习（rl）在机器人控制方面面临几个关键问题。 首先，很多环境里的reward设计并不理想。在locomotion上，我可以明确告诉模型每一步该做什么，这样 reward 是比较清晰的，rl也比较有效。但是在操作（manipulation）任务中，大部分步骤其实没有明确的reward，导致很难学到好的操作策略。 另外一个问题是状态空间。做locomotion时，观察到的状态维度很低，sim和real差异不大，所以基于rl的策略还能奏效。但做全身控制或操作时，物理差异大，状态空间也非常高，直接用rl从仿真训练到真实环境的效果很难保证。 最后，任务的horizon（时间跨度）也更长。locomotion可以每步给 reward，但操作任务往往要经过几千步之后才有反馈，这导致 rl 很难有效学习。 综上，这些是我觉得强化学习在机器人控制，尤其是复杂操作上的最大挑战。 尽管有人依然在尝试用rl解决操作问题，但尝试大多数还没真正奏效。通常他们只是在做一些非常简单的任务，比如让机械手抓一个立方体，然后转动一下。这样的任务 reward 设计比较明确，状态空间也相对简单，往往也不用复杂地操作整个机械臂，只是做一些局部动作。 所以目前强化学习在操作领域的应用，更多还是停留在解决这些比较简单的问题上。 我觉得现在要解决通用智能的问题，关键点有好几个，但我认为还有更大的挑战。 首先，一个特别大的问题是现在大多数策略模型根本没有记忆。它们通常只根据当前这一帧的观测来预测动作，完全不利用之前的历史信息。举个例子，如果机器人在环境中走动，环境变化了，某个物体可能暂时看不到了，但模型没有记忆，它就“忘了”这个物体在哪里。现在的模型一般只在固定场景里工作，物体位置不变，所以没这个问题。但如果要做真正智能的机器人，必须有“记忆”，这点非常关键，但目前大家很少涉及。 第二个问题是快速学习能力。人类遇到新环境或新工具时，可以很快学会使用，而现有模型缺乏持续学习的机制，不能不断地吸收和适应新知识。 第三，在线学习也很重要。人其实大部分时间是在与环境交互过程中学习的，而目前很多模型训练和部署是分离的，缺少这种持续的在线适应。 最后一个我觉得同样重要的是感知的多样性。我们人类在操作时不仅靠视觉，还依赖触觉、力觉等多种感知信息。比如说做精细操作（dexterous manipulation）时，触觉和力觉特别关键，但目前这些感知信号很少被用到，这也是一个被忽视但非常重要的方向。 刚才提到的第一个问题——记忆，其实跟现在很多定位和导航系统里的空间记忆不太一样。比如自动驾驶汽车有三维地图记忆，但我说的记忆更多是动态和任务相关的。 举个例子：如果我想做操作任务，比如打开一个柜子门，然后翻找里面的东西，再把门关上。模型要怎么记住自己之前看过柜子里的哪些东西呢？你光用三维模型来记忆，很难做到这一点。因为三维地图只能告诉你空间结构，但它没法帮你记住“我在柜子里翻找过，那里没有我要的东西”。 所以，光靠三维空间记忆，往往是不够的。真正的智能体需要一种更灵活、更语义化的记忆，能够记住操作过程中发生的具体细节。 23. 怎么对比语言中获得的智能和从物理载体中获得的智能？ 我的感觉是，如果你去看人的发展历史，其实我们花了大量时间在学习各种运动控制的技能，或者是在环境中学习物理规律等等。这些学习远早于语言的出现——语言其实只是在人类历史的最后一万年才突然发展出来的。也正是有了语言，才有了后来的所谓“智能”。 所以我觉得，从历史上看，人类的技能其实是在与真实环境互动中逐步形成的。如果我们要理解人的智能，可能真的需要先造出一个“聪明的机器人”。这就意味着智能本质上不是从语言中来的，而是从与世界的交互中来的。 现在大家很关注语言模型，但我觉得如果你仔细观察就会发现，这些模型其实并不真正理解物理世界。比如说，我给你几个物体，让你想象从一个地方把它搬到另一个地方，这类涉及物理因果的推理，当前的大语言模型往往效果都不太好。再比如，我给你几张照片，问你“我想把这个东西扔到那边，应该怎么做”，模型也常常回答不上来。 所以我怀疑：如果没有真正的物理世界经验，仅靠语言，我们真的能学到智能吗？尤其是当你希望一个模型完成一些长程、复杂的任务，比如持续进行十几步、二十几步的推理和操作时，现在的模型就会开始出问题。 我觉得，这类能力可能只有在智能体与环境进行真实交互时，才能慢慢学会。也就是说，要获得真正的智能，可能还是得回到物理世界，从生物或历史的角度看，这基本是绕不开的。所以，光靠语言模型，我看不太清楚它们能不能最终达到我们想象中的人工智能。我知道很多人在尝试这条路线，但在我看来，这种路径并没有那么清晰能通向“真正的 ai”。 其实我也说不清楚下一个最大的突破到底是什么。如果我知道的话，我可能早就去做了（笑）。但我现在的感觉是，大家做的东西都太像了。我记得大概五年前，每次去开会的时候，每篇 paper 都挺不一样的，各种方向都有，每个人都在探索不同的思路。但现在感觉几乎全是跟 llm 或者 diffusion model 有关的 paper，而且内容都很相似。 我自己是觉得，我们应该多去想一些不一样的方向，这才是最有意思的。现在很多人做研究都有一种共识，觉得只要把一个 llm 或者 vision model套到机器人上，智能问题就能解决了。但我其实不太相信这条路是那么直接的。 这让我想到 2015 年、2016 年那会儿，大家也特别乐观，觉得“我们有 perception，有操作，加上点 rl，不就能搞定通用智能了吗？”但实际上一点都没那么简单。现在这波思路其实跟那会儿也差不多，就是把已有的模块往上一叠，以为就能跑通所有任务。我觉得稍微想一想就知道，这事可能没那么容易。 总的来说，我觉得现在很多人做研究的视角还是太近了，太关注当下已有的框架，而没有去往远处多看一步。 25. 为什么具身不火的时候百花齐放，反倒现在火了方向却单一了？ 我觉得现在这种研究同质化的趋势，其实背后有几个原因。 首先就是，有太多公司在做这个方向了，特别是聚焦在 llm + vision + action 这一套 pipeline 上。所以当你看到很多公司都在用这种方式出 demo、发 paper、拿融资，那大家自然也就会跟着去做。毕竟你身边的人都在做，而且你未来可能也想去这些公司，那你就更容易被这个风向带着走了。我觉得这是一个很现实的动因。 lessons learned 没办法真正传下来。比如我们这一批人已经研究了几年，可能已经意识到某些方向其实并不好做，或者效果有限。但新进来的人还是会选择那些看上去最简单、最直接的路径去试，比如“我加一个 llm，再堆点 data，就能出个结果”。 于是，这就变成一个循环：越来越多人重复去做那些“看上去最靠谱”的路线，但其实整个领域就被卡在那，缺少真正的进步。
