movements, with some ability to learn and adapt. it also supports avoiding obstacles without conscious thought and certain automatic safety behaviors. these are the functions i wanted to build into a robot module. [editorial note: this is the interviewee’s engineering analogy. automatic avoidance and safety involve several neural systems, rather than being functions exclusively of the biological cerebellum.] over my six years as a phd student at berkeley, i explored this extensively. i feel we are very close to robots that can truly “think.” of course, much follow-up work remains, but i think the next step may be to move from the cerebellum toward the cerebrum. by incorporating more perception and environmental information, those two systems could work together on harder tasks, giving robots real environmental understanding and more complex behavioral capabilities. my research has three keywords: agility, intelligence, and safety. within those directions, the technical approach breaks down into five modules. our first module was what i call structured motion intelligence. the core idea was to embed the robot's dynamics model in a structured optimization framework. we wanted to run optimization either online or offline and have the robot directly execute the resulting solution. we did a great deal of work along this path. our earliest achievement was expressive motion on a bipedal robot, entirely through optimization. we first designed a trajectory by hand, then solved for a control strategy with an optimization algorithm, allowing the robot to execute the movements precisely without relying on learning. we also explored automatic parameter tuning: adjusting certain parameters on top of an existing controller to improve overall performance. that work still sat within the model-based control framework. but we soon ran into problems. reinforcement learning had not yet become part of our approach, and we relied entirely on optimization for motion control. we gradually recognized some fundamental limitations of model-based methods. [editorial note: the original says “there was not yet a concept of reinforcement learning.” in this research narrative, that describes its absence from the team’s approach at that stage, rather than the historical invention of rl.] first, there is a substantial mismatch between the model and the real robot. even a very detailed dynamics model has a gap from physical hardware. we later called this the model-to-real gap. however good the model is, it cannot fully describe nonideal effects such as friction, compliance, hysteresis, and other nonlinearities. we tried several ways to close that gap. one was to increase the optimization rate. if the optimizer runs fast enough, many errors can be treated as disturbances without separately modeling compensation for them. but that introduces another problem: high-speed, real-time optimization with a complex model is difficult at the control layer. most optimization models are too complex to meet the required control frequency. a second approach was manual tuning. we began by adjusting many controller parameters by hand; sometimes we also put those parameters into an optimizer. in essence, though, it was like a person manually running reinforcement learning. you define something like a reward function, then use intuition, experience, and experimental results to tune parameters until the system's behavior matches what you want. the biggest problem is how slow the development process becomes. parameters that work today may fail tomorrow. a robot is a dynamic system that changes every day: motors wear, mechanical structures loosen, joints overheat, and friction changes. those hardware factors directly affect controller performance. this approach can really only serve as a demonstration-oriented route: keep refining it in one direction and you can certainly produce a beautiful demo. boston dynamics, for example, has very capable controllers and produces visually impressive, stable demos. but the problem is that this method is difficult to scale up or extend, and cannot generalize. that is my assessment of this development route. we began asking whether we could dispense with an explicit control model and let reinforcement learning teach the robot highly dynamic, broadly useful motion control. could it train itself to walk, run, and perform long jumps rather than have us tune each capability by hand? that was a radical idea at the time. people generally did not believe rl could run directly on physical hardware; the prevailing view was that it worked in simulation but would fail on a real robot. xue bin peng's work was a representative example. deepmimic looked excellent in simulation and produced very expressive behavior. but as robotics researchers, we initially doubted whether it could transfer to real robots. one main reason was its idealized assumptions. in simulation, training can access the robot's complete state, including every joint's position and velocity, and the model matches the training environment. after training, the controller is deployed in that same simulator. those assumptions do not hold in the real world, so we felt the approach was still far from hardware deployment. fortunately, we were all at berkeley. our group and the group led by sergey levine and pieter abbeel, where xue bin peng worked, were tackling the same problem: how to deploy reinforcement learning on real hardware. we did a series of projects, mainly on cassie. our first task on cassie was walking. we first made it work around mid-2020; the paper was published in 2021, but the actual result was achieved in 2020. that put our work in the same period as early rl controller research at eth and other teams. looking back, that wave was among the earliest groups to apply rl in practical locomotion control. the systems were still relatively basic, but they created real momentum. [editorial note: this describes an early wave, rather than claiming the first hardware deployment. eth’s anymal work, learning agile and dynamic motor skills for legged robots, was published in 2019.] the major breakthrough in our paper was not only showing that an rl controller could run on hardware. more importantly, we demonstrated strong compensation and robustness, which surprised many people at the time. in our experiments, if the robot was almost falling and you helped it back a little, the controller did not break down. it kept running, recovered the robot from a highly unstable state, and continued walking. that is extremely difficult for model-based methods. once the system goes outside what is called the region of attraction, it breaks down and cannot recover. in other words, once a disturbance pushes it beyond that boundary, no amount of effort can bring it back. this is how i characterize the limitation we encountered. [editorial note: a region of attraction specifies states from which a particular closed-loop system converges; being outside it does not universally prove that every model-based controller must fail.] the rl controller behaved differently. its policy implicitly captured extensive experience of responding to disturbances. once you pulled the robot back, it could adapt to the current state and stabilize again. that recovery ability was unprecedented at the time and was very impressive. those results made many people reconsider the potential of reinforcement learning for real-world robot locomotion. more researchers entered the field because they saw that rl could actually run on physical systems and offer practical value, rather than remain confined to simulation. we explored many methodological ideas that i think were valuable. over these few years, our direction went through the whole progression from nothing to a first working result, then to many capabilities. it was not easy: systematic progress in rl for bipedal control has really concentrated into just these recent years. we kept advancing the work. we started with basic walking control, then tried more complex jumps—long jumps, high jumps, and other dynamic jumping maneuvers. our goal was to accomplish many kinds of jump with one controller: a standing long jump, a jump onto a table, a backward jump, or a jump with a turn. it was an ambitious idea, aimed at pushing the generality of bipedal motion control to a very high level. we spent a lot of time on it, recorded many videos, and ultimately achieved good results. for example, two controllers performed 19 different jumping movements. they did not require a separately programmed strategy for each jump. given a landing target, the robot could jump to it. training took place entirely in simulation, followed by direct deployment on the real robot without additional parameter tuning. we developed several methods to support that generalization. first, we designed multi-stage training so that the controller could handle the different stages and objectives of the task. second, we proposed a dual-history architecture: it encodes a longer history of the robot's inputs and outputs while also giving direct access to short-term feedback. together, those histories help the controller infer the robot's current dynamics more quickly and accurately. the design gives the controller implicit adaptation. without external intervention, it can adapt to changes in the hardware, such as drifting dynamics parameters or changing contact conditions. that is a central technical reason a controller can perform so many different jumping movements. we then worked on running control, including sustained runs of 100 and 400 meters. the point of that paper was not the number of demos, but the systematic reinforcement learning methodology we developed. we wanted to answer how a broadly applicable controller architecture, with suitable training and control structures, could support different kinds of task. the resulting controllers were also stable in practice. we repeatedly tested one walking controller over a year and a half, redeploying and running it periodically, and its performance remained consistent. we have similar long-term validation for jumping and running controllers. they showed consistent behavior without obvious degradation. that consistency over time is crucial and valuable for deployment in real systems. a crucial dividing line between a demo and a practically usable controller is that a robot always has a model-to-hardware gap. we can obtain a model, but it can never describe reality perfectly. important parameters—joint friction, rotational inertia, and friction between the feet and ground—change over time on the real robot. for example, in one running experiment, the robot wore through its sole after just one lap. the friction changed, and we had to replace the sole before running again. its dynamic response was then different from training. joints wear too. long-jump experiments generate large impacts, and after several jumps the joints' condition changes. a controller that looked excellent in simulation or training can therefore fail a few days after deployment. we realized early that without adaptation, a controller cannot truly be deployed. you might record a beautiful video, then have the controller fail completely a few days later as the robot changes. to demonstrate that our controllers could adapt to the body, we deliberately tested them repeatedly while the hardware's condition was changing. we wanted to know whether they could stay stable through those changes in dynamics. our robot control research followed a progression. we began with optimization and structured models, then gradually moved toward reinforcement learning, letting the robot learn policies from experience without an explicit model-based control law. we started from the agility of a single bipedal robot and pushed its capabilities as far as possible. many projects now attempt similar things and draw on some of our early methods or ideas. i think that is natural; these were fairly frontier efforts at the time. of course, that work was still about a single agent: building the capabilities of one robot. but from the start, we knew that walking, running, and jumping were not enough. a robot ultimately needs to do useful work to deliver value as a system. so early in my phd, we began thinking about more complex tasks, including manipulation. we began asking early in my phd whether legged robots could perform manipulation tasks. around 2021–2022, humanoid platforms were much less mature than they are now, configurations with multiple kinds of embodiment were uncommon, and many robots did not even have “hands.” so we asked: could legged robots still do useful work without hands? we found a promising starting point: use the feet to kick, push, and pull, accomplishing tasks without grasping. we call this nonprehensile manipulation. rather than rely on a dedicated end effector such as a robot hand, we interact with the environment through the feet or other body parts without grasping the object. [editorial note: the original says “non-contact” here; these actions involve contact. “nonprehensile” means without grasping.] opening, pushing, or pulling a door, or even switching off a light, does not always require a hand to grasp a handle. sometimes a gentle touch is enough to open the door. we started implementing such actions on legged robots, initially using a quadrupedal platform. the first task was precise soccer shooting: kick a ball to a specified target. we then expanded to other scenarios, such as saving penalties. when a ball arrived from different directions, the robot used different control strategies to respond. it could take a step to intercept the ball, jump to block it, or switch gaits to chase or dive for it. we tried many combinations of movements, effectively combining several low-level controllers into a highly dynamic manipulation task that looked very complex as a whole. we then explored harder tasks, such as dribbling while walking and going around obstacles or holes in the ground. those tasks require dynamic coordination among locomotion, obstacle avoidance, and interaction with the ball. we took a further step by using imitation learning to learn human manipulation demonstrations. the idea was to teach the robot to use its legs through human demonstrations. a person could guide a robot leg directly by hand through a movement, and the robot would learn the control pattern: the action sequence, contact strategy, and force level. this lets it both perform tasks and learn from human behavior how to deal with new manipulation settings. the core idea is hierarchical control. many people discuss hierarchy now, but we built our system around it. at the lower level, we use a general rl controller whose job is to make the legs track different end-effector trajectories. on top of that capability, we train a controller focused on task planning: planning the trajectories of those end effectors, in this case the legs. the upper controller can take several forms. it might be an rl policy or an imitation learning model. it can learn in simulation, be trained on real-world data, or combine the two—for example, pretraining in simulation and fine-tuning on real data. we explored this framework extensively and validated the general applicability of its structure. we conducted many experiments on quadrupeds in this loco-manipulation framework. moving from quadrupeds to humanoids is not complicated: you can view the front limbs as hands and the hind limbs as legs. the underlying logic is similar. it is still a problem of interaction between a single robot and an object. we then asked: if one agent can accomplish a task, how can several agents cooperate? my earliest work in this direction was human–robot cooperation rather than a multi-robot task. we used a robotic dog to guide a blindfolded person as they walked, functioning as a guide dog. that is a collaboration problem between a robot and a person. we then had three quadrupedal robots cooperate to pull a heavy box. they used cables to tow it through a very narrow passage. that task used centralized optimization, with substantial work to accelerate computation. later, we published work in which several quadrupeds towed a load together without needing centralized information during execution. each robot ran its own controller without depending on the states of the others, making the control decentralized. we could even remove a robot during the task—for example, reduce a team from four robots to three—and they would quickly adjust their formation and complete the task. that work used multi-agent reinforcement learning. multi-robot cooperation is difficult: controlling even one robot is challenging, and coordinating several in the real world is harder. we made progress through hierarchical architectures and reinforcement learning. how multiple robots cooperate, especially on physical hardware in real environments, is a substantial challenge. all the projects i have described underwent extensive real-world experiments; they were not purely simulation results. that matters because many rl systems look excellent in simulation but encounter unforeseen problems when deployed. the overall idea remains hierarchical control, which is especially effective for complex systems such as quadrupeds, bipeds, and humanoids. at the lower level is a stable, reliable controller that responds quickly and maintains dynamic stability. the upper level handles task planning: target trajectories, cooperation strategies, and other decisions. this division makes the system more scalable and adaptable. we explored each direction extensively: optimizing single-robot tasks, learning cooperation among agents, and combining methods such as reinforcement learning and imitation learning. we enabled several robots to cooperate without centralized information during execution. doing that in the real world is far from easy. beyond cooperation, i think the most important issue is safety. that is especially true for humanoids, which are designed to operate in human environments. safety has to be the highest priority there. if a large language model says something wrong, it may amount to incorrect information. if a robot controller makes a mistake, however, the robot could hit a person and cause physical injury. that is unacceptable. we therefore focus on adding control-theoretic safety assurance to learning-based methods. learning, especially rl, can perform very well on highly dynamic tasks, with flexible movements, fast responses, and strong generalization. but its behavior is not always predictable; we do not know exactly when it will fail. control theory can provide a safety layer or boundary around the policy. for example, as the robot approaches an obstacle—a wall, a structure, or a person—the system can guarantee no collisions or violations of the specified formal safety constraints. [editorial note: such formal guarantees depend on the model, assumptions and constraints used; they do not amount to an unconditional guarantee for every real-world situation.] we have explored how to construct verifiable safe sets and how probabilistic methods can model a policy's reliability boundaries. this can ensure that even a learning-based controller does not make decisions that injure people when deployed in the real world. i have always felt that “cerebellum” is somewhat vague in robotics, especially when we discuss humanoids; people do not share one understanding of it. the definition becomes easier if we narrow the discussion to legged robots or quadrupeds. their first tasks are clear: maintain balance and perform basic movement control, including standing, walking, running, and jumping. in the human nervous system, the cerebellum is primarily involved in motor control, coordination, and balance, while the cerebrum is more involved in perception, cognition, and decision-making. as an analogy for a robot architecture, the cerebellum corresponds to the low-level module that controls the body's movements. locomotion control, whole-body coordination, adaptation, and rapid reflex-like safety responses can all be placed within what i call the robot cerebellum. for instance, many controllers in our research enable highly dynamic movement and adapt automatically to changes in robot dynamics, such as joint damage or worn soles. that reflects the adaptive aspect of the biological analogy. continuing to walk after “injury” does not require complex planning by the cerebrum; it happens within the motion controller. another example is a person's fast response to danger, such as pulling a hand away immediately after touching a flame. that happens through a reflex pathway rather than deliberate, complex thought. from a robotics perspective, this is one capability we want in the cerebellum-like system: automatic safety responses. [editorial note: this is an architectural analogy. biological withdrawal reflexes are mediated by spinal circuits and should not be attributed exclusively to the cerebellum.] i would therefore include the following functions in the robot cerebellum: basic movement such as walking, running, and jumping; dynamic adaptation that implicitly compensates for friction changes, disturbances, and mechanical wear; immediate responses and safety mechanisms, including rapid obstacle avoidance, posture recovery, and collision avoidance without higher-level decisions; and low-level execution and feedback integration, such as trajectory tracking, stabilization, and processing proprioception. the cerebrum covers higher-level cognition and task decisions. examples include perceiving a target and deciding whether to pick up coke or sprite; processing multimodal information such as vision, language, and semantics; planning long-horizon tasks, such as getting to school through route planning and navigation; and coordinating multiple agents by deciding who does which task and how they divide the work. my research aims to build a cerebellum-like module that gives a robot not just movement, but adaptation, safety, and reflex-like intelligence. ultimately, it should provide basic, stable, reliable bodily control without intervention from the higher-level “brain.” there are still gray areas in practice. whether cooperation strategy belongs to the cerebellum, for instance, is open to interpretation. but from the perspective of engineering architecture and biological inspiration, i find the distinction fairly clear and useful: the cerebellum handles low-level movement and safety; the cerebrum handles cognition and task decisions. i still believe model-based control is very valuable in robotics. companies such as boston dynamics have not abandoned it; they continue using it while also obtaining increasingly good results with reinforcement learning. over roughly the past five years, the robot control community has undergone a clear shift in thinking. our group embraced rl quickly because we deployed policies on real hardware early and the results were excellent. that made the whole team excited. some researchers were initially skeptical. they felt rl control policies were not “elegant” in the way model-based methods are, with explicit mathematical structure, analytic forms, and strong interpretability. they preferred more constructive approaches such as optimal control and nonlinear model predictive control (mpc). as experiments increasingly demonstrated rl's performance advantages on real systems, however, acceptance grew. around 2020, groups at eth, our lab, oregon state university, google, and elsewhere began systematically advancing real-world rl locomotion deployment. by 2024, the community had largely reached the view that model-based methods and reinforcement learning are complementary rather than mutually exclusive, with each suited to different tasks and system constraints. i think two factors drove rl's rapid growth. first, the entry requirements for mathematical modeling are relatively lower. compared with traditional optimization-based control, you do not need to formulate a complete dynamics model or solve a complex constrained optimization problem, so newcomers can get started more easily. second, open-source work and toolchains have greatly reduced the barriers to learning and experimentation. eth, nvidia, and others released simulation platforms, gpu-accelerated engines, and training frameworks, with plentiful tutorials and examples. undergraduates and graduate students can quickly build rl control systems without implementing an optimization solver from scratch. as a result, more newcomers now begin directly with reinforcement learning rather than traditional model-based control. from a research perspective, though, i do not think this is necessarily a good thing. rl is practical to implement, but several important problems remain. first, adaptation is not reliably achieved. a controller may work well today, yet if its training or design is poor, changes such as friction shifts or motor degradation may prevent effective adaptation. long-term consistency remains difficult. second, formal safety guarantees are lacking. an rl controller is often a black-box neural network, and the robot itself is highly complex. combined, their behavior in unknown scenarios can be hard to predict. the robot may take a dangerous action in the wrong state, collide with someone, or fall—outcomes that are unacceptable in real applications. we have continued exploring control-theoretic safety for rl policies. one important finding is that, when a robot is trained well and its control performance is sufficiently good, the closed-loop behavior can be approximated by a globally linear system. that lets us turn a black-box problem into a linear control problem, then apply traditional model-based methods to formally verify and constrain safety. it is a pragmatic and implementable approach. [editorial note: the published result identifies a low-dimensional linear approximation of the tested closed-loop cassie behavior; it does not establish that every coordinate of the full robot is globally linear or that all trained robots have this property.] many questions remain. which systems or training conditions produce linear-looking closed-loop behavior? is the linear approximation universal across robot platforms? how can we extract and use that structure effectively? i think these are among the most promising questions in combining reinforcement learning and control theory over the next few years. adaptation can indeed be seen as a first step toward a general-purpose robot controller. the field is discussing generalist control, but generality has multiple levels and dimensions. first: adaptation on one physical robot—generality over time the most basic level is adaptation over time on the same embodiment. take cassie: the hardware platform stays the same, but its dynamics change with use as joints wear, friction decreases, and motor performance degrades. a genuinely general controller should automatically adapt to those changes without retraining and maintain stable performance. we repeatedly validated this in the experiments discussed earlier, making it a first foundation for generality. second: transfer across robot platforms—structural generality the next level is cross-embodiment generalization, which attracts a great deal of attention. can one controller operate boston dynamics' atlas, unitree's go1, and even humanoids or quadrupeds with entirely different shapes and joint structures? that demands strong adaptation to underlying dynamics, the arrangement of degrees of freedom, and even mechanical configurations. i believe it is possible; in theory, i am confident it can be achieved. but is it actually necessary? one controller supporting many platforms sounds powerful, but training costs might grow exponentially. whether performance can remain good enough on every embodiment is a practical question. it may also sacrifice the finely optimized performance of a controller dedicated to one platform. rl already has limitations in generalization, particularly when the distribution has multiple modes. if the state–action distribution changes substantially, one policy struggles to adapt. that is a real bottleneck. third: task-level generality—adaptation across tasks and modes another level is generalization across tasks or skills. whether the robot is walking, running, jumping, turning, or moving from locomotion into basic manipulation, and whatever the environment or goal, the controller should perform consistently and transfer some capability between tasks. here, i think we can borrow ideas from large models. if many tasks and robot configurations are jointly trained in one system, the controller should theoretically do more than remember them: some degree of emergent behavior might appear on new combinations and tasks. for example, learning task a, long jumping, and task b, obstacle avoidance, might enable task c, jumping while avoiding obstacles. control abilities learned on a humanoid might transfer to a quadruped. or imitation learning might allow rapid generalization after seeing a human demonstrate a new task. i do think rl falls short in controller generalization, and our experiments provide very direct examples. in our locomotion work, we trained separate controllers for walking, jumping, and running. the running controller is very capable, supporting changes in speed, turns, and other complex behavior, but it always operates within the basic running mode. it does not transfer to jumping or ordinary walking. we tried unified rl controllers that learned several tasks, such as walking and running together. but their performance across those tasks was worse than that of separately trained and deployed controllers. the multi-task controller was usable, yet specialist controllers were clearly better. this exposes a limitation in rl task generalization, especially when task distributions differ greatly and involve very different dynamic regimes. it is hard to find one policy that performs well on all of them. at first, we suspected insufficient data. but increasing the amount did not noticeably improve convergence speed or results. it is not something that simply training more will solve. we then observed newer humanoid work combining upper-body manipulation with lower-body locomotion—walking, running, and jumping—in one system. these controllers work in simulation and appear more general. on closer inspection, however, most use a teacher–student architecture. rl first trains a task-specific policy for each task; imitation learning or policy distillation then combines those policies into one larger network. each underlying policy can perform well, and the distilled controller gains some ability to switch and combine tasks. this avoids the training-efficiency and stability problems of directly training the general-purpose controller with rl. personally, i think that is a reasonable engineering path for now. we work around rl's limited native generalization by using imitation learning for policy fusion and general control, while rl remains responsible for training optimal task-level policies. that division is more pragmatic. it also means that the goal of one controller learning every task with true emergent capabilities remains challenging, especially for highly dynamic, high-dimensional locomotion. we still have a long way to go in understanding better training structures, stronger policy representations, and more natural ways to unify multi-task learning. we initially thought rl could work only in simulation and could not succeed on real hardware. i find the shift from that view very interesting. the first change was using history. early work such as xue bin peng's trained rl models using complete simulator state: every link's position and every joint's position and state were directly available. such complete information is unavailable on a physical robot. base linear velocity, for example, cannot be measured directly with the robot's ordinary onboard sensors. it previously had to be estimated with a state estimator, and those estimates still are not especially precise. rather than rely only on the current frame's state, we began providing a history of inputs and outputs—motor commands and sensor readings over a period of time. that history can be used to infer the current base state. we further found that it can reveal internal dynamics properties, such as joint inertia and mass parameters. these estimation processes can be described mathematically. once we can infer the relevant states and properties, we can adjust control to adapt to changes in the body, instead of having it fail as the robot's condition changes or wears. many subsequent projects studied whether to use history, how long it should be, and how to encode it as input. we also ran extensive comparative experiments. i feel our approach is somewhat more generally applicable, although platforms differ substantially, so it is hard to make a blanket claim. the second issue is hardware. however good a controller is in simulation, it cannot be deployed if the hardware cannot keep up. actuator performance is especially important. if the joints cannot respond properly and track the simulated reference trajectory, the system will not work. some robots use inexpensive hobby servos with poor response and controllability. a requested velocity may be unachievable; the joint may oscillate or overheat and shut down. an rl controller is fundamentally a module issuing commands at high frequency, often target joint positions or velocities. in simulation, we assume those targets can be executed as the simulation advances step by step. on hardware, if the actuator cannot achieve the requested target, control can fail completely. platforms such as cassie and some high-performance quadrupeds have capable joints that respond quickly and track accurately. that hardware can support genuinely dynamic rl policies on real robots. i therefore see real-world rl deployment as the result of two developments coming together. algorithmically, we began using history to compensate for unobserved states, enabling estimation and adaptive control. at the same time, better hardware let actuators actually track the targets produced in simulation. there is another gap: the simulator's model can itself be inaccurate. mass parameters or friction coefficients, for example, may differ considerably from their real values. that is another source of mismatch between simulation and hardware. methods such as domain randomization can help close this gap: perturb simulation parameters to improve policy robustness. but it is even more important that hardware executes the controller’s commands well. in simulation, each step assumes that the ideal torque command has been executed before advancing to the next step. real actuators have delays and nonlinear responses and may not keep up with that torque command. that introduces another sim-to-real error. [editorial note: the original contains an apparent transcription error in the chinese word for torque.] if the hardware is not good enough, algorithmic improvements may be wasted. i see this transition as algorithms and hardware advancing toward each other until they meet. that is an excellent question and deserves a detailed answer. we recently released berkeley humanoid lite, an open-source humanoid with transparency down to the joint level, precisely because our control work exposed real problems with many commercially available joints. that experience motivated several recent projects in our group, including colleagues' efforts to redesign those underlying systems. from a control engineer’s perspective, hardware must be transparent. from issuing a desired joint velocity or position—or a torque command—to its conversion into current, transmission to the motor and actuation of the joint, we need to know what happens along the entire chain. [editorial note: the apparent transcription error in the original’s parenthetical is read as “torque command.” position, velocity and torque are distinct command types.] we may not care about every intermediate control detail, but we are highly sensitive to performance characteristics. for a robot of a given size, what is the motor's maximum rotational speed? at that speed, what acceleration or velocity can it actually deliver? is the response linear? are there significant dead zones or unstable regions? all of these directly determine the upper limits of controller performance. when the actuator becomes a black box, controller developers lose their footing. we cannot tell whether a policy failed because of the algorithm or because of a nonideal actuator response. externally integrated joint modules and commercial closed systems can both create this problem: we do not know what happens after a command is sent. if the hardware is poor, that response chain cannot be trusted. however good the algorithm is, poor execution below it means poor control. that is deeply frustrating for control engineers. our group recently developed two complete humanoid designs. one motivation was to gain more transparency and control over the hardware so that we could test more dynamic, higher-performance controllers. only when we understand the complete chain, from issuing commands through the closed-loop current response, can we confidently push the limits of control. that is also why we open-source the system. everyone can see how a control command is ultimately executed. when something goes wrong, you do not have to guess. you can investigate the possible layer: torque calculation, communication delay, insufficient current-loop bandwidth. you can debug it step by step. the idea resembles the distinction between end-to-end policies and hierarchical controllers. end-to-end is exciting, but a failure can be difficult to localize. hierarchy is more complex, yet you can identify the problematic component precisely. the open-source joints in berkeley humanoid lite follow a similar principle: make the hardware response system layered, with each layer traceable, debuggable, and verifiable, so that it can properly support higher-performance control policies. the result is a solid foundation. 12. recruitment as noted at the beginning, dr. 专访xue bin(jason) peng：探索人形机器人全身运控的通用控制器 与jason peng回顾deepmimic、amp、ase、maskedmimic与通用控制器。 全身运动控制 对于从事人形机器人运动控制的朋友来说，xue bin（jason）peng 的名字一定不会陌生。过去一年中，我们看到大量高质量的人形机器人拟人演示出现在各个平台上，而这些演示背后的技术基础，很多都可以追溯到 jason 早期提出的一系列开创性工作，包括 deepmimic、amp（adversarial motion priors） 和 ase（adversarial skill embedding） 等。这些方法极大地降低了人形机器人模仿学习（imitation learning）的技术门槛，可以说，jason 的研究奠定了今天人形机器人实现灵活、自然运动控制的重要基础。 xue bin（jason）peng目前是西蒙弗雷泽大学（simon fraser university, sfu）的助理教授，同时也是英伟达（nvidia）的研究科学家。他的研究工作主要位于计算机图形学与机器学习的交叉领域，重点关注使用强化学习进行虚拟角色运动控制。 值得一提的是，jason 的学术成长路径也极具代表性。他的导师——michiel van de panne、pieter abbeel和sergey levine，分别是角色动画（character animation）和机器人强化学习（robotics + rl）领域最具影响力的顶尖教授。 jason 在硕士阶段，师从不列颠哥伦比亚大学（ubc）的图形学专家 michiel van de panne，这位教授不仅是 character animation 领域的奠基人物之一，同时也是 andrej karpathy（前 tesla ai 总监）的硕士导师和 eth computational robotics lab教授 stelian coros 的博士导师。 随后，jason在加州大学伯克利分校（uc berkeley）攻读博士学位，师从机器学习领域重量级学者 sergey levine 和 pieter abbeel，在强化学习（reinforcement learning）与机器人智能领域打下了扎实而深远的基础。 这期访谈，我们的话题覆盖jason的研究经历以及他的几篇人形机器人全身运控的奠基性工作，包括他对未来通用控制器构建的思路以及对人形机器人硬件的建议。相信这期访谈对于从事人形机器人软硬件开发的朋友们多少会有些帮助。 对目前的人形机器人硬件有什么建议？ 1. 你的两位导师michiel（角色动画领域最具影响力的教授之一）和 pieter abbeel（机器人强化学习的开创者之一）分别是如何影响你的研究和思维方式的？ michiel他是我在英属哥伦比亚大学（ubc）读本科和硕士期间的导师。说实话，如果不是因为他，我现在可能根本不会从事我目前这份研究工作。当时我对计算机图形学很感兴趣，想在这个领域尝试做一些研究。michiel是 ubc 做角色动画方面的教授，于是我主动联系他，希望能参与一些动画方向的研究项目。这也就是我进入这个领域的起点。 那时我其实还没有考虑过机器人领域，只是单纯想做和图形学相关的方向。动画看起来很有趣，但那时基本还没有引入机器学习，主要还是靠传统的运动学方法或手工设计的控制器。 直到后来，deepmind发表了一篇关于使用深度q学习做运动控制的论文（continuous control with deep reinforcement learning）。我们看到那篇论文后，开始深入研究强化学习和深度强化学习，把它作为训练虚拟角色控制器的一种方法。这是一个转折点，让我慢慢进入了机器学习这个领域，并将其与动画结合。 之后，我在伯克利（uc berkeley）读博士，开始和 sergey levine 以及 pieter abbeel 合作研究，也就逐渐将这些技术应用到真实机器人的控制上，而不只是虚拟世界。 所以无论是 michael，还是后来的 sergey 和 pieter，对我的职业生涯都产生了非常深远的影响。我感到非常幸运能与他们合作，如果没有他们的引导，我可能现在完全在做另一条路的事情了。 2. 你的研究经历了一次转变，从图形学中虚拟角色的技能学习，转向了基于奖励机制的真实机器人训练，可以说是一种 sim-to-real（从仿真到现实）的转变。在你看来，这两个方向之间最大的区别是什么？ 我觉得当我开始接触真实机器人时，有一件事让我很意外：很多在仿真中理所当然的事情，在现实中其实非常难做到。 举个例子，状态估计（state estimation）在真实机器人中比我想象的要难得多。在仿真环境中，我们拥有完全可观测性，可以轻松获取所有信息，比如位置信息、速度、甚至智能体的全部内部状态，这些数据都是直接可用的。 但在现实中，当我开始做机器人项目后，哪怕只是获取机器人的线速度这种最基本的状态信息，都变得非常困难。你需要额外的传感器、估计算法，最终得到的结果还可能是带噪声的、不太准确的。 所以我认为，“部分可观测性”（partial observability）是我从仿真转向现实机器人时遇到的最突出的挑战之一，直到现在，这仍然是一个非常棘手的问题。 什么叫部分可观测性： 在一个系统或环境中，如果智能体（agent）无法获取关于系统完整状态的全部信息，那么这个环境就是部分可观测的。换句话说，智能体做决策时，只能“看到”环境的一部分，它的观察是不完整、不确定或带噪声的。举个例子，一个机器人在房间中移动，但只有前方的摄像头输入，它看不到身后和侧面的情况，这就是一个“部分可观测”的问题。要解决这个问题，机器人需要“记住”它从哪里来，或者通过多次动作建立对环境的估计。 全可观测环境（fully observable） 你在下棋，能看到棋盘上每一个棋子的位置和状态 —— 所有信息都可见，你可以基于完整信息做出最优决策。 部分可观测环境（partially observable） 你戴着墨镜在迷雾中开车，只能看到前方几米的路况，而不是整条路线。这时候你必须根据有限的观察、过去的经验和内部记忆来判断当前状态并做出行动。 3. 在与真实机器人打交道的过程中，给你留下最深刻印象的是什么？ 状态估计确实是让我印象非常深刻的一个挑战。但除了这个，还有一个很大的问题就是：现实中的动力学系统并不是静态的（non-stationary）。在仿真中，系统的动力学几乎是固定不变的。这意味着你可以很容易地复现实验：一个控制器只要成功运行一次，基本上就可以无数次重复，每次的行为表现都非常一致。 但在真实机器人上，动力学系统是持续变化的。一个控制器今天可能运行得很好，但过一段时间，它的表现就可能完全不同。举个例子，机器人使用时间长了以后，电机发热，就会导致系统动力学发生变化。所以，一个10分钟前还能正常运行的控制器，可能在你再次运行时就不再有效了。 4. 你是如何应对 sim-to-real 转移中的挑战的？ 我认为在进行 sim-to-real 转移（即从仿真到真实环境迁移）过程中，主要面临的挑战包括：部分可观测性、系统不确定性，以及现实中机器人动力学的非静态性。我们目前应对这些挑战的核心方法是使用域随机化（domain randomization）。在大多数研究中，我们会在仿真环境中训练控制器，然后将其直接部署到真实机器人上。 为了缩小仿真与现实之间的“现实差距（reality gap）”，我们在训练时会对仿真中的物理参数进行大量随机扰动，比如质量、摩擦、延迟和传感器噪声等。这种方法可以促使控制器学习到更强健、适应性更强的策略，从而更好地泛化到真实环境中的不确定性。所以到目前为止，域随机化仍然是我们在 sim-to-real 转移中使用的最主要的工具。 您能否为我们系统性地梳理一下您的主要研究方向与项目？这些工作的核心思想是什么？它们分别在解决哪些关键问题？ 我可以从我们早期的一个工作 deepmimic 说起。deepmimic 的核心思路其实很简单：就是将深度强化学习与动作跟踪（motion tracking）结合起来。这项研究的初衷是想构建虚拟角色，能模仿人类执行各种动作技能，用于动画或虚拟环境中。 deepmimic 在 deepmimic 之前，很多动画领域的控制器设计都在借鉴机器人学的做法，比如轨迹优化、最优控制、或有限状态机（finite state machines）等。这些方法的最大问题在于：不具备通用性，需要大量人工设计。每种新技能都要从头设计一个控制器。比如要模拟“走路”就要一套专门的控制器，“跳跃”又得重新设计一套。如果是翻滚或杂技类更复杂的技能，那需要投入的时间和精力就更多了。这种方法在长远来看是不可扩展的。所以很多过去的研究只能聚焦于极少数具体行为。 我们在 deepmimic 中希望构建一个通用的框架，可以再现任意人类动作技能。为此，我们采用了深度强化学习，通过它训练神经网络控制器。神经网络是一种非常强大的函数逼近器，可以表达非常灵活和复杂的策略。它使我们无需为每个技能去手工设计有限状态机，而是可以使用统一的神经网络架构来适配所有技能。 什么叫有限状态机： “有限状态机”（finite state machine，简称 fsm）是计算机科学和人工智能中一种非常经典的建模方法，用来表示系统在不同状态之间的转移关系。有限状态机是一种在任意时刻只处于一个状态的模型，系统会根据输入触发状态之间的转移。 deepmimic 的另一个关键部分是动作跟踪（motion tracking）。当我们有了神经网络控制器，接下来的问题是：如何训练它去执行各种不同的技能？在传统做法中，你通常需要为每种技能设计一个定制的奖励函数。比如“走路”用一套 reward，“跑步”又是另一套。但这种方式同样不具备扩展性。 我们的方法是采用统一的奖励机制：就是让控制器去跟踪一个参考动作（reference motion）。给它一个目标动作（比如动捕数据），然后让控制器逐帧去模仿它。我们发现，只用这个简单的跟踪型奖励函数，配合策略梯度强化学习方法，就可以让模型学会各种动作技能，而无需为每种技能都手工设计控制器或奖励。 所以相比为每个技能设计控制逻辑，我们只需要提供不同的参考动作，再用相同的训练目标去优化，就能得到对应的控制策略。这就是 deepmimic 的基本思想。 在 deepmimic 之后，我们的一个重要后续项目是 amp（adversarial motion priors）。deepmimic 提供了一个通用框架，可以通过动作跟踪（motion tracking）逐帧模仿参考动作来训练控制器。这种方式在希望角色精准复现某一特定动作时非常有效。事实上，现在我们在很多人形机器人展示中看到的精彩行为，很多背后都是基于这种跟踪技术实现的。 但它的一个关键限制是：这种训练方式下的控制器非常“僵硬”。它们往往只能一遍遍“播放”相同的动作序列，不能偏离预设轨迹，也不能很好地适应新任务。 amp 因此，在 amp 项目中，我们希望构建一个更加灵活的模仿学习目标，让控制器不再被“逐帧跟踪”所限制。我们的核心想法是：用“分布匹配”来替代“轨迹跟踪”。与其要求角色复刻某个精确轨迹，不如训练控制器去生成与数据集整体动作风格相匹配的动作。 我们使用了类似 gan（生成对抗网络） 的思路，进行对抗式模仿学习：首先训练一个判别器，判断一个动作是来自真实数据集，还是模拟角色生成的；同时训练控制器，去“骗过”这个判别器，也就是生成看起来像是真实动作的数据。 这种方法带来了更高的灵活性，控制器不需要逐帧跟随某一条特定动作；它可以拼接、组合不同动作片段；它可以泛化到数据集中没有出现过的新行为；还能在此基础上完成一些数据中并未明确包含的任务目标。所以 amp 提供了一个更强大、更适应性的模仿学习框架，用以推动动作控制的发展。 在使用 amp（adversarial motion priors）时，很多尝试复现的用户反馈说，策略往往只学到单帧之间的转换，结果导致角色“原地踏步”，无法移动。你在实验中有遇到类似的问题吗？你觉得这是 amp 方法本身的局限吗？ 是的，这种“原地踏步”的现象确实可能发生，具体取决于你的设计选择。如果策略陷入一个局部最优，它可能只在一两帧之间来回转换，导致角色看起来卡住了，无法产生移动。 但这个问题通常可以通过扩大判别器的时间窗口来解决。也就是说，不是让判别器只看到两帧，而是给它比如说10帧的动作序列。当判别器能观察更长时间范围的行为时，像这种“卡在单一状态转换中”的不自然行为就会更容易被识别出来，从而促使策略学到更流畅、真实的动态动作。 在机器人运动技能训练的过程中，很多方法会使用隐空间（latent space）来提取各种特征，但隐空间并不是人类可以直观理解的空间。您在研究过程中如何控制隐空间上数据的安全性（即防止异常数据造成策略行为异常）？ 这是一个非常关键的问题。我们在后续的一个工作中提出的方法叫 ase（adversarial skill embedding，对抗式技能嵌入），就是专门为了解决这个问题而设计的。 在很多模型中，特别是采用 vae（变分自编码器）结构的模型中，一个很常见的问题是隐空间中会出现“空洞区域” —— 有些 latent 编码会被解码成完全不像训练数据的行为。虽然目前还没有完全完美的解决方案，但 ase 尝试通过一种类似 gan（生成对抗网络） 的方法来缓解这个问题。 具体来说，ase 中我们把控制器视作一个解码器，它的任务是把一个 latent 编码映射成一个动作序列，这个动作要看起来像真实的数据动作。然后，我们再引入一个判别器，来判断这个生成的动作是否符合真实数据的风格 —— 和训练 gan 的方式很类似。 这种对抗式训练的一个重要优势是：它会促使模型尽可能让隐空间的每一个点都能被映射成看起来“像样”的行为。这能有效减少latent 空间中出现“异常区域”的概率，降低策略出错的风险。 当然，我们也不能保证百分之百不会出现奇怪的行为，有些 latent 编码可能还是会导致不自然的动作输出。但我们发现，像 ase 这样用对抗训练得到的模型，整体上比传统方法更鲁棒、更稳定。 maskmimic的sim2real gap怎么样？ maskmimic与在真实机器人上的部署之间仍然存在非常大的差距。在模拟环境中，我们已经可以训练出控制器，能够复现上千条动作片段。但在现实机器人上，目前大多数系统还处于一种我称之为 "deepmimic阶段" —— 也就是说，一个控制器往往只能执行单个技能或单个动作片段。 masked mimic 相比之下，动画系统现在已经能训练出支持上千种技能的控制器，但要将这样的高容量控制器可靠地迁移到真实机器人上，目前还做不到。 关键的问题在于 “从模拟到现实的迁移”（sim-to-real transfer）：哪怕你在模拟中训练得很好，把控制器部署到真实机器人上，通常还是需要在现实中进行大量手动调参才能让它跑起来。而如果你训练的控制器包含了成千上万种技能，那在现实中对这些技能逐个调试和验证的成本几乎是无法接受的，这就是当前技术最大的瓶颈之一。 9. 在你看来，模仿学习（imitation learning）和强化学习（reinforcement learning）在运动技能学习中的优缺点分别是什么？你认为哪一个更有长期潜力？ 我不太确定模仿学习和强化学习是否真的可以直接类比。因为这两者本质上是正交的范式（orthogonal paradigms）。模仿学习可以通过监督学习或强化学习来实现，具体取决于你手头的数据类型。而强化学习也可以作为一种实现模仿学习的方法，但它也可以完全不依赖演示数据，通过 reward 直接训练控制器。所以它们并不是严格意义上的对立方法。 但如果一定要比较的话，比如模仿学习 vs 纯强化学习（pure rl），后者完全不依赖演示数据，那我们可以从以下角度来看： 纯强化学习的优点是：你不需要依赖任何演示，你只需要定义一个目标，然后直接训练控制器来优化这个目标。这种目标可能是人类设计出来的 reward function。好处在于，它有可能会发现一些更优的行为模式，甚至是人类没有想到的策略。比如像 alphago 这样的系统，它能发现一些超出人类策略的解决方案，这就是强化学习的力量所在。 但纯强化学习的问题也很明显：你通常需要非常复杂的 reward 设计，才能引导 agent 学到你想要的行为。比如你希望 agent 完成一个特定行为，那 reward function 就要非常精心设计，否则 agent 可能不会学习到期望的结果。所以这就是强化学习的一些优点与缺点。 至于模仿学习，它的优劣基本上正好是反过来的：它的优势在于你可以通过引入演示数据（demonstration），更容易地引导 agent 的行为，因为训练目标就是去模仿数据中的行为。 这样可以让 agent 更容易产生人类风格的行为，或者更符合预期的动作表现。 但模仿学习也有自己的缺陷：收集高质量演示数据并不容易，这取决于你研究的具体任务，有些任务可能很少有人类能够很好地完成，那相应的数据也就难以获取。另一个问题是：模仿学习训练出的控制器，行为空间会更受限，它往往只能学习人类曾经做过的行为，缺乏发现新颖策略的能力。换句话说，它可能会在某种程度上限制 agent 的探索性和创造性。 我觉得现在强化学习在操作任务（manipulation）中没有像在运动控制（locomotion）中那么广泛使用，一个主要原因可能是，操作任务中还有“低垂的果实”可以先做 —— 比如用行为克隆（behavior cloning）和监督学习，这些方案目前已经相当有效。对于操作任务，你可以比较容易地构建一个远程操控（teleoperation）系统，然后收集大量人类演示数据。拿到这些数据之后，就可以用监督学习训练一个控制器，这个方案效果通常还不错。 但在运动控制这块，比如腿式机器人，你很难收集到高质量的演示数据。所以在这个领域，我们几乎一开始就被“逼着”用强化学习。因此，目前在操作任务里，大多数控制器还是基于监督学习和行为克隆训练出来的。不过我认为，随着发展，操作任务最终也会走上类似的路径。 不过我认为，这类vla模型最终也会遵循llm的发展趋势。在大型语言模型（llm）中，我们通常也是先经历一个监督学习阶段，在这个阶段，我们使用大量人类数据对模型进行预训练。但如果希望模型在特定任务上有更好的表现，或者要让模型针对某一具体任务进行专门优化，我们通常还需要进行微调，或者是进行针对特定任务的强化学习。 我想，未来对于操作模型来说，可能也会走上类似的路线。也就是说，现阶段我们可以通过监督学习，利用大量遥控操作的数据对模型进行训练；但如果真的想在某一个具体的操作任务上达到最优性能，那么在这个基础上，可能仍然需要借助强化学习微调（rl fine-tuning）来进一步优化模型表现。 11. 越来越多的人开始关注将大型模型（如 vla）应用于机器人领域。您如何看待大规模架构在机器人技能学习中的作用？ 我认为这类大型多模态模型非常有前景。而且我们确实已经从这些模型中观察到了非常有趣的涌现特性，也就是说，这些大型模型能够展现出一些自发产生的复杂行为。 但我认为当前的主要瓶颈在于这些模型的推理速度。推理时间较长，使它们很难在实时的低层控制中发挥作用。这有点像“慢思维”和“快思维”之间的差别。我觉得很多vla模型未来可能更多地作为高层规划器使用，运行频率较低，它们主要负责制定总体规划。而这些规划最终需要由更小、更快、更高响应性的低层控制器来执行。所以我认为这些多模态模型确实很有前景，但目前特别是在低层控制方面，还缺少一个优秀的控制器，能将高层的指令有效地转换为具体的低层动作执行。 我认为这些vla模型可以应用在一些节奏较慢、动态性较低的任务中，比如操作类任务，像是简单的抓取与放置。这类任务用运行较慢的vla模型是没问题的。但如果你想实现像全身的敏捷运动控制这种高动态的操作，那就必须依赖能以更高频率运行的控制系统。而现在，我们的计算能力还不足以让这些大型的多模态模型实现那样的目标。 12. 在机器人运动控制（locomotion）领域，您认为工业界在某些方面是否已经超过了学术界？ 是的，我认为在某些方面，工业界已经变得更擅长让机器人展现出高度敏捷、类似人类的行为。这是因为，如果你是机器人制造商，你会对机器人系统的底层结构有非常深入的理解，也知道如何从特定的机器人中发挥出最佳性能。而我认为，这类见解往往是像我们这样在学术界的人所缺乏的，因为我们本身不造机器人，我们只是从制造商那里购买机器人。所以在展示类人机器人令人惊艳的敏捷动作演示方面，工业界确实比学术界具备明显的优势。 但我认为，当前学术界也有其优势，尤其是在开发一些更通用的控制模型方面。这些模型并不仅限于复现某个具体行为，而是朝着更通用的控制基础模型方向发展，目标是能够复现人类能够执行的各种行为。从这个角度看，我觉得学术界在这些通用控制模型的探索上可能略领先于工业界。不过话说回来，这些学术模型所产生的运动质量，可能还达不到工业界展示中那样流畅或自然的水平。 13. 在未来的研究方向中，您有哪些感兴趣的领域？或者您认为哪些方向是特别有前景的？ 目前我感兴趣的研究方向是开发更通用的控制模型。与其为某一个特定技能设计专门的控制器，我们更希望能构建出可以复现人类各种运动技能的通用模型。我认为我们已经从一些研究中看到了希望，比如maskedmimic和cmu团队的一些成果(phc) 。但目前这些控制方法中仍然缺少一个关键问题的解决方案——我们该如何确保控制器能够生成看起来自然的行为？另外，当你拥有了这样一个通用控制器之后，又该如何有效地将它迁移或重用于新的任务？目前我们能够复用的控制器，大多仍局限于非常简单的任务，比如简单的导航行为。因此，我们未来希望努力的方向就是：如何发展这些更强的通用模型，并使它们能够被复用于更复杂的任务中。 14. 未来的“通用控制器”应该是什么样的？我们在构建更大规模控制系统时，可以从生成模型中学到什么？ 我认为未来的通用控制模型，其本质也会是生成模型。我的看法是：未来的控制器将不再是传统意义上的控制模块，而是像生成图像或文本那样的生成式模型，只不过它们生成的是运动指令（motor commands）。未来我们会看到越来越多生成模型直接作为控制系统的核心架构。 接下来要解决的问题就是：我们该如何以可扩展的方式训练这些生成式控制器，使其能处理大规模数据集？如果数据集中包含动作标签，那目前来看，监督学习依然是在多个领域中最具扩展性的训练方法。但如果没有明确动作信息，就需要采用强化学习。在我们的实践中，基于运动跟踪的强化学习方法在大规模数据集训练上效果最好。 正如你提到的，像amp这样的算法，以及一些对抗式模仿方法，在扩展规模时容易出现模式坍缩问题（mode collapse），即模型只输出少数几类行为，丢失了多样性。但我们发现，如果使用运动跟踪作为目标函数，这个问题会大大减轻。这类似于监督学习与对抗式学习（如 gans）之间的差别。 因此，在我们近期的研究，比如 masked mimic 项目中，我们重新采用了基于跟踪的训练方式，来训练生成式控制模型。 15. 您认为我们是否需要引入一个潜在空间（latent space）？比如使用高斯分布，或者傅里叶变换之类的方式来构建？在设计控制器时，是否需要一个这样的潜在空间结构？ 我并不认为潜在空间（latent space）是绝对必要的，它不是一个“必须有”的组件。潜在空间只是生成模型用来表达复杂分布的一种机制，但我们也可以在没有潜在空间的情况下构建出优秀的生成模型。比如大语言模型（llms）就是非常强大的生成模型，它们并没有显式地依赖潜在空间。我认为在控制任务上，也可能采用类似的方式。 不过话说回来，目前我们使用的很多主流生成模型，确实都采用了某种形式的潜在空间。比如扩散模型（diffusion models）就是典型代表，它们在当前来看是效果最好的生成模型之一。因此，虽然潜在空间可能会有帮助，但它并不是非用不可的关键。我们真正需要的，是一个足够灵活且强大的生成架构，能够捕捉和表达多模态行为的复杂分布。 16. 通用控制器会是某种形式的moe吗？ 总的来说，我不太倾向于使用“专家混合模型”（mixture of experts）那种每个专家分别训练的方式。问题在于，如果你为不同技能分别训练控制器，然后再尝试将它们组合在一起，其实很难保证它们之间能够很好地协同工作。 比如，不能保证不同专家之间的动作能够稳定地切换与衔接，这会让整个系统变得脆弱、不稳定，难以实现最优的控制性能。当然，在大模型（比如语言模型）中确实也有“专家混合层（moe layer）”，但那种结构不是简单把多个独立模型拼接在一起，而是作为一个整体架构的一部分，进行端到端训练的。 我个人认为，这种集成式的 moe 架构 —— 即模型内部使用专家层、并进行统一训练 —— 比将多个分开的专家模型后期组合起来要更有前景。作为一种基本的研究理念，我个人更倾向于端到端训练，而不是将模块分开训练后再试图组合在一起。 对我来说，由于我的大部分研究依赖于仿真到现实迁移（sim-to-real transfer），所以我对硬件设计者最大的期望是：尽量设计出更容易模拟的机器人。 具体来说，希望能够确保，第一，电机的行为尽可能接近理想的pd控制（比例-微分控制）；第二，机器人的运动学结构（kinematic structure）可以在物理仿真中轻松复现。这样可以最大限度地缩小仿真与现实之间的差距（sim-to-real gap）。机器人电机的动力学特性（motor dynamics），可能是我们在实际工作中最常遇到的最大仿真到现实差距（sim-to-real gap）之一。 什么是pd控制： pd控制，全称是 比例-微分控制（proportional-derivative control），是一种非常常见的控制策略，尤其在机器人学、自动控制和仿真物理引擎中大量应用。它的核心思想是：控制器根据当前位置误差（位置差）和误差变化率（速度差）来计算控制输出，去驱动系统达到目标状态。简单来说，p控制负责驱动，d控制负责刹车与稳定。 在仿真和实际机器人之间迁移（sim-to-real transfer）时，如果电机行为能很好地近似一个理想的 pd 控制器，那么仿真器里的动作与真实机器人动作差距就会更小，也更容易控制。 references： jason peng主页 https://xbpeng.github.io/ maskedmimic, sim-to-real transfer, generative control and humanoid hardware. whole-body control anyone working on humanoid motion control will be familiar with xue bin (jason) peng. over the past year, high-quality demonstrations of human-like humanoid movement have appeared across many platforms. much of their technical foundation can be traced to his pioneering work, including deepmimic, amp (adversarial motion priors) and ase (adversarial skill embeddings). these methods substantially lowered the barrier to motion imitation for humanoids and helped establish the foundations for flexible, natural movement. the discussion retains its april 2025 context. at the time of this interview, xue bin (jason) peng is an assistant professor at simon fraser university (sfu) and a research scientist at nvidia. his work lies at the intersection of computer graphics and machine learning, particularly reinforcement learning for motion control of simulated characters. his academic path is also noteworthy. his advisers—michiel van de panne, pieter abbeel and sergey levine—are among the most influential leading professors in character animation and robotic reinforcement learning. during his master's studies at the university of british columbia (ubc), jason worked with graphics researcher michiel van de panne. in addition to his foundational contributions to character animation, van de panne supervised the master's research of andrej karpathy, formerly tesla's ai director, and the phd of stelian coros, who leads eth zurich's computational robotics lab. jason then pursued his phd at the university of california, berkeley, advised by sergey levine and pieter abbeel, building a strong foundation in reinforcement learning and robot intelligence. in this interview, we discuss his research journey and several foundational contributions to humanoid whole-body motion control, along with his ideas for general-purpose controllers and recommendations for robot hardware. i hope it will be useful to people developing humanoid software and hardware. special thanks to dr. dun yang and dr. qiang zhang for helping prepare the interview and correct the transcript. i also thank dr. zhicheng wang, dr. haojie shi and dr. ziwen zhuang for contributing several important questions. the podcast episode can be found by searching for respark on xiaoyuzhou. contents ↓ from graphics to perspectives on mixture-of-experts architectures 17. recommendations for humanoid hardware 1. how did michiel van de panne, one of the most influential professors in character animation, and pieter abbeel, a pioneer of robotic reinforcement learning, shape your research and thinking? michiel was my adviser during my undergraduate and master's studies at ubc. honestly, without him, i might not be doing this research at all. i was interested in computer graphics and wanted to try research in the field. michiel worked on character animation at ubc, so i contacted him about participating in animation research. that was how i entered the area. i was not thinking about robotics then; i simply wanted to work in graphics. animation looked interesting, but machine learning had not yet become central to the work we were considering. much of it relied on traditional kinematic methods or hand-designed controllers. later, deepmind published continuous control with deep reinforcement learning. after reading it, we began studying reinforcement learning and deep reinforcement learning more closely as a way to train controllers for virtual characters. that was a turning point that gradually brought me into machine learning and its connection with animation. editorial note: the original calls the method deep q-learning; the cited paper introduces deep deterministic policy gradient (ddpg), an actor-critic method extending ideas from deep q-learning to continuous actions. during my phd at berkeley, i began working with sergey levine and pieter abbeel and gradually applied these techniques to controlling real robots, rather than only characters in virtual worlds. michiel, and later sergey and pieter, had a profound influence on my career. i feel very fortunate to have worked with them. without their guidance, i might now be doing something entirely different. 2. your research shifted from learning skills for virtual characters in graphics to reward-based training of real robots—a move from simulation to reality. what is the biggest difference between those directions? when i started working with real robots, i was surprised by how difficult things that seem obvious in simulation become in reality. state estimation, for example, was much harder than i had expected. in simulation, we can have full observability: positions, velocities and even the agent's complete internal state are directly available. on a real robot, even obtaining something as basic as linear velocity can be difficult. you need additional sensors and estimation algorithms, and the final estimate may still be noisy and inaccurate. partial observability was therefore one of the most striking challenges in my transition from simulation to real robotics. it remains a difficult problem today. what is partial observability? an environment is partially observable when an agent cannot access all information about the system's complete state. its decisions are based on only part of the environment, with observations that may be incomplete, uncertain or noisy. a robot moving through a room with only a forward-facing camera, for example, cannot see behind itself or to its sides. it may need to remember where it came from or estimate the environment through a sequence of actions. a fully observable environment in chess, every piece and its position are visible on the board. the game state is available, allowing decisions based on complete information, though finding the optimal move still requires computation. a partially observable environment imagine driving through fog while wearing dark glasses. you can see only a few meters ahead, rather than the whole route. you must infer the present state and choose actions using limited observations, past experience and internal memory. 3. what has left the deepest impression on you when working with real robots? state estimation certainly stands out, but another major issue is that real-world dynamics are non-stationary: they change over time. in a typical simulation, the dynamics are largely fixed. that makes experiments easy to reproduce. once a controller works, it can generally be run repeatedly with very consistent behavior. a real robot's dynamics keep changing. a controller may work well today and behave differently later. motors heat up after prolonged use, for example, changing the system dynamics. a controller that worked ten minutes ago might no longer be effective when you run it again. 4. how do you address challenges in sim-to-real transfer? the main challenges include partial observability, system uncertainty and changing real-robot dynamics. our central tool is domain randomization. in most of our studies, we train controllers in simulation and then deploy them directly on real robots. to reduce the reality gap, we randomly perturb physical parameters and observation conditions during training, including mass, friction, latency and sensor noise. this encourages stronger, more adaptive policies that generalize better to uncertainty in reality. domain randomization remains our main tool for sim-to-real transfer. could you give us a systematic overview of your main research directions and projects? what is the central idea behind each, and which important problems do they address? i can begin with deepmimic, an early project. its basic idea is simple: combine deep reinforcement learning with motion tracking. we wanted simulated characters to imitate a wide range of human movement skills for animation and virtual environments. before deepmimic, many animation controllers borrowed approaches from robotics, including trajectory optimization, optimal control and finite-state machines. their biggest problem was a lack of generality and substantial manual design. each new skill required designing a controller from scratch: one for walking, another for jumping, and much more time and effort for flips or complex acrobatics. this was not scalable over the long term, so much earlier research focused on very few specific behaviors. with deepmimic, we wanted a general framework capable of reproducing any human movement skill. we used deep reinforcement learning to train neural-network controllers. neural networks are powerful function approximators that can represent flexible, complex policies. instead of manually designing a finite-state machine for every skill, we can use a shared network architecture to adapt to all skills. what is a finite-state machine? a finite-state machine, or fsm, is a classical model in computer science and ai for representing transitions between a finite set of states. the system occupies one state at a time and changes state in response to inputs. motion tracking is the other key part of deepmimic. once we have a neural-network controller, how do we train it to perform different skills? conventionally, each skill might require its own reward function—one for walking and another for running—which is also difficult to scale. we use a shared reward mechanism: tracking a reference motion. give the controller a target motion, such as motion-capture data, and train it to imitate the sequence frame by frame. we found that this simple tracking reward, combined with policy-gradient reinforcement learning, can teach many skills without manually designing a new controller or imitation reward for each one. rather than designing separate control logic for every skill, we provide different reference motions and optimize the same training objective to learn the corresponding policies. that is the basic idea of deepmimic. an important project after deepmimic was amp, or adversarial motion priors. deepmimic provides a general framework for training controllers by tracking reference motions frame by frame. that is effective when a character should reproduce a particular motion precisely. many impressive humanoid demonstrations today are built on this kind of tracking technique. a key limitation is that controllers trained this way are very rigid. they often just play the same motion sequence over and over, cannot deviate from the prescribed trajectory, and cannot adapt well to new tasks. [editorial note: this describes the limitation motivating amp, rather than every capability of deepmimic. the original deepmimic work also combines imitation with task objectives and demonstrates recovery and multi-skill behavior.] in amp, we wanted a more flexible imitation objective that would not constrain the controller to frame-by-frame tracking. the idea is to replace trajectory tracking with distribution matching. instead of reproducing one precise trajectory, the controller generates behavior whose motion style matches the dataset overall. we use adversarial imitation learning, similar to a generative adversarial network, or gan. a discriminator learns to distinguish motion from the reference dataset from motion generated by a simulated character. the controller simultaneously learns to fool the discriminator by producing behavior that resembles the reference data. this offers more flexibility. the controller does not need to follow one sequence frame by frame. it can stitch together or combine motion fragments, generalize to behaviors not explicitly present in the dataset, and pursue task objectives that the demonstrations do not directly contain. amp therefore provides a stronger, more adaptive framework for motion imitation. some people reproducing amp report that their policy learns only transitions between individual frames, leaving the character stepping in place instead of moving. have you encountered this? is it a limitation of amp itself? yes, that can happen, depending on the design choices. a policy may get trapped in a local optimum, switching back and forth between one or two frames so that the character appears stuck and does not move. it can often be addressed by expanding the discriminator's temporal window. instead of showing it only two frames, show it a sequence of perhaps ten. observing a longer period makes unnatural behavior such as getting trapped in a single transition easier to recognize, encouraging smoother and more realistic dynamic movement. many methods for learning robot movement skills use a latent space to represent features, but that space is not intuitively interpretable to people. how do you control the safety of data in it, preventing unusual latent inputs from causing abnormal policy behavior? this is an important question. in a subsequent project, we introduced ase—adversarial skill embeddings—to address this kind of problem. many models, especially those using variational autoencoders, or vaes, have holes in their latent space: some codes decode into behavior that looks nothing like the training data. we do not have a perfect solution, but ase uses an approach resembling gan training to reduce the problem. in ase, we treat the controller as a decoder. it maps a latent code into a motion sequence that should resemble real reference motions. a discriminator judges whether the generated behavior matches the reference style, much like training a gan. an important advantage of adversarial training is that it encourages every point in the latent space, as far as possible to map to plausible behavior. this can reduce the likelihood of abnormal regions and lower the risk of policy errors. we cannot guarantee that strange behavior will never occur. some latent codes may still produce unnatural motions. but in our experiments, adversarially trained models such as ase are generally more robust and stable than traditional methods. how large is maskedmimic's sim-to-real gap? there is still a substantial gap between maskedmimic and deployment on real robots. in simulation, we can train controllers to reproduce thousands of motion clips. most real-robot systems are still at what i call the deepmimic stage: a controller often performs only one skill or one motion clip. maskedmimic animation systems can now support thousands of skills in one controller, but reliably transferring such high-capacity controllers to real robots is not yet something we can do. sim-to-real transfer is the central issue. even a well-trained simulated controller often needs substantial manual tuning on the real robot before it works. with thousands or tens of thousands of skills, debugging and validating each one individually in reality becomes prohibitively expensive. that is one of the largest current bottlenecks. 9. what are the strengths and weaknesses of imitation learning and reinforcement learning for movement skills? which has greater long-term potential? i am not sure they can be compared directly because they are essentially orthogonal paradigms. imitation learning can be implemented through supervised learning or reinforcement learning, depending on the available data. reinforcement learning can implement imitation, but it can also train a controller directly from rewards without demonstrations. they are not strictly opposing approaches. if we insist on comparing imitation learning with pure reinforcement learning that uses no demonstrations, we can consider the following trade-offs. the advantage of pure rl is that no demonstration data is required. you define an objective, perhaps a human-designed reward function, and train a controller to optimize it. the agent may discover better behaviors or strategies that people have not considered. systems such as alphago illustrate rl's ability to discover solutions beyond established human play. editorial note: the original alphago also learned from human games; alphago zero and alphazero are clearer examples of the demonstration-free learning discussed here. the disadvantage is that reward design can be complicated. to guide an agent toward a particular behavior, you may need a carefully designed function; otherwise it may learn something different from what you intended. those are some of rl's strengths and weaknesses. imitation learning largely reverses the trade-off. demonstrations make it easier to guide behavior because the training objective is to reproduce what appears in the data. that makes it easier to obtain human-like behavior or movement that matches our expectations. but collecting high-quality demonstrations can be difficult. for some tasks, few people can perform them well, making suitable data hard to obtain. the controller's behavior can also be more constrained: it often learns what humans have already done and has less ability to discover new strategies. in that sense, imitation may limit exploration and creativity. 10. what are the bottlenecks for rl in manipulation? one reason rl is less widely used in manipulation than in locomotion may be that easier opportunities remain. behavior cloning and supervised learning already work well. for manipulation, it is relatively straightforward to build a teleoperation system, collect many human demonstrations and train a controller with supervised learning. that often gives good results. with legged locomotion, high-quality robot demonstrations are much harder to collect, so we were almost forced to use reinforcement learning from the outset. most manipulation controllers today are still trained with supervised learning and behavior cloning, but i think manipulation will eventually follow a similar path. i think vision-language-action models, or vlas, will ultimately follow the development pattern of large language models. llms usually begin with predictive training on large amounts of human-produced data—supervision from the data itself in pretraining. to improve performance on a particular task or specialize the model, we then use fine-tuning or task-directed reinforcement learning. manipulation models may take a similar route. at present, we can train with supervised learning on large quantities of teleoperation data. to reach the best performance on a specific manipulation task, we may then need rl fine-tuning to optimize the model further. 11. more people are exploring large models such as vlas for robotics. what role do you see for large-scale architectures in learning robot skills? i think large multimodal models are very promising. we have observed very interesting emergent properties: complex behaviors that arise from these models. the main bottleneck, in my view, is inference speed. slow inference makes it difficult to use them for real-time low-level control. it resembles the distinction between slow and fast thinking. many vlas may serve as high-level planners running at a lower frequency, with their plans executed by smaller, faster and more responsive low-level controllers. the multimodal models are promising, but particularly for low-level control, we still need good controllers that turn high-level instructions into concrete actions. a relatively slow vla can work for slower, less dynamic tasks such as simple pick-and-place manipulation. agile whole-body motion, however, requires much higher-frequency control. at present, our computational resources are not sufficient to make these large multimodal models meet that requirement. 12. in locomotion control, has industry surpassed academia in some respects? yes. in some respects, industry has become better at producing highly agile, human-like robot behavior. manufacturers understand their robots' underlying systems deeply and know how to extract the best performance from a particular machine. academics like us often lack that insight because we buy robots rather than build them. industry therefore has a clear advantage in demonstrations of strikingly agile humanoid motion. academia also has strengths, especially in developing more general control models. instead of reproducing one behavior, we are moving toward control foundation models capable of many human skills. academia may be slightly ahead in exploring these general models. their motion quality, however, may still fall short of the smoothness and naturalness of industrial demonstrations. 13. which future research directions interest you, or seem especially promising? i am interested in more general control models. rather than designing a controller for one skill, we want models that reproduce many human movement skills. maskedmimic and work from cmu such as phc show promise. important questions remain: how can we ensure that the controller generates natural-looking behavior, and how can we transfer or reuse it effectively for new tasks? today, reusable controllers are often limited to simple tasks such as basic navigation. we want stronger general models that can be reused for more complex tasks. 14. what should a future general-purpose controller look like? what can larger control systems learn from generative models? i think future general control models will fundamentally be generative models. instead of traditional control modules, they will resemble models that generate images or text, except that they generate motor commands. we will see more generative models serving as the core architecture of control systems. the next question is how to train these generative controllers in a scalable way on large datasets. if the data includes action labels, supervised learning remains among the most scalable approaches across many domains. without explicit action information, we need reinforcement learning. in our experiments, motion-tracking-based rl has worked best for training on large motion datasets. as you mentioned, algorithms such as amp and other adversarial imitation methods can suffer from mode collapse when scaled: the model produces only a few kinds of behavior and loses diversity. we find that using motion tracking as the objective substantially reduces this problem. it resembles the difference between supervised and adversarial learning, such as gans. in recent work such as maskedmimic, we therefore returned to tracking-based training to develop generative control models. 15. do we need a latent space, perhaps built with a gaussian distribution or something like a fourier transform? is that structure necessary when designing a controller? i do not think a latent space is absolutely necessary. it is one mechanism for representing complex distributions in a generative model, but strong generative models can be built without a separately sampled latent-code space. large language models, for example, are powerful generative models that do not explicitly depend on that kind of latent space. a similar approach may be possible for control. this does not mean llms lack internal hidden representations. many leading generative models we use do employ some form of latent variables. diffusion models are an example and are among the strongest generative approaches at present. a latent space may therefore help, but it is not indispensable. what we need is a sufficiently flexible and powerful architecture that captures the complex, multimodal distribution of behavior. editorial clarification: noise variables in diffusion and a learned, compressed latent space are different concepts; not every diffusion model requires the latter. 16. will a general-purpose controller use some form of mixture of experts? i am generally less inclined toward a mixture of experts in which each expert is trained separately. if controllers are trained independently for different skills and combined afterward, it is difficult to ensure that they cooperate well. smooth, stable transitions between experts are not guaranteed, making the whole system fragile and limiting control performance. large models such as language models do use moe layers, but that is different from simply joining independent models. those layers are part of a single architecture trained end to end. i find an integrated moe architecture—with expert layers inside a jointly trained model—more promising than combining separate experts afterward. as a general research principle, i prefer end-to-end training to training modules independently and then trying to assemble them. 17. what recommendations do you have for current humanoid hardware? since much of my work relies on sim-to-real transfer, my main request to hardware designers is to make robots easier to simulate. specifically, first, motor behavior should approximate ideal proportional-derivative, or pd, control as closely as possible. second, the kinematic structure should be easy to reproduce in a physics simulator. that minimizes the sim-to-real gap. motor dynamics are among the largest sources of mismatch we encounter in practice. what is pd control? proportional-derivative control is widely used in robotics, automatic control and physics simulation. it calculates a control output from the current position error and its rate of change—the velocity error—to drive the system toward a target state. in simple terms, the proportional component drives the correction, while the derivative component provides damping and stability. when transferring between simulation and a real robot, motors that closely approximate an ideal pd controller reduce the difference between simulated and actual behavior, making control easier. references jason peng's homepage deepmimic: https://xbpeng.github.io/projects/deepmimic/index.html
