osh-ep01-toddlerbot: osh ep1：toddlerbot——来自斯坦福的小型人形机器人开源项目 讨论toddlerbot的开源硬件、运动与操作算法、开发生态与社区。 开源硬件（osh） 石麻笔记静悄悄，一定是在憋大招，欢迎来到石麻笔记新系列open source hardware（osh），这是即robot data ep10 robot data第一季访谈总结和robot foundation model （rfm）rfm ep01：pi和π0具身基础模型之后的第三个连载系列。osh系列访谈比较特色的地方在于，除了作者访谈，我们也会尝试复现，让各位看官更直观的对比“卖家秀”和“买家秀”，来看看到底这些开源机器人项目work不work。osh第一期，我们选择了来自斯坦福的开源小人形toddlerbot。 toddlerbot（https://toddlerbot.github.io/）是一款低成本（$6000）、开源的人形机器人，专为机器人与人工智能研究而设计。toddlerbot的两个一作分别是haochen（https://hshi74.github.io/）和weizhuo（http://me.weizhuowang.com/）。haochen目前是斯坦福大学计算机科学专业的二年级博士生，导师是 karen liu 和 shuran song。weizhuo是斯坦福大学机器人方向的博士三年级在读生，目前由 monroe kennedy iii 和 c. karen liu 两位教授共同指导。感谢两位博士接受我的访谈邀请以及复现指导。本次toddlerbot的复现工作由来自厦大机器人队的雨涵和锦标完成。 以下为本文目录 👇 1.toddlerbot简介 2. 为什么想做开源小人形 3. 硬件设计思路 4. 为什么小人形就只能用舵机方案？ 5. 移动算法层面的创新 6. 操作算法 7. 机器人开源与商业公司之间的竞争 8. 关于toddlerbot的其他特点 9.鸣谢 10.小调研 1. toddlerbot简介 toddlerbot是一款低成本、开源的人形机器人平台，专为可扩展的策略学习以及机器人与人工智能领域的研究设计。它的身高56厘米，体重3.4公斤，全身有 30 个主动自由度（dof）：每只手臂 7 个自由度，每条腿 6 个自由度，脖子 2 个自由度，腰部 2 个自由度。下图绿色标记表示两种末端执行器设计 —— 一个柔顺式手掌和一个平行夹爪。紫色标记表示传感器和电子系统的布局（采用爆炸视图展示），包括两颗鱼眼摄像头、一个扬声器、两个麦克风、一个惯性测量单元（imu）以及一台 jetson orin nx 计算机。全身零部件采购和3d打印结构件成本大约在6000美金。 toddlerbot“卖家秀”- by 斯坦福haochen&weizhuo toddlerbot“买家秀”- by 厦门大学 雨涵&锦标 我们最开始想做这样一个开源人形机器人是2023年的corl，当时在corl逛了一圈，发现关于人形机器人的研究论文并不多，但在互联网上，大家似乎对人形机器人相关研究很感兴趣，那是什么因素阻止了大家在人形机器人方向上的科研探索呢？（那个时间点还不像现在大家可以买到宇树的h1或者g1）。我们意识到，核心问题在于硬件——大多数研究者缺少一个好用的平台，难以在算法上做出创新。以前也有过很多人形机器人的平台，但是他们大多数都无法满足现在从事ai 算法的科研需求。对于适用于 ai算法的人形硬件，我们认为有几点要求：相对便宜，比较好用耐用，上手门槛低，比较好维修，可以做 locomotion rl sim2real, 也可以做 manipulation behavior cloning。 而我个人一直很喜欢leap hand这个工作，甚至在家里做了一个，发现使用体验不错。这让我觉得，开源硬件可能是一个有影响力的方向，也能为整个研究社区带来真正的贡献。 我们就想能不能做一个开源的人形机器人？刚开始和导师们讨论时，他们都觉得难度太大，因为之前已经有不少开源人形机器人的尝试，但大多未能成功。尽管如此，我们依然相信自己可以做到。因此，从项目一开始，我们就确立了核心目标——一定要开源，一定要让其他研究者能够复现我们的成果。 在这个过程中，我们始终围绕这一前提，不断优化和迭代性能，最终做出了一个既能完成各种运动和操作，又能被他人复现的人形机器人。 大家都知道，人身上有非常多的肌肉，要完美模拟人体结构，仅依靠几十个电机是不可能的。但是所有这些肌肉最终都会作用在具体的关节上。经过我们的分析，人的动作最关键的关节大约是32个左右。 我们希望机器人具有全功能性，因此对自由度的数量非常重视，尽可能将所有需要的自由度都包含进来。例如，我们的手臂设计了7个自由度，而通常人型机器人的手一般只有4到6个自由度。腿部方面，我们在脚踝处设计了两个自由度，大腿部分则设计了全部三个自由度。这个部位的设计经过了多次迭代，大约制作了五六个版本。我们还在迭代更好的设计，预计近期会发布。 腰部本来计划设计三个自由度，但由于技术难度，最终实现了两个，包括侧弯和绕z轴的旋转动作。舍弃了前弯，是因为这个动作已经包含在髋关节的俯仰（hip pitch）自由度中了。考虑到后续与人交互和动作创新的需求，我们在脖子部分设计了两个自由度，能够实现转头和俯仰动作，未来有需求时可能会加上一个侧头的自由度。整体而言，我们的机器人共有30个自由度。作为参考，宇树g1自由度为29个。 另外，为确保机器人的可复现性，我们的设计思路是让机器人越小越好。小型化带来的优势明显，例如所需设备和空间少，一张书桌即可进行制作。经过优化，我们的机器人高度最终确定在55厘米左右，重量仅为3.5千克，一只手即可轻松拎起。 小型化不仅有助于实现敏捷的运动，因为功率密度更高，也更加安全。在家庭环境中， 这样的小型机器人不太可能伤害小孩或宠物，反而是机器人更容易被小孩或宠物损坏。此外，较小尺寸和轻重量也让开发过程更容易。如果机器人出现问题，可以很方便地用手直接搬起。 现在的 ai 算法因为本质上都是黑箱，很难在算法层面提供安全性的保障，所以足够小可以更好地保证安全。相比之下，全尺寸机器人在科研和教育环境中存在安全风险。如果控制策略（policy）出现问题，机器人可能执行危险动作，对周围人或环境造成伤害。 因此，我们的核心设计原则是尽可能小的尺寸、足够多的自由度，以及高可复现性。为进一步提高可复现性，我们的机器人除电机外的所有构件都采用3d打印制作。因为在家庭环境中，不方便使用车床或cnc加工设备，但随着3d打印技术的快速发展，现在在家就能完成制作。 我们也看到过身边使用全尺寸机器人，曾经发生过由于机器人的意外动作导致人员受伤的事件，这种情况非常危险，我们希望通过上述设计策略避免这样的风险。 我们采用的是传统的减速齿轮方案即舵机方案，而不是准直驱（qdd）。其实这里涉及到一个物理原理。当电机的尺寸非常小的时候，电机内部的线圈绕组必须非常细。这导致线圈无法承载较大的电流，只能通过提高电压来提升转速，但同时能够提供的扭矩却非常有限。因此在这种情况下，如果仍然采用传统的无刷电机方案，其性能表现实际上与普通舵机就没有太大区别。 这也意味着，在这个尺寸下，准直驱（qdd）的优势可能比不上舵机方案。根据我们的粗略估计，我们机器人尺寸大约在80厘米左右可能是 qdd 方案的一个 sweet spot，更小尺寸的机器人无法有效实现qdd驱动方式。 舵机实际上指的是一种包含空心杯小型电机的装置，其内部配备了高倍率的减速齿轮组。具体来说，舵机内有一个空心杯电机（coreless motor），最初应用时只需通电即可旋转，因此控制电路相对简单。一般情况下，它的编码器安装在输出轴位置，精度相对较低。同时，由于舵机最显著的特点是使用了非常高的减速比（通常远超过准直驱qdd方案的减速比），这使得舵机与无框力矩电机的准直驱（qdd）方案有明显差别。准直驱电机常见的减速比一般在5倍到40倍之间，而舵机的减速比则可能达到数百倍甚至更高。这种高减速比结构通常封装在一个长方体的盒子内，因此在结构和性能上与qdd有着明显的差异。 我们算法在 rl 这块用的是比较标准化的。整个流程是，先做一个舵机的 model，也就是sysid。使用一些 position tracking 数据来拟合sysid的参数。 基于拟合后的sysid参数，再去调整mujoco里面 urdf 等动力学（dynamics）参数，使得模型尽可能精准地反映真实情况。 其次就是训练一个 rl policy，并且加上非常多的 domain randomization。在训练 rl policy 时，我们用 zmp 生成一个 reference motion，让 rl policy 去 track。 在 simulation 里面 train 出 policy 之后，只要之前做的 sysid digital twin 足够精确，并且 domain randomization 参数调得比较好的话，就可以直接 deploy，也就是尝试将仿真和真实世界做到非常非常相似。这样一来，只要你看到在 simulation 里面训练出来的东西能 work，基本上它在现实生活中也能差不多地 work。 做这个sysid流程的目的是通过系统辨识的方式找到一套可以准确描述电机特性的参数集合，再把这些参数放入仿真环境里去使用。每个电机都有自己独特的特性，不同型号的电机之间存在差异。比如电机本身具有一定的惯性，电机转动起来时，它的速度能达到多少，它可以提供多少扭矩等等。这些特性你都需要明确地在仿真环境里体现出来，因为只有这样，你的策略（policy）才能知道，当给出一个特定的位置目标（position target）时，电机会怎样去反应。 因为这个机器人关节数量比较多，所以通过遥杆等其他方式去操控会比较困难。目前我们也在尝试用 vr 或者 mocap 等方式进行遥操作，这个方向也在进行中，之后可能会 release 相关成果。 我们现在之所以采用 aloha 风格的操作方式，是因为我们知道 aloha style 能够采集到质量有保证的数据，这样用这些数据来训练 diffusion policy 时，成功率会更高一些。 关于 aloha style，指的其实就是两套同构的机器人系统，其中一套机器人动作会被实时复制粘贴到另一套上去。大家习惯上就称这种方式为 aloha style。 商业公司很难做到完全开源，因为最终他们还是靠卖硬件盈利。对只想购买整机而不想从零开始组装的人来说，买整机确实更方便。但是，人形机器人总会面临损坏的问题，一旦出现问题，如果你购买的是整机，自己可能很难维修，需要向原厂定制零部件并进行替换。除非厂商能做到高度模块化，否则维修仍会是个问题。 而完全开源的机器人则有明显优势，比如在我们这里，一旦机器人某个部分坏了，你只需要重新3d打印出来就可以解决。这正是开源的好处之一。修理机器人几乎是无法避免的，尤其是涉及人形机器人时，必然会出现各种需要维护的问题。 在我看来，组装开源机器人本身就是一次动手能力的培训过程。通过亲自动手，你不仅能提升自己的技能，更能深入理解机器人的工作原理。当机器人出现问题时，你能迅速定位故障点，这对未来的开发也会有极大的帮助。 虽然购买完整的机器人套餐对用户来说很方便，但对于学术界或研发领域来说，培养动手能力和深入理解机器人的过程同样重要，甚至是必不可少的。 我们在设计时，有一个比较独特的点，就是机器人的手臂力量和腿部力量是均衡的。目前大多数人形机器人设计时都会更侧重于腿部运动（locomotion），导致腿部很强壮，但手臂的自由度很少、力量也相对较弱。而我们的机器人则不同，手臂和腿的力量是差不多的，因此可以轻松完成引体向上、俯卧撑之类的动作。 未来，我们可能还会进一步开发更具动态性的任务，因此在设计时就提前考虑了这一点，特意把机器人的结构做得更强壮些，同时预留了许多扩展接口，以便之后能有更多发挥空间。 另外，在人形机器人领域，有一点是特别值得关注的，就是机器人和人的交互。严格来说，在完成具体的实用任务时，人形机器人可能并不比轮式或四足机器人在特定场景下更有优势。虽然人形机器人常被认为是最通用的形式，但这种通用性是在算法和控制完全成熟的前提下才能体现的。 我个人认为人形机器人最突出的优势是它与人类形态相似，这种相似性使它在与人交互时具备一些独特的优势。因此，我们考虑未来将机器人向社交方向进一步拓展，让它更自然地与小朋友和成年人进行互动。借助人形机器人的可爱外形，可以让人们更愿意、更快速地接受并与它进行自然交流。 这种想法其实带有一定的产品化思路，但同时也可以为开发者提供一个平台，在此基础上继续提升人机交互方面的能力。 过去很多社交机器人通常只是预先编程几个特定动作或技能，通过简单反馈来重复执行一些预设的轨迹，但这远远不够通用。如果想实现真正自然且通用的互动，就可能需要借助大模型，从真实的人机交互数据出发，在基础模型之上进行微调，深入进行科研探索。 我认为 toddlerbot 最令人激动的一点，就是我们会有更多的同学参与到这个平台的开发和使用中来，不断地迭代提升软件和硬件，所以我比较期待几年之后 toddlerbot 会变成什么样子。 特别感谢两位十年老友dj和aj的支持，帮我们这次toddlerbot复现提供设备；也要感谢来自厦大机器人队的雨涵和锦标，两位学弟是我们复现toddlerbot的主力。当然还要感谢我的老师，厦大机器人队指导教师胡天林老师一路支持。 osh ep01: toddlerbot—an open-source small humanoid from stanford an interview with toddlerbot's creators on reproducible humanoid hardware, locomotion, manipulation and community development, alongside our own build. open-source hardware (osh) when smart note goes quiet, it usually means something new is taking shape. welcome to our new open source hardware series, or osh—our third ongoing series, following robot data, whose first season concluded with ep10: robot data season one interview roundup, and robot foundation model, introduced in rfm ep01: pi and the pi0 embodied foundation model. what makes osh different is that, alongside interviews with the creators, we will also try building their projects ourselves. this gives readers a more direct comparison between the creators' demonstrations and a user's own results, and lets us see whether these open-source robotics projects really work. for our first episode, we chose toddlerbot, an open-source small humanoid from stanford. toddlerbot (https://toddlerbot.github.io/) is a low-cost, open-source humanoid designed for robotics and ai research, with a cost of about $6,000. its two joint first authors are haochen shi (https://hshi74.github.io/) and weizhuo wang (http://me.weizhuowang.com/). at the time of this interview, haochen is a second-year computer science phd student at stanford, advised by karen liu and shuran song. weizhuo is a third-year robotics phd student at stanford, jointly advised by monroe kennedy iii and c. karen liu. thank you both for accepting my interview invitation and advising us on reproducing the project. our toddlerbot build was completed by yuhan and jinbiao from the xiamen university robotics team. contents 1. introducing toddlerbot 2. why build an open-source small humanoid? 3. hardware design 4. why use servo motors for a small humanoid? 5. locomotion algorithms 6. manipulation algorithms 7. open-source robots and commercial competition 8. other features of toddlerbot 9. acknowledgements 10. a short survey toddlerbot is a low-cost, open-source humanoid platform designed for scalable policy learning and research in robotics and ai. it stands 56 cm tall, weighs 3.4 kg and has 30 active degrees of freedom: seven in each arm, six in each leg, two in the neck and two in the waist. green markers in the diagram indicate two end-effector designs: a compliant palm and a parallel-jaw gripper. purple markers show the sensor and electronics layout in an exploded view, including two fisheye cameras, a speaker, two microphones, an inertial measurement unit (imu) and a jetson orin nx computer. purchasing all the components and producing the 3d-printed structural parts costs approximately $6,000. toddlerbot: the creators' demonstration, by haochen and weizhuo at stanford toddlerbot: our reproduction, by yuhan and jinbiao at xiamen university we first wanted to build an open-source humanoid at corl 2023. walking around the conference, we noticed that there were not many papers on humanoid robots, even though people online seemed very interested in humanoid research. what was preventing researchers from exploring this area? at that point, people could not buy unitree's h1 or g1 as they can today. we realized that hardware was the central problem: most researchers lacked a usable platform on which to innovate in algorithms. many humanoid platforms had existed before, but most did not meet the needs of today's ai research. we felt a humanoid platform for ai algorithms should be relatively inexpensive, easy to use, durable, accessible to newcomers and easy to repair. it should support reinforcement learning for locomotion with sim-to-real transfer, as well as behavior cloning for manipulation. i have always liked the leap hand project. i even built one at home and found it worked well. that made me feel that open-source hardware could be an influential direction and make a real contribution to the research community. so we asked ourselves whether we could build an open-source humanoid. when we first discussed it with our advisers, they felt it would be too difficult: there had already been several attempts at open-source humanoids, and most had not succeeded. still, we believed we could do it. from the start, we established a core goal: it had to be open-source, and other researchers had to be able to reproduce our results. throughout the process, we kept that premise at the center of our work, continuously improving and iterating on performance. eventually, we built a humanoid that could perform a range of locomotion and manipulation tasks and could also be reproduced by other people. the human body has a great many muscles, and it is impossible to perfectly reproduce its structure with only a few dozen motors. but all those muscles ultimately act on specific joints. our analysis suggested that approximately 32 joints are the most important for human movement. we wanted a versatile robot, so we paid close attention to the number of degrees of freedom and tried to include all those it would need. each arm, for example, has seven degrees of freedom, whereas humanoid arms often have only four to six. each ankle has two degrees of freedom, and the upper leg includes all three. that part of the design went through roughly five or six versions. we are still working on improvements and expect to release a better design soon. we originally planned three degrees of freedom in the waist, but technical difficulties led us to implement two: lateral bending and rotation around the z axis. we omitted forward bending because hip pitch already provides that movement. to support future interaction with people and new movements, we gave the neck two degrees of freedom for turning and pitching the head. we may add lateral head tilt if it becomes necessary. overall, the robot has 30 degrees of freedom. for comparison, unitree's g1 has 29. to make the robot reproducible, we also wanted it to be as small as possible. miniaturization has clear benefits: it requires less equipment and space, and it can be built on a desk. after optimization, we settled on a height of about 55 cm and a weight of just 3.5 kg, so it can easily be lifted with one hand. a smaller robot can move more nimbly thanks to higher power density, and it is also safer. in a home, a robot this small is unlikely to hurt a child or a pet; the robot is more likely to be damaged by them. its size and weight also make development easier. if something goes wrong, you can simply pick it up by hand. current ai algorithms are essentially black boxes, making it difficult to guarantee safety at the algorithmic level. keeping the robot small helps reduce the consequences of failures. full-size robots, by comparison, carry risks in research and educational settings. if a control policy goes wrong, the robot may perform dangerous movements that harm people or its surroundings. our central design principles are therefore the smallest practical size, enough degrees of freedom and high reproducibility. to further improve reproducibility, all structural components other than the motors are 3d-printed. lathes and cnc machining equipment are inconvenient to use at home, whereas the rapid development of 3d printing now makes home fabrication possible. we have also seen incidents around us in which unexpected movements from full-size robots injured people. that is very dangerous, and we hope these design choices help avoid such risks. we use conventional geared servo motors rather than quasi-direct drive, or qdd. there is a physical reason for this. when a motor is very small, its internal coil windings must be extremely thin. they cannot carry a large current, so higher voltage is needed to increase speed, while the available torque remains very limited. under these conditions, a conventional brushless motor does not actually perform very differently from an ordinary servo motor. at this scale, qdd may therefore offer fewer advantages than servos. our rough estimate is that a robot around 80 cm tall could be a sweet spot for qdd. in our assessment, a smaller robot of this design cannot use qdd effectively. here, a servo refers to a unit containing a small coreless motor and a high-ratio gearbox. a coreless motor can rotate as soon as power is supplied, so its control circuit is relatively simple. the encoder is usually mounted at the output shaft and has comparatively low precision. a defining feature of these servos is their very high reduction ratio, usually far higher than in qdd. that distinguishes them from qdd systems using frameless torque motors. qdd motors commonly have reduction ratios between 5:1 and 40:1, while servos may reach several hundred to one or more. this high-ratio assembly is usually enclosed in a rectangular housing, with a structure and performance quite different from qdd. technical note: this describes the high-ratio servo design being discussed, not a universal definition of a servo. servo actuators may use different motor types; the ratios and size threshold above are the interviewees' engineering estimates. our reinforcement learning approach is fairly standard. we first build a servo model through system identification, or sysid, fitting its parameters with position-tracking data. we then use those fitted parameters to adjust the dynamics parameters in mujoco, including the urdf-related model parameters, so that the model reflects reality as accurately as possible. next, we train an rl policy with extensive domain randomization. during training, we use the zero-moment point, or zmp, to generate a reference motion for the policy to track. once the policy is trained in simulation, we can deploy it directly if the system-identified digital twin is accurate enough and the domain randomization parameters are well tuned. the goal is to make simulation and the real world extremely similar. then, if something works in simulation, it will generally work about as well in real life. system identification gives us a set of parameters that accurately describe the motor's characteristics, which we then use in simulation. each motor has its own properties, and different models behave differently. a motor has inertia, a maximum achievable speed and a certain torque capacity, for example. these characteristics must be explicitly represented in the simulator so that the policy can understand how the motor will respond to a particular position target. the robot has many joints, so controlling it with a joystick or similar interfaces is difficult. we are also exploring teleoperation with vr and motion capture. that work is ongoing, and we may release the results later. for now, we use an aloha-style interface because we know it can collect reliably high-quality data. training a diffusion policy with that data gives us a better success rate. aloha-style control means using two robots with the same structure: the movements of one are copied to the other in real time. people generally refer to this arrangement as aloha-style teleoperation. it is difficult for a commercial company to make everything fully open-source, because ultimately it earns money by selling hardware. buying an assembled robot is certainly more convenient for someone who does not want to build it from scratch. but humanoids inevitably get damaged. if you bought a complete robot, it may be difficult to repair yourself: you may need custom replacement parts from the manufacturer. unless the company achieves a high degree of modularity, repair remains a problem. a fully open-source robot has clear advantages. with ours, if a part breaks, you can simply 3d-print it again. that is one benefit of open source. robot repairs are almost unavoidable, especially for humanoids, which inevitably need various forms of maintenance. in my view, assembling an open-source robot is itself a form of practical training. working on it yourself improves your skills and gives you a deeper understanding of how the robot works. when a problem occurs, you can quickly locate the fault. that is extremely useful for future development. buying a complete robot package is convenient, but for academic researchers and developers, gaining hands-on skills and a deep understanding of the robot is equally important—even essential. one distinctive choice in our design is that the arms and legs have comparable strength. most humanoids prioritize legged locomotion, resulting in strong legs but weaker arms with fewer degrees of freedom. our robot is different: its arms are about as strong as its legs, so it can easily perform movements such as pull-ups and push-ups. we may develop more dynamic tasks in the future, so we planned for that from the outset. we deliberately made the structure more robust and included many expansion interfaces to leave room for further development. human–robot interaction is another particularly interesting aspect of humanoids. strictly speaking, for specific practical tasks, a humanoid may not have an advantage over a wheeled or quadruped robot in a given setting. humanoids are often described as the most general-purpose form, but that generality depends on algorithms and control becoming fully mature. personally, i think the humanoid's most striking advantage is its resemblance to a person. this gives it distinctive strengths in human interaction. we are therefore considering developing the robot further in a social direction, so it can interact more naturally with children and adults. its cute humanoid appearance may make people more willing to accept it and start interacting naturally with it. there is an element of product thinking in this idea, but it can also provide a platform on which developers can continue improving human–robot interaction. many earlier social robots only had a few preprogrammed movements or skills. simple feedback caused them to repeat preset trajectories, but that is far from general-purpose interaction. to achieve genuinely natural and general interaction, we may need large models, using real human–robot interaction data to fine-tune foundation models and pursue deeper research. to me, the most exciting thing about toddlerbot is that more students will participate in developing and using the platform, continuously improving its software and hardware. i am looking forward to seeing what toddlerbot becomes in a few years. special thanks to dj and aj, two friends of ten years, for supporting our toddlerbot reproduction with equipment. i also want to thank yuhan and jinbiao from the xiamen university robotics team, the two younger alumni who did the main work on our build. and, of course, thank you to my teacher, hu tianlin, the team's faculty adviser, for his continued support. we will select another nine open-source hardware projects to reproduce and will continue improving and iterating on these platforms. recommendations for good open-source hardware projects are welcome. we also particularly need people who understand robot joints, mechanical body design and motion control algorithms. do you think small humanoids, approximately 50–70 cm tall, are valuable? options: yes; no. what kind of development support do you prefer? options: open-source hardware/software; modular design; a complete sdk; community support. have you developed a small humanoid robot before? options: yes; no. would you participate in early testing or crowdfunding for a small humanoid? options: yes; no. what price range would you accept? options: rmb 2,000–5,000; rmb 5,000–10,000; rmb 10,000–20,000; rmb 20,000–30,000. are you a student or currently working? options: undergraduate student; graduate student; software development engineer; robotics hardware development engineer; other employed role. would you prefer a small humanoid to use servo motors or dedicated joint actuators? options: servo motors; joint actuators. original poll: please take part in the original wechat article.
rfm-ep05-hi-robot: rfm ep05：hi robot——和史潇洋聊一聊如何教机器人更好地“听懂”与“思考” 与史潇洋讨论hi robot、语言理解、高层策略与vla的结合。 机器人学习与基础模型（rfm） 在机器人基础模型（robot foundation model，rfm）系列，我在rfm ep04：pi0 vs helix vs go-1三类vla模型框架对比解析总结了以π0为代表的vla模型结构，在rfm ep01：pi和π0具身基础模型根据sergey的talk总结了关于π0的总体思路和介绍。 今天介绍的hi robot是pi在2025年2月末公布的一个工作，它的核心思想是让机器人能够“思考”复杂的指令、反馈和插话。大家都知道vlm可以直接控制机器人，但如果指令太复杂，机器人无法直接理解和执行怎么办？hi robot就是用于解决这个问题。我也非常荣幸的邀请到hi robot: open-ended instruction following with hierarchical vision-language-action models（基于层级视觉-语言-动作模型的开放式指令跟随）这篇工作的一作史潇洋博士进行访谈。 史潇洋是斯坦福大学计算机专业的博士生，导师是 chelsea finn，同时也是 physical intelligence（pi）的研究员。此前，她曾在 nvidia research 与 yuke zhu 和 jim fan 合作工作。她在南加州大学（usc）获得了计算机科学学士学位，导师是 joseph j. lim 和 youngwoon lee。史潇洋的研究兴趣广泛集中在机器人学习领域，研究目标是打造能够自然完成复杂、长周期任务的通用机器人。 关于π0，相信大家在科技媒体上经常会看到诸如“对标π0大脑”之类的字眼。有些pr文，我深度看完之后会非常困惑，这些创业公司pr的业务和π0并没什么相关性。在阅读今天这篇科普博客之前，各位读者可以思考一个问题：你们理解的π0这类vla是更偏向high-level policy还是low-level policy？对应到国内的说法是更偏向大脑还是小脑？ 以下为本文目录 👇 1. 关于hi robot 2. hi robot和π0解决问题的差异性？ 3. π0的指令和hi robot的指令有什么异同？ 4. hi robot和直接接入一个vlm有什么区别？ 5. 为什么hi robot指令理解比vlm做得好？ 6. 怎么解决grounding的问题 7. vla和rl怎么结合？ 8. hi robot方法介绍 9. 关于π0的数据问题 10. 怎么理解high-level policy的训练过程？ 11. 怎么理解第2步数据生成vlm 12. hi robot使用的数据是怎么构建的 13. hi robot模块对vla是必须的吗？ 14. 实时交互场景hi robot是必需的吗? 在进入采访内容之前，我们可以先从pi的官网了解一些关于hi robot的总体介绍。hi robot的初衷是为了让机器人在面对复杂任务时，也像人一样“思考”，有个小声音在脑中指导它下一步该怎么做。hi robot将vla（如 π0）整合进一个两层的推理流程中。π0是反应快速、执行动作的“s1快系统”，而高层的vlm则扮演“s2慢系统”的角色，负责思考和语言理解，通过“自我对话”的方式，把复杂任务拆分成简单的中间步骤，再交给π0去完成。 hi robot视频介绍 hi robot这个high-level policy是一个vlm，实际上它使用的vlm骨干网络与π0完全相同。它被训练用于处理复杂的指令提示、观察场景，并将任务拆解为π0能理解的小任务，以“耳语”的方式逐步向π0 vla模型下达具体操作（例如：“拿起一片全麦面包”）。这个高层策略还能够融入实时的上下文反馈。 更重要的是，vlm 是用大规模互联网数据训练出来的，它本身就擅长根据图像和语言上下文生成文字，比如回答“机器人接下来该抓哪个物体”。hi robot 利用了这种能力，相当于让机器人具备了“看图理解人说话”的基础常识，不完全依赖自己过往的动作经验，也能像人一样，调动外部知识去做任务。 2. hi robot和π0解决问题的差异性 π0是pi开发的一个低层策略（low-level policy）模型，其核心功能是直接生成机器人的控制动作，即动作轨迹，使机器人能够在真实世界中与多种物体进行交互。例如，它可以操作一件 t 恤并将其折叠完成，具备实际执行复杂操作的能力。在π0的设计中，我们重点强调了 dexterity（操作灵巧性）。 同时，π0也具备一定的语言理解能力（language following），可以根据用户的自然语言指令执行任务。也就是说，用户发出指令后，系统能够“听懂”并完成操作。然而，这种语言理解能力存在限制：它只能执行那些在训练数据中出现过、模型已经学习过的任务。比如，当用户说“叠衣服”时，机器人只能按照它训练中学到的方式、在相似环境下、对已知类型的衣服进行折叠。此外，模型所能理解的语言也仅限于一个相对封闭、有限的词汇集合，即训练语料中出现过的词汇或句式。 我们也讨论到在实际应用中的“落地问题”：当机器人部署在真实环境中时，用户的语言表达往往是开放的、自然的，而非严格受限于训练数据。比如，家中长辈可能会对机器人说：“帮我把这杯水端过来。”这类指令可能从未出现在模型的训练数据中，因而系统无法理解。 为了解决这一问题，我们在 hi robot 项目中提出了一个目标：构建一个支持开放词汇指令（open-vocabulary instruction）的机器人系统。这个系统允许用户使用任意自然语言表达指令，包括模型未见过的表达、复杂的长指令等。核心机制在于引入一个高层策略（high-level policy），它能理解人类语言，将其转化为机器人能够执行的中间表示，再交由π0这样的低层策略（low-level policy）生成具体动作，从而在真实世界中完成任务。 这种架构的优势主要体现在三个方面：第一，他显著提升了人机交互的通用性，使非专业用户也能够自然指令机器人；第二，系统具备了一定的语言推理能力，可以在语言空间中进行更复杂的理解与转换；第三，在训练阶段具备更强的任务泛化能力，能够在多任务间实现知识共享与迁移学习。 举个例子，比如在π0中，如果我们想让机器人制作一个三明治，输入的指令通常是类似“拿起一片面包”这种格式化的操作指令，它必须是明确、具体、结构化的动作描述。 但在 hi robot 中，情况就不同了。你可以直接对机器人说：“我是一个素食主义者，你帮我做个三明治吧。”系统会推理出，“你是素食主义者”意味着桌上的肉类不能被使用。你还可以说：“我对某种食材过敏。”它就能理解并排除相关食材，不会将它们用于制作过程。 只做素食三明治 换句话说，hi robot 能够理解更自然、更复杂、更个性化的指令，并据此做出合适的推理与行为选择，而不仅仅依赖预定义的动作脚本。在任务理解或者说指令理解这一层面，hi robot 的表现相比π0要更加出色。 当然，在实际开发过程中，hi robot和π0是并行推进的。一方面，在π0中我们也在做语义理解相关的工作，比如提高标注阶段的质量，尤其是 label 的定义和精度。与此同时，在 hi robot 的开发过程中，我们也在同步优化 synthetic data（合成数据）的质量。 在这个过程中，我们的团队也在协作探索这两个模型（π0和 hi robot）之间如何交互，每个模块的架构如何设计，才能让整体系统具备更强的语义理解能力和更好的泛化能力。 对于 high-level policy，我们其实也尝试过直接使用像 gpt-4 这种大型模型，特别是可以处理图像的版本（例如 gpt-4v），目前在市面上算是最强的通用多模态模型之一。 但问题在于，它其实并不能很好地理解机器人的能力边界——它不知道这个机器人“能做什么、不能做什么”，缺乏 grounding。它本身没有足够强的空间理解能力，也缺乏对任务的持续理解能力。 而我们所做的 hi robot，则不同：我们有自己的 vla，也有自己的机器人数据库，并且我们可以利用这些 vlm 来生成更贴合实际的合成数据。把这些能力整合在一起，我们训练了一个真正为具身智能和机器人控制设计的 high-level policy。 这样的模型在任务理解和指令执行上，表现明显优于那些直接拿来使用的外部模型，比如gpt-4 系列。 5. 为什么hi robot在指令理解层面比vlm做的好？ 这里面最核心的问题其实就是 grounding。这个“grounding”在科研领域其实是一个老生常谈的话题了。很多大模型，比如说在做数学题、写代码方面表现非常强，但一旦你希望它去控制一个机器人、与真实世界交互、与人进行互动，甚至是执行一个非常简单的动作，比如“把手机拿起来”，它就完全做不了。 这是因为这些模型从未真正与世界发生过交互——它们缺乏反馈（feedback）。在训练过程中，它们只是从静态数据中学习，从来没有真正通过感知和行动去影响环境，也没有建立起对动作后果的因果理解。 而目前的多模态模型，包括很多state-of-the-art的vlm 和vla，在空间推理（spatial reasoning）方面仍然表现较差。 你可以把 grounding 的问题理解为由两个层面组成，首先是外在 grounding：模型对真实世界缺乏物理空间和时间维度的理解，它不知道物体之间的空间关系、交互逻辑；其次是内在 grounding：模型对它自身控制的实体——比如机械臂、小车等——也没有清晰认知，它不知道“我能做什么，不能做什么”、“做什么会成功，做什么会失败”。 这种缺乏内外双重 grounding 的问题，使得当前的大模型虽然语言强、逻辑强，但在具身智能场景中依然难以真正落地。 这是一个仍然非常开放（open）的研究问题。目前谁都无法给出确切答案，它仍属于科研探索的范畴。但根据我的经验来看，这本质上还是一个数据问题，同时也是训练方法的问题。如果有足够高质量的数据，尤其是那种真实世界中人与环境交互的数据，并且这些数据中包含了明确的反馈，那么模型是有可能学会有效的 grounding 的。 在训练方法上，很多人提到强化学习。强化学习就是一种让智能体能够与环境进行主动交互的机制。比如，它可以尝试做某个动作——“我试试看这样做”、“我换个方式再试一下”——通过不断试错，从环境中获得奖励或惩罚，进而逐步建立起因果关系的理解。 可以说，这种机制是目前在具身智能、机器人控制等领域比较火的一个方向，也是在尝试解决 grounding 问题的重要路径之一。 其中一种可能的类比是类似于 deepseek 的方法。它有一个预训练阶段，先利用一个大规模的数据集进行模仿学习，然后再通过强化学习进行微调。 对π0，我们也在考虑类似的思路：既然我们已经完成了基于模仿学习的一整套流程，接下来能不能把模型放到真实或模拟环境中，让机器人自主地进行尝试，从环境中获取 reward（奖励）或估算 value function（价值函数），再利用这些反馈去微调已有的模型，这其实也是一种可能的路径。 至于为什么像 vlm 或 vla这类模型现在强化学习做得相对较少，倒不是没人做强化学习，而是因为目前能用于训练这些大模型的、带有环境交互能力的数据和平台非常有限。 此外，算力也是一个现实因素。在学校实验室的常规算力配置下，其实是很难训练得起这样规模的模型的，这在实际推动中也是一大限制。其实现在能把这些 vla 模型真正训练起来的地方就不多。 而即使有能力训练的机构，很多也还没到已经把整个 vla 的 recipe 在模仿学习阶段完全跑通的程度。大多数还停留在模仿学习阶段，这一阶段里其实还有很多 low-hanging fruit，可以通过比较简单的方法就实现显著提升。 强化学习本身依然是一个非常“科研向”的方向。比如 alphago，它是通过强化学习训练出来的，它一旦成功，效果非常惊人，但问题是：它太难成功了。强化学习有点像在炒非常不稳定的股票——潜力巨大，但极其难以把控。 所以，当训练强化学习模型的成本非常高昂时，很多组织在资源分配上就会更加谨慎。也因此，至今仍有不少地方尚未真正去尝试将强化学习大规模用于此类模型。 根据hi robot论文里关于整体架构的描述：hi robot的整体架构是由高层策略和低层策略组成。高层策略接收开放式自然语言指令，以及来自基础相机和手腕相机的图像输入，生成低层语言指令。低层策略则结合这些语言指令、图像信息以及机器人的状态，生成具体的动作指令，并可选地输出语言回应。 我们这里面分一个high-level policy和一个low-level policy。high-level policy是相当于system two（s2）一样，就是它负责思考；low-level policy像是 system one（s1），或者说它负责执行。 这里面high-level policy向左边这个箭头指向的是一些图片，这些图片来自于机器人本身对世界的观察，就是它各个相机拍下来的现在周围正在发生的事情。然后这个上面写的 user prompt and instruction 是指不管人对它说什么，比如说我说“我想要一个有牛肉、有西红柿、有青菜的三明治”，就是这样一串对机器人的指令被放了进来。这个是它的输入。 它的输出，一个是 low-level language command，也就是给机器人实际执行的指令，比如说它会把刚才这一串指令翻译成“拿起一片全麦面包”或者“拿起一片西红柿”，这样非常具体的操作指令。然后它还会输出另一个内容，是机器人对人的回答，比如说你跟它说“我对某个东西过敏”，它就会回应说它了解了，它不会把这个东西放到你的三明治里。它会有这样一个口头上的回应。 然后这就是刚才说的这个 low-level language command，比如说“拿起一片西红柿”这样的指令，这个连同这些照片一起发给 low-level policy，也就是这里面用的是π0。再加上机器人本身的一些状态信息，比如它的关节（joints）、它自己的观察值、内部的数值，比如它当前的速度。然后通过这个 model inference，它会预测出后续的行为轨迹，然后再执行出来。 这里面high-level policy的确可以理解为“大脑”，但像π0，其实更适合理解为“小脑”。我们做的是端到端的学习，所以在这个架构里，其实并没有 vlm 和 action expert 明确区分的存在，整个系统是连成一体的，是一个整体的模型，负责具体的感知-运动映射，整个模块就是一个s1的结构。 之所以很难去训练这个 low-level policy，是因为它需要在真机上采集数据，数据必须来自真实硬件的交互过程。而且首先要有足够大的数据量，这就意味着需要非常多的机器人硬件设备。第二个问题是数据的质量，这其实更加关键。高质量的数据对训练效果影响非常大。在数据质量这方面，还有一段路要走。 像在π0这样的项目里，我们其实已经有了一定的经验，知道什么样的数据是“好数据”。这件事情我们已经做了很多年，因此已经积累了一些直觉（intuition），知道哪些数据是有价值的，哪些是不够好的。 所以我们会基于这些经验和直觉去主动控制数据采集的过程，通过优化采集策略、调控环境和操作方式，来尽量确保采出来的数据是高质量的、对训练真正有用的。 数据质量的问题是渗透在方方面面的，比如说，机器人上每一个摄像头放在哪里，这件事都非常关键。很多时候我们看到一些公司在给机器人采数据的时候，相机的位置设置就存在很大问题。比如：有的相机位置太远，导致它根本看不清自己在干什么。人类在操作时可以依靠自身的眼睛做出判断，但相机看的范围和分辨率可能远达不到这个能力；有的相机位置太近，以至于完全不知道周围发生了什么。当机器人犯了错，它也没有足够的信息去判断自己错在哪里，也就不知道下一步该怎么纠正。 所以我们通常不会只用一个相机，会使用至少三个。它们之间如何布置、如何协同，都会直接影响数据中到底包含了哪些信息，以及有哪些本该进入数据的信息却缺失了。 举个例子，我们发现，把相机放在机器人的手腕上会比较有效，这种我们称为 wrist camera。它能在非常近的距离内观察机器人实际在操作的物体，是非常关键的。 这只是一个相机位置的例子，但它反映出来的问题，其实涉及到不同机器人之间的协调、感知信息的设计等等，这些都会直接影响最终的数据质量。 另外，也存在有经验的遥操员和新手遥操员采集到的数据差异问题，在实际训练中，我们不可能只雇佣大量的有经验的遥操员，现实情况是一定会有大量新手数据。这些数据混在一起，该如何处理？如何建模其中的差异性和不稳定性？这其实也是我们在π0中讨论和研究的重要问题之一。 所以这其实也有点像是 chatgpt 背后的例子。比如说，gpt4同一时期的其他模型，为什么整体表现都不如gpt4？并不是因为 openai 拿到了比其他家多十倍的数据，大家基本上都用的是类似的互联网数据量。 真正的差异在于那些无数个细节，特别是在数据处理这部分——可能需要一千个细节同时做到位，每一个都很关键。尤其是数据的清洗、筛选、组织、权重分配、格式化等，都会对训练结果产生巨大影响。 所以像 google 发的一些论文，通常会花很多篇幅去讲模型结构、架构层次，但其实最终效果的好坏，往往背后隐藏的是他们在数据处理上做了很多深入、精细的工作。只是这些细节往往不会全部写在 paper 里。 因为模型结构大家都很好奇，而且有时候确实只是换一个模型结构，性能就能提升个 20%。所以大家更关注结构层面的创新，也更愿意在论文里去讲这个。 但实际上，他们通常不会讲数据是怎么洗的。怎么去清洗、筛选、组织这些数据，往往才是决定模型能不能提升 60%、70% 性能的关键。而这些部分，才是真正的“秘密武器”。 10. 用于训练高层策略的数据采集与生成 根据hi robot论文里关于训练高层策略的数据采集与生成过程的描述：首先采集由人远程操控的机器人演示数据，并将其分割为短技能片段（例如“拿起一块 kitkat”）。基于这些标注数据，我们使用视觉-语言模型（vlm）生成合成的用户指令（例如：“你能帮我拿点甜的东西吗？”）以及机器人的回应。最终生成的数据集用于训练高层策略，该策略将图像观测和用户指令映射为语言回应和技能标签。 第0步是采集数据的过程，也就是在真实世界中控制机器人执行任务，比如说一个“去超市买东西”的任务。我们会让机器人自主导航，比如说跑到货架前面，然后由人远程操控它进行各种操作。这里需要说明的是，我们采集的原始数据是一整段长序列，比如一条数据可能长达十分钟。 然后进入第1步，我们会把这十分钟的数据切分成几秒几秒的小段，每一小段都对应机器人正在进行的一个动作或任务。我们会给这些小段加上自然语言的标注，描述“机器人此刻正在做什么”。比如在数据中有一段是“把这块巧克力拿起来”，我们就会给这一段加上相应的标签。 但这时候，仅仅有自然语言的动作描述还不够。比如说，某一段数据被标注为“我在超市里，我想吃点甜的”，这类描述非常模糊。机器人并不知道“甜的”和“巧克力”之间有什么联系，它无法从这种模糊描述中准确理解任务。 所以就进入了第2步，我们通过 synthetic data（合成数据）的生成来补充信息。我们会使用一个比较强的 vlm（视觉-语言模型），给它输入一张图片和一个明确的动作标签，比如“拿起一块巧克力”，让模型去想象：如果这是一个真实世界的场景，有一个用户正在与机器人交互，那用户可能会说什么指令？ 比如，在这个场景中，用户可能说的是：“你去帮我买一些甜的零食。”然后我们也会让模型想象，如果机器人听到这样的指令，它该如何回应，比如它说：“好，我去给你买一些巧克力吧。” 接下来是第3步，我们会将前面采集的数据、标注的数据以及生成的 synthetic data 全部汇总，用来训练一个 high-level policy，也就是 hi robot 中负责“思考”的部分。训练的输入包括图片和用户可能发出的指令；训练的目标是让模型预测两个输出：机器人该如何回应用户的指令；机器人该实际执行什么动作。 这里生成的是用户的指令。比如我们回到刚才那个三明治的例子，它在这个过程中要“想象”的是：现在正在制作的这个三明治里有生菜、有西红柿、有芝士，但没有白菜，也没有肉。那么它就可以去推理，这样的一个配料组合对应的可能是什么样的用户意图。它可能会联想到，用户说的是：“我想要一个没有肉的三明治。” 所以它的能力在于能从当前行为和视觉信息中联想到用户可能发出的指令，把某种配料组合对应到一类语义场景上，建立起语言和动作之间的对应关系。 当然我们也可以在真实世界中采集人与机器人交互的数据，但这种数据非常昂贵。你不仅需要一个人在控制机器人执行操作，还需要另一个人在现场不停地说话，比如“我想要这个”“我想要那个”“你等会儿”之类的，整个过程人力成本非常高。 但现在的情况是，市面上一些最强的 vlm（视觉语言模型）本身已经具备了这类能力。因为它们是基于整个互联网的大规模数据进行训练的，虽然它们不一定见过“人和机器人”之间的对话，但起码见过大量“人与人”之间的交流。比如，一个人请另一个人帮忙，会怎么表达；那个人是怎么回应的；又是怎么执行对方要求的。 在这种场景中，即使没有明确写出“这个人请求了什么”，模型也可以通过后续的行为来反推他可能说了什么。这种能力使得我们可以通过合成数据模拟“人机对话”的过程，而不用完全依赖真实交互采集。 很大一部分都是来自真实机器人采集的数据。比如说，整个动作理解的过程，其实还是一个监督学习的过程。 也就是说，模型之所以能够理解动作、理解指令，很大程度上是因为它在真实环境中，通过大量人工采集和标注的数据进行训练的。所以这也就解释了你后面提到的问题：它的能力，其实在很大程度上是建立在之前那些高质量、真实交互数据的基础之上的。hi robot未来可能会开源，取决于是否有时间。 13. hi robot这样的high-level模块对vla是必须的吗？ 我觉得不是，这其实非常取决于具体的用途。比如说，如果这个模型本身并不需要和用户进行任何交互，或者它也不需要在新的场景中进行泛化，那它根本不需要一个像 hi robot 这样的高层模块，甚至它都不一定需要一个完整的 vla 模型。它可能只需要一个很简单的模型就足够完成任务。 所以这其实取决于模型最终要部署在哪个场景中：它有没有交互的成分？有没有需要做逻辑推理的部分？ 14. 在需要实时交互的场景，hi robot是必需的模块吗? 我只能说，hi robot 会赋予它这样的能力，但这并不是唯一的方式。当然也可以想象未来会出现一个单一的大模型，把这些能力全部整合在一起。或者说，现在这个问题仍然是一个非常开放的研究方向（open-ended research question），其实也没人能给出最终的标准答案。 references： hi robot interview, here is an overview of hi robot based on pi's website. the motivation is to let a robot reason through complex tasks, as if a small voice were telling it what to do next. hi robot integrates a vla such as π0 into a two-level reasoning process. π0 is the fast, action-executing system 1, or s1, while the high-level vlm acts as the slower system 2, or s2, handling reasoning and language understanding. through a form of self-directed dialogue, it breaks complex tasks into simple intermediate steps for π0 to perform. these system labels are functional analogies. an introduction to hi robot. hi robot's high-level policy is a vlm using the same underlying vision–language backbone as π0. it is trained to process complex prompts, observe the scene and divide a task into subtasks π0 understands. it effectively whispers concrete instructions to the vla, such as “pick up a slice of whole-wheat bread.” the high-level policy can also incorporate feedback from the ongoing interaction. a vlm pretrained on large-scale internet data is already good at producing text from images and linguistic context—for example, answering which object a robot should pick up next. hi robot uses that ability, giving the robot commonsense knowledge for interpreting what a person says in relation to what it sees. it need not depend entirely on its previous action experience; it can bring broader knowledge to the task. π0 is a low-level policy developed by pi. its central function is to generate robot-control actions directly: action trajectories that let a robot interact with different objects in reality. for example, it can manipulate a t-shirt and fold it, executing a complex physical operation. in designing π0, we especially emphasized dexterity. π0 also has some language-following ability: it can perform tasks from natural-language instructions. a user gives an instruction, and the system understands and executes it. but this understanding is limited by what the model has learned from its training tasks. if the user says “fold the clothes,” the robot follows the procedures it learned, for familiar clothing types in similar settings. the language it handles is also comparatively closed and limited to the vocabulary or expressions represented in its training data. here, “closed” describes the demonstrated task and instruction distribution, not a literal restriction of the tokenizer to those words or an inability to process any new phrasing. deployment exposes this limitation. in real environments, people speak naturally and openly rather than restricting themselves to the training vocabulary. an older family member might say, “bring me that glass of water.” if that expression was absent from the model's training, the system may not understand it. hi robot therefore aims to support open-vocabulary instructions. users can express requests naturally, including unfamiliar wording and long, complex instructions. the key is a high-level policy that understands human language and converts it into an intermediate representation the robot can execute. a low-level policy such as π0 then generates the physical actions. the language interface is broader, while execution still depends on the robot's available skills. the architecture offers three main advantages. first, it makes interaction more general, letting non-experts instruct robots naturally. second, it provides language reasoning, enabling more complex understanding and transformation within language space. third, it strengthens task generalization rfm ep04：pi0 vs helix vs go-1三类vla模型框架对比解析 解析pi0、helix与go-1三类vla模型框架及通用操作路线。 机器人学习与基础模型（rfm） 2025年刚进入3月，机器人领域好不热闹，除了人形机器人跳舞、翻跟头、鲤鱼打挺等各种酷炫的demo，具身智能公司也动作频频，pi发布hi robot，figure发布helix，google发布gemini robotics，智元发布go-1，英伟达gtc发布groot n1。随之而来的是各种搞不清楚的概念。这些所谓的“vla”模型到底是什么？各种vla模型之间的区别是什么？vla和模仿学习有什么关系？真机数据的重要性体现在哪里？ 在robot foundation model断更几个月后（rfm ep01：pi和π0具身基础模型，rfm ep02：octo，rfm ep03：清华rdt及具身大模型框架对比），终于在公众号后台粉丝的催更下，隆重推出机器人基座模型第四期。 我整理了目前几个主要vla模型的模型结构，以及对一些概念的理解。这篇文章的成文，在我自己对几个vla模型结构的梳理基础上，在模型结构理解和概念确认方面采访了智元启元大模型（genie operator-1，简称go-1）的共一刘迟明。希望这篇文章可以成为中文互联网上最容易理解的vla科普文章。 刘迟明目前就职于智元机器人负责基座大模型架构和研发，是agibot world colosseo文章共一，主导研发go-1基座模型。他曾就职于阿里巴巴和腾讯担任技术专家岗位，负责大规模互联网系统机器学习和深度学习技术研发；曾开发和训练千亿参数llm，相关工作发表于顶会和头部期刊；参与过很多开源社区项目建设，贡献代码给如huggingface/transformers等头部项目。 以下为本文目录 👇 1.什么是vla 2.pi0 vla模型结构理解 3.figure helix vla模型结构理解 4.智元go-1 vla模型结构理解 5.通用操作的一些想法 1. 什么是vla vla 是一种整合视觉（vision）、语言（language） 和 动作（action） 的多模态模型，用于推动机器人更自然地理解和执行任务。它的目标是让机器人像人一样，通过“看图 + 听指令”来“做事情”。 在传统控制系统中，视觉、语言和动作模块往往是独立处理的，而 vla 模型尝试构建一个统一的架构，让模型从感知（图像）、理解（语言）到执行（动作）之间具备连贯性和一致性。vla 模型通常包括以下几个部分： 第一部分：视觉编码器（vision encoder）：输入图像、视频等视觉信号，将其编码为特征向量。通常使用 vit（vision transformer）、resnet 或更高级的图像模型。 第二部分：语言编码器（language encoder）：输入自然语言指令，将其转换为语言嵌入（text embedding）。使用如 bert、t5、gpt、clip text encoder 等。 第三方部分：多模态融合模块（cross-modal fusion）：将图像和文本信息进行对齐，学习视觉和语言之间的关系。可以是 cross-attention 机制、多模态 transformer 或 clip-style 对比学习。 第四部分：动作生成器（action decoder / policy head）：根据融合后的视觉和语言特征，生成动作指令（可以是连续控制向量，也可以是离散 token）。动作可能通过 diffusion、flow matching、rl policy head 等生成。 如果对应到核心能力来源，第一到第三部分核心能力都来自于以openai和google为代表的大模型公司的视觉语言模型（vlm），第四部分的核心能力来自于以pi0为代表的具身智能公司。 根据具象的解释，可以把 vla 模型想象成一个训练有素的机器人助理：它“看到”一张图，比如一张厨房桌子，桌上有盘子、叉子、鸡蛋。你对它说：“把鸡蛋翻个面。”它“理解”你的语言，与它看到的图像一起思考：鸡蛋在哪里？手该怎么动？用什么工具？然后它“动起来”，做出一系列精确的动作，比如拿起锅铲、翻转鸡蛋。这个过程中，它就是把视觉感知、语言理解和动作控制三个过程无缝结合起来了。 2.pi0 vla模型结构 在rfm（robot foundation model）系列，我们根据sergey的几个talk整理了一篇关于pi0的科普（rfm ep01：pi和π0具身基础模型）。根据pi的官方披露信息，pi的通用机器人策略采用了一个预训练的视觉-语言模型（vlm）作为基础骨干，并使用了一个跨形态、多样化的操控任务数据集。为了适配机器人控制，我们在模型中加入了一个独立的动作专家模块，通过流匹配（flow matching）生成连续动作，从而实现精确且流畅的操控能力。该模型既可以通过提示实现零样本控制（zero-shot control），也可以在高质量数据上进行微调，从而完成复杂的多阶段任务，例如折叠多件衣物或组装一个盒子。 这段文字，在理解了模型框架的基础上看其实非常精准，但在不理解的基础上，一些概念就不会很清晰。结合我自己的理解以及被访者的交流，我将pi0模型结构的理解进行来拆分。 整个pi0的模型架构用我自己的话来理解：pi0是一个机器人收到人类指令和结合观察直接输出动作的端到端vla模型，这个模型训练分两个阶段，第一阶段预训练，在基于大模型公司开发的vlm对文本和语言对有理解的基础上，通过模仿学习的框架用真实机器人数据作为监督信号训练出机器人动作生成策略；在后训练阶段，针对特定任务，用模仿学习框架进一步训练提高特定任务的成功率。对这个理解的进一步拆解是： vla及其输入和输出 结合pi0的公开资料以及访谈，我们将pi0 vla的模型结构做了进一步理解，如上图。整个模型的输入是机器人接收到的图像观察（vision）和语言（language）指令，即模型最左侧的input部分；整个模型的输出是机器人动作（action），即模型最右侧的output部分。简单理解vla就是，一个机器人在收到指令的情况下（language），结合对周围环境的视觉输入（vision），去完成指令要求的任务对应的动作输出（action），整个过程在一个大的神经网络里闭环完成，也就是所谓的“端到端”。 pi0 vla模型结构 模型的训练分两个阶段，第一大阶段是预训练，第二阶段是后训练；两个阶段的区别在于训练规模和对输出质量的要求不同。预训练模型的入参与 vlm 类似，都包括图像和文本数据，但同时还额外加入了机器人本体的关节角度数据作为输入信息。 预训练阶段 预训练阶段有两个主要部分构成，依靠三类数据来源。预训练的第一个组成部分是一个依靠互联网规模的数据预训练的vlm，这个vlm通常是个由大模型公司训练好的开源模型或api。在pi0的工作中他们选择了google的paligemma 3b模型权重，这个部分和pi的团队没什么关系，他们仅仅是选择了一个适合他们的由别的公司开发的vlm。 预训练的第二个组成部分是一个由两组真实机器人数据集（开源真机数据集oxe和pi自己收集的高质量遥操真机数据）训练的action expert（动作专家），这个action expert通过模仿学习的框架对比与真机数据损失函数最小来获得最优解，用到了类似diffusion model这样的结构（flow matching）将token denoise成连续的动作输出。 预训练vlm pi0模型预训练阶段的 pretrained vlm，实际上就是指谷歌的paligemma那套开源模型，即之前google的vlm团队利用互联网规模（internet-scale）的图文数据所训练出来的一组3b规模的模型权重。这里需要说明一下，现在“pretrain”这个词在不同业务领域里可能各有不同的具体含义，即便我们说的是一个vlm（视觉语言模型）领域的pretrain，它的含义也可能有所不同。 比如刚提到的paligemma，其实是基于 gemma 模型构建的。gemma 本身是google推出的一个语言模型，而paligemma则是在这个语言模型基础上，额外加入了视觉编码器（vision encoder），通过进一步训练后，形成了一个视觉语言模型（vlm）。这样就实现了文本与视觉之间的对齐（text-vision alignment）。 实际上，physical intelligence（pi）团队并没有从头开始用互联网规模的图文数据训练vlm模型，而是直接使用了google团队的开源 vlm paligemma的预训练权重。在这个基础之上，他们进一步利用约10万小时的机器人数据集，对模型进行了训练，最终得到了他们自己的pi0模型。 动作专家（action expert） action expert 本质上是一种 flow matching，可以简单理解成一种diffusion model，但其损失函数与其他 diffusion model 不同。它从 vlm 获取的是每一层 transformer 输出的 hidden state，即每个 token 的隐藏向量（hidden vectors）。llm和vlm都是基于 transformer 架构的，它们以 token 为基本载体，将图像和文本统一切分成一系列 tokens。这些 tokens 在网络中每一层 transformer 前向传播时都会产生相应的隐藏状态（hidden states），即 tokens 对应的特征向量（vectors）。每层 transformer 产生的这些特征向量会被传递给 action expert，后者再通过类似diffusion model的方法对这些信息进行去噪（denoise），从而生成相应的控制指令。 zero-shot能力 预训练阶段的vla具备一定的零样本（zero-shot）输出能力，图中所描述的情况一般适用于训练中已经见过的任务（即 in-distribution tasks），但实际上，基于 vlm 训练出来的策略通常具备一定的泛化能力，可以推广到训练过程中未见过的物体，体现出一定的 zero-shot 能力。 后训练阶段 pi0的vla大模型第二个训练阶段是后训练，后训练阶段仅仅依靠pi自己收集的高质量真机数据集，通过模仿学习框架，进一步提高模型在特定任务上的成功率。后训练过程类似于将一个通用模型（generalist）进一步训练为成功率更高的专用模型（specialist），即实现从通用到专用（from generalist to specialist）的转变。 这里面提到的真机数据其实是一类机器人数据的获取方式，通常是由人类“遥控”操作机器人所获得的机器人数据。遥控方式有多种，包括同构遥操例如mobile aloha，头显遥操例如open television等。 怎么理解vla是个端到端模仿学习的框架？ 整体来说，这套称为 vla 的方法其实就是一种端到端的模仿学习。这里的模仿学习具体体现在，它的监督信号来源于人遥操机器人产生的动作数据。具体来说，模型中的 action expert 会通过去噪（denoise）输出动作信号，而这些动作信号需要计算损失才能进行梯度回传优化。计算损失时，模型输出的动作信号与真实动作进行比较，而真实动作就是人遥操机器人过程中机器人的动作数据，这就构成了模仿学习的监督信号。 端到端模仿学习仅在action expert部分吗？ 他整个模型在训练时用到的仅仅是模仿学习的损失，没有采用其他类型的损失函数。比如，训练 vlm 时通常会计算 token 与 token 之间的交叉熵（cross entropy，action expert部分提到）损失，但在这个模型中并没有使用这种 token-level 的损失，而只用到了模仿学习中的动作监督信号作为唯一的损失进行训练。 怎么理解diffusion transformer？ 这里使用的模型架构其实不应该称作 dit（dit），因为 dit 一般特指的是 meta 提出的那个特定的 transformer 架构，这里的模型虽然也是基于 transformer 架构的 diffusion 模型，但与 dit 并不相同。可以称它为 diffusion transformer 会更合适一些，但最好不要直接使用 dit 这个名称，以免造成混淆。 后训练和预训练的区别 pi0后训练和预训练中的action expert部分，都是采用同一个 diffusion transformer架构，二者唯一的差别在于训练时所使用的数据不同。后训练使用更高质量和更有针对性的机器人真机数据来提高任务成功率，比如使用同样的机器人本体，或者在复杂任务上进行有针对性的训练。 3. figure-helix vla模型 根据figure披露的官方信息，helix 是首个结合 “system 1 / system 2” 架构的 vla（视觉-语言-动作）模型，专为高频率、灵巧控制整个人形机器人上半身而设计。 以往的方法面临一个根本性的权衡问题：视觉-语言模型（vlm）作为骨干网络具有广泛的泛化能力，但运行速度较慢；而传统的机器人视觉-运动策略速度很快，但泛化能力弱。helix 通过两个互补的系统解决了这一矛盾，这两个系统是端到端训练，并能高效通信的： system 2（s2）：一个部署在机器人上的、基于互联网预训练的视觉-语言模型，运行频率为 7-9 hz，负责场景理解和语言理解，使机器人具备对物体和语境的广泛泛化能力。 system 1（s1）：一个快速响应的视觉-运动策略网络，将 s2 生成的潜在语义表示转化为 200 hz 的精确连续动作，实现高速、实时的控制。 这种解耦的架构使两个系统能在各自最适合的时间尺度上运行：s2 负责“慢思考”，处理高层语义和目标规划；s1 负责“快反应”，实时执行和调整动作。例如，在协作行为场景中，s1 能快速适应伙伴机器人动作的变化，同时保持对 s2 所设定语义目标的执行。 结合上述信息，helix最大的特色在于引入了快慢思考的概念，他的结构看上去和pi0不一样，但实际上是类似的。pi0里的动作专家（action expert）可以看成是helix里的s1，action expert 的输入其实就是 vlm 中每个 token 的 hidden vector，这个 hidden vector就相当于是helix中的latent vector。helix的s2和s1就可以对分别应到pi0预训练框架中的pretrained vlm和action expert两个部分。 怎么理解helix双系统的频率差别 从频率的角度来看，figure helix中提到的 s2 是 7 到 9 赫兹，s1 是 200 赫兹，两者频率差别非常大。如果没有双系统架构，可能整体架构就只有单一频率运行，比如pi0目前的控制频率是 50 赫兹。 pi0和 gemini robotics 目前都采用了同步架构，没有使用双系统异步架构。因为同步架构的响应速度对于绝大多数任务来说已经足够快，也更流畅了。异步架构真正带来的好处到底是什么？比如，让 s1 更快、更高频，这种提升在实际应用中能带来多少收益？这些问题还需要进一步了解。 在figure发布helix之前，智元曾在24年10月份，发了一篇robodual的双系统异步架构文章，比helix早了5个月。而最近智元发布的go-1的架构（本文第4部分会详细介绍）则采用了单系统同步架构，也是暂时认为在操作大模型上串行架构在5-10hz的模型推理频率上已经有比较好的效果。2025英伟达gtc上发布的groot n1也采用了和figure helix类似的s1和s2双系统。所以从单双系统的选择上，不同公司在不同时期都会有不同的尝试，目前尚未有定论。 关于频率和运行时间的换算关系，我自己之前也搞不太清楚，为了便于后文的理解，这里将频率和时间的换算关系做一个解释：频率与周期互为倒数 频率（f）：单位时间内周期性事件重复的次数，单位为赫兹（赫兹 = 1/s）。 周期（t）：完成一次完整周期性事件所需的时间，单位为秒（s）。 如果周期为1秒一次，那么频率就是1赫兹，如果周期为每20毫秒（0.02秒）完成一次，那么频率就是50赫兹。 具体到pi0架构，它每推理一次的时间约为 80 到 100 毫秒，也就是模型整体的执行频率大约是 10 赫兹（1/0.1=10）。这实际上与helix中提到的 s2 频率（7-9赫兹）是相近的，谷歌的gemini robotics 端到端模型的推理时间是 200 毫秒，即 5 赫兹。这几个模型（pi0、gemini robotics 和 figure heliex 中的 s2）整体推理频率量级都差不多。 虽然这些模型推理频率在 5-10 赫兹左右，但它们的 s2 都能够输出更高频率（如 50 赫兹）的控制信号。这是因为，尽管模型推理一次可能需要较长时间（比如 200 毫秒），但每次推理可以预测未来一段时间（例如未来两秒）的控制信号，因此可以实现高频控制输出。 既然这些模型的大脑部分本身就能达到 50 赫兹的控制信号输出，那么再额外增加一个频率更高的 s1 系统到底是为了解决什么样的问题？也许 helix 看到了某些特别的问题，但他在论文里并未清晰说明。 怎么理解它的推理速度？为什么它的推理速度慢，但控制信号输出的频率却可以这么高？ 因为每次推理的时候预测的是未来两秒钟的动作轨迹。每秒钟可以推理五次（每200毫秒推理1次，1秒=5*200毫秒，模型推理频率5赫兹），每次都可以推理出未来两秒的轨迹，相当于每 次推理。模型虽然只有5赫兹的推理速度，但可以执行50赫兹的控制频率。 模型推理频率：模型推理一次是200ms(0.2s)的话，它连续推理可以做到1/0.2s = 5hz的频率。动作控制频率：模型推理一次，推理出的action，是一个有50个frames的chunk（假设对应预测未来1秒本体的运动）。 这50个frames，按间隔20ms(0.02s)发送给本体，进行本体动作控制。1/0.02s= 50hz。模型预测的action频率是50hz，可以大概理解为模型一次推理50个未来的动作控制信号。这50个控制信号在1秒内执行完。 这里涉及到一个技术概念叫做action chunk：action chunk（动作块）是近年来在机器人学习和强化学习中提出来的一个概念，它的本质是将一段连续时间内的动作序列作为一个整体进行处理，而不是逐帧、逐步地预测动作。在传统的机器人控制中，模型每一步都会输出一个瞬时动作（例如每 20ms 控制一次电机），这叫做 step-wise control。而 action chunking 的想法是：一次性输出多个时间步的动作序列，把这几个时间步的动作合成一个“chunk”（块），可以看作是短时段的运动计划。 一个 action chunk 通常是指一段固定长度的连续动作向量，比如：模型每次输出一个 chunk，包含未来2秒的动作，每秒50帧，那么一个 chunk 就是 100 帧动作。这些动作可以是连续值（如关节角度），也可以是离散的 token（如 index 到一个动作字典中）。 总结来说，模型推理频率并不高，但由于每次推理都预测未来一段时间内的大量动作（如两秒内100帧），所以它可以支撑较高频率（如50赫兹）的控制输出。而实际上50赫兹的控制频率已经足够满足使用需求了。至于把控制频率从50赫兹提高到200赫兹，看起来可能更丝滑一些，但并非必要，这一点可能还有一些未被公开分享的额外观察。 怎么理解helix的s1频率更快？ pi0的s1和s2是串行执行的，也就是说pi0的s2执行完后再执行s1，s1执行完之后再等待下一次s2的执行。而helix的s1和s2是串并行的，s1是一个更小的模型（80兆），它独立执行，有更高的推理速度（200赫兹）。串并行的意思是它既可以是串行的，也可以是并行的。它有串行的部分，s1依赖于s2给它的信息。并行的部分就是s1可以单独去执行，不需要等待s2的推理结果。因为s1是独立执行的模型，他的模型结构可以做的更小，大概是80m大小，也就是8000万参数量的小模型，所以运行效率更高。这种结构使得它的s1动作输出频率达到200赫兹，而pi0的动作输出频率是50赫兹。 s1本质上也是一个action expert，但它额外引入了一个叫做latent conditional visual motor transformer的结构，即它额外增加了视觉信息（图像）作为输入，这意味着它不仅仅是直接从latent vector进入diffusion过程去denoise出一个action，而是额外加入图像信息后再进行denoise动作的过程。它额外引入图像输入的作用，主要是为了实现闭环控制，因为s1模型是独立执行的。 4. 智元villa 根据智元官方的资料，为了有效利用高质量的agibot world数据集以及互联网大规模异构视频数据，增强策略的泛化能力，智元提出了 vision-language-latent-action (villa) 这一创新性架构。go-1这个通用具身基座大模型基于villa构建，与vla架构相比，villa 通过预测latent action tokens(隐式动作标记)，弥合图像-文本输入与机器人执行动作之间的鸿沟。在真实世界的灵巧操作和长时任务方面表现卓越，远远超过了已有的开源sota模型。 villa架构是由vlm(多模态大模型) + moe(混合专家)组成，vlm 采用internvl2.5-2b，接收多视角视觉图片、力觉信号、语言输入等多模态信息，进行通用的场景感知和指令理解；latent planner是moe中的一组专家，基于vlm的中间层输出预测latent action tokens作为cop(chain of planning，规划链)，进行通用的动作理解和规划；action expert是moe中的另外一组专家，基于vlm的中间层输出以及latent action tokens，生成最终的精细动作序列；在推理时，vlm、latent planner和action expert三者协同工作。 潜在动作模型（lam） 从大规模视频数据（如 ego4d 中的人类视频）学习通用动作表示，并将其量化为离散的潜在动作 token。潜在规划器 通过预测潜在动作进行时间推理，在图像-文本输入与动作专家生成的机器人动作之间建立桥梁。 值得一提的是，最近gtc大会上，英伟达的nvidia isaac gr00t n1和go-1一样用的是三阶段（中间有一阶段是latent action）的预训练范式。而且真机数据中80%是用的是智元开源的agibot world百万真机数据。 为了和pi0的模型结构做直观的对比，我将villa的模型结构抽象成上图。villa如果只看stage2和stage3，它与pi0的主要区别就在于中间的latent planner。为了训练这个latent planner，才有了stage1的lam模型。 为什么要在中间加一个lam，因为现在机器人的数据太少了，尤其是模仿学习的真机数据极其有限，我们考虑如何利用人类视频数据来某种程度的解决机器人真机数据稀缺的问题。在模仿学习训练之前，引入人类操作物体的一些数据，让模型直接预测视频的未来帧。 假如我们要训练机器人去翻锅里的鸡蛋，这个动作和人类的操作——伸手拿铲子翻鸡蛋——在动作空间上是非常类似的。所以，我们先用人的数据，即人的视频数据，让模型学会预测。例如，看到人准备翻鸡蛋，就能预测未来鸡蛋是如何被翻过来的，把这种隐含的 latent action 预测能力先让模型学习到。 当模型再去训练机器人的模仿学习时，它就有更强的能力，可以更快理解机器人在翻鸡蛋时应该如何行动。这样在隐空间上的动作规划方向就更清晰，从而加速机器人的学习过程。 这些动作上的语义被压缩成 latent action tokens，然后模型去预测这些 latent action tokens，这就相当于模型具备了预测动作趋势的能力。而重建部分是由 lam 的 decoder 负责完成的。 在villa这个模型里，为了让它在一些具体任务上有更高的成功率，go-1也有做一个后训练的部分。在文章里面，我们把这个过程叫做 sft（supervised fine-tuning），这个部分和pi0里的后训练部分是类似的作用。 go-1在自主推理的表现可以参看以下视频： 通用操作路线至少有四五条，以pi0为代表的这种大规模端到端模仿学习路线，分层路线（对话李昀烛：通用操作新解法——基于学习的动力学模型和voxposer & rekep：从任务表征的角度探究机器人的零样本任务泛化），还有世界模型和仿真+sim2real相关的路线。也非常期待后续会有更多创业公司，在端到端模仿学习以外的路线上，做出成果。 what is vla? 2. understanding the π0 vla architecture 3. understanding figure's helix vla architecture 4. understanding agibot's go-1 vla architecture 5. some thoughts on general-purpose manipulation vla is a multimodal model that combines vision, language and action to help robots understand and execute tasks more naturally. the aim is for a robot to do things by looking at images and understanding instructions, much as a person does. in traditional control systems, vision, language and action are often handled by separate modules. a vla model tries to bring them into a unified architecture, maintaining continuity and consistency from perception through images, to understanding through language, to execution through actions. a vla model typically includes the following components. part 1: vision encoder. it takes visual signals such as images and video and encodes them as feature vectors. common choices include vit, or vision transformer, resnet and more advanced image models. part 2: language encoder. it takes a natural-language instruction and converts it into a text embedding. examples include bert, t5, gpt and the clip text encoder. part 3: cross-modal fusion. it aligns image and text information and learns the relationships between vision and language. this can involve cross-attention, a multimodal transformer or clip-style contrastive learning. part 4: action decoder or policy head. using the fused visual and linguistic features, it produces action commands, which can be continuous control vectors or discrete tokens. actions may be generated through diffusion, flow matching, an rl policy head or other methods. if we trace where the core capabilities come from, parts 1 through 3 draw on the vision-language models, or vlms, developed by foundation model companies such as openai and google. part 4 draws on the robotics capabilities developed by embodied ai companies, exemplified here by physical intelligence and π0. for a concrete picture, imagine a well-trained robotic assistant. it sees an image of a kitchen table with a plate, a fork and an egg. you tell it, 'flip the egg.' it understands your words and considers them together with what it sees: where is the egg? how should its hand move? which tool should it use? it then acts, performing a precise sequence such as picking up a spatula and turning the egg over. in this process, visual perception, language understanding and action control work together seamlessly. 2. the π0 vla architecture in the rfm, or robot foundation model, series, we put together an introduction to π0 based on several talks by sergey levine: rfm ep01: physical intelligence and the π0 embodied foundation model. physical intelligence's published description explains that its generalist robot policy builds on a pretrained vision-language model and a diverse, cross-embodiment manipulation dataset. for robot control, the model incorporates a separate action expert that generates continuous actions through flow matching, enabling precise, smooth manipulation. the model can be prompted for zero-shot control or fine-tuned on high-quality data for complex, multistage tasks, such as folding multiple garments or assembling a box. once you understand the architecture, that description is quite precise. without that background, however, some of its concepts are difficult to make sense of. combining my own understanding with the interview, i have broken the π0 architecture down below. here is how i understand the overall architecture in my own words. π0 is an end-to-end vla model that directly produces actions from a robot's observations and a human instruction. training has two stages. during pretraining, it builds on a vlm developed by a foundation model company, with its existing understanding of visual and textual information, and learns a robot action policy through imitation learning supervised by real-robot data. during post-training, it uses imitation learning again to improve success on particular tasks. let us unpack that description. vla: inputs and outputs using the public π0 materials and the interview, we worked through the architecture shown above. at the far left, the model receives the robot's visual observations and language instructions. at the far right, it outputs robot actions. in simple terms, a robot receives an instruction, combines it with visual information about its surroundings, and produces the actions needed to carry out the task. these functions are integrated within one large neural network—the sense in which the model is called end-to-end. the robot then receives new observations as it acts, closing the perception–action loop. the π0 vla architecture training has two main stages: pretraining and post-training. they differ in training scale and in the quality required of the output. like a vlm, the pretrained policy takes images and text as inputs, but it also receives the robot's own state, including joint angles. pretraining pretraining has two main components supported by three kinds of data. the first component is a vlm already pretrained on internet-scale data. more generally, such a vlm may be available as an open model or through an api. in π0, the team selected google's paligemma 3b weights. pi did not develop that original vlm; it chose a suitable model developed by another company. the second component is an action expert trained using two broad sources of real-robot data: open datasets such as oxe and pi's own high-quality teleoperated robot data. in the imitation learning framework, the model is optimized against supervision from these demonstrations. it uses flow matching, a generative approach related to diffusion, to turn noisy action representations into continuous action outputs. the pretrained vlm the pretrained vlm in π0 refers to google's open paligemma model: a set of roughly three-billion-parameter weights learned from internet-scale image and text data. one point needs clarification: the word 'pretrain' can mean different things in different fields. even when we are discussing vlm pretraining, its specific meaning depends on the context. paligemma, for example, is built on gemma. gemma is a language model from google. paligemma adds a vision encoder to that language model and trains the combination further to form a vision-language model, establishing alignment between text and vision. the physical intelligence team did not train a vlm from scratch on internet-scale image–text data. it started with google's pretrained paligemma weights and trained the resulting robot policy on a large robot dataset to obtain π0. editorial correction: the chinese original gives approximately 100,000 hours; the original π0 paper reports about 10,000 hours of pi demonstrations, supplemented by open robot datasets. the action expert the action expert uses flow matching. at an intuitive level, it resembles a diffusion model, although its training objective differs. it is conditioned on information from the vlm's transformer layers: hidden states, or feature vectors, associated with the image and text tokens. llms and vlms use transformer architectures in which token representations acquire hidden states as they pass through successive layers. the action expert uses that contextual information to generate control commands through an iterative generative process. editorial clarification: the original describes denoising these vlm vectors themselves. more precisely, flow matching transforms a noisy action chunk into actions, conditioned on the vlm representations; the vlm hidden states are not the noisy actions being denoised. zero-shot capability the pretrained vla has some zero-shot control capability. the situation shown in the diagram generally concerns tasks already represented in training—the in-distribution tasks. a policy built on a vlm can also have some generalization ability, including handling objects not encountered during robot training. that is another sense in which it can demonstrate zero-shot capability. post-training the second training stage is post-training. it uses pi's own high-quality real-robot data in an imitation learning framework to improve success on particular tasks. this resembles refining a generalist into a specialist with a higher success rate: a transition from general-purpose capability to task-specific expertise. here, real-robot data refers to a way of obtaining robot demonstrations, usually by having people teleoperate the robot. there are several methods, including mechanically matched teleoperation such as mobile aloha and headset-based teleoperation such as open-television. in what sense is vla an end-to-end imitation learning framework? overall, this particular vla approach is end-to-end imitation learning. its supervision comes from actions recorded while people teleoperate robots. the action expert generates actions through its denoising or flow-based process, and a loss is computed to optimize the model by backpropagation. the demonstration actions provide the targets: they are the actual robot actions recorded during human teleoperation. this is where imitation learning's supervision enters. in flow matching, that supervision is expressed through the generative training objective rather than simply comparing a final sampled trajectory with a demonstration. does end-to-end imitation learning apply only to the action expert? during this robot-policy training, the model uses an imitation learning objective rather than adding other kinds of objectives. for example, vlm training commonly uses cross-entropy between predicted and target tokens. that separate token-level objective is not used here; the robot policy is trained from action supervision through the flow-matching loss. the fact that this supervision enters through action generation does not mean that only the action expert can be optimized: the training is end-to-end. the earlier pretraining of the original vlm is a separate stage with its own objectives. how should we understand 'diffusion transformer'? it is useful to distinguish a generic diffusion transformer from dit as the name of a specific architecture introduced by researchers at meta. the model discussed here also uses a transformer-based generative architecture, but it is not simply that original dit implementation. calling it a diffusion transformer in the broader descriptive sense is reasonable; calling it dit without qualification can be confusing. more precisely, π0's action-generation objective is flow matching. post-training versus pretraining the action expert uses the same architecture during π0 pretraining and post-training. the difference emphasized here is the training data. post-training uses higher-quality, more targeted real-robot data to improve task success—for example, demonstrations from the same robot embodiment or focused training on a complex task. 3. figure's helix vla model in its official announcement, figure presents helix as the first vla of its kind to combine a system 1/system 2 architecture for high-frequency, dexterous control of a humanoid robot's entire upper body. that is figure's positioning of the system, rather than a claim that no earlier robotics work had used a dual-system approach. earlier approaches face a fundamental trade-off. a vlm backbone provides broad generalization but runs relatively slowly. traditional visuomotor policies are fast but have weaker generalization. helix addresses this with two complementary systems that are trained end-to-end and communicate efficiently. system 2, or s2, is an onboard, internet-pretrained vlm running at 7–9 hz. it handles scene and language understanding, giving the robot broad generalization across objects and contexts. system 1, or s1, is a fast visuomotor policy. it translates the latent semantic representation produced by s2 into precise continuous actions at 200 hz, enabling fast, real-time control. this decoupled architecture lets the systems operate on the timescales best suited to them. s2 performs the slower thinking, dealing with high-level semantics and goals. s1 provides fast reactions, executing and adjusting actions in real time. in cooperative behavior, for example, s1 can adapt quickly to a partner robot's changing movements while continuing to pursue the semantic goal set by s2. on this account, helix's most distinctive feature is the separation of fast and slow thinking. its architecture looks different from π0's, but there is a useful analogy between their roles. π0's action expert can be compared with helix's s1, while the vlm's hidden token representations provide contextual information comparable in function to helix's latent vector. in this conceptual mapping, helix's s2 and s1 correspond to the pretrained vlm and action expert in π0. this is an analogy between functions, not a claim that the architectures or generation methods are identical. understanding the frequency difference between helix's two systems figure reports s2 running at 7–9 hz and s1 at 200 hz, a substantial difference. without separately scheduled systems, the overall model has a single inference cycle, even though the actions it generates can be executed at another rate. for comparison, π0 produces actions for 50 hz control. model inference frequency and action execution frequency need to be distinguished. the comparison made in this interview treats π0 and gemini robotics as synchronous end-to-end systems, rather than helix-style asynchronous dual systems. for many tasks, that arrangement may already be responsive and smooth enough. i still want to understand the practical benefit of asynchronous execution: how much does making s1 faster improve real applications? this is a question to investigate, not a definitive statement about every implementation of these models; in particular, the public details of gemini robotics do not establish every aspect of its runtime scheduling. before figure announced helix, the robodual work associated with agibot collaborators had explored an asynchronous dual-system architecture in october 2024. the recently released go-1, discussed in section 4, instead uses a synchronous pipeline; at this stage, its developers consider serial inference at roughly 5–10 hz effective for manipulation foundation models. nvidia's gr00t n1, announced at gtc 2025, also separates s1 and s2, in a way conceptually similar to helix. different companies have therefore explored different arrangements at different times, and the choice is not settled. editorial correction: the original says robodual preceded helix by five months. robodual was submitted on october 10, 2024, and helix was announced on february 20, 2025—approximately four months apart. i used to be unclear about the relationship between frequency and runtime myself. to make the discussion easier to follow, here is the conversion: frequency and period are reciprocals. frequency, f: the number of repetitions of a periodic event per unit time, measured in hertz, where 1 hz = 1/s. period, t: the time needed to complete one cycle, measured in seconds. if an event occurs once every second, its frequency is 1 hz. if it occurs once every 20 milliseconds, or 0.02 seconds, its frequency is 50 hz. the π0 inference time quoted in this discussion is around 80–100 milliseconds per pass, corresponding to roughly 10–12.5 hz—1/0.1 = 10. this is close in order of magnitude to helix's s2 at 7–9 hz. the discussion quotes approximately 200 milliseconds, or 5 hz, for end-to-end gemini robotics inference. these figures place π0, gemini robotics and helix's s2 in a similar broad range. they are the timings used in this comparison, not hardware-independent performance guarantees. a model that runs inference at around 5–10 hz can nevertheless generate actions to be executed at a higher frequency, such as 50 hz. even if one inference pass takes 200 milliseconds, it can predict a sequence of controls for a future interval, such as the next two seconds. that sequence supports higher-frequency action execution. here, it is the complete policy's action output we are discussing; helix's s2 itself supplies a semantic representation to s1 rather than directly issuing a 50 hz motor-control sequence. my question was: if a model's brain can already generate actions for 50 hz execution, what problem does an additional, faster s1 solve? perhaps helix has identified particular difficulties, but in my view the published description did not explain them clearly. editorial clarification: executing a precomputed chunk at 50 hz is different from updating a policy with fresh observations at 200 hz. figure's explanation emphasizes that s1 keeps responding to new visual and robot-state information between slower s2 updates. the question of the practical benefit remains worth studying, but that feedback distinction matters. why can inference be slow while action execution is fast? suppose each inference pass predicts the next two seconds of motion. at one pass every 200 milliseconds, the model performs five passes per second: one second equals 5 × 200 milliseconds, so its inference frequency is 5 hz. each of those passes produces a trajectory covering a longer future interval. in other words, each inference pass predicts an action sequence. even with only 5 hz inference, the robot can execute those predicted actions at 50 hz. model inference frequency: if one pass takes 200 ms, or 0.2 seconds, continuous inference can run at 1/0.2 = 5 hz. action execution frequency: suppose a pass produces an action chunk with 50 frames representing the robot's next second of motion. those frames can be sent to the robot every 20 ms, or 0.02 seconds, for control. since 1/0.02 = 50 hz, the action sequence runs at 50 hz. roughly speaking, one inference pass predicts 50 future control commands, which are executed within one second. this introduces the concept of an action chunk. action chunking, used in robot learning and reinforcement learning, treats a sequence of actions over a continuous time interval as a single unit, rather than predicting only one frame or step at a time. in step-wise control, the model outputs an instantaneous action at each step—for example, controlling a motor every 20 ms. with action chunking, it outputs several future timesteps together. the resulting chunk can be viewed as a short motion plan. an action chunk typically contains a fixed-length sequence of action vectors. if the model predicts two seconds of motion at 50 frames per second, the chunk has 100 action frames. depending on the model, actions can be represented as continuous values, such as joint angles, or discrete tokens, such as indices into an action dictionary. thus, a relatively low inference frequency can support a higher action execution frequency by predicting many future actions at once—for example, 100 frames over two seconds. my view in this discussion was that 50 hz control is sufficient for many intended applications, and that increasing it to 200 hz might look smoother without necessarily being essential. there may be additional observations that have not been shared. that is my assessment, not a universal requirement: the value of faster control depends on the task, and faster execution of an existing chunk should not be confused with faster updates from new sensory feedback. why does helix's s1 run faster? using s1 and s2 as a conceptual analogy, π0 processes the vlm context and action generation within one inference pipeline: the next full cycle follows the previous one. helix instead combines dependency with concurrent execution. its s1 is a smaller, roughly 80-million-parameter model that can run independently at 200 hz. it depends on information from s2, which is the serial aspect, but does not need to wait for a new s2 result before every action, which is the parallel aspect. it uses the latest available semantic representation while continuing to process current observations. keeping s1 small makes this efficient. helix consequently updates its action policy at 200 hz, whereas π0's generated actions are associated with 50 hz control. again, π0's vlm and action expert are not literally separately scheduled helix-style s2 and s1 systems. s1 plays the role of an action-generating policy, using a latent-conditioned visuomotor transformer. crucially, it also receives current visual information, rather than relying only on the semantic latent vector. that fresh image input enables closed-loop control while s1 runs independently between s2 updates. editorial correction: the original describes s1 as denoising actions through diffusion. figure describes helix's s1 as trained with a standard regression loss; it should not be equated with π0's flow-matching action expert. 4. agibot's villa architecture agibot's published materials introduce vision-language-latent-action, or villa, to make better use of high-quality agibot world demonstrations and large-scale heterogeneous internet video, improving policy generalization. go-1 is a generalist embodied foundation model built on this architecture. compared with a vla, villa predicts latent action tokens as an intermediate bridge between image–text inputs and the robot's executable actions. agibot reports strong performance on real-world dexterous manipulation and long-horizon tasks, substantially outperforming the open-source baselines evaluated in its study. that comparison concerns the reported evaluation, not every model or task. as explained in the interview, villa combines a vlm with specialized expert modules, described here as a mixture of experts, or moe. it uses internvl2.5-2b as its vlm backbone to support general scene perception and instruction understanding. the interview describes multimodal information including multiview images, force-related signals and language. the latent planner uses intermediate vlm representations to predict latent action tokens, forming what the interview calls a chain of planning, or cop. the action expert uses the vlm context and latent action information to produce the final fine-grained action sequence. at inference, the vlm, latent planner and action expert work together. editorial clarification: the released paper explicitly specifies images and language for the planner and proprioceptive state for action generation; it does not establish force signals as a separate vlm input. its two expert modules should also not automatically be read as a conventional sparsely routed moe. the latent action model, or lam, learns general action representations from large-scale video data, such as human videos in ego4d, and quantizes them into discrete latent action tokens. the latent planner reasons over time by predicting those latent actions, linking the image–text inputs to the robot actions generated by the action expert. it is worth noting the parallel with nvidia isaac gr00t n1, announced at gtc: the original discussion compares its training recipe with go-1's three-stage approach, including a latent-action stage, and states that 80% of its real-robot data came from agibot's open million-trajectory agibot world dataset. editorial clarification: gr00t n1 does use latent-action learning from video, but its training recipe is not identical to go-1's. nvidia's original paper states that it used the 140,000 agibot-alpha trajectories available when training began, alongside other real-robot datasets. it does not identify 80% as a universal share of all its real-robot training data; the original percentage lacks a specified counting or sampling basis and should not be treated as independently established. to make the comparison with π0 more intuitive, i abstracted villa's architecture into the diagram above. looking only at stages 2 and 3, the main difference emphasized here is the intermediate latent planner. stage 1, the lam, provides the latent action representations needed to train that planner. why add a lam in the middle? robot data is scarce, especially real-robot imitation learning data. we wanted to explore whether human video could help address that shortage. before robot imitation training, the model can learn from videos of people manipulating objects, using future-frame prediction and reconstruction to learn about the changes produced by actions. suppose we want to teach a robot to flip an egg in a pan. at the level of the manipulation being performed, that resembles a person reaching for a spatula and flipping the egg, even though human and robot control coordinates differ. we first use human video to teach predictive representations: when someone is about to flip an egg, the model learns about how the egg will change in subsequent frames. the idea is to learn this implicit latent-action capability before training on the robot's own actions. when the model subsequently learns from robot imitation data, that prior understanding can help it grasp more quickly how the robot should act to flip the egg. the direction of action planning in latent space is clearer, potentially accelerating robot learning. the semantics of these changes are compressed into latent action tokens. predicting those tokens gives the model a representation of how an action is likely to change the scene. the lam's decoder handles the reconstruction component. to improve success on particular tasks, go-1 also undergoes post-training. the paper calls this supervised fine-tuning, or sft. it serves a similar purpose to π0's post-training stage. the following video demonstrates go-1's autonomous inference. using agibot's go-1 embodied foundation model together with adc, the adversarial data collection approach, this demonstration shows autonomous inference in a water-pouring task. the robot follows and moves toward the kettle, then grips its handle steadily. it quickly locates and continuously tracks cups of different types and colors. its pouring motion is smooth, and the demonstration presents it as recognizing the water level in the cup to avoid overflow, aiming for efficient, safe operation. #embodiedai #embodiedfoundationmodels #agibot. watch in the original wechat article. 5. some thoughts on approaches to general-purpose manipulation there are at least four or five approaches to general-purpose manipulation. one is the large-scale, end-to-end imitation learning route exemplified by π0. another is the hierarchical route, discussed in conversation with yunzhu li: a new approach to general-purpose manipulation through learned dynamics and voxposer & rekep: exploring zero-shot robot task generalization through task representations. there are also approaches involving world models and simulation with sim-to-real transfer. i look forward to seeing more startups make progress along routes beyond end-to-end imitation learning. over lunch recently, a leader from a mobile internet company said something i expect to remember for years: 'the people who will eventually win are probably already in the arena.' in a field with a long horizon, i want to look past the noise, settle down, follow particular people and their work, and keep building my understanding. all that preparation is about recognizing the person who will ultimately succeed when i meet them. references
