to grasp and put down a usb plug, for example, or pull a belt. exploration produces these behaviors, while continued training and feedback improve them. rl's connection to dynamic programming helps it attain higher performance. this paper does not address generalization from one task to another. serl and hil-serl primarily solve the problem of making rl for real-world manipulation work at all. for multi-task learning, earlier work has shown that single-task rl models can rapidly generate data, which can then be distilled into a larger model supporting multiple tasks. that offers a route toward broader adaptability. we aim to provide a reliable, usable foundational tool that researchers can build on for more complex work. many subsequent projects can develop from it, with a clearer understanding of how to implement the necessary components. one reason people abandon this work is that it requires deep understanding of both robotic systems and rl algorithms. you need a high level in both, and that is not easy. frankly, there is no obvious shortcut: you learn through mistakes and accumulate experience step by step. fast results are difficult, so people may give up. i also think it is risky and may offer limited short-term rewards. over the long term, however, rl will clearly be a major part of the solution. at the time of this interview, i predicted that startups relying heavily on imitation learning would, after experiencing its limitations, begin using rl the following year to improve success rates, cycle times and robustness. why have i persisted? around 2019, 我们为什么一定要用这些复杂的遥操作来获取模仿学习需要的数据？这里有一个非常重要且丰富的数据源，就是人类的视频，例如在youtube或抖音上的视频，包含了丰富的物理信息和运动行为，这些视频本质上是宝贵的先验知识来源。然而，目前还无法有效利用这些视频，因为它们通常缺乏动作标签，没办法直接用来进行模仿学习。就算它们有动作标签，不同的研究组可能使用不同的动作标签定义和收集方式，导致数据不统一，比如，有的组喜欢用机械臂末端的移动来作为动作，有的组喜欢用每一个轴的转动来作为动作，这种不统一的数据标签也很难被用来做模仿学习。atm这个工作就是研究如何从视频中提取经验知识。 我们的atm的主要想法是什么？我们不想做视频预测。未来的视频图像长什么样，对于机器人控制没有任何意义。我们只需要知道每个物体的移动方向，而不在乎画面的精美程度。我们只关心运动信息。我们参考以前的人是如何建模运动的。比如，在游戏或仿真引擎中，他们不会把某一个物体建模成一个对象，而是把物体中的每一个粒子建模成一个对象，通过建模粒子之间的碰撞、挤压和相对移动来对整个场景进行建模。特别是在复杂的流体、软体物体和沙子等场景中，这种方法非常有效。 atm的主要想法是，既然像素级的视频建模不是一个好的表征方法，那么我们能否利用类似的想法，把视频变成一些粒子的集合，建模每个粒子的运动来反映整个场景的物理规律，来为控制模型服务。ep1对话高阳、汶川：如何利用互联网人类视频训练机器人大模型（atm—rss 2024满分论文） mimicplay的想法是从人类行为数据中学习机器人的控制和策略。直接从人类行为中学习机器人的动作是不可能的，因为通过相机很难精确捕捉手在三维空间中的具体位置，这导致了最终的数据无法直接用于训练机器人，因为机器人的运动方式会有所不同。因此，我们的想法是退一步，不直接学习机器人的电机动作，而是学习策略。比如说，一个较长的任务是将某个食物放进碗里，再放入微波炉加热，最后取出。虽然人类手部轨迹和机器人的轨迹会有所不同，但做这件事的先后策略，比如去哪里找把手，去哪里拉托盘，这些策略是可以共享给机器人的，这套策略我们称之为高层次的规划。低层次的控制器（low level controller）则是在拿到规划后，控制机械臂的末端复现这些动作。 高层次和低层次分开之后的一个很大优势是，高层次的规划器（planner）可以直接从人类视频中学习。这种数据是比较便宜的，可以称之为“play data”。你不需要对这些数据进行标注，比如标注你在做a还是b。只需要给定一个目标，比如某道菜，希望高层次的轨迹规划能规划出相应的策略。你可以想象在家里的厨房放一个相机，它可以捕获你每天在厨房里的策略。比如，你做一道菜时，先打开冰箱，从冰箱里拿出某个菜，然后在切菜板上切开。这些都是可以用第三视角相机轻松获取的数据。 低层次的控制器因为高层次有更多人类数据的支持，学习所需的数据量也会减少。它只需要按照规划的轨迹去执行20个步骤即可，不需要再考虑高层次的规划问题。这样，低层次控制器的数据需求很少，可能只是学了一个抓取问题或移动问题。这些移动可能只需控制机器人向某个方向移动几厘米，有时甚至不需要学习。 通过高层次轨迹规划的数据，可以很好地帮助整个系统减少机器人数据的需求。将规划问题和控制问题分开是我们当时的一个想法。高层次轨迹规划的数据通过人类行为数据来实现泛化，可以很好地帮助系统减少对机器人数据的需求。这样可以使整个系统更高效，数据需求更少。这是我们一直以来的核心思路。ep4对话王辰：mimicplay & dexcap——如何利用人类视频和人体动捕数据进行机器人训练 在humanplus的阶段，我们尝试将合成数据和机器人遥操数据的特点融合：一种是海量的合成数据，虽然在仿真软件中的数据量大，但质量不高；另一种是高质量的真实世界数据，但采集速度慢，无法达到海量。因此，human plus的主要目标是能否结合这两者的优点，即在真实世界中收集高质量数据，同时利用海量的合成数据。 humanplus结合了两种数据来源：一边是机器人仿真数据，另一边是人类的运动数据。关于机器人仿真数据，我们不能直接将人类的运动信息复制到机器人上，因为机器人的重量和关节结构与人类不同，直接复制可能会导致机器人失去平衡并倒下。因此，在最低层次的控制逻辑上，我们仍然使用强化学习在仿真环境中生成大量的仿真数据训练机器人。这意味着，当机器人接收到人类关节位置信号时，它会根据这些信号主动控制自己的动作，以模仿人类的动作，但同时也会考虑到自身的物理限制，以保持平衡。这种方法可以确保机器人既能够模仿人类动作，又不会因为不稳定而倒下。 通过模仿学习人类视频数据，我们可以将人类的运动模式转化为机器人控制策略。感觉就像是神经网络在控制一个人的动作，最终的神经网络输出可以直接映射到人形机器人上。由于人形机器人在形态上与人类相似，这种映射过程相对简单和直观。这使得我们可以更有效地利用人类数据来训练和控制机器人，使其能够执行类似人类的动作和任务。ep5对话符梓鹏：humanplus和mobile aloha的数据故事——从合成数据到真实数据再到两者的结合 在 eureka 的工作中，我们提出了一个设想：能否通过llm自动设计仿真环境，使我们能够在仿真中快速学习新技能，并迅速将其转移到现实世界中。eureka 使用大型语言模型（llm）来自动编写用于仿真机器人任务的奖励函数（reward function）。在仿真中，奖励函数就像仿真中的其他代码一样，是可以在计算机上运行的代码，而像 gpt-4 这样的llm非常擅长编写代码。因此，在 eureka 中，我们使用llm来自动编写奖励函数代码。但这还不是全部，我们还要求llm改进奖励函数代码。 为了实现从仿真到现实的强化学习，除了设计奖励函数，你还必须让仿真到现实的转移能够顺利进行。通常，仿真环境和现实世界环境之间存在很多不匹配，特别是在物理模型方面。模拟器无法完美地模拟现实世界中的重力、摩擦力等。因此，现在很流行的一种做法是进行领域随机化（domain randomization），即在仿真中随机化物理参数。但在domain randomization的过程依然有一个问题，那就是人类必须手动涉及这个domain randomization的参数。在dreureka中，除了自动编写奖励函数，我们还自动化了域随机化设计。 现在，我们已经实现了奖励函数和域随机化的自动选择，我们可以部署在奖励函数分布和域随机化参数上表现最佳的策略。令人惊喜的是，我们发现将这些策略直接部署到现实世界中竟然是可行的。这意味着我们现在拥有了一个端到端的、完全自动化的仿真到现实世界的流程。整个过程完全由大型语言模型自动化完成，中间不需要任何人工干预。 这一突破性进展展示了大型语言模型在自动化强化学习任务中的强大潜力，从奖励函数的设计到域随机化的选择，再到最终策略的部署，全程无需人类专家参与。这不仅大大提高了效率，也为解决更复杂的现实世界问题开辟了新的可能性。ep6对话马也骋：eureka和dreureka如何利用llm解决仿真+rl最重要的难题 关于跑酷工作，我认为核心问题主要有两个方面：一是如何设计和调整一个有效的训练策略，二是如何克服sim2real gap。训练策略的设计是一个复杂的任务，涉及不同动力学约束的强化学习训练，以及技能模型的蒸馏。 过去，四足的工作不带视觉，主要依赖本体感知，而现在，我们引入了视觉感知，特别是双目深度相机，sim2real gap问题在引入视觉系统后变得尤为重要。为了有效地克服sim2real gap，我们需要在仿真中尽可能真实地模拟视觉感知中的深度，同时调整真实世界中的数据，使其尽量接近仿真器中的理想图像，将仿真数据和真实数据的分布尽可能接近，从而缩小这两者之间的差距。 在缩小sim2real gap过程中，我们采用了多种方法进行尝试，比如填洞、去噪等，深度图在这方面表现尚可。在跑酷任务中，挑战相对简单，主要是克服地形，而克服地形的关键在于了解其深度。但是未来真正的实用机器人不应仅仅依赖深度图，而需要能够处理rgb图像。 此外，multitask learning（多任务学习）在机器学习中一直是一个长期存在的问题。当一个模型同时学习多个任务时，不同任务的回传梯度往往会发生冲突，会遇到每个技能的性能下降的问题。调试单个技能其实比较容易，但同时调试多个技能则很困难。因此，子文在尝试了各种方法后发现了一个比较好的策略：先单独训练每个技能，将这些技能作为教师模型，然后共同训练一个学生模型。这样的方法可以最大限度地减少性能下降，最终的成果是一个系统化的解决方案，不只是单点创新，而是全面提升了能力。ep7对话赵行、庄子文：机器人跑酷和自动驾驶——机器人数据从哪里来 robogen这个工作背后的思路是这样的：首先，我们将相关信息提取出来，然后利用这些信息去构建一个供机器人训练的环境。这个环境包括多个方面：机器人需要掌握的技能、每个技能适用的具体环境、环境的外观设计、机器人与环境的交互方式等。此外，我们还要为每个任务定义明确的完成标准，这通常通过奖励函数或损失函数来实现。值得注意的是，这些函数可以通过像语言模型这样的大型模型生成代码的方式来自动创建。我们希望自动化训练前的每一个环节，打通整个流程。这意味着从奖励函数的定义到生成代码，每个环节都可以自动化处理，使整个训练过程从头到尾实现高度自动化。这是我们想要实现的目标，也是我们最早提出的全自动化训练流程的核心理念。 在处理刚体交互时，强化学习非常有效，无论是用于运动（locomotion）还是操控刚体（manipulation）。然而，当涉及到柔性物体时，情况变得复杂，可微分模块至关重要。柔性物体，比如流体或会变形的衣服，与刚体不同。强化学习在这种情况下需要对状态空间进行有效的表示。如果我们希望超越刚体的交互，开始处理柔性物体，挑战就在于状态空间的复杂性。例如，仿真环境中通常会用粒子系统来表示这些物体，一块布可能由几十万个粒子组成。在这种情况下，用传统的基于代码的奖励函数来描述这些粒子状态是非常困难且昂贵的。第一，粒子数量巨大，直接对其状态进行描述和判断目标达成与否的成本非常高。第二，很难用明确的函数来描述像衣物对折这样的复杂形变过程及其对应的粒子状态。因此，传统方法难以适用于这些复杂的情况，这也是我们需要可微分模块的原因。它们可以帮助我们更有效地处理与软体物体的交互，简化并加速训练过程。 对于这类问题，使用梯度信息确实可以加速策略的学习效果，尤其是在与纯强化学习相比时，通过利用梯度来指导强化学习过程可以加速优化。然而，这个方向在学界仍是一个活跃研究领域，尚未有成熟的框架来将这两种方法有效结合。同时，由于梯度本身并非总是理想的，在实际优化过程中，例如接触力的梯度可能会导致优化景观不连续，从而引入噪声，影响训练效率。梯度提供的信息往往是局部的，在解决复杂的非凸问题时，局部信息可能不足以实现全局优化。这些都是当前学界试图解决的挑战。ep8对话淦创、周衔：robogen如何通过生成模型和可微分模拟大规模合成机器人示教数据（附可微分物理引擎论文综述） umi的核心是一个物理api，我们找到了一个物理接口，使它既包含了与机器人足够相似的物理形态，同时又不限制于具体的机器人形态，成本也比机器人低很多。我可以从三个方面具体说明。 首先是可移植性（portability）问题。我们假设即使机器人本身成本很低，例如每个机器人只有1000到2000元，按照目前机器人的重量，如果我想去餐厅采集数据，需要把机器人运到卡车上，再开到餐厅，然后卸下来安装调试，基本上半天时间就过去了。每次进入一个新环境都要有这个前期设置成本，这使得获取多样化环境数据的成本非常高。umi通过其手持设备很好地解决了这个问题。虽然umi的夹子现在有点重，有800克，但可以放在包里随身携带。因此，我们只要人到了一个环境，比如我们去餐厅吃饭，坐下就可以开始收集数据，两分钟内就能开始工作，大大简化了获取多样化真实世界数据的过程。 其次是物理形态的相似性。在学术界中使用的研究机器人往往是一个工业机器人，加上一个平行夹爪，umi设计时考虑到了这种常见的机器人形态。因此，umi记录的是夹爪在空间中的六维运动轨迹，只要机器人能到达任何一个位置，具体的关节角度并不重要，甚至可以用无人机达到所需位置。因此，它在一定程度上实现了对机器人形态的无关性，无论实验室使用的是什么牌子的机器人，只要有六个自由度都可以使用。 最后是数据收集的直观性。例如，我们尝试了一个任务是投掷方块，有两类物体，圆的和方的，机器人前面有两个盆，一个是圆的，一个是方的，任务是将方块投到方的盆里，圆块投到圆的盆里。这是一个高速的动态动作，用遥控机器人来完成是非常困难的。我们之前做实验，15分钟内遥控机器人没有成功投进一个方块。如果用umi，因为人类用这种夹子的直觉非常强，因此用umi收集同样任务的数据速度是人类用手的一半，虽然听起来慢，但相比遥控操作任务收集速度为零已经是很大的提升。在另一个任务——转动杯子上，我们发现umi收集数据的速度是人手的一半，而遥控操作机器人收集数据的速度比umi慢三倍。这使得umi在数据收集方面具有显著的优势。ep2对话迟宬、许臻佳：umi——机器人训练的物理api dexcap中手上的相机是用来做slam的场景追踪，所以它提供的手特别是手指的精度，都是在厘米级别的，都是在一厘米以内的左右级别。所以dexcap，我称为它是一个“核武器”，它给你一个更高精度的数据。相比于第三方视角的mimicplay的人类数据，它给的精度本来就更高。dexcap手上的相机是用来做追踪（tracking），它的目的不是为了获得图像。因为人的手和机器人的手还是长得不一样，所以出现在画面里之后还是有domain gap。所以你并不能单纯用人类手上相机的数据去直接学习机器人方案，我们试过了不太work。 dexcap手套是动作捕捉手套，每根手指上都有一个电磁场传感器，手上的相机用于定位手掌在六自由度空间里的位置。相机下方有一个电磁发射器，每个手指的指尖都有一个电磁接收器。通过电磁场实现毫米级别精度的定位，确定每个手指指尖相对于手掌的三维空间位置。再加上手掌上的相机，可以给手掌相对于胸口的相对位置，那进一步就可以获得手指指尖在相机画面中的相对位置。这个精度由胸口和手腕上的相机，以及动捕手套这套设备共同保证。 胸口相机用来定位人体相对于世界坐标系在空间的位置，手腕上的相机用来定位手掌相对于胸口的空间位置，动捕手套来定位手指指尖相对于手掌的空间位置。所以你背着这套东西走，胸口的摄像机可以告诉你人在哪里，手腕上的摄像机可以告诉你手掌相对于胸口在哪里，动捕手套可以告诉你手指相对于手掌在哪里，最终可以获得一个手指在空间中的绝对位置。这个绝对位置是高精度的，这直接保证了当你将机器人推入场景时，只需让机器人进行inverse kinematic（逆向运动学）来完成操作动作。ep4对话王辰：mimicplay & dexcap——如何利用人类视频和人体动捕数据进行机器人训练 open-television针对目前遥操作的问题和人形机器人时代的特性提出的一种新方法。对于人形机器人而言，操作人员不可能站在机器人后面，因为会被其躯干挡住；站在旁边歪着头看也不直观，还得一直扭着脖子。此外，人形机器人是移动平台，设置过多的固定摄像头并不实际。因此，最直观的方式是让操作人员沉浸式地控制机器人，就像自己变成机器人一样。open-television这个工作也是受这个想法启发，它的主要特点是操作人员无需站在机器人旁边或后面，也不需要以第三人称视角操作，而是戴上头盔后沉浸式地操作机器人。 这种远程操作具有以下特点：第一，沉浸式（imversive）体验，操作人员通过沉浸式远程操作看到的不是2d视频，而是3d视频，就像观看3d电影一样。左右眼看到的图像不同，从而形成自然的立体视觉。这种立体视觉可以实现对空间距离的精确估计，使操作人员能够完成很多精细的任务。第二，我们的机器人系统还配备了活动颈部（active neck），使头部能够移动。人眼在执行任务时，会使用中心视网膜的一个小区域来聚焦（foveal vision）。使用固定摄像头时，如果需要看其他地方，只能斜视或用边缘视觉，非常不便。因此，加入活动颈部使系统更加沉浸和直观。操作人员只需转动头部即可看到目标区域，而不需要歪着眼睛或使用边缘视觉。第三，活动颈部还降低了计算成本，因为操作人员只需要看到摄像头中心的一小部分图像，而不需要处理高分辨率的广角图像。大分辨率图像中有很多无用的视觉信息，处理这些信息对计算机的需求很高。聚焦于中间小部分图像后，只需转头就能看到所需内容，从而大大提高了计算效率。我们的系统可以达到大约80赫兹的帧率，而处理更大图像时只能达到40赫兹，高帧率对系统的直观性帮助很大。对话程旭欣：open-television教你如何沉浸式遥操机器人 ep5 mobile aloha 到了mobile aloha的阶段，相当于我们完全没有用到任何仿真软件的信息，完全利用真实世界的数据来让机器人进行学习。收集机器人在真实世界中的数据，这些数据由人类通过遥操作方式采集，并通过高效的模仿学习用少量的数据进行训练；这时候可以获得更好的、比较真实的视觉信号，比如rgb数据，还有一些语义上的数据。 这种方法面临的一个挑战是，真实世界数据的收集速度较慢。所以，mobile aloha相当于是结合了一个高效的模仿学习算法，只需提供大约50次人类采数据的尝试，就可以让机器人学习并完成各种任务。这种方法高效地帮助人类采集数据，相比以往使用vr设备或3d鼠标键盘等工具采集数据，不仅速度快且易于上手。mobile aloha的主要作用在于快速让人们掌握如何操作机器人，以解决几乎所有真实世界中可能遇到的问题。ep5对话符梓鹏：humanplus和mobile aloha的数据故事——从合成数据到真实数据再到两者的结合 机器人数据获取难度大很大一部分原因是机器人的形态很多，在不同的机器人上，会有不同的方法来表示它们的某些模态，分散的机器人载体和多模态的数据模式是导致目前机器人没有完整模型的一个主要原因。我们提到的多模态，即包括rgb视觉信息、文字信息也包括点云和触觉等这些对灵巧操作任务至关重要的信息模态。为了与目前大家常说的多模态大模型里的模态加以区分，我们将这些数据类别统称为多样性（heterogeneity）而不再称之为多模态。 除了数据多样性问题，机器人训练所用到的数据领域（domain）也存在巨大差异，比如人类视频、真实机器人数据以及仿真数据，这也是机器人学或具身智能领域特有的挑战。每个domain都有自己的优势和劣势，仿真中我们可以生成大量数据，但有些东西可能无法模拟，存在仿真与现实之间的差距；人类视频数据在网上有大量可用，但可能缺少动作标签，训练起来较难；而真实机器人数据非常昂贵，因此，跨domain的研究非常困难。 如何将机器人训练数据多样性和跨多个领域的数据组合起来，提高机器人训练的通用性是poco这个工作最核心的思想。在poco中，我们把不同的策略拆分成了几个层次：第一，task level：在不同的任务，比如不同的工具使用，我们可以进行一些训练，使用 classifier-free的diffusion training。这样就可以在任务层次上进行组合，利用不同的工具。第二，domain level：在不同的领域来源，比如仿真和真实机器人上进行组合。我们可以研究如何将这两个领域的策略组合在一起。第三，behavior level：在测试时可以指定一些成本，比如让它的行为更加顺滑或者更加安全。我们可以直接手动编写一些任务或目标，然后进行组合。 我的 phd 论文主要是关于异构性数据（heterogeneous data），其中包括了我之前的两个工作 fleet learning（robot fleet learning via policy merging）和dec ssl（does decentralized learning with non-iid unlabeled data benefit from self supervision？）其实包括poco，它核心思路也是如何更加高效地处理和利用这种异构性数据。这是一个更广泛、更基础的问题，除了视觉和语言领域外，几乎所有其他领域都面临数据不足的问题，但却希望能够应用机器学习。因此，他们都会遇到异构性数据的问题。 如何高效地从这些数据中提取信息？这个大问题在当前的研究中仍然未被充分探索。在整个学术界，很多研究者可能会专注于单个问题，比如一种机器人、一种任务、一个模拟环境或一个真实世界的任务，或者某种特定的算法，比如模仿学习或强化学习。但其实，把这些各类要素整合在一起，进行综合研究，我认为是非常有价值的。 现在大家都在关注大模型，如何训练一个大模型来支持多样化的任务，这其实是一个非常有意义的问题。比如到底是 30% 的模拟数据加 50% 的真实世界数据，还是 10% 的模拟数据加 70% 的真实世界数据，这些比例如何选择，目前其实并没有太多的理解，很多时候都是凭感觉进行调整。我认为，对异构性数据的研究会在未来全面支持大模型的训练和应用，这对于整个领域的发展是非常重要的。 gpt4o是一个很好的例子。过去，大家通常是以语言为中心，中间的模型必定是语言模型，输出也只能是语言。但现在显然他们提前把数据都tokenize好了，然后进行了一些异构预训练，这就是hpt里的一个想法。这样做的好处是，它能够融会贯通。最近也有一些工作表明，这种表示不同的模态最终会收敛，因为它们都是从不同的视角看待世界。ep9对话王理睿：如何处理机器人领域中极为异构的数据集和任务 references： robot data, episode 10: a full review of season 1 revisiting all nine season 1 interviews: human videos, simulation, motion capture, teleoperation and the composition of heterogeneous robot data. all nine interviews in robot data season 1 have now been published. my sincere thanks to the researchers who accepted my invitations and to everyone who has followed the series. the interviews revolve around a robot-data pyramid. at its base are internet and synthetic data: abundant and inexpensive, but less directly aligned with a particular robot's training needs. at the top are demonstrations collected by a person teleoperating the target robot itself: highly relevant, but difficult to obtain and relatively scarce. in the middle is human motion-capture data, bridging synthetic data and robot-specific demonstrations. robots have diverse embodiments, limited data for any one embodiment, and many sensor modalities, making frameworks that combine different sources essential. every season 1 interview explores a level of this pyramid or how to bring those levels together. the pyramid's 'quality' ranking refers to direct usefulness for a target robot, not an absolute ranking of all datasets. robot data season 1, ep01–ep09 to bring the nine interviews together, i will revisit their explanations of each data route and the core ideas behind the individual projects. the earlier episodes are linked below. the first-person passages that follow retain the researchers' voices from those interviews. ep1: yang gao and chuan wen on learning from internet human videos — atm at rss 2024 (reported perfect review scores) ep2: cheng chi and zhenjia xu on umi — a physical api for robot training ep3: xuxin cheng on open-television — immersive robot teleoperation ep4: chen wang on mimicplay and dexcap — learning from human videos and motion capture ep5: zipeng fu on humanplus and mobile aloha — synthetic data, real data and their combination ep6: yecheng jason ma on eureka and dreureka — using llms to address key challenges in simulation and rl ep7: hang zhao and ziwen zhuang on robot parkour and autonomous driving — where robot data comes from ep8: chuang gan and zhou xian on robogen — generating robot demonstrations with generative models and differentiable simulation, with a differentiable physics review ep9: lirui wang on heterogeneous robot datasets and tasks contents ↓ 1. internet videos of human activity ep1: atm ep4: mimicplay 2. synthetic data ep5: humanplus ep6: eureka and dreureka ep7: robot parkour ep8: robogen 3. motion-capture data ep2: umi ep4: dexcap 4. robot teleoperation data ep3: open-television ep5: mobile aloha 5. combining robot data ep9: poco and hpt why must we use complicated teleoperation systems to obtain the data needed for imitation learning? human videos—from youtube or douyin, for example—are an important, abundant source. they contain physical information and patterns of movement, making them valuable prior knowledge. but using them effectively is difficult, because they usually lack action labels and cannot directly serve as conventional action-supervised imitation data. even where action labels exist, research groups may define and collect them differently. some represent end-effector motion; others represent the rotation of each joint. those incompatible definitions make combining demonstrations difficult. atm studies how to extract useful experiential knowledge from video. what is our main idea in atm? we do not want to predict entire video frames. for our control objective, we care about where objects move, not how beautiful the future image looks. motion information is what matters. we drew inspiration from earlier ways of modeling movement. game and simulation engines sometimes represent an object as a collection of particles, modeling their collisions, compression and relative motion to describe the scene. this is especially useful for complex materials such as fluids, deformable objects and sand. the original says future video appearance has 'no meaning' for control; here that expresses our choice of motion-focused representation, not a universal claim that video prediction can never help a robot. atm asks whether, instead of modeling video pixel by pixel, we can represent it as a set of points and model their movement to capture information about a scene's physical behavior for control. the analogy is to particle-based modeling, while atm itself predicts image-point trajectories rather than simulating literal physical particles.
ep1: yang gao and chuan wen on learning from internet human videos — atm at rss 2024 (reported perfect review scores) mimicplay aims to learn robot policies and control from human behavior. directly obtaining a robot's motor actions from ordinary human video is difficult: a camera cannot easily recover exact hand positions in three-dimensional space, and the robot moves differently from a human. our idea was therefore to take a step back, learning a higher-level strategy rather than motor commands directly. consider a long task: put food in a bowl, place it in the microwave, heat it and take it out. human and robot hand trajectories differ, but the sequence and strategy—where to find a handle or pull out a tray—can be shared. we call this high-level planning. a low-level controller then uses that plan to control the arm's end effector and carry out the movements. separating the two levels has a major advantage: the high-level planner can learn directly from human videos. this relatively inexpensive source is called play data—open-ended interaction, not necessarily playing games. you need not label every action as task a or task b. give it a goal, such as the dish you want to make, and the high-level planner should produce an appropriate strategy. imagine a camera in your kitchen recording your daily activity: opening the refrigerator, taking out ingredients and cutting them on a chopping board. a third-person camera can readily capture those behaviors. with more human data supporting the high-level planner, the low-level controller needs less robot data. it can focus on executing, say, twenty planned steps, without also learning the overall task plan. its data requirements may therefore be modest: perhaps learning a grasping or movement skill. some movements just require moving a few centimeters in a direction, and may not need to be learned at all. the twenty steps are an illustrative explanation, not a fixed horizon imposed by mimicplay. high-level planning learned from human activity can substantially reduce the system's need for robot demonstrations. separating planning from control was our central idea. generalization in the human-data planner supports the rest of the system, making it more efficient and reducing data requirements. that remains our core approach. in the published system, the high-level guidance takes the form of learned latent plans rather than simply replaying human trajectories as robot motor commands.
ep4: chen wang on mimicplay and dexcap — learning from human videos and motion capture with humanplus, we tried to combine the strengths of synthetic data and robot teleoperation data. simulation can produce huge quantities, though its data may not match reality closely enough; real-world data is highly relevant but slow to collect and difficult to scale. humanplus asks whether we can collect high-quality data in the real world while also benefiting from abundant simulation experience. humanplus combines robot simulation with human motion. we cannot simply copy human motion onto a robot, because their masses and joint structures differ; direct copying may make it lose balance and fall. for the lowest-level control, we therefore still use reinforcement learning and large amounts of simulation experience. when the robot receives human joint-position targets, it actively controls its motion to imitate them while respecting its own physical limitations and maintaining balance. this is designed to make imitation stable; it is not an unconditional guarantee that the robot never falls. through imitation, we can turn human movement patterns into robot policies. it feels as though a neural network is controlling a person's movements, with its output mapped onto a humanoid. because humanoids resemble people, that mapping can be relatively intuitive, allowing us to use human data more effectively for human-like movements and tasks. editorial clarification: humanplus does not directly behavior-clone arbitrary internet videos into motor actions. its simulation-trained low-level policy enables real-time shadowing of human motion; demonstrations collected on the robot through shadowing then train an autonomous skill policy.
ep5: zipeng fu on humanplus and mobile aloha — synthetic data, real data and their combination in eureka, we asked whether an llm could automate parts of simulation design so that we could learn new skills quickly and transfer them to reality. eureka uses a large language model to write the reward functions for simulated robot tasks. a reward function is executable code, like other code in the simulation, and a model such as gpt-4 is good at writing code. we therefore use an llm to generate reward code—but not just once. we also ask it to improve that code iteratively. for sim-to-real reinforcement learning, designing a reward is not enough; the policy must transfer successfully. simulation and reality differ in many ways, especially in their physical models. a simulator cannot perfectly reproduce all relevant gravitational, frictional and other physical effects. a popular response is domain randomization: vary the physical parameters during training. but people normally have to design the parameter ranges manually. in dreureka, we automate that design as well as reward generation. with automatic reward and domain-randomization design, we can select policies that perform best under the generated rewards and randomized physics settings. to our delight, we found that these policies could transfer directly to the real world in our evaluated tasks. this gives us an automated sim-to-real design pipeline, avoiding iterative manual intervention in reward and randomization tuning. editorial clarification: 'fully automated' describes this algorithmic design loop. researchers still supply the task simulator, task and safety instructions, hardware setup and physical deployment; the llm does not build and operate the entire experiment unaided. this demonstrates the potential of llms to automate reinforcement-learning design, from rewards and domain randomization to policies suitable for deployment, reducing dependence on repeated expert tuning. that improves efficiency and opens possibilities for more complex real-world problems. the reported automation and transfer results are within the experimental tasks and assumptions, rather than proof of a universal autonomous deployment system.
ep6: yecheng jason ma on eureka and dreureka — using llms to address key challenges in simulation and rl for the parkour work, i see two central questions: how to design and tune an effective training strategy, and how to overcome the sim-to-real gap. designing the training strategy is complicated, involving reinforcement learning with different dynamics constraints and the distillation of skill policies. many earlier quadruped systems used proprioception without vision. here we introduce visual perception, particularly a stereo depth camera, which makes the sim-to-real gap more important. we try to simulate depth sensing as realistically as possible and process real-world data to resemble the cleaner, idealized images in simulation. bringing the two distributions closer helps narrow the gap. we tried several ways to narrow that gap, including filling holes and removing noise. depth images work reasonably well for this purpose. the parkour challenge is comparatively focused: traversing terrain, for which understanding its geometry and depth is crucial. but future practical robots should not rely only on depth. they will also need to use rgb images. multitask learning is another longstanding challenge. when one model learns several tasks at once, their backpropagated gradients may conflict and each skill can lose performance. tuning one skill is relatively easy; tuning several together is hard. after trying different approaches, ziwen found a useful strategy: train each skill separately as a teacher, then train a shared student from them. this minimizes performance degradation. the result is a systematic solution and a broad capability improvement, rather than one isolated innovation.
ep7: hang zhao and ziwen zhuang on robot parkour and autonomous driving — where robot data comes from the idea behind robogen is to extract relevant information and use it to build a robot-training environment. that includes the skills a robot should learn, the setting for each skill, the environment's appearance and how the robot interacts with it. we also need clear completion criteria, usually expressed as rewards or losses. large models, such as language models, can generate the code for those functions automatically. we want to automate every preparation step and connect the pipeline—from defining rewards to generating code—so the training process becomes highly automated from beginning to end. this is the goal and core idea behind the fully automated training pipeline we first proposed. reinforcement learning works well for many rigid-body interactions, both locomotion and manipulation. deformable objects complicate matters, making differentiable components important. fluids and clothing differ from rigid objects, and rl needs an effective representation of their state. if we move beyond rigid-body interaction, the complexity of that state space becomes a challenge. simulators often use particle systems; a piece of cloth might contain hundreds of thousands of particles. writing a conventional reward function that assesses those particle states can be difficult and expensive. first, the particle count makes describing the state and checking goal completion costly. second, it is hard to write an explicit function for a deformation such as folding clothing and its corresponding particle configuration. these difficulties motivate differentiable components, which can make learning soft-object interaction more efficient. this explains their role in our approach, rather than establishing that every deformable-object task requires differentiable simulation. gradient information can accelerate policy learning and optimization compared with relying on reinforcement learning alone. combining the approaches effectively is still an active research topic, without a mature framework that resolves all these issues. gradients are not always ideal. contact can make the optimization landscape nonsmooth or discontinuous, introducing noise and harming training efficiency. gradients also convey local information, which may be insufficient for global optimization in complicated nonconvex problems. these are challenges the research community is still addressing.
ep8: chuang gan and zhou xian on robogen — generating robot demonstrations with generative models and differentiable simulation, with a differentiable physics review at the heart of umi is a physical api. we found a physical interface with a form sufficiently similar to a robot's, yet not restricted to one particular robot embodiment, and much cheaper than a robot. i can explain it from three perspectives. first, portability. suppose a robot cost only rmb1,000–2,000. with the weight of today's robots, collecting restaurant data would still involve loading it onto a truck, driving there, unloading, installing and calibrating it. half a day could disappear. every new environment incurs that setup cost, making diverse-environment data expensive. umi's handheld device addresses this. its gripper is still somewhat heavy, around 800 grams, but fits in a bag. once we arrive somewhere—for example, sit down at a restaurant—we can begin recording within two minutes. that greatly simplifies collecting diverse real-world data. the robot price here is a hypothetical example, not the price of the umi system. second, similarity of physical form. many research platforms combine an industrial robot arm with a parallel-jaw gripper, and umi was designed around that common form. it records the gripper's six-degree-of-freedom trajectory in space. if a robot can reach a required pose, the particular joint angles used to get there are less important; in principle, even another platform such as a drone could reach a position. in that sense, umi is relatively independent of the robot's embodiment: the brand matters less than its ability to execute the demonstrated poses. editorial clarification: having six degrees of freedom alone does not guarantee compatibility. reachability, gripper geometry, actuation, timing and other constraints still matter; the drone is a conceptual example, not a demonstrated universal transfer result. third, intuitive data collection. we tried a dynamic throwing task with round and square objects and two corresponding bins: throw each object into the bin of the matching shape. this fast movement is difficult to demonstrate through robot teleoperation. in our earlier tests, fifteen minutes of teleoperation did not successfully throw a single block into the bin. with umi, people have a strong intuition for using the gripper, and collection ran at about half the speed of using bare hands. that sounds slow, but it is a major improvement over obtaining no successful teleoperated demonstration. in another task, turning a cup, umi again collected data at roughly half bare-hand speed, while robot teleoperation was about three times slower than umi. these examples show its collection advantages.
ep2: cheng chi and zhenjia xu on umi — a physical api for robot training dexcap's wrist cameras track the scene using slam. in the interview, i described the combined spatial tracking as having roughly centimeter or subcentimeter accuracy, and called dexcap a 'nuclear weapon,' metaphorically for obtaining higher-precision data than third-person mimicplay videos. the wrist cameras are for tracking rather than primarily collecting policy-training images. human and robot hands look different, creating a domain gap in those images. we tried learning directly from human wrist-camera footage, and it did not work well. editorial clarification: this overall tracking figure is distinct from the millimeter-level relative fingertip measurement supplied by the electromagnetic glove below. dexcap uses motion-capture gloves with an electromagnetic sensor on each fingertip. a wrist-mounted camera tracks the hand's six-degree-of-freedom pose. an electromagnetic transmitter sits below it, with receivers at the fingertips. the electromagnetic measurements give millimeter-level estimates of fingertip positions relative to the hand. combined with the wrist camera's hand pose relative to the chest, this lets us recover fingertip positions in the camera's coordinate frame. the chest camera, wrist cameras and gloves work together to provide the overall measurement. the chest camera tracks the person's pose in world coordinates; the wrist cameras track the hands relative to the chest; and the gloves track the fingertips relative to the hands. as you walk wearing the system, combining those measurements gives absolute fingertip positions in space. those high-quality trajectories can then guide a robot through inverse kinematics. editorial clarification: inverse kinematics is one part of retargeting, not a guarantee that any robot can replay every human motion without accounting for its embodiment and physical constraints.
ep4: chen wang on mimicplay and dexcap — learning from human videos and motion capture open-television proposes a new teleoperation method suited to humanoids and today's collection challenges. an operator cannot simply stand behind a humanoid, because its torso blocks the view. standing beside it and craning one's neck is also unintuitive and tiring. a humanoid is mobile, so installing many fixed cameras is impractical. the most intuitive approach is therefore immersive control—as if you had become the robot. this inspired open-television: operators need not stand beside or behind the robot or control it from a third-person view. they wear a headset and operate it immersively. there are three main features. first, immersion: the operator sees stereoscopic video rather than a flat 2d view, like a 3d film. different images reach the left and right eyes, giving natural depth cues that help estimate distances and perform fine tasks. second, our system has an active neck so its head can move. when people act, they focus using the small foveal region at the center of the retina. with a fixed camera, looking elsewhere may require sideways glances or peripheral vision. the active neck makes control more intuitive: turn your head and the view follows, without awkwardly shifting your eyes. third, it can reduce computational cost. the operator can focus on a smaller central view rather than processing an extremely high-resolution wide-angle image containing much irrelevant information. turning the head brings the desired area into view. in our setup, this supported around 80 hz, compared with about 40 hz when processing larger images. a higher frame rate helps the experience feel more immediate and intuitive. these rates describe the interview's setup, not a guaranteed rate on all hardware.
ep3: xuxin cheng on open-television — immersive robot teleoperation with mobile aloha, we used real-world data rather than simulation. people collected demonstrations through teleoperation, and efficient imitation learning allowed training from a relatively small amount of data. that provides realistic visual signals, such as rgb images, and information about the task's semantics. one challenge is that real-world data is slow to collect. mobile aloha combines an accessible collection system with an efficient imitation-learning algorithm: around fifty human demonstrations per task can teach a range of skills. compared with earlier collection methods using vr equipment, a 3d mouse or keyboard, this interface can be quicker and easier to learn. its value is helping people rapidly learn to operate robots and collect demonstrations for many real-world problems. editorial clarification: the paper reports selected tasks, including co-training with static aloha data. the original's phrase 'almost all problems in the real world' is an aspirational description, not an experimentally established capability.
ep5: zipeng fu on humanplus and mobile aloha — synthetic data, real data and their combination a major reason robot data is difficult to collect is the diversity of embodiments. different robots may represent the same sensor modality differently. fragmented platforms and varied data formats are a major obstacle to a comprehensive shared model. by multimodal data, we mean not only rgb images and text but also point clouds, touch and other modalities crucial for dexterous manipulation. to distinguish these broader differences from the usual image-and-language discussion of multimodal foundation models, we use the term heterogeneity. there are also substantial differences between data domains: human videos, real robot demonstrations and simulation, for example. that is a distinctive challenge in robotics and embodied intelligence. each domain has strengths and weaknesses. simulation supplies abundant data but cannot perfectly reproduce everything. human videos are plentiful online but often lack action labels, making training difficult. real robot data is expensive. cross-domain research is therefore challenging. poco's core idea is to combine heterogeneous policies across domains to improve robot learning's generality. we consider three levels. at the task level, policies trained for different tasks, such as using different tools, can be combined through diffusion training and classifier-free guidance. at the domain level, we can compose policies trained from sources such as simulation and real robot data. at the behavior level, we can specify costs at test time—for example, to favor smoother or safer behavior—and combine those objectives with the learned policies. the composition operates through compatible policy distributions and their scores or energy representations, rather than simply averaging unrelated action vectors. my phd thesis mainly concerns heterogeneous data, including my earlier work robot fleet learning via policy merging and does learning from decentralized non-iid unlabeled data benefit from self supervision? poco also asks how to process and use such data more efficiently. it is a broader, foundational problem: outside vision and language, many fields have too little data but still want to apply machine learning. they therefore face heterogeneity as well. how do we extract information efficiently from these datasets? this larger question remains underexplored. researchers often focus on one robot, task, simulator, real-world setting or algorithm, such as imitation learning or reinforcement learning. i think studying these elements together, rather than only in isolation, is highly valuable. people are now focused on large models, and training one model to support diverse tasks is a meaningful challenge. for example, should we use 30% simulation data and 50% real-world data, or 10% simulation and 70% real-world data? we still have limited understanding of how to choose such mixtures, and often adjust them intuitively. those example pairs are partial mixtures rather than complete recipes summing to 100%. i believe research on heterogeneous data will broadly support the training and application of large models and be important to the field's development. gpt-4o provides a useful analogy. earlier systems were often language-centered, with a language model in the middle and language as the only output. we can instead think about tokenizing different data types and pretraining them jointly, which is an idea behind hpt. that offers the possibility of integrating information across modalities. some recent work also suggests that representations from different modalities may converge, because they describe the same world from different perspectives. editorial fox教授合作。他的研究兴趣在于机器人技术和机器学习，特别致力于开发能够在复杂且无结构的现实环境中进行泛化的机器人算法和系统，从事于可以处理异构机器人数据的群体学习研究。 poco: policy composition from and for heterogeneous robot learning的作者包括lirui wang, jialiang zhao, yilun du, edward adelson, russ tedrake，它被rss 2024收录。 以下为本文目录 👇 1. poco介绍 2. poco的核心思想 3. 如何理解跨domain的数据融合？ 4. 怎么理解policy composition？ 5. 为何特别关注异构数据？ 6. poco只针对工具使用类的任务吗？ 7. 为什么加入触觉信息？ 8. 其他关于poco的问题 9. 关于hpt 10. 关于fleet learning 一些想法 如何应对机器人领域中极为异构的数据集和任务？机器人数据来自不同领域，例如仿真环境、真实机器人操作以及人类视频。我们研究了使用扩散模型的策略组合（poco）方法，以应对这些挑战。 poco介绍 我们专注于能够泛化的机器人工具使用任务，这些任务强调了在现实世界操控中的组合性和丰富的接触特性。工具使用任务在机器人应用中非常重要，并且有大量真实人类视频资源可供使用。为支持这一研究，我们在drake仿真环境中开发了一个基准测试。 data poco 的核心理念是优化动作轨迹的组合能量景观。这个推理过程无需重新训练，可以应用于不同的任务（例如锤子和扳手任务）、行为（例如平滑度成本目标）和领域（例如仿真和现实环境）。 poco方法简介 poco 展示了在不同场景中的泛化能力，能够适应变化的物体和工具姿态、干扰物、新物体以及动态场景。受人类学习方式的启发，poco 能够在不同模态（如rgb、点云、触觉）和领域（如仿真、真实机器人、视频）中组合策略。 我们组合的多任务策略在具有外部接触、可变形物体、强力操控和外部干扰的任务中展示了任务级的泛化能力。此外，它在这四个工具使用任务中的表现也优于直接在多任务上训练的无条件策略。 工具1-饭勺子 工具2-扳手 工具三-小锤子 工具四-刀子 机器人数据获取难度大很大一部分原因是机器人的形态很多，在不同的机器人上，会有不同的方法来表示它们的某些模态，分散的机器人载体和多模态的数据模式是导致目前机器人没有完整模型的一个主要原因。我们提到的多模态，即包括rgb视觉信息、文字信息也包括点云和触觉等这些对灵巧操作任务至关重要的信息模态。为了与目前大家常说的多模态大模型里的模态加以区分，我们将这些数据类别统称为多样性（heterogeneity）而不再称之为多模态。 除了数据多样性问题，机器人训练所用到的数据领域（domain）也存在巨大差异，比如人类视频、真实机器人数据以及仿真数据，这也是机器人学或具身智能领域特有的挑战。每个domain都有自己的优势和劣势，仿真中我们可以生成大量数据，但有些东西可能无法模拟，存在仿真与现实之间的差距；人类视频数据在网上有大量可用，但可能缺少动作标签，训练起来较难；而真实机器人数据非常昂贵，因此，跨domain的研究非常困难。 如何将机器人训练数据多样性和跨多个领域的数据组合起来，提高机器人训练的通用性是poco这个工作最核心的思想。在poco中，我们把不同的策略拆分成了几个层次：第一，task level：在不同的任务，比如不同的工具使用，我们可以进行一些训练，使用 classifier-free的diffusion training。这样就可以在任务层次上进行组合，利用不同的工具。第二，domain level：在不同的领域来源，比如仿真和真实机器人上进行组合。我们可以研究如何将这两个领域的策略组合在一起。第三，behavior level：在测试时可以指定一些成本，比如让它的行为更加顺滑或者更加安全。我们可以直接手动编写一些任务或目标，然后进行组合。 在真实机器人上，我们有一些传感器，例如摄像头、手部摄像头和第三视角摄像头，还有触觉传感器。在我们进行远程操作时，这些传感器会收集数据，这些数据可以用来训练模型，并且模型也可以工作，但常常会有一些问题，例如泛化能力不足。我们发现，很多时候这些演示数据会导致模型过拟合。举个最基本的例子，在一个桌面环境中，机器人需要用锤子去敲击钉子。如果我将钉子的位置移动到一个模型训练时未见过的位置，它可能就无法正确执行任务了。更不用说在场景中添加障碍物或快速移动目标物体了，这些都会暴露出模型在泛化能力上的问题。 然而，在仿真环境中，针对这些场景相关的挑战，可以很容易地被设计出来。在仿真环境中，我们可以添加各种杂乱的物体，并使用规划器生成演示数据。这样一来，基于仿真训练的策略甚至可以通过另一种模态（比如点云数据）表现出更好的泛化能力。 因此，在测试阶段，如果我们有两个策略——假设一个来自仿真，一个来自真实机器人操作，且它们已经分别完成了训练，我们能否将它们结合起来，从而实现两者的优势互补？也就是说，既能保有现实世界中的流畅动作，又能利用仿真环境中的泛化能力。这正是这篇论文的动机所在。 我们假设这两个策略已经各自训练完毕，且在训练过程中并没有共享数据。例如，一个公司训练了一个模型，另一个公司也训练了一个模型。现在我们想将它们结合起来，以在两个模型都未曾见过的全新场景中进行测试，看看能否实现更好的泛化能力。在机器人领域，我们可以将这种情况称之为组合泛化（compositional generalization）。举个例子，我们可以用锤子来钉钉子，也可以用扳手来拧螺丝。然而，如果我们想用扳手来钉钉子（tool use generalize to tool use），直接训练一个基于rgb的策略往往是无法实现的，我们可以通过策略组合（policy composition）的方式，实现这种组合泛化的能力。 policy composition就是每个领域的策略都是在各自的领域中独立训练的，然后将这些训练出来的策略进行组合。策略的组合（policy composition）其实并不常见，基本上很少有人做这种工作。我们之所以能够进行这种组合，是因为我们利用了扩散策略（diffusion policy）这个隐式模型的结构。 具体来说，扩散策略学习的是一个能量景观（energy landscape），它隐式地表示了这个能量景观。所以我们可以将两个或多个能量景观组合起来，而这在之前的研究中是比较少见的。另一种理解这种方法的方式是想象做梯度下降（gradient descent），由两个不同的策略模型提供不同的梯度，然后在测试时将它们组合起来，这实际上是一个在测试阶段进行的组合过程。 在传统的机器人学中，比如轨迹优化领域，我们经常定义一些目标，比如我们可能会定义轨迹要尽可能平稳，也要避免碰撞等，这其实是两个目标，在优化过程中，要为其提供梯度使其同时满足这两个目标或约束。策略组合相当于将这两个目标替换为两个策略，它可以非常灵活地选择不同的策略，就像选择多个组件一样，然后将它们组合成一个模块，用来执行特定的任务。 如果是一个简单的前馈策略，比如两个mlp或两个transformer，一个预测左移，一个预测右移，简单地平均，它们就往中间，可能会产生奇怪的效果。比如，如果我们需要避开中间的障碍物，有些目标是往左移动，有些是往右移动，简单地平均它们反而可能会撞到中间的障碍物。但因为diffusion policy并不是简单的平均，他是iterative和implicit的，因此在数学上这样compose它是合理的，因此它可以真的支持一些组合的问题。 针对diffusion policy的这个特性，应该就是之前采访迟宬博士提到diffusion policy可以很好的解决多模态分布（multimodal distribution）。感兴趣的朋友可以去之前的文章查看（diffusion policy—基于扩散模型的机器人动作生成策略） diffusion policy 是我们采用的一种策略类别，其基本假设是它需要是一种基于能量的模型，而diffusion policy算是一种基于能量的模型。在训练时，diffusion policy就在预测一个降噪（denoise）的步骤，在测试时，它会持续预测，从一个随机噪声轨迹开始，一直不断的降噪它，根据当前观察到的情况，把它降噪成训练阶段设定的期望轨迹或可行动作。在这个持续降噪的过程中，如果我们有两个不同的 diffusion policy，根据当下的观测和噪声轨迹，它们各自会生成一个预测，我们就可以把这两个预测组合起来。 最理想的情况是，它为我们提供了一个用户界面，其中包含许多不同的模块。例如，你可以选择使策略的轨迹更安全，或者使其行为更像仿真中的策略，或者让它执行更多类似于锤击的任务，你就选择即可。在选择完毕后，在测试时将这些模块组合在一起即可，但这些策略都可以是分开训练的。 上面是针对不同领域训练的策略组合，那针对不同模态的数据训练的策略组合是类似的逻辑。不同模态下产生的不同策略，只要它们的动作空间是相同的，就可以被组合起来。因此，它们可以是同一个领域内，两个不同模态的数据训练出的两个策略，也可以是两个不同的领域，同样的模态数据训练出来的两个策略。 还有一个没有提到的是人类视频，在这里，我们建立了一个数据管道，能够追踪人类视频中“手-工具-物体”的点云，利用这些点云可以训练出一些策略。这也是一个非常可扩展的方法，用于收集人类数据。这样训练出来的策略可以与其他两个领域的策略一起组合，从而提升效果。 在实验中，比如说结合了仿真和真实环境比单独使用仿真或者单独使用真实环境效果更好。这里面使用了仿真的时候是用到了3d点云，而在真实环境中则是用到了摄像头和触觉，所以这种情况下加入了不同的模态。 在策略组合方面，其实之前已经有很多工作涉及类似的想法，比如 classifier-free diffusion model，这些都与我们的工作有一定联系。我们相当于是从一个新的视角出发，特别是从数据的异质性角度来考虑这个问题，尽量使其更加通用，这正是我们这个工作的创新之处。 具体来说，有一个既定目标，怎么用这个既定目标来偏置（bias）采样过程。举例来说，假设我们训练一个扩散策略（diffusion policy），在一个迷宫场景中，如果目标设定在迷宫的右上角，那么策略就会被引导向右上角移动，这可以看作是一种引导性采样过程。 我们的方法可以类比为，有一个现实机器人的策略，和一个仿真环境的策略，通过设定奖励策略，把奖励策略真实机器人策略往仿真环境的策略拉一下，使其更像仿真训出来的策略。反过来， 真实机器人策略也可以把仿真策略往真实机器人策略方向拉一点，使其更像真机策略。 我的 phd 论文主要是关于异构性数据（heterogeneous data），其中包括了我之前的两个工作 fleet learning（robot fleet learning via policy merging）和dec ssl（does decentralized learning with non-iid unlabeled data benefit from self supervision？）其实包括poco，它核心思路也是如何更加高效地处理和利用这种异构性数据。这是一个更广泛、更基础的问题，除了视觉和语言领域外，几乎所有其他领域都面临数据不足的问题，但却希望能够应用机器学习。因此，他们都会遇到异构性数据的问题。 如何高效地从这些数据中提取信息？这个大问题在当前的研究中仍然未被充分探索。在整个学术界，很多研究者可能会专注于单个问题，比如一种机器人、一种任务、一个模拟环境或一个真实世界的任务，或者某种特定的算法，比如模仿学习或强化学习。但其实，把这些各类要素整合在一起，进行综合研究，我认为是非常有价值的。 现在大家都在关注大模型，如何训练一个大模型来支持多样化的任务，这其实是一个非常有意义的问题。比如到底是 30% 的模拟数据加 50% 的真实世界数据，还是 10% 的模拟数据加 70% 的真实世界数据，这些比例如何选择，目前其实并没有太多的理解，很多时候都是凭感觉进行调整。我认为，对异构性数据的研究会在未来全面支持大模型的训练和应用，这对于整个领域的发展是非常重要的。 gpt4o是一个很好的例子。过去，大家通常是以语言为中心，中间的模型必定是语言模型，输出也只能是语言。但现在显然他们提前把数据都tokenize好了，然后进行了一些异构预训练，这就是hpt里的一个想法。这样做的好处是，它能够融会贯通。最近也有一些工作表明，这种表示不同的模态最终会收敛，因为它们都是从不同的视角看待世界。 它不仅仅针对工具使用类任务，可以针对各类机器人任务，只是我认为工具使用类任务在机器人操作中非常有趣，也应该是比较具有挑战性的，因为它对泛化能力的要求非常高。所以我选择将工具使用这类任务作为主要关注点之一，但这并不意味着poco仅能做这种任务。 工具更换与灵巧手使用工具有所不同，我觉得现在工业界里比较流行的还是工具更换。如果你要换一个工具，可能就需要重新训练那个策略，这就很麻烦了。最好的情况是有一个基础的策略，然后每次更换工具时只需要进行适配。甚至在理想情况下，连适配都不需要。 我当时选择操作任务时，觉得grasping和pushing这些任务已经有很多人做了，所以决定选择一个新的任务，挑一些不同的技能。我认为工具使用其实几乎涵盖了所有的东西。我们在这里写的是用锤子和扳手，实际上，烹饪也是在使用工具。虽然工具使用听起来包罗万象，但我的想法是，这样的技能是可以被学习的。就像人类一样，如果我要用石头砸东西，我其实知道怎么做，这些基本的物体之间的互动是可以被学出来的。所以我选择了这个任务，尽管我知道它可能定义模糊，还涉及到很多力学方面的东西，但我觉得这个任务非常有意思。这就是我的基本思路。我认为，不论是数据的异构性还是工具使用，我们增加了更多的任务，相当于增加了更多的工具和更多的embodiment，虽然更有挑战，但可能具身大模型就是这样才能训练出来。 增加了这些数据异构性、工具和任务，把这些放在一起为什么会有帮助？怎么可能会work？怎么可以加在一起训练？但如果你看大语言模型，比如说加入代码数据，这些数据对模型的性能提升是非常显著的。直觉上，一个正常人不会觉得代码数据能帮助学习英语或者中文。但实际上，我们给模型增加了更难的任务，这些任务配合一些好的目标，比如next token prediction，让模型面临挑战，它必须去学会一些抽象的、有推理能力的技能和知识，来完成各种不同的任务。所以我认为这种思维方式是非常基础的。 因为我们在使用工具时，特别重要的是能够感知到当一个物体碰撞另一个物体时的具体力量，这时就需要触觉传感器来获取这些信息。如果只有视觉，可能无法获得这些信息。另外一个重要的方面是确定工具在手中的位置和姿态。这在工具使用中非常关键，因此很多工具使用的研究都会使用触觉信息。poco这个工作里我们用的触觉传感器是gelsight svelvt，jialiang的一个触觉传感器，（关于gelsight相关触觉传感器，我们在gelsight十五年——简述视触觉传感器发展史有详细介绍）。 without retraining怎么理解？ 不需要像chatgpt那样把数据放在一起训练，我们可以分开训练，却能在多个领域中达到类似的效果。这其实是一个更具挑战性的设置，因为这些数据都是分开来使用的，你需要确保如何有效地整合它们在一起。 poco哪里可以改进 poco有一个问题就是在实践中可能速度不够快，因为需要在测试时运行多个策略。不过这个问题应该可以比较容易解决，只需要更多的计算资源就行了。分布式计算可以很好地解决这个主要问题。另外，在算法上我们其实还有很多可以改进的地方。 对poco我们有一个follow-up的工作，叫做heterogeneous pre-trained transformer（hpt，异构预训练变换器）。hpt的想法比poco简单很多，也更通用，就是把所有数据放到一起，把openx、仿真数据、以及人类视频数据等多达50多种不同的数据集汇总在一起训练，这可能是最异构的数据集了。训练的方法就是，我们对每个embodiment进行了单独的tokenize。你可以想象，针对不同模态的数据，我们把不同模态的数据进行tokenize，但在robotics里有embodiment这个概念，如果有不同的观测和不同的动作，都需要单独对待。所以我们tokenize embodiment，然后将其映射到一个中间的transformer，然后再将其映射回到每个独立的任务。因此，在这种情况下，我们开发了一种新的架构，并观察了他的可扩展性，我们研究了通过增加数据或模型大小是否可以提升性能。 hpt效果 效果就是我们可以将其迁移到一个新的领域，而不必重新训练中间的那个 transformer。假设每个模态都有了自己的tokenizer，我们只需要训练一个非常小的网络，将其调整到新的机器人领域即可，效果还挺好的，这个工作最近会发布。 hpt我们既是加了更多的数据，也是在增加更多的挑战，通过这些挑战让模型不得不去学习一些可以通用的东西。这可能类似于不同层次的数据金字塔（pyramids of data），有些数据比较容易获取，有些则比较昂贵，但每个数据的质量都不一样，因此需要一个好的方法将它们结合在一起。 集群学习（fleet learning）是我们提出了一个新的想法，包括russ tedrake也非常感兴趣，tri也一直在说这个概念。这个想法一直在讨论，尤其是随着越来越多的机器人技术的发展和投资，会有成百上千的机器人出现。每个机器人遇到一些数据或场景时，如果其他机器人不知道如何处理，它们是不是也得先看到相同的信息才能学习？因此，我们想要实现的目标是，比如有1000个机器人，一个机器人学到了某些信息或遇到了某些场景，其他所有机器人都应该能够立即学习到这些信息。因此，我们在这里研究的这个想法叫做“fleet learning”。 它的一个例子是自动驾驶。实际上，每辆车都可以生成大量的数据，每天都会产生大量数据，而目前最基本的做法是将这些数据经过复杂的数据处理流程。fleet leanring实际上是在研究集群学习的问题，每个机器人在执行不同任务时，就像我们之前提到的不同的模态一样，因为它们是被设计成这样，它们执行不同的任务，所以它们是非常异构的。那么我们如何高效地处理这种异构性？或者如何在这种异构性中高效地学习数据和表示？这就是集群学习的理念。 所以，我可以总结一下这四个工作：hpt、fleet learning、dec ssl和poco。hpt相当于是将这些异构的数据放在一起，然后对这些数据进行tokenize，训练一个大模型。fleet learning在训练时将它们的权重进行平均，将神经网络的权重组合起来，这样更加高效，可能权重只有几mb，而不是每天上传几tb的数据。这些大量的数据比如说在一个月内完成训练，然后在完成后对几mb的数据进行平均。然后，对于dec ssl，假设这些数据甚至都没有标签，是未标记的，那我能不能先做自监督学习，先学习到一种表示，然后再平均，再组合。最后是poco，如果这些策略都训练完毕，我们能不能在它们的动作空间进行一些组合。所以实际上，这些工作是从不同的角度去解决这个问题。 因为最近几天睡前陪读《恐龙王国》，我第一次了解曾经和人类共同生存在同一个星球上的物种的点滴。从最早出现在2亿多年前的三叠纪晚期到6600万年前因未知灾难的灭绝，恐龙在地球上生活了1.6亿年。从身长长达30米的梁龙，小到几十厘米的美颌龙，进化了1亿多年的恐龙生存能力比人类强太多，但如今它们也只能以地下的化石来证明他们曾经存在过。反观人类文明，更进步一步到中华五千年文明，与以千万年为单位计量的恐龙时代相比，真的是微不足道，人类文明下2024年的我们更是沧海一粟。每个当下的无灾无难、平安健康都是值得被珍惜和庆幸的瞬间。恐龙帝国的消亡也许意味着人类文明的终点逃不过一些宿命，我也突然有些理解elon musk常说的火星殖民和人类文明的延续之间的关系。如果某一个轮回我站在了人类文明的终点，我会非常感谢今天的人们在脑机接口、星际飞船、通用机器人、新能源、人工智能这些领域做出的不懈努力。人类文明过于绚烂和精彩，穿越世代后，它不可以仅仅以化石的形式被埋藏在地下，它必须以某种形式延续下去！ robot lirui wang on heterogeneous robot data and policy composition the complete poco interview on combining simulation, human video, real robots and tactile information, followed by hpt, fleet learning and a personal reflection. in the first eight episodes of robot data, we worked through the robot data pyramid, introducing strong research that learns from human video, motion capture, teleoperation and simulation. these projects often focus on using one kind of data to advance robot learning. can robots make use of all these modalities together? the answer is yes—and they must. human learning through interaction with the physical world also combines different sources. a child may mentally imitate a cartoon character's movements, analogous to simulated data; imitate an adult, analogous to human video; or need an adult to guide their hands through a difficult task, analogous to teleoperation. with help from these different kinds of experience, people become better at tasks. how, then, do we handle the extremely heterogeneous datasets and tasks found in robotics? data comes from simulation, real-robot operation and human video demonstrations. today's paper, policy composition, or poco, uses diffusion models to combine information across domains, modalities and tasks. its composed policies demonstrate strong scene-level and task-level generalization in tool-use tasks. i invited the paper's first author, lirui wang, to explain poco. at the time of this september 2024 interview, lirui was a phd student at mit, advised by professor russ tedrake at mit csail, and also worked closely with professor kaiming he. before mit, he earned his bachelor's and master's degrees at the university of washington, working with professor dieter fox. his interests span robotics and machine learning, particularly algorithms and systems that generalize to complex, unstructured real-world environments, and fleet learning that can handle heterogeneous robot data. poco: policy composition from and for heterogeneous robot learning was written by lirui wang, jialiang zhao, yilun du, edward h. adelson and russ tedrake, and accepted at rss 2024. contents ↓ 1. introducing poco 2. poco's core idea 3. understanding data combination across domains 4. what does policy composition mean? 5. why focus on heterogeneous data? 6. is poco only for tool-use tasks? 7. why include touch? 8. other questions about poco 9. hpt 10. fleet learning some reflections how do we address robotics' highly heterogeneous datasets and tasks? robot data comes from domains such as simulation, real-robot operation and human video. we investigate policy composition using diffusion models—poco—to meet these challenges. an introduction to poco we focus on generalizable robotic tool use, which highlights the compositional and contact-rich nature of real-world manipulation. tool use is important in robotics, and there is a substantial supply of real human video involving tools. to support this work, we developed a benchmark in the drake simulation environment. poco's core idea is to optimize a composed energy landscape over action trajectories. this composition takes place during inference without retraining, and can apply across tasks, such as hammer and wrench tasks; behaviors, such as a trajectory-smoothness objective; and domains, such as simulation and reality. an overview of the poco method poco generalizes across scenes with changing object and tool poses, distractors, new objects and dynamic conditions. inspired by human learning, it composes policies across modalities such as rgb, point clouds and touch, and across domains such as simulation, real robots and human video. our composed multitask policy demonstrates task-level generalization in tasks involving contact with the environment, deformable objects, forceful manipulation and external disturbances. it also outperforms an unconditional policy trained directly on the four tool-use tasks. tool 1: a rice paddle tool 2: a wrench tool 3: a small hammer tool 4: a knife a large part of the difficulty in collecting robot data comes from the diversity of robot embodiments. different robots represent their sensor modalities differently. fragmented hardware platforms and diverse data formats are among the reasons we still lack a unified robot model. by multimodal data, we mean not only rgb and text but also point clouds and touch, which are crucial to dexterous manipulation. to distinguish this broader challenge from how 'multimodal' is often used for foundation models, we describe it as heterogeneity. beyond modality differences, training domains vary enormously: human video, real-robot data and simulation data. this is a distinctive challenge in robotics and embodied ai. each domain has strengths and weaknesses. simulation can provide large quantities of data, but some phenomena are difficult to simulate and a sim-to-real gap remains. human video is abundant online but may lack action labels, making learning harder. real-robot data is expensive. research across these domains is therefore difficult. poco's central question is how to combine this diversity across domains to make robot learning more general. we consider composition at three levels. first, the task level: train for different tasks, such as using different tools, with classifier-free diffusion training, then compose task-related behaviors. second, the domain level: combine policies learned in domains such as simulation and real robots. third, the behavior level: specify costs at test time, for example to favor smoother or safer trajectories. we can manually define such objectives and compose them with the policies. a real robot may have several sensors: cameras on the hand, external cameras and tactile sensors. during teleoperation, they collect data for training a model. the resulting model may work, yet have limited generalization. we often find that demonstrations lead to overfitting. consider a tabletop task in which a robot uses a hammer to hit a nail. move the nail to a position not seen in training, and the policy may fail. add obstacles or move the target quickly, and its generalization problems become even clearer. in simulation, those scene variations are easy to design. we can introduce clutter and use a planner to generate demonstrations. a simulation-trained policy can consequently generalize better to such variations, potentially using another modality, such as point clouds. at test time, suppose we have two already-trained policies, one from simulation and one from real-robot operation. can we combine them so their strengths complement each other—retaining smooth real-world behavior while benefiting from simulation's generalization? that is the motivation for this paper. we assume the policies were trained separately, without sharing data. for example, two companies might each train a model. we then combine them and test in a new setting neither has encountered, asking whether the combination generalizes better. in robotics, we can call this compositional generalization. we might know how to hammer a nail and how to turn a screw with a wrench, but want to hammer the nail using the wrench. a directly trained rgb policy may not manage that transfer; policy composition offers a way to combine skills and support such generalization. each domain's policy is trained independently, and the trained policies are then composed. at the time of this work, this kind of composition was relatively uncommon in robot learning. we can do it because of diffusion policies' implicit generative structure. a diffusion policy can be interpreted through an implicit energy landscape. that gives us a way to combine two or more landscapes. another intuition is gradient-based optimization: different policy models provide different directions, which we combine during inference. the composition happens at test time, not by pooling all the data and retraining a single policy. in traditional trajectory optimization, we often define several objectives—for instance, making a trajectory smooth and avoiding collisions. their gradients guide optimization toward satisfying both. policy composition replaces such objectives, conceptually, with learned policies. we can select different policies like components and compose them to carry out a task. simply averaging the outputs of two feedforward policies, such as mlps or transformers, can behave strangely. if one chooses left and another right, their mean points down the middle. if an obstacle is in the middle, averaging two individually sensible routes could produce a collision. diffusion-policy composition is not merely averaging final actions: it is iterative and implicit, which gives a mathematical basis for composing distributions in this framework. that supports forms of composition that a naive action average would not. this relates to cheng chi's point in our earlier interview that diffusion policy handles multimodal action distributions well. here, 'multimodal' means several plausible action modes, rather than several sensor types. for more, see diffusion policy: generating robot actions with diffusion models. diffusion policies are the policy class we use. the key is their connection to energy-based or score-based modeling. during training, a policy learns a denoising prediction. at test time, it starts with a noisy trajectory and repeatedly denoises it, conditioned on the current observation, toward plausible actions represented in its training distribution. with two diffusion policies, each produces a prediction from the current observation and noisy trajectory, and we combine those predictions during the iterative process. editorial clarification: this energy-landscape explanation is an interpretation of diffusion scores; it does not mean that every diffusion implementation explicitly outputs a scalar energy or that an arbitrary pair of policies can be combined without compatible representations. ideally, this would give us an interface with different modules to choose from. you could select a safer trajectory, behavior closer to a simulation-trained policy, or more hammer-like actions. after selection, the modules would be composed at test time, even though each policy was trained separately. that is an envisioned use of the method, rather than a guarantee that a safety preference establishes safety. the same logic applies to policies trained on different modalities, not only different domains. if their action spaces and representations are compatible, policies using different modalities can be composed. they might come from the same domain with different sensors, or from different domains using the same modality. we have not yet discussed human video. we built a data pipeline to track hand–tool–object point clouds in human video and use them to train policies. this is a scalable way to collect human data. such policies can then be composed with policies from the other two domains to improve performance. in our experiments, composing simulation and real-world policies performed better than using either one alone. the simulation policy used 3d point clouds, while the real-world policy used cameras and touch, so this combination also crossed modalities. earlier work, including classifier-free diffusion methods, contains related composition ideas. we approach the problem from the perspective of data heterogeneity and try to make the method more general. that perspective is central to our contribution. one way to think about it is to use an objective to bias the sampling process. suppose we train a diffusion policy for a maze. if the goal is in the top-right corner, sampling is guided toward that corner. this is guided generation. similarly, imagine a real-robot policy and a simulation policy. composing their guidance can pull the real-robot distribution toward simulation-like behavior, and the simulation distribution toward real-robot behavior. the interview uses the intuition of reward or objective guidance here; poco performs the combination through its diffusion-policy predictions. my phd research focuses on heterogeneous data. it includes my earlier work on robot fleet learning via policy merging and does learning from decentralized non-iid unlabeled data benefit from self supervision?, which we refer to here as dec ssl. poco also asks how to use heterogeneous data more efficiently. this is a broader, fundamental issue: outside data-rich fields such as language and vision, many areas have limited data but still want to use machine learning, and therefore encounter heterogeneity. how can we efficiently extract information from this data? that broad question remains underexplored. researchers often focus on one robot, one task, one simulator, one real-world problem or a particular algorithm such as imitation learning or reinforcement learning. i think it is valuable to integrate these factors and study them together. many people now want to train large models for diverse tasks, which is a meaningful goal. but how do we select data mixtures? should we use, for example, 30% simulation and 50% real-world data, or 10% simulation and 70% real-world data, alongside other sources? we do not yet understand those choices well; they are often adjusted intuitively. i believe research on heterogeneity will support foundation model training and application more broadly, and is important for the field. gpt-4o offers an analogy. earlier approaches often centered on a language model and language outputs. the idea of bringing different modalities into token representations and learning from them together is also behind hpt: different sources can inform a shared representation. some recent research suggests that representations across modalities may converge because they offer different views of the same world. editorial clarification: the speaker's description of gpt-4o's internal tokenization and training is an analogy and interpretation, not independently established knowledge of its private training pipeline. no. it can apply to other robot tasks. i chose tool use because it is interesting and challenging, with demanding generalization requirements. making it our main focus does not mean the method is limited to it. changing tools is different from using tools with a dexterous hand. tool changing is common in industry, but if each new tool requires retraining a policy, that is inconvenient. ideally, you would have a base policy that only needs adaptation when a tool changes—or, in the best case, no adaptation at all. when choosing manipulation tasks, i felt grasping and pushing had already received considerable attention. i wanted something new, with different skills. tool use encompasses a great deal. we discuss hammers and wrenches, but cooking also involves tools. although the category is broad, i believe these interactions can be learned. a person who wants to strike something with a stone has an intuitive idea of how to do it. these basic interactions between objects are learnable. i chose the problem despite its somewhat loose definition and its mechanical complexity because i found it interesting. adding tool tasks adds heterogeneity, skills and embodiments. it makes learning harder, but perhaps that is precisely how an embodied foundation model needs to be trained. why should combining more heterogeneous data, tools and tasks help? how can it work, and how can we train them together? consider language models: code data can substantially improve their capabilities. at first, one might not expect code to help a model learn english or chinese. but harder tasks, paired with useful objectives such as next-token prediction, force the model to develop abstract knowledge and reasoning skills that serve different tasks. i think that way of thinking is fundamental. in tool use, it is important to sense the forces involved when one object contacts another. tactile sensors provide information vision alone may not reveal. it is also crucial to know the tool's position and orientation within the hand, which is why many tool-use studies include touch. in poco, we use gelsight svelte, a tactile sensor developed by jialiang zhao. for more about this sensor family, see fifteen years of gelsight: a brief history of vision-based tactile sensors. editorial correction: the original spells the sensor name 'svelvt'; the published name is svelte. what does 'without retraining' mean? we do not have to gather all the data into one training process, as in the comparison with chatgpt. policies can be trained separately and then achieve cross-domain behavior through composition. that is a more challenging setting in one respect: the data remains separate, so we must make the learned policies work together effectively. 'without retraining' refers to the composition stage, not to eliminating the initial training of the policies. where can poco improve? one practical issue is speed, because several policies have to run at test time. more compute and distributed execution could help address this, though the speedup depends on the implementation and communication overhead. there is also plenty of room for algorithmic improvement. we have a follow-up direction called heterogeneous pre-trained transformers, or hpt. its idea is simpler and more general than poco's: bring together more than 50 datasets, including open x-embodiment, simulation and human video, and train with them jointly. this is an extremely heterogeneous collection. we tokenize each embodiment separately. you can imagine tokenizing different modalities, but in robotics an embodiment also brings its own observations and actions, which must be handled appropriately. embodiment-specific tokenizers map the inputs into a shared transformer, and task-specific outputs map the representations back into actions. we developed this architecture and studied whether more data or larger models improve performance. hpt results we can transfer the representation to a new domain without retraining the central transformer. by training a small input tokenizer and output network for the new robot, we adapt to its observations and action space while keeping the shared trunk fixed. the results are promising. at the time of this interview, we expect to release the work soon. hpt adds both data and challenges, pushing the model to learn reusable representations. this resembles the data pyramid: some sources are easier to obtain and others more expensive, with different qualities. we need an effective method for bringing them together. fleet learning is an idea we have been developing, one that also interests russ tedrake and has been discussed by tri. as robotics technology and investment expand, hundreds or thousands of robots will appear. when one robot encounters new data or a new situation, must every other robot experience the same thing to learn it? we would like a fleet of, say, 1,000 robots to share what any one of them learns. ideally, the others could benefit immediately. that is the goal behind fleet learning, rather than a claim that immediate transfer has already been achieved for any robot fleet. autonomous driving is an example. each vehicle produces large amounts of data daily, which conventionally passes through a complex processing pipeline. fleet learning asks how to learn across the collection. robots perform different tasks and have different sensors and designs, so their experiences are heterogeneous. how do we handle that efficiently, and learn useful data representations across it? those are the questions behind the idea. let me summarize the four directions: hpt, fleet learning, dec ssl and poco. hpt pools heterogeneous data, tokenizes it and trains a shared large representation. fleet learning combines policy parameters rather than uploading all the original data. a policy update might be only a few megabytes, compared with terabytes of daily raw data; after a period of local training, such as a month, the policies can be merged. these quantities are illustrative. editorial clarification: the policy-merging method accounts for neural-network permutation symmetry; it is not simply naive averaging of arbitrary independently trained weights. dec ssl asks whether unlabeled decentralized data can first support self-supervised representation learning, then combination. finally, poco asks whether already-trained policies can be composed in action-distribution space. they tackle heterogeneity from different angles. for the past few nights, i have been reading dinosaur kingdom at bedtime with my child, and learning about species that once inhabited the same planet we do. dinosaurs appeared in the late triassic, more than 200 million years ago, and non-avian dinosaurs disappeared around 66 million years ago after a catastrophe—a span of roughly 160 million years. from diplodocus reaching around 30 meters in length to the much smaller compsognathus, described in my original account as only a few tens of centimeters long, i feel that more than a hundred million years of evolution gave dinosaurs far greater survival abilities than humans. their long history makes me reflect on how fragile our own tenure is. many of those creatures now survive for us only as fossils underground. even five thousand years of chinese civilization is tiny beside an age measured in tens of millions of years. we, living in 2024, are smaller still. every ordinary moment of health, peace and freedom from disaster is worth cherishing. the fall of that dinosaur world makes me wonder whether human civilization could face a similar end. i suddenly understand a little more of the connection elon musk draws between settling mars and continuing civilization. if i were someday standing at the end of human civilization, i would be grateful for the relentless work people are doing today on brain–computer interfaces, spacecraft, general-purpose robots, new energy and artificial intelligence. human civilization is too rich and extraordinary to survive across generations only as fossils buried underground. it must continue in some form. editorial clarification: the original suggests dinosaurs and humans shared an era and calls the extinction an unknown catastrophe. humans did not coexist with non-avian dinosaurs; the end-cretaceous extinction is strongly associated with an asteroid impact, and birds are surviving dinosaurs. the reflection above concerns our shared planet across different ages. the original size comparison is a rough description, and the survival comparison is my reflection, not a biological measurement. the final research interview in robot data season 1 is complete. i sincerely thank the scholars who accepted my invitations and everyone who has continued following the series. the diagram below summarizes the robot data pyramid explored across all nine interviews. general-purpose robots represent a far-reaching ambition for productivity and a formidable application challenge for frontier technology. that future may take longer than people expect, but i believe it will come. along the way, perhaps these notes will offer a small spark of insight to an entrepreneur, researcher or practitioner: someone looking up at the same stars while doing grounded work in a different field. robot data simulation）自动学习多种机器人技能的机器人代理。与其他生成式机器人代理不同，robogen并不是利用已有的大语言模型或生成式ai直接生成策略或者低层动作，而是采用一种生成方案，自动生成多样化的任务、场景和训练监督，从而在最小化人工干预的情况下扩展机器人技能的学习规模。 robogen概览 值得一提的是，robogen的几个关键能力都是通过genesis获得的，比如通过生成式模拟和渲染进行场景生成，比如通过可微分物理引擎进行快速技能学习等。genesis 是一个用于通用机器人学习的生成式和可微分的物理引擎，提供了一个统一的模拟平台，支持各种材料的模拟，能够模拟广泛的机器人任务，同时完全支持可微分特性。genesis作为下一代模拟基础设施，原生支持生成模拟：这一未来范式结合了生成式人工智能和基于物理的模拟，旨在为机器人代理解锁无限且多样化的数据，让它们能够在前所未有的各种环境中学习广泛的技能。genesis 已经接近开发完成，预计下个月就会公开发布。 robogen这个工作背后的思路是这样的：首先，我们将相关信息提取出来，然后利用这些信息去构建一个供机器人训练的环境。这个环境包括多个方面：机器人需要掌握的技能、每个技能适用的具体环境、环境的外观设计、机器人与环境的交互方式等。此外，我们还要为每个任务定义明确的完成标准，这通常通过奖励函数或损失函数来实现。值得注意的是，这些函数可以通过像语言模型这样的大型模型生成代码的方式来自动创建。我们希望自动化训练前的每一个环节，打通整个流程。这意味着从奖励函数的定义到生成代码，每个环节都可以自动化处理，使整个训练过程从头到尾实现高度自动化。这是我们想要实现的目标，也是我们最早提出的全自动化训练流程的核心理念。 在处理刚体交互时，强化学习非常有效，无论是用于运动（locomotion）还是操控刚体（manipulation）。然而，当涉及到柔性物体时，情况变得复杂，可微分模块至关重要。柔性物体，比如流体或会变形的衣服，与刚体不同。强化学习在这种情况下需要对状态空间进行有效的表示。如果我们希望超越刚体的交互，开始处理柔性物体，挑战就在于状态空间的复杂性。例如，仿真环境中通常会用粒子系统来表示这些物体，一块布可能由几十万个粒子组成。在这种情况下，用传统的基于代码的奖励函数来描述这些粒子状态是非常困难且昂贵的。第一，粒子数量巨大，直接对其状态进行描述和判断目标达成与否的成本非常高。第二，很难用明确的函数来描述像衣物对折这样的复杂形变过程及其对应的粒子状态。因此，传统方法难以适用于这些复杂的情况，这也是我们需要可微分模块的原因。它们可以帮助我们更有效地处理与软体物体的交互，简化并加速训练过程。 对于这类问题，使用梯度信息确实可以加速策略的学习效果，尤其是在与纯强化学习相比时，通过利用梯度来指导强化学习过程可以加速优化。然而，这个方向在学界仍是一个活跃研究领域，尚未有成熟的框架来将这两种方法有效结合。同时，由于梯度本身并非总是理想的，在实际优化过程中，例如接触力的梯度可能会导致优化景观不连续，从而引入噪声，影响训练效率。梯度提供的信息往往是局部的，在解决复杂的非凸问题时，局部信息可能不足以实现全局优化。这些都是当前学界试图解决的挑战。 robogen是一个完全自动化的流水线，用于无尽且多样化的技能获取。robogen的流水线包括四个阶段：a) 任务提议，b) 场景生成，c) 训练监督生成，以及 d) 使用生成的信息进行技能学习。robogen实现了一个自我引导的“提议-生成-学习（propose-generate-learn）”循环：首先，代理会提出感兴趣的任务和技能；接着，通过合理配置空间布局，填充相关的对象和资产，生成相应的模拟环境。然后，代理将提出的高级任务分解为子任务，选择最优的学习方法（如强化学习、运动规划或轨迹优化），生成所需的训练监督，最终学习相应的策略以掌握所提议的技能。 robogen工作原理 这个阶段让语言智能体能够自主不断提出新任务。为实现这一点，需要通过经典的“上下文学习”（in-context learning）方法提供一些示例，让智能体理解当前任务的要求，并基于这些示例生成新的任务。在这个过程中，存在如何控制任务多样性的问题，因此需要采用有效的策略。我们的策略包括从大型物体数据集中自动采样物体，并基于这些物体的语义信息生成与其交互的有意义任务。例如，当智能体接收到一个微波炉的样本时，它可能会提出加热汤或其他食物的任务。 此外，任务生成策略还可以基于物体的affordance（即物体的可操作性），或是通过场景设定，如在客厅中指示机器人完成某些任务。智能体可以通过这些示例举一反三，生成更多有意义的新任务。给于任务的例子不是唯一的方法，但它们对激发灵感至关重要。虽然理论上可以直接询问机器人哪些任务有意义，但实际操作中需要通过具体例子来启动和引导机器人的思考过程。 一个场景基本由两部分组成：背景（房间的外观）和前景（可交互的物体）。每个物体实际上是一个三维资产（3d mesh），这些资产的生成依赖于txt to 3d或image to 3d技术。这些领域发展迅速，经常有新方法生成更高质量的3d资产，这些是我们的一些上游模块。我们的想法是如何将这些3d资产按照一定有意义的空间配置进行摆放。最初的做法相对粗糙：首先提出任务，然后确定任务所需的物体，并将这些物体以较合理的方式放置在场景中。当时的场景中通常只有不到十个物体。 为了增加视觉信息的多样性，我们会在训练过程中添加一些干扰项。这可以帮助提高训练的全面性。我们现在的方法包括在视频或图片空间中生成像厨房这样的场景，然后提取这些图片中的信息，并将其应用到3d虚拟世界中。对于每个物体，我们可以从大型物体数据集中检索，并使用3d生成模型进行生成。此外，我们在设计一套可以生成开放世界中不局限物体种类的可交互物体（articulated object）的方法，预计很快会公开。3d gs并不是一种生成方法，而是一种表示方法。它的优势在于比以前的渲染方法更快。你可以使用3d gs表示从现实场景中拍摄的视频，通过生成方法在3d gs表示空间中学习这些场景。 现在也很流行一种利用3d gs来扩增现实数据，real2sim（关于real2sim在对话赵行、庄子文：机器人跑酷和自动驾驶——机器人数据从哪里来有提及）。但值得注意的是，3d gs本身只是渲染方式，没有物理属性，适合用于背景。如果背景不需要交互，可以直接放入虚拟环境中。但如果需要交互，则需要将其转换为实际的mesh，因为3d gs仅由点构成，无法进行物理交互。需要将其表面重建为mesh，并将所有前景物体从3d gs中提取出来，添加物理属性（如刚体、软体的重力和摩擦力），以实现真实交互。这种方法的核心目的是通过现实世界的数据多样性来增加在虚拟环境中交互场景的多样性。与之相对的是，你可以从头开始生成，利用噪声和生成方法在空间中创建新的内容，这些生成方法和3d gs可以在高层空间中结合，模块之间可以相互耦合。 强化学习的核心在于优化目标，这个目标是奖励函数。例如，如果你想以每秒三米的速度跑步，你会设定奖励函数：速度越接近三米每秒，奖励越大。如果没有这个信息，强化学习的代理就不知道目标是什么，也不知道该如何行动。当你提出一个任务，比如向前跑时，需要定义相应的奖励函数。例如，可以设定奖励函数为当前速度与目标速度的差值，差值越小，奖励越大。这将抽象的任务转化为可以用代码表示的奖励函数。强化学习通过优化这个奖励函数来学习和掌握技能。最终，代理会知道如何完成任务，并为了实现目标而努力。具体来说，大语言模型帮助设计奖励函数，之后强化学习通过训练来实现这些奖励函数所定义的目标。 robogen的最后一步是通过上述训练获得在仿真环境下的各种各样的机器人示教数据。这些示教数据可以有两种呈现形式：一种是强化学习生成策略（policy），这是一个闭环控制系统，能够根据不同的状态采取不同的行动。这种方法适合复杂任务，通过学习来优化策略，以适应不同情况。另一种是路径规划：生成的是一个轨迹（trajectory），即在固定的状态下每一步的动作是预先确定的。适用于较简单的任务，比如将手从一个位置移动到另一个位置，不需要强化学习，只需在空间中进行规划。生成的数据也需要后续验证，失败的数据需要被筛除。 关于策略和轨迹的区别，可以从最小的层面考虑，比如说你记录了一次洗碗的轨迹，这就是一个轨迹。如果你录制了100条这样的轨迹，你可以将这些轨迹通过学习方法整合成一个策略（policy）。这个策略能够应对不同的状态（如碗的位置、颜色），并根据不同的情况采取相应的行动。一个特定的策略可能只适用于某种厨房环境和洗碗的任务，但最终目标是创建一个能够处理1000种不同任务的通用策略。实现这个目标的方法是通过模仿学习，将各种演示数据（无论是轨迹还是小规模的策略）蒸馏到一个大策略中。最终，我们得到的是一个综合了多种任务的策略。 作为robot data文章的主题“可微分物理引擎（differentiable physics）”，这个词是不是给人一种每个字都能看懂但凑到一起就看不懂的感觉。查遍了知乎和b站等科普网站，除了一些关于胡渊明博士taichi和difftachi的资料，也没有看到关于可微物理引擎在机器人领域应用更系统的科普。所以，矮子里拔大个，我还是决定就可微分物理引擎这个话题先写一篇科普文章。 解释：可微分物理引擎（differentiable physics engine）是一种用于模拟物理系统的工具，其主要特点是可以对其输入参数进行微分。传统的物理引擎通常是基于数学模型和物理定律来模拟物体之间的相互作用和运动规律。然而，这些传统的物理引擎在计算梯度方面通常是不可微的，这使得它们难以直接应用于需要梯度信息的机器学习任务中。可微分物理引擎通过引入可微分的物理模型或数值计算技术，使得其在输入参数上具有可微分性。 什么是simulation，比如现在有一个物体的状态，你对物体进行一个操作，机器人有了一个动作，通过动作，物体的状态发生变化，从一个状态到另一个状态，整个过程是forward（前向）的。这种给定状态，机器人做动作，再预测下一步会发生什么的过程叫physical dynamic或者前向仿真（forward simulation）。这个过程中，对机器人任务到最终的目标的距离可以算一个奖励，和rl有点像，这一步做完之后离目标更近了还是更远了，算出来一个奖励值。如果模拟器不可微，只能做搜索，这个非常低效，你可能需要几千万上亿的数据去找到哪个轨迹是最好的。所以前向仿真本质是搜索问题。 可微分物理模拟的好处是，有梯度信息，可以用梯度下降的方式找到最优解。从状态到动作到状态，每一步都有导数，有导数之后可以用梯度下降的方法求解，让奖励的数值最大。对于不可微分的物理引擎只能用搜索或者近似的梯度，可微分物理模拟是每一步都用数学公式可以精确的算出每一步的梯度，用这个梯度来做优化，结果肯定是更好和更快。 现有的大多数物理引擎实际上都不支持可微分性，这导致它的解法有局限性，必须依赖于rl或者一些motion planning来进行。从使用的工具角度来看，这非常受限制。但是做机器人的人可能都知道，做trajectory optimization是一个非常高效的方法，比rl更高效，但因为支持可微分性门槛非常高，所以这个领域的发展进展缓慢。但一旦这个问题得到解决，对于机器人学习来说，是一个革命性的进步。虽然目前rl是在仿真环境中机器人学习技能很常用的方法，但实际上，绝大多数做机器人学习的人都不认为rl是一个非常高效的学习机器人技能的方法，但是又没有其他更好的方法。我们希望能够构建这样一个具有可微分性的高效系统，尽管这条路非常漫长，工程量非常大，但是我们认为这是一条必须走的道路。 我们这套可微分物理引擎系统最早是和胡渊明的taichi合作，可微分模拟在计算图形学（computational graphics）是一个很大的分支，但他们的侧重是用可微分的方式让模拟做的更准更快。在机器人领域，我们考虑的是怎么让skill learning（技能学习）更高效，用梯度的方式去做机器人技能学习。 比如我们21年和胡渊明合作的plastinelab，对于ppo或者rl他们的学习效率非常低，而我们的方法学习效率是rl几个数量级的提升，这也是我们为什么后面坚定的去创建这套可微模拟系统来做机器人技能学习。当我们有了这种很高效机器人学习技能的方法之后，可以在模拟器里收集大量的机器人示例（demonstration）的数据，再去学一些真实世界技能迁移（real world skill transfer）。所以我们整体的逻辑是通过构建强大的可微分物理模拟系统，来生成和收集大量机器人操作的数据，有了数据之后，可以训练机器人技能学习的基础模型，然后再学习一个adaptive policy，将这个模型迁移到真实世界。 包括到后面和shuran组合作的roboninja也是这样一套思路，这个工作是切割各种各样的物体。这个工作里每个物体都不一样，包括中间有核的物体，这种用遥操作等是非常难构建的。我们在模拟器里构造和收集无限量的数据，让他在模拟器里学习一个policy再tansfer到真实世界。包括到后面的fluidlab、softzoo以及今年iclr的一篇工作thinselllab都是这个逻辑。 roboninja demo 很多任务，rl训练不出来，很痛苦，policy训练了很久也找不到，而用我们的可微引擎训练个半小时就可以找到policy。所以可微分物理引擎是比rl更有效的寻找机器人技能学习策略的方式。但现在有个问题，现在大多数的仿真器不支持可微，这也是现在整个机器人领域的痛点。如果不支持可微，你就没有其他解法，你就只能做rl或motion planning，没有trajectory optimization的选择。可微物理引擎门槛很高，全世界做机器人可微模拟的人没多少，会写可微物理引擎的不超过100人。这也是我们做genesis的初衷，把会写可微分物理引擎的华人都聚到一起去做这个事情。可微物理引擎对数学和编程的门槛很高，即使在计算机图形学，可微模拟也是个出力不讨好的事情。 我们整个一套东西是希望给机器人构建世界模型。人为什么学技能快，人是有一个世界模型的。robot intelligence从哪里来，我一直认为这个智能应该从世界模型来，这就需要给机器人建立一个“状态-动作-状态”的能力，包括需要给他建立一个非常有效的寻找动作序列做规划的能力。这个能力从哪来来，我一直比较坚持的认为需要建立一个强大的可微分物理引擎来作为机器人的大脑，来支持他学习各种技能。当然这个世界模型也可以从现实世界里学习，但共同的目的是怎么给机器人构建一个大脑，不一定是某个技能，而是更广泛的对物理世界的理解，你只有真正的有了这么一个大脑，真正的有个对物理世界的建模，你才能真正的generalize。 目前机器人模拟器的两大难题，一个是怎么更快的在仿真里学会技能，可微模拟可以迅速地找到对于一些任务比较好的policy。另一个难题是怎么减少sim2real gap，可微模拟整个概念也是将sim和real更好的结合，它可以获得更好的sim2real alignment，这也是可微模拟和pybullet这类物理引擎不同的一点。对于pybullet这种物理引擎，解决sim2real gap的办法就是domain randomization，但这个方法非常不可控。可微分模拟有一个好处是，它可以用真实数据校正模拟数据（digital tune），比如有一个现实世界的视频，可以利用现实世界的视频来校正这个可微模拟器。假设，我们现在有一个真实世界视频，怎么在仿真里给他重建出来？对于可微分物理引擎，可以用真实世界视频作为目标，相当于我对仿真引擎的参数做优化，让他仿真的结果和真实世界的结果做匹配。我们可以用梯度下降迅速找到参数，让仿真和真实接近。 这里有几个概念区分下，rl、differentiable physics（可微模拟）和motion planning这些都是解决在仿真里怎么找策略（policy）的问题；diffusion policy，diffusion transformer，imitation learning包括offline rl这些都是有了数据之后怎么学技能这件事。数据的来源有两种，一种是通过遥操作在真实世界里采集，一种是模拟器里来，这是两条路线。两条路线采集的数据，在这个后面可以接diffusion policy，diffusion transformer，il，offline rl，这些都是有了机器人数据（demonstration）让机器人去学习技能。 我们希望通过可微分物理引擎，构建一个可以广泛适用刚体、软体，到各种类型的特殊物体的模拟器，同时还有好的渲染能力。这其实是回到了一个问题，就是怎么构建一个仿真环境，使得机器人能够在这个虚拟世界里学习并将所学应用到现实世界中。将虚拟的转化为真实的，这是我们的一个使命。因为机器人领域目前最大的问题就是缺乏数据，尽管很多人用遥操作采数据，但遥操作产生的数据很难scale，我更相信在模拟器里采数据，但模拟的问题是，写物理引擎的门槛比搭一个遥操作系统的门槛高很多。 很多机器人实验室会倾向于遥操作，门槛更低，但这是不是最终的路径是一个问题。现在的仿真有点像八十年代的深度学习，很多人都觉得这个门槛很高，不是那么多人愿意投入精力。我们愿意沉下来做一些对这个领域有革命性意义的事情，尽管可能需要三五年甚至更长的时间。我们还是认为，通过模拟器和可微模拟来生成数据这条路线是真正能解决机器人领域数据从哪里来的手段。 通用机器人模拟器和物理引擎大多只针对刚体，其中一些比较知名的物理引擎也有可微分分支，比如由stanford大学开发的nimble physics，它是dart物理引擎的一个解析可微分支。关于dart物理引擎，在聊一聊“sim”（上）——一览机器人模拟器生态做过介绍。mujoco xla(mjx)则是在 jax 中重新实现的 mujoco 物理引擎，具有可微性。 和通用机器人模拟器相比，可微分物理模拟器大都由学术团队自己开发，生态非常分散，并没有哪一个可微模拟器是被广泛应用的。simulately（聊一聊“sim”（下）——simulately作者访谈）对这部分特殊模拟器进行了总结和分类，常见的机器人可微模拟器典型代表包括diffsim，fluidlab，disect，plasticinelab，diffarticulated，thinshelllab，daxbench，nimblephysics，mujoco xla（mjx），softmac等。接下来逐一看看这些模拟器的特点。 diffsim diffsim是一个支持大量刚体和可形变物体交互的可微分物理引擎。过往的可微分物理引擎大多只能对特定的物体类别，例如球体或二维多边形，而无法泛化到更广泛的对象类别。diffsim是一个可扩展的可微分物理框架，可以支持大量对象及其相互作用。为了适应具有任意几何和拓扑结构的对象，作者采用网格作为表示，并利用接触的稀疏性进行可扩展的可微分碰撞处理。与基于粒子的方法相比，diffsim在内存和算力需求方面节省至少两个数量级。diffsim使用c++进行开发。 plasticinelab plasticinelab是一个针对软体操作的可微物理引擎。现有的机器人模拟器通常只模拟刚体物理，软体动力学在模拟、控制和分析方面更为复杂。其中最大的挑战之一来自于其无限自由度（dofs）及相应的高维控制方程。plasticinelab提供了一个新的可微分物理基准，包括各种软体操纵任务，底层物理引擎使用difftaichi系统支持可微的弹性和塑性变形。 diffarticulated diffarticulated是一种可微分的关节体模拟方法。作者使用伴随方法推导了关节体模拟的梯度，几乎不需要额外计算，比自动微分（autodiff）工具快一个数量级，将内存需求降低了两个数量级。自动微分（autodiff）模拟器在模拟步骤很多时会占用大量内存，这会导致学习受到时间限制或者需要采用较大时间步长，限制了学到的行为范围，降低模拟稳定性。 fluidlab fluidlab是一个支持多种材料的可微物理仿真环境，可以处理涉及复杂流体动力学的操作任务，例如流体之间以及流体和固体之间的相互作用。fluidlab平台的核心是一个完全可微分的物理模拟器fluidengine，它支持多种材料的建模，包括固体、液体和气体，弹性、塑性和刚性物体，牛顿和非牛顿液体，以及烟雾和空气等多种材料。fluidengine使用物理引擎编程语言taichi进行开发，支持在gpu上进行大规模并行计算。此外，它以完全可微的方式实现，为下游优化任务提供有用的梯度信息。 daxbench daxbench是一个用于可变形物体操纵（deformable object manipulation, dom ）的可微分仿真框架。与现有工作通常专注于特定类型的可变形物体不同，daxbench支持流体、绳索、布料等；它提供了一个通用基准，用于评估不同的 dom 方法，包括规划、模仿学习和强化学习。 thinshelllab thinshelllab是一个专为机器人与具有不同材料特性的薄壳材料（纸片、布料）进行交互而定制的可微分仿真平台。先前的研究主要依赖启发式策略或从真实世界的视频演示中学习策略，只关注有限的材料类型和任务（例如，展开布料），当扩展到更多种类的薄壳材料和各种任务时，这些方法面临显著挑战。thinshelllab设计了一系列围绕不同薄壳对象的操纵任务。作者通过几个真实世界的实验展示了thinshelllab如何通过真实到仿真的系统识别（real-to-sim system identification）和仿真到真实的技能转移（sim-to-real skill transferring）来弥合仿真和现实之间的差距。 为了在仿真中重建真实场景，thinshelllab首先通过基于视觉的触觉传感器和力传感器收集真实世界的数据。 softmac softmac是一个可微分仿真框架，它将软体与关节刚体和衣物耦合在一起。为了在各种机器人操纵场景中应用可微分仿真，一个关键的挑战是在一个统一的框架中集成各种材料。softmac使用基于连续力学的material point method (mpm)来模拟软体，基于每种模态的仿真器和接触模型，作者开发了一种可微分耦合机制，以模拟软体与其他两种材料之间的相互作用。 jade jade是一种用于关节刚体的可微物理引擎，它在nimble physics基础上进行改进，解决nimble physics在穿透（penetration）方面的问题。jade将接触建模为线性互补问题（lcp），与现有的可微模拟相比，jade提供了一些功能，包括无交点碰撞模拟和多个摩擦接触的稳定lcp解决方案。jade使用连续碰撞检测来检测碰撞时间，并采用回溯策略来防止具有复杂几何形状的物体之间的相交。
