robot demonstrations, learning skills with differentiable simulation, and the research behind key physics platforms. more than two months have passed since i first conceived the robot data series, and seven episodes have been published. for episode eight, we explore robogen, a particularly interesting project. unlike collecting demonstrations through human teleoperation or motion capture, robogen generates robot learning experiences in simulation using generative models and differentiable simulation. its authors come from cmu, tsinghua, mit, umass amherst and the mit–ibm ai lab: yufei wang*, zhou xian*, feng chen*, tsun-hsuan wang, yian wang, katerina fragkiadaki, zackory erickson, david held and chuang gan. the asterisks denote equal contribution. i was delighted to interview two of the authors, professor chuang gan and dr. zhou xian. in this august 2024 introduction, chuang gan was a faculty member at umass amherst and a research manager at the mit–ibm watson ai lab. he earned his phd at tsinghua under andrew chi-chih yao and was a postdoctoral researcher at mit, working with antonio torralba, daniela rus and joshua tenenbaum. his research connects computer vision, ai, cognitive science and robotics, with the overall goal of building a human-like autonomous agent able to perceive, reason and act in the physical world. zhou xian is introduced here as a phd graduate of carnegie mellon university's robotics institute, advised by katerina fragkiadaki. his interests span robotics, computer vision and world-model learning. before cmu, he completed his undergraduate studies at nanyang technological university in singapore, working with quang-cuong pham and i-ming chen. his research focuses on unified neural policies and data engines for robotics and beyond. these introductions retain the original interview's timeframe. join me for robot data episode eight as we explore automated generation of robot demonstrations and an introduction to differentiable physics engines. contents ↓ part i: zhou xian on generating robot demonstrations at scale with robogen 1. introducing robogen 2. robogen's core idea 3. how robogen works task proposal scene generation training-supervision generation learning skills using the generated information part ii: chuang gan on building world models with differentiable simulation 1. how differentiable physics engines work 2. differentiable simulation for robot learning 3. differentiable simulation and the sim-to-real gap 4. differentiable simulation and robot data part iii: a review of differentiable physics research some reflections robogen is a robotic agent that automatically learns diverse skills through generative simulation. rather than using a language model or generative ai directly to produce policies or low-level actions, it takes a generative approach to creating tasks, scenes and training supervision. the aim is to scale up robot skill learning with minimal human intervention. robogen overview several important capabilities in robogen come from genesis, including scene generation and rendering and fast skill learning through differentiable physics. genesis is presented here as a generative, differentiable simulation platform for general-purpose robot learning, unifying the simulation of different materials and a broad range of tasks. its ambition is to combine generative ai with physical simulation to create abundant, diverse data and let robots learn many skills in varied environments. at the time of this august 2024 interview, the team said development was nearly complete and expected a public release the following month. editorial clarification: that was a forecast, not a current release promise; the public project dates its launch to december 2024. 'fully differentiable' describes the goal, not blanket support across every solver and interaction. official documentation identifies differentiable mpm and tool-based interaction while other solver capabilities differ. the idea behind robogen is to extract relevant information and use it to build a robot-training environment. that includes the skills a robot should learn, the setting for each skill, the environment's appearance and how the robot interacts with it. we also need clear completion criteria, usually expressed as rewards or losses. large models, such as language models, can generate the code for those functions automatically. we want to automate every preparation step and connect the pipeline—from defining rewards to generating code—so the training process becomes highly automated from beginning to end. this is the goal and core idea behind the fully automated training pipeline we first proposed. reinforcement learning works well for many rigid-body interactions, both locomotion and manipulation. deformable objects complicate matters, making differentiable components important. fluids and clothing differ from rigid objects, and rl needs an effective representation of their state. if we move beyond rigid-body interaction, the complexity of that state space becomes a challenge. simulators often use particle systems; a piece of cloth might contain hundreds of thousands of particles. writing a conventional reward function that assesses those particle states can be difficult and expensive. first, the particle count makes describing the state and checking goal completion costly. second, it is hard to write an explicit function for a deformation such as folding clothing and its corresponding particle configuration. these difficulties motivate differentiable components, which can make learning soft-object interaction more efficient. this explains their role in our approach, rather than establishing that every deformable-object task requires differentiable simulation. gradient information can accelerate policy learning and optimization compared with relying on reinforcement learning alone. combining the approaches effectively is still an active research topic, without a mature framework that resolves all these issues. gradients are not always ideal. contact can make the optimization landscape nonsmooth or discontinuous, introducing noise and harming training efficiency. gradients also convey local information, which may be insufficient for global optimization in complicated nonconvex problems. these are challenges the research community is still addressing. robogen is an automated pipeline for acquiring diverse skills repeatedly. it has four stages: a, task proposal; b, scene generation; c, training-supervision generation; and d, learning skills with that information. it follows a self-guided propose–generate–learn cycle. the agent first proposes tasks and skills of interest, then populates a simulated environment with relevant objects and assets in appropriate spatial arrangements. it decomposes the high-level task into subtasks, chooses a suitable method—reinforcement learning, motion planning or trajectory optimization—generates the supervision and learns policies for the proposed skills. repeating this loop can yield many demonstrations; 'endless' describes repeatable generation rather than a guarantee of unlimited successful skills. how robogen works this stage lets the language agent keep proposing new tasks autonomously. we use conventional in-context learning, providing examples that explain the requirements and allow it to propose further tasks. controlling diversity is important. our strategies include automatically sampling objects from large datasets and using their semantic information to generate meaningful interactions. given a microwave, for example, the agent might propose heating soup or another food. tasks can also be generated from an object's affordances—the actions it makes possible—or from a scene, such as asking a robot to perform activities in a living room. the agent generalizes from examples to propose more meaningful tasks. examples are not the only method, but they help stimulate useful ideas. in principle, we could simply ask which tasks are meaningful; in practice, concrete examples help initiate and guide the agent's reasoning. a scene broadly has two parts: the background, such as the room's appearance, and the foreground of interactive objects. each object is represented by a 3d asset or mesh, obtained using techniques such as text-to-3d or image-to-3d generation. these areas are advancing quickly, with new methods producing better assets, and serve as upstream modules for us. we ask how to arrange those assets meaningfully in space. our initial approach was fairly rough: propose a task, identify the required objects and place them reasonably in a scene. there were usually fewer than ten objects. we add distractors during training to increase visual diversity and make training more comprehensive. we are also working on generating scenes such as kitchens in image or video space, extracting information from them and bringing it into a virtual 3d world. individual objects can be retrieved from large datasets or created with 3d generative models. we are developing methods for creating articulated objects beyond a fixed set of categories and expect to release them soon, as of this interview. 3d gaussian splatting, or 3dgs, is a representation and rendering technique, not a generative method by itself. its advantage is faster rendering than some earlier methods. we can represent videos of real scenes using 3dgs and train generative methods in that representation space. using 3dgs to expand real-world data through real-to-sim reconstruction is also becoming popular; we discussed this in hang zhao and ziwen zhuang on robot parkour and autonomous driving: where robot data comes from. but a standard 3dgs representation has no physical properties of its own, making it naturally suited to noninteractive backgrounds. if interaction is needed, we can reconstruct surfaces as meshes, extract foreground objects and assign physical properties, such as mass and friction, for rigid or deformable simulation. the point is to use real-world diversity to enrich interactive virtual scenes. alternatively, generative methods can start from noise to create new content. generation and 3dgs representations can be combined and coupled at higher levels. editorial clarification: mesh reconstruction is one implementation route. gaussian representations can also be coupled to separate physical models; they are not inherently impossible to use in an interactive system. reinforcement learning optimizes an objective defined by a reward function. if you want a robot to run at three meters per second, you can give higher rewards as its velocity approaches that target. without such an objective, the agent does not know what behavior is desired. a task such as running forward must therefore be translated into an appropriate reward—for example, penalizing the difference between current and target velocity. this turns an abstract task into executable code. the language model helps design that reward, and rl then trains a policy to pursue the objective it defines. the final stage produces varied robot demonstrations in simulation. one form comes from an rl policy: a closed-loop controller choosing different actions for different states, appropriate for complex tasks that require adaptation. another comes from motion planning: a trajectory whose actions are predetermined for a given setup. simpler tasks, such as moving a hand from one position to another, may need spatial planning rather than rl. generated data still needs validation, and failed demonstrations must be filtered out. to distinguish a policy from a trajectory, consider recording one dishwashing attempt: that is a trajectory. if you record a hundred, learning can combine them into a policy able to respond to differences such as a bowl's position or appearance. one policy may still cover only a particular kitchen and dishwashing task. the eventual goal is a general policy handling, say, a thousand different tasks. through imitation learning, demonstrations from trajectories or smaller policies can be distilled into a larger policy that brings multiple tasks together. our topic, differentiable physics engines, can feel like one of those phrases whose individual words make sense but whose combination does not. i searched popular explainers on zhihu and bilibili. apart from material about yuanming hu's taichi and difftaichi, i found little systematic discussion of differentiable physics in robotics. with no better explainer at hand, i decided to write an introductory account myself. explanation: a differentiable physics engine simulates a physical system while allowing derivatives of its outputs with respect to relevant inputs or parameters to be computed. conventional engines use mathematical models and physical laws to approximate motion and interaction, but often do not expose gradients suitable for direct use in learning or optimization. a differentiable engine incorporates differentiable models or numerical techniques to make that gradient information available. this concerns the represented numerical system; contacts and other nonsmooth phenomena can still make derivatives difficult. what is simulation? start with an object's state, let a robot take an action and predict how the state changes. that is forward dynamics or forward simulation: state, action, next state. for a robot task, we can then measure progress toward a goal and assign a reward, as in rl. if the simulator does not supply gradients, searching for an effective action sequence may be inefficient and require tens or hundreds of millions of samples. editorial clarification: the original calls forward simulation itself a search problem. forward simulation evaluates dynamics; searching or optimizing actions is the separate process that calls it. the advantage of differentiable simulation is access to gradients, allowing gradient-based optimization of actions and parameters to increase reward or reduce loss. derivatives through state–action–state transitions can guide that optimization. without them, one can use search or approximate gradients. i see directly available gradients as a route to better and faster solutions. editorial clarification: the original describes every gradient as mathematically exact and the result as necessarily better and faster. gradients are of a discretized model and depend on numerical and contact approximations; gradient descent does not guarantee a global optimum or universal speed advantage. many existing physics engines do not provide the differentiability needed by our workflow, which limits convenient access to gradient-based solutions and leads researchers toward rl or motion planning. trajectory optimization can be very efficient—sometimes more so than rl—but implementing suitable differentiable models is technically demanding, and progress has been slow. i believe solving this could transform robot learning. rl is commonly used to learn skills in simulation, yet many researchers find it sample-inefficient and would welcome alternatives. we want to build an efficient differentiable system. the road is long and the engineering effort substantial, but we believe it is a necessary path. editorial clarification: trajectory optimization is still possible with analytic models, finite differences or approximate derivatives; it is not categorically unavailable without a differentiable engine. the efficiency comparison expresses our experience and research position, not a consensus ranking of every method. our work on differentiable physics began in collaboration with yuanming hu's taichi project. differentiable simulation is an important branch of computer graphics, where the emphasis may be making simulation more accurate and efficient. in robotics, we focus on learning skills more efficiently, using gradients to guide the process. for example, in our 2021 collaboration on plasticinelab, ppo and other rl approaches learned inefficiently, while our gradient-based approach was orders of magnitude more efficient on the evaluated tasks. that strengthened our conviction to build a differentiable simulation system for robot skill learning. with an efficient learning method, we can collect many demonstrations in simulation and work on real-world skill transfer. our overall logic is to build powerful differentiable physical simulation, generate and collect abundant manipulation data, train a foundation model for skill learning, and then learn an adaptive policy to transfer those capabilities to reality. the reported speed advantage is tied to the benchmark and comparison, not every robot task. roboninja, our later collaboration with shuran song's group, follows this logic too. it cuts varied objects, including soft objects with rigid cores—situations that are difficult to cover through teleoperation alone. we construct and collect large quantities of simulation data, train a policy and transfer it to reality. fluidlab, softzoo and this year's iclr project, thinshelllab, follow a similar line of thought. 'unlimited data' describes repeatable simulation generation, subject to computational resources and the model's coverage. roboninja demonstration some tasks are frustrating with rl: train for a long time and you still cannot find a useful policy. in our experience, a differentiable engine can sometimes find one in half an hour. that is why i see differentiable physics as an effective route to robot skill policies. but most simulators do not expose the needed gradients, which is a pain point. building such an engine requires substantial mathematical and programming expertise; i estimate there are fewer than a hundred people worldwide who can write one. this motivated genesis: bring together chinese researchers with that expertise to tackle it. even in graphics, differentiable simulation can be demanding work with limited recognition. editorial clarification: the half-hour figure and expert count are the interviewee's examples and estimates. lack of built-in differentiability does not rule out trajectory optimization through other derivative methods, despite the original's categorical wording. our broader aim is to build a world model for robots. why do humans learn skills so quickly? they have a model of the world. i have long believed robot intelligence should come from world models: the ability to predict state–action–state transitions and efficiently plan action sequences. i believe a powerful differentiable physics engine can act as a robot's brain, supporting the acquisition of many skills. a world model can also be learned from real-world experience. the shared goal is more than one particular skill: it is a broad understanding and representation of the physical world. i think that kind of model is essential to meaningful generalization. robot simulation faces two major challenges. one is learning skills faster; differentiable simulation can quickly find useful policies for some tasks. the other is narrowing the sim-to-real gap. differentiability can help align simulation with reality, which distinguishes our workflow from using an engine such as pybullet without accessible gradients. domain randomization is commonly used there, but its parameter choices can be difficult to control. differentiable simulation offers another option: calibrating the model with real data. given a real-world video, for example, we can optimize simulator parameters so the simulated outcome matches what the video shows, using gradient descent to bring them closer. editorial clarification: the transcript calls this 'digital tune'; the process described is parameter calibration or system identification. domain randomization is not the only calibration method available to a nondifferentiable simulator. let us distinguish a few concepts. rl, differentiable physics and motion planning can help find policies or action sequences in simulation. diffusion policy, diffusion transformers, imitation learning and offline rl can then learn skills from available data. demonstrations may come from real-world teleoperation or from a simulator—two collection routes. either source can feed those later learning methods. these are distinctions between stages of a workflow, not mutually exclusive algorithm families; rl and learned models can also be combined within either stage. we hope to build a differentiable physics platform broadly covering rigid bodies, deformable bodies and other specialized materials, together with good rendering. that returns us to the question of how to create a virtual world where robots learn and then apply their learning in reality. turning virtual experience into real capability is our mission. a major bottleneck in robotics is data. teleoperation is popular but difficult to scale, so i place more faith in simulation-generated data. the difficulty is that writing a physics engine has a much higher entry barrier than building a teleoperation system. many robot labs prefer teleoperation because it is easier to get started. whether it is the ultimate route is another question. simulation today feels to me a little like deep learning in the 1980s: the barrier looks high and relatively few people want to invest the effort. we are willing to work patiently on something we believe could transform the field, even if it takes three to five years or longer. we still believe simulation and differentiable simulation can address the fundamental question of where robot data will come from. general-purpose robot simulators and physics engines have largely emphasized rigid bodies, and some now have differentiable branches. nimble physics, developed through stanford research, is an analytically differentiable fork of dart. i introduced dart in let's talk about sim, part i: the robot simulator ecosystem. mujoco xla, mjx, includes a jax reimplementation of mujoco with automatic-differentiation support. here, differentiability refers to the jax implementation; it should not be assumed for every later mjx backend or every nonsmooth contact configuration. compared with general-purpose simulators, differentiable simulation is often developed by individual academic teams. the ecosystem is fragmented, without one platform dominating the applications discussed here. simulately, introduced in let's talk about sim, part ii: interviewing the simulately authors, organizes these tools. examples include diffsim, fluidlab, disect, plasticinelab, diffarticulated, thinshelllab, daxbench, nimble physics, mujoco xla and softmac. below, i review their main characteristics. diffsim is a differentiable physics framework supporting interactions among many rigid and deformable objects. earlier frameworks often focused on limited object classes, such as spheres or two-dimensional polygons. diffsim instead seeks scalable support for broader geometry and topology, representing objects as meshes and exploiting sparse contacts for differentiable collision handling. its authors report up to two orders of magnitude less memory use and computation than the evaluated particle-based methods. the original says 'at least' two orders of magnitude; the paper says 'up to,' an important distinction. the implementation uses c++. plasticinelab is a differentiable physics benchmark for soft-body manipulation. many existing robot simulators focus on rigid bodies, whereas deformable dynamics are more difficult to simulate, control and analyze. a major challenge is the continuum's effectively infinite degrees of freedom and corresponding high-dimensional equations after discretization. plasticinelab supplies varied deformable-object manipulation tasks, using difftaichi for differentiable elastic and plastic deformation. diffarticulated presents an efficient method for differentiable articulated-body simulation. it derives gradients using spatial algebra and the adjoint method, with little additional computational overhead. in the reported comparisons, it runs about ten times faster than differentiation through general autodiff tools and reduces memory requirements by roughly two orders of magnitude. autodiff through many simulation steps can consume large amounts of memory, forcing shorter horizons or larger time steps. that can restrict learned behaviors and compromise simulation stability. these improvements are benchmark-dependent. fluidlab is a differentiable simulation environment for manipulation involving complex fluid dynamics, including interactions between fluids and between fluids and solids. at its core is fluidengine, a differentiable simulator covering multiple materials: solids, liquids and gases; elastic, plastic and rigid bodies; newtonian and non-newtonian liquids; and smoke and air. it is implemented using taichi, a programming system suited to numerical and physics computation, and supports large-scale parallel gpu computation. its gradient information supports downstream optimization tasks. daxbench is a differentiable simulation framework for deformable object manipulation, dom. unlike approaches limited to one type of deformable object, it covers materials including fluids, ropes and cloth. it provides a common benchmark for comparing approaches such as planning, imitation learning and reinforcement learning. thinshelllab is a differentiable platform for robotic interaction with thin-shell materials, such as paper and cloth, with different physical properties. earlier work often used heuristic strategies or learned from real-world demonstrations and focused on limited material types and tasks, such as unfolding cloth. extending those methods to more varied thin shells and tasks is challenging. thinshelllab provides a suite of manipulation tasks and demonstrates real-to-sim system identification and sim-to-real skill transfer in several physical experiments, addressing the gap between simulation and reality. to reconstruct a real scenario in simulation, thinshelllab first collects physical data using vision-based tactile and force sensors. softmac is a differentiable framework coupling soft bodies with articulated rigid bodies and cloth. bringing different materials into a unified simulation is a central challenge for robot manipulation. softmac models soft bodies using the continuum-mechanics-based material point method, mpm. with simulators and contact models for each material, it introduces a differentiable coupling mechanism to model the interactions of soft bodies with the other two material classes. jade is a differentiable physics engine for articulated rigid bodies that builds on nimble physics and addresses interpenetration. it models contact as a linear complementarity problem, lcp, providing intersection-free collision simulation and stable solutions for multiple frictional contacts. continuous collision detection identifies impact times, and a backtracking strategy prevents intersections between bodies with complicated geometry. in the week of this august 2024 article, i went to beijing for the world robot conference, wrc. it was packed. i saw many companies' robots, and plenty were brought out to walk around. the atmosphere was lively, but the products' forms were very similar. i cannot necessarily come up with ingenious new forms myself, yet i still hope to see some robots that look and work differently. [an expressive reaction] i also met many groups of children on study trips. start robotics education young: tinkering with robots is joyful. building something from nothing, then seeing it move, gives a tremendous sense of accomplishment. i hope next year's conference brings more products and technologies that make us say 'wow.' references nimble physics: https://nimblephysics.org/ diffsim: yi-ling data这个话题下，大规模仿真+强化学习解决移动（locomotion）可能是在当今机器人学习领域共识度最高的路线。从2020年开始，用强化学习在英伟达issacgym上解决四足移动的论文持续获得了很高的关注。来到2023年末，随着硬件的突破，用强化学习解决双足人形移动的问题逐渐获得了更多的关注。 在robot data第七期，我非常荣幸能够邀请到在四足和双足人形移动方面非常有代表性的两个工作robot parkour learning和humanoid parkour learning的指导老师赵行和一作庄子文来为大家介绍机器人移动相关问题。因为赵行老师在自动驾驶行业的深厚积累，我们也探讨了自动驾驶作为初代具身智能落地代表，在数据方面的历史经验。 robot parkour learning：ziwen zhuang*, zipeng fu*, jianren wang, christopher atkeson, sören schwertfeger, chelsea finn, hang zhao；*共同一作 humanoid parkour learning：ziwen zhuang, shenzhe yao, hang zhao。 庄子文是清华大学交叉信息研究院的一年级博士生，研究方向包括运动智能、具身人工智能和机器人技术。庄子文在上海期智研究院担任研究助理，由赵行教授指导。在此之前，他曾是上海科技大学mars实验室的成员，师从soeren schwertfeger教授。 非常感谢两位学者的细致解读，相信以下文字可以让你对大规模仿真+强化学习对解决局部移动问题，以及自动驾驶行业的数据经验有新的认知，enjoy！ 以下为本文目录 👇 第一部 对话庄子文：大规模仿真下的机器人跑酷 1. robot parkour learning方法介绍 2. 仿真+rl之于locomotion 3. 仿真的sim2real gap 4. 关于具身数据集 5. 控制理论 vs 强化学习 第二部 对话赵行：机器人跑酷和自动驾驶—机器人数据从哪里来 1. robot parkour解决的核心问题 2. rgb视觉之于未来机器人的感知 3. 自动驾驶行业在数据问题上的历史经验 4. 特斯拉怎么做端到端模仿学习的呢？ 5. 自动驾驶仿真—感知仿真vs行为仿真 6. 行为仿真数据—训练or测试 7. 感知仿真—real2sim 8. 关于机器人学习的路线 一些想法 跑酷任务在机器人学习中的应用，特别是在四足机器人和人形机器人的不同实现中，通常分为三个阶段：预训练、微调、和蒸馏。 阶段 1：带有软动力学（soft dynamics）约束的强化学习预训练 在强化学习预训练阶段，我们引入soft dynamics约束。soft dynamics 的概念源于模拟器中物理碰撞的局限性。在传统的模拟器中，物体只能发生硬碰撞。例如，当机器人腿部遇到地形时，只能直接发生碰撞，无法实现逐步减少的穿透效果。而在 soft dynamics 中，当我们在系统中编写代码时，我们知道某处有一个障碍物，但在实际的模拟环境中并不告知机器人这个障碍的存在。这样一来，模拟器在进行物理模拟时，当机器狗接近该区域时，不会计算碰撞。然而，当它实际穿透这个障碍物时，我们通过奖励函数给它一点惩罚，告诉它这种穿透是不正确的，从而降低其奖励值。 soft dynamics 阶段 2：带有硬动力学（hard dynamics）约束的强化学习微调 在强化学习的微调阶段，我们严格执行所有动力学约束，并在真实的动力学条件下对预训练阶段学到的行为进行微调。把障碍物实际放上去的时候，在模拟中允许机器人进行微调，因为在模拟环境中，轻微的穿透可能不会导致问题，但在现实环境中，如果真的有障碍物挡在那里，轻微的穿透就行不通了。为了适应这种差异，机器人需要在模拟中进一步微调，以确保在实际环境中也能顺利应对障碍物。 hard dynamics 阶段 3：通过蒸馏学习基于视觉的跑酷策略 在学会每个单独的跑酷技能后，我们使用 dagger 算法将这些技能蒸馏为一个基于视觉的跑酷策略。这个策略可以在只依赖机器人自身的感知和计算能力的情况下部署到四足机器人上。 distill 关于蒸馏，它的初衷其实是为了解决几年前 isaacgym 渲染速度过慢的问题。在 isaacgym上，用 3090 显卡进行渲染时，速度非常慢。比如，如果在不渲染的情况下，完成一次强化学习训练可能只需要 3 个小时，但如果启用渲染，可能需要长达三天的时间，差距非常明显。因此，蒸馏的解决方案是先伪造一个传感器，让它去感知地形信息，然后通过蒸馏的方法让模型学会如何在真实世界中使用传感器来应对地形，或是encode这个地形。其实，只要问题定义得足够清晰，即使使用 4090 显卡直接进行训练，也可以不用蒸馏。 蒸馏的另一个重要好处是可以更方便地更换传感器。例如，你可以先使用深度相机进行训练，然后如果发现深度相机效果不佳，可以通过蒸馏将知识迁移到激光雷达等其他传感器上。这样，换传感器的成本就会降低，因为你不需要从头开始重新训练模型，这是蒸馏方法的一个显著优势。 在2020年之前，强化学习领域的学者以及在做机器人移动（locomotion）研究的学者都在努力提升算法的效率。像 mujoco 和 pybullet 这样的仿真平台主要依赖 cpu 进行模拟，每台服务器最多只能同时运行 256 个模拟器。2020年，瑞士联邦理工学院（eth）的 marco hutter 团队（rsl 实验室）的一名成员在英伟达实习，决定尝试通过增加数据量来提升效果，并利用英伟达的资源在 isaac gym 平台上进行了大规模的仿真实验，这可以说是最早的一次大规模仿真尝试，结果一试就成功了。英伟达显卡的并行处理是其强项，一上来就能同时运行 4,096 个模拟器，这就是一个通过规模化实现突破的例子。自此之后，几乎没有人再提强化学习算法的效率问题了。 在locomotion方面，sim2real gap的问题目前已经有很好的解决，但操作方面还有很多挑战。操作研究通常简化了整个物理过程，导致很多操作模型的定义实际上违反了物理定律。例如，在操控一个物体时，需要施加足够的力，但操作库或模型输出的指令可能忽略了物体的重量，可能导致无法实际搬起物体。因此，模型在实际应用中的表现总会存在与真实情况之间的差距，因为总会有一些被忽略的因素。 此外，在进行操作时，碰撞面和碰撞关系非常复杂。例如，当用手指操作物体时，涉及到大量的碰撞面，这使得模拟更加复杂。相较于机器人移动任务，操作的碰撞数量级更大，因此模拟器的实现也变得更加困难。当前许多通用模拟器采用的是迭代式的仿真方法，它们通过计算下一个时间点的系统状态来进行模拟。这种方法虽然可以逐步逼近真实情况，但也存在模拟精度的问题，尤其是在处理复杂碰撞和物理交互时，这使得模拟过程更加复杂和计算更加密集，这种复杂性往往会导致仿真速度变慢。 在整个具身智能的研究中，以前做计算机视觉的很多研究人员习惯于使用大家公认的标准数据集和指标，这种惯性导致在新领域也希望有一个统一的数据集供大家训练和测试，以便在公认的指标上进行竞争。例如，最早imagenet出来后，成功率指标是非常直观的指标，后来出现了一些基于transformer的可视化图，大家也可以从中去分析问题。但在机器人领域，目前还没有足够直观或者说被广泛认可的数据集出来，这样的标准还没有完全形成。尤其是当数据集无法涵盖所有可能的情况，或者是即使没有真机的一些课题组也可以用的数据集，这种情况还没到来。 此外，机器人领域的任务成功率通常较低，很多操作任务的成功率可能都在10%以下，甚至更低。因此，成功率的细微差异（比如从3%到4%）并没有显著的区别。这种低成功率和指标的不确定性，使得评估机器人性能更加复杂。为了提高成功率，机器人操作往往在简化的场景下进行机器人系统的测试，但简化场景下的问题也变得相对简单，这样的系统在真实世界中可能无法有效处理复杂的情况。我们可以看到，许多成功率较高的工作在展示时的视频都是经过加速的，有些甚至需要加速四倍、八倍，即使是稍微好一些的系统，可能也需要加速两倍来显示机械臂的动作。这是因为，在许多早期的机器人操作任务中，问题被简化为所谓的准静态动力学（quasi-static dynamics）。 这种简化忽略了许多动态因素，比如一个物体突然掉落的情况。这也意味着，机器人无法完成需要动态处理的任务，比如铺床单或抖动衣物。而在准静态动力学设定中，这些复杂的动态操作从定义上就被排除了。因此，aloha在技术上产生了较大的影响力，因为它们几乎全部都是实时的，它把控制问题引入到学术界的视野。最早引起这一关注的是宋舒然组的几篇工作，包括swingbot，他们明确指出，机器人在操作时必须考虑动力学因素，包括环境的高速移动和惯性等。 在人形机器人领域，直接将收集到的人类数据集映射到机器人上，并不符合物理定律。如果你看过一些早期计算机图形学领域的工作，他们往往通过人类的视频数据训练神经网络，然后让神经网络生成一系列人的行为动作。然而，这种研究的一个问题在于，生成的动作经常不符合物理定律。例如，有些动画中人会像走太空步一样，在地面上滑动，这种现象就是典型的不符合物理定律的表现，这中间还是需要一层网络来将人类的动作映射为机器人能够执行并满足物理定律的动作。 从数学角度来看，强化学习和控制理论确实有很多相似之处。但强化学习涉及到大量的概率分析，比如对先验和后验分布的分析。而在控制理论中的规划和系统动力学通常是确定性的，系统的行为是可以精确预测的。相比之下，强化学习则是通过不确定性的方式来建模。这两者的联系主要体现在这些方面。 对于强化学习来说，它的最大优点在于能够应对突破边界的意外场景。比如，deep tracking control这篇文章中提到的，mpc（模型预测控制）和类似的算法在应对这些意外情况时存在局限。具体来说，mpc 在规划过程中，面对小范围的偏差，比如atlas机器人在跳跃时目标平台距离原计划有0.1米时，只需稍微调整力道即可解决。然而，当情况变得更复杂，例如目标平台距离为0.5米，超出了机器人的跳跃能力时，mpc可能无法及时调整并规划出有效的保护动作。这种情况下，机器人可能会碰撞到平台，导致损伤。而强化学习能够处理这些突破边界的意外情况，通过学习和适应，能够在面对超出预期的挑战时，规划出新的应对策略。 robot parkour learning获得了2023 corl最佳系统论文提名，这说明我们的整体系统设计比较完善，而不仅仅是某个单点技术的突破。关于跑酷工作，我认为核心问题主要有两个方面：一是如何设计和调整一个有效的训练策略，二是如何克服sim2real gap。训练策略的设计是一个复杂的任务，涉及不同动力学约束的强化学习训练，以及技能模型的蒸馏。 过去，四足的工作不带视觉，主要依赖本体感知，而现在，我们引入了视觉感知，特别是双目深度相机，sim2real gap问题在引入视觉系统后变得尤为重要。为了有效地克服sim2real gap，我们需要在仿真中尽可能真实地模拟视觉感知中的深度，同时调整真实世界中的数据，使其尽量接近仿真器中的理想图像，将仿真数据和真实数据的分布尽可能接近，从而缩小这两者之间的差距。 在缩小sim2real gap过程中，我们采用了多种方法进行尝试，比如填洞、去噪等，深度图在这方面表现尚可。在跑酷任务中，挑战相对简单，主要是克服地形，而克服地形的关键在于了解其深度。但是未来真正的实用机器人不应仅仅依赖深度图，而需要能够处理rgb图像。 此外，multitask learning（多任务学习）在机器学习中一直是一个长期存在的问题。当一个模型同时学习多个任务时，不同任务的回传梯度往往会发生冲突，会遇到每个技能的性能下降的问题。调试单个技能其实比较容易，但同时调试多个技能则很困难。因此，子文在尝试了各种方法后发现了一个比较好的策略：先单独训练每个技能，将这些技能作为教师模型，然后共同训练一个学生模型。这样的方法可以最大限度地减少性能下降，最终的成果是一个系统化的解决方案，不只是单点创新，而是全面提升了能力。 目前，利用强化学习训练机器人处理rgb图像遇到的domain gap还是很难克服的。这也可能是今年或者明年大家研究里非常想去解的一个问题：机器人不再依赖深度图或者点云图，而是仅仅通过rgb图来感知。rgb图像包含丰富的信息，包括物体的材质、地面的特性以及周围的环境。例如，它可以显示一个标志，指示某个区域不可进入。这些语义信息在rgb图像中非常丰富，提供了深度图无法提供的详细上下文。 解释：这里提到的rgb是相对于点云信息，rgb图像由红、绿、蓝三种颜色通道组成，可以捕捉场景的彩色视觉信息。每个像素点记录了颜色信息，组合成我们肉眼可以看到的图像，目前互联网上存在的大量图片和视频数据也是rgb数据。点云是一组三维空间中的点，每个点包含位置坐标（x, y, z）和有时附带的强度值等信息。它通常由激光雷达或深度相机生成。 首先rgb不一定只有二维感知能力，双目rgb也可以提供深度信息。我这里强调rgb的意思是，从未来发展的角度来看，大概率不会使用激光雷达或者深度相机的点云，而是会选择单目或者双目的rgb，这不仅仅是出于成本的考量，更重要的是泛化性。单目或双目的rgb在视觉感知模块中具有最好的泛化性，因为数据量最大。互联网上有海量的通过相机和视频拍摄的rgb数据，它符合构建感知大模型（foundation model）对庞大数据量的需求。 我们需要参考现在互联网上有多少文本数据量才能训练出语言大模型，视觉或者视频是有机会训出感知大模型的。但其他传感器的数据，比如激光雷达、深度相机，甚至力学，触觉，几乎不可能成为感知大模型的基础，主要原因是这些领域连标准都没有。到目前为止，激光雷达还没有一个大家广泛接受的标准，无论是数据格式、传输、压缩方面都缺乏统一标准。在这种情况下，很难真正开发出感知大模型。 视觉数据之所以有如此大的优势，是因为它依赖于已经非常成熟的相机行业，再加上互联网在视觉数据的压缩和传输方面也非常方便。因此，未来机器人感知大模型很可能是基于rgb数据的。现阶段多传感器融合的三维重建是有用的。但从长期来看，imu 加上激光雷达的数据很难进入到感知大模型里，可能还是会和机器人数据管道解耦。这些数据可以帮助生成更好的真值数据集，或者作为测试集的基准。 在自动驾驶发展的初期，并没有如今机器人行业面临的数据短缺以及scaling up的问题。早期，自动驾驶都是依赖传统的机器人学方法，这些方法就是通过建图来识别静态环境，用激光来识别动态障碍物，利用规则结合搜索优化算法来规划自动驾驶汽车的轨迹，从而解决导航和移动问题。因此，自动驾驶的移动问题在那之前几乎都是通过传统方案来解决的。当时大家并没有深入考虑数据的重要性。 以waymo为例，2009年开始涉足自动驾驶，为什么选择那个时间点呢？这是因为他们观察到了2004年和2007年的darpa urban challenge，在那些比赛中，各个高校参赛团队已经能够通过传统的机器人学方法实现自动驾驶。这种传统方法通常是模块化的，比如感知分为检测与跟踪，地图包括高精度建图和定位，规控包括轨迹预测、位置速度规划等等。参赛团队看到了这些传统技术的可行性，因此waymo在2009年开始投入自动驾驶，并且一直沿用了2007年darpa urban challenge的技术路线。 实际上，到了2016年，自动驾驶真正火爆起来时，大多数人仍然沿着waymo的路线在推进，包括百度阿波罗也在较早期进行探索，基本上也是遵循这套技术路线。我认为真正的转折点是在2017年和2018年，特斯拉开始全面采用ai路线，从那个时间点开始，大家才逐渐意识到并开始探索用ai方法来解决自动驾驶问题。特斯拉开创了一个全新的方向，他们提出了完全通过ai、端到端地解决自动驾驶问题的理念。我认为这确实是特斯拉开了先河，改变了大家的思考方式。正是特斯拉的这种创新，使得大家对在机器人领域采用类似的模仿学习方法充满了信心，认为这种方法也可以在机器人领域取得成功。 在自动驾驶行业，最初大家认为有些公司的强大算法能力会带来明显的优势，但现在来看，纯靠算法的公司优势已经不明显了。实际上，跑的快的公司不是这些有算法优势的公司，反而是主机厂，比如国内的新造车势力和特斯拉，这些公司和专注于做自动驾驶算法的创业公司比也许算法不是最好的，但通过成功建立数据闭环，他们的实际自动驾驶体验是很不错的。这些主机厂之所以能跑得更快，核心原因是他们拥有大量的数据，他们需要做的事情就是对这些数据筛选和自动标注，然后再训练模型，问题就解决了。 公开信息虽然不多，但大家普遍认为特斯拉的方法是通过图像作为输入，轨迹或控制信号直接作为输出，训练了一个模型。不过，这个模型中还有一些中间输出，比如占用图、车道线检测和物体检测的输出。基本上，这是一个多头（multi-head）模型，而其中最重要的head是规划出来的轨迹或控制信号的。包括所有的中间输出，整个模型是直接进行训练的。 而他训练的数据来源就是所有卖给车主在路上跑的tesla车，这种方法非常巧妙。用现在机器人的数据视角来看，特斯拉的方法其实就是一个同构遥操作，类似于mobile aloha。驾驶员操作与机器人本体相同的系统，不断收集数据，收集后直接用来训练模型。特斯拉给出了一个最佳示范，证明这条路径可以达到非常高的上限，虽然还未完全达到l4水平，但已经非常接近。 仿真可以分为几个部分：感知的仿真，比如激光雷达和视觉图像的仿真；行为的仿真，比如模拟其他车辆的行驶轨迹。对于机器人来说，可能还有动力学仿真和物理参数的仿真，因机器人在操作时，需要与物体接触。在自动驾驶领域，主要关注的就是感知的仿真和行为的仿真。waymo在行为的仿真这方面做了很多工作。几年前，waymo的主要宣传点就是他们拥有几千万英里的真实驾驶数据，再加上几千万英里乘以一千到一万倍的仿真数据。 waymo这里提到的仿真指的是行为仿真。比如，在真实驾驶中遇到一个醉汉以一米每秒的速度穿过马路，waymo可以通过仿真将他的速度调整为两米每秒或0.5米每秒，从而生成新的行为数据。类似地，在执行无保护掉头时，可以模拟对方车辆是否让行，从而仿真出各种不同的行为数据。 而像特斯拉这样的公司，更倾向于做端到端的解决方案，因为他们的数据主要是图像数据，因此更倾向于做感知的仿真。感知的仿真在过去，包括特斯拉和英伟达在内的一些公司，会在游戏引擎中渲染新的场景进行感知仿真。特斯拉之前在这方面做得很多，但最近由于他们拥有大量的真实数据，已经不再需要依赖仿真，所以他们现在可能不再进行仿真。总体来说，对于数据量足够大的公司，大概率不会那么需要仿真。 6. 行为仿真—训练or测试 预测是用来预测其他车辆的行为，而规划是用来规划自己车辆的行为，当这两者结合起来时，就形成了一个行为仿真器。这种行为仿真器生成的数据被广泛的应用在了测试中，但没有被广泛应用在训练中。原因在于，仿真数据的分布与真实数据之间存在偏差。如果将仿真数据用于模型训练，可能会把我的模型带偏，特别是当仿真数据与真实环境差异较大时。 尽管如此，仿真数据在测试中仍然有价值。它可以用来验证模型在处理各种边界情况（corner cases）时的能力。我们可以将仿真数据视为这种边界情况，就是他很假，但假也有用，假就是这个边界情况。通过测试模型在这些情况下的表现，来评估模型是否能够在超出其能力边界时仍保持安全驾驶。 最近几年计算机视觉领域最大的进展有两个方面：一个是视频生成模型，另一个就是可微分渲染（nerf和3d gs）。我认为可微分渲染尤其值得关注。过去的感知仿真主要依靠数字资产的绘制和游戏引擎的渲染，但无论我们如何绘制资产，都很难复刻真实环境中物体的多样性分布，所以我认为纯仿真这条路很难走下去。现在可微渲染给我们提供了一个新的思路，那就是基于一条真实数据，利用3d gs渲染新的视角，合成出新的数据。具体来说，我们可以基于一条真实的路测视频，渲染出”我如果开在旁边这条车道可能看到什么样的图像？” 这种方法我们把它称为real2sim。 real2sim2real的流程基本如下，通过采集机器人的真实数据，在仿真器中对这些真实数据进行增广。接着，可以用这些合成数据来训练模型，最终在实际环境中使用。3d gs 是纯视觉的，主要关注物体的新视角渲染，但并不模拟物体的物理特性或动力学。 当下比较主流的机器人学习技术路线：在操作方面，主要依靠模仿学习；而运动控制方面，依靠强化学习；这种算法组合是较为明确的。至于数据问题，强化学习的数据靠高度并行化的仿真器；模仿学习的真机数据通过遥操作采集，包括vr遥操作或同构遥操作等，采集到的真实数据可以做数据增强来提升模型训练的泛化性。当下主流的技术路线差不多是这些，对于学术界来说，我们要持续探索数据效率更高的算法，对于业界来说，要找到合适的商业场景并将数据闭环。 未来的数据利用确实可能会形成一个金字塔结构，包括真实机器人数据、仿真数据和视频数据。拥有更多真实数据会使模型的性能更强，这是确定的。仿真数据的效果则取决于仿真的质量，仿真数据的价值可以通过仿真质量的高低来衡量。高质量的仿真数据系数大，低质量的则系数小。让机器人从视频数据中学习，尤其是开放世界中的视频数据，是未来的最终目标，但还需要进一步的科研探索。 最近一段时间，国内外在机器人领域的创业公司每隔一阵子都会公布最新的进展，持续刺激这个行业的热度。与此同时，也有越来越多的人持续涌入机器人创业浪潮，作为关注这个领域的早期投资机构打工人，身在其中，每天都可以有惊喜，当然也充满了遗憾。具身智能的这波热度已经持续了一年半，在肉眼可见的未来半年，随着硬件demo的持续进化，热度应该依然可以持续。 在持续的热度和眼花缭乱的demo里，我非常庆幸能够以文字的形式记录下和这些优秀学者的对谈。把如今的困惑和突破通过一系列对最有代表性论文的探讨记录下来，也许在三年、五年或十年后，再回头看这些文字的时候，会不禁感慨，原来当初的主流路径并非最后work的路径，感谢某些人在某些方向上的坚持不懈，通用机器人才得以实现。 references： robot parkour learning robot the parkour learning approach can be understood through three stages: pretraining, fine-tuning and distillation. the discussion begins with the quadruped framework and relates it to humanoid locomotion. stage 1: rl pretraining with soft dynamics constraints we introduce soft dynamics constraints during pretraining. rather than immediately enforcing a hard collision with every obstacle, we allow the robot to penetrate obstacle regions and penalize that penetration through the reward. we know the obstacles' geometry in code, but initially do not enforce the corresponding physical collision in the simulator. as the robot enters an obstacle, its reward decreases. this makes it easier to learn a behavior that progressively avoids penetration. 'soft dynamics' here describes the learning curriculum, not a claim that all conventional simulators are incapable of compliant contact. soft dynamics stage 2: rl fine-tuning with hard dynamics constraints during fine-tuning, we enforce the full dynamics constraints and refine the pretrained behavior under realistic simulated contact. now the obstacle is physically present. a small penetration that was tolerated during the relaxed stage cannot occur in reality, so additional training is needed to adapt the behavior to proper collision constraints before deployment. hard dynamics stage 3: distilling a vision-based parkour policy once the individual parkour skills have been learned, we use dagger (dataset aggregation) to distill them into a single vision-based policy. it can run on a quadruped using only onboard perception and computation. distillation one motivation for distillation was the rendering bottleneck in earlier isaac gym workflows. in the setup we used with an rtx 3090, an rl run might take three hours without rendering but around three days with rendering. those figures illustrate that particular setup. we could first give a teacher privileged terrain information—a virtual terrain sensor—and then distill the policy into a student that learns to interpret deployable sensor observations. if the problem and compute budget permit direct visual training, such as with an rtx 4090, distillation is not inherently required. another benefit is easier sensor replacement. a policy might initially use a depth camera, then transfer through distillation to a different sensor such as lidar if the depth camera proves unsuitable. that can reduce the need to relearn all the motor skills from scratch. before around 2020, many rl and locomotion researchers focused on algorithmic efficiency. cpu-based workflows using simulators such as mujoco and pybullet offered much less parallelism in the setups being discussed—for example, roughly 256 environments on a server. around that time, a member of marco hutter's robotic systems lab at eth zurich explored scaling data through an internship at nvidia and large isaac gym experiments. gpu parallelism made thousands of environments, such as 4,096, practical, producing an important breakthrough through scale. in my account, this shifted attention strongly toward parallel data generation. editorial clarification: these counts are setup examples, not universal cpu or gpu limits. a representative published milestone is rudin and colleagues' learning to walk in minutes using massively parallel deep reinforcement learning, first released in 2021. scaling did not eliminate the research problem of rl sample efficiency. the sim-to-real gap has been addressed effectively for many locomotion settings, but manipulation still presents substantial challenges. manipulation models can simplify physics too aggressively. to lift an object, for instance, sufficient force must be applied, yet an abstract action representation may ignore its mass or force limits. such omitted factors can make a simulated solution fail on real hardware. this is progress in particular locomotion applications, not a claim that sim-to-real transfer has been solved universally. manipulation also involves complex contact geometry. finger–object interaction can create many contact surfaces, and the number of contacts can be orders of magnitude greater than in the locomotion examples we discuss. this makes simulation harder. general simulators often use iterative numerical methods to compute successive states. complex contacts introduce accuracy challenges and computational cost, which can slow simulation substantially. researchers coming from computer vision are accustomed to widely accepted datasets and metrics, and naturally want unified training and evaluation benchmarks in robotics. imagenet, for example, offered an intuitive accuracy metric; later visualization methods also helped analyze models. in robotics, an equally broad and widely accepted standard had not emerged at the time of this discussion. we still lack a dataset covering the range of situations and supporting meaningful evaluation even for groups without real hardware. in the difficult manipulation settings i have in mind, success rates can be below 10%. differences such as 3% versus 4% may be difficult to interpret without adequate evaluation. this makes performance assessment challenging. to improve success, systems are often tested in simplified scenes, but those tests may not show how they handle real-world complexity. demo videos may also be sped up two, four or eight times. many earlier manipulation formulations use quasi-static dynamics, simplifying the problem by neglecting some dynamic effects. these observations concern particular research settings and demos, not all robotics work; small percentage changes can be meaningful when supported by sufficient trials. quasi-static assumptions exclude many dynamic events, such as an object suddenly falling, or fast motions involved in shaking clothing or spreading a bedsheet. aloha helped draw attention to real-time execution and control in this context. earlier work such as swingbot, associated with research on dynamic manipulation, also emphasized the importance of high-speed environmental motion and inertia. editorial clarification: the interview attributes this early line broadly to shuran song's group, but swingbot's published authors include chen wang, shaoxiong wang, branden romero, filipe veiga and edward adelson; it should not be treated as a paper authored by shuran song. for humanoids, directly mapping human motion data to a robot does not ensure physical feasibility. early graphics models could generate plausible-looking human movement that violated contact or dynamics—for example, feet sliding over the ground as though doing a moonwalk. a robot needs a layer that converts human reference motions into executable behavior consistent with its own physics. mathematically, rl and control theory have many connections. in the comparison i am drawing, rl often handles uncertainty through probabilistic formulations, including analyses of prior and posterior distributions, whereas many model-based planning and control implementations use deterministic dynamics. editorial clarification: this is a simplified comparison of common implementations. control theory also includes stochastic and robust control, and rl is not defined by bayesian prior/posterior analysis or excluded from deterministic settings. an advantage of learned control is the possibility of responding robustly when a situation goes outside the planner's expected conditions. consider the comparison with deep tracking control. if a jumping platform is displaced by 0.1 meters, a model-based planner might adjust the motion slightly. if it is displaced by 0.5 meters, beyond the robot's reachable jump, the original plan may become infeasible and require a protective response. a trained policy can learn recovery behavior for such deviations, although that ability depends on its training. rl-trained tracking controller; it is not evidence that rl always succeeds where mpc fails. robot parkour learning was a finalist for the corl 2023 best systems paper award. i see that as recognition of a complete system, rather than only one isolated technical advance. the two main challenges were designing an effective training strategy and overcoming the sim-to-real gap. training required rl under different dynamics constraints followed by distillation of the skills. earlier quadruped systems often relied mainly on proprioception, without vision. we add visual perception, particularly stereo depth, making the perceptual sim-to-real gap important. we try to simulate depth observations realistically and process real observations to resemble the simulator's idealized images, bringing the distributions closer together. we tried approaches such as hole filling and denoising. depth images work reasonably well here because parkour primarily requires understanding terrain geometry. but future practical robots should handle rgb images as well, rather than rely only on depth. multitask learning is also a longstanding challenge. gradients from different skills can conflict, degrading performance. debugging one skill is easier than debugging several simultaneously. after exploring alternatives, ziwen found a useful strategy: train each skill separately as a teacher, then train a shared student. this reduces performance loss and brings the components together into a systematic solution. at the time of this 2024 interview, the domain gap remains difficult for rl policies using rgb observations. i expect researchers to work hard on this over 2024 and 2025: robots perceiving through rgb rather than relying exclusively on depth or point clouds. rgb contains rich information about materials, surfaces and context—for example, a sign marking a restricted area. those semantics provide context that geometry-only depth observations do not convey. a clarification: rgb images robot-data-ep06-eureka-dreureka: ep6对话马也骋：eureka和dreureka如何利用llm解决仿真+rl最重要的难题 与马也骋讨论llm、奖励函数生成、强化学习与sim2real。 robot data 在robot data的前几期，我们介绍了用人类视频数据、遥操数据以及动捕数据进行机器人学习的典型论文，这些论文都以人类专家经验为基准。在机器人学习领域有另一大主流分支就是仿真+强化学习，在四足和双足locomotion的训练方面，仿真+强化学习的效果毋庸置疑。但在操作方面，仿真+强化学习却面临着非常大的瓶颈：仿真环境和奖励函数搭建费时费力，强化学习搜索速度慢，sim2real gap等问题。eureka和dreureka利用大语言模型自动设计仿真环境和奖励函数，在仿真中快速学习新技能，并迅速将其转移到现实世界中。 我们很荣幸的邀请到eureka和dreureka的一作马也骋博士，对仿真、强化学习、以及llm在仿真+强化学习领域的潜力做了详细讲解。以下万字长文，希望带你一起了解eureka和dreureka。 eureka和dreureka的作者包括来自宾大grasp、英伟达等机构的学者。eureka: human-level reward design via coding large language models作者包括jason ma, william liang, guanzhi wang, de-an huang, osbert bastani, dinesh jayaraman, yuke zhu, linxi "jim" fan, anima anandkumar，其中jason ma（马也骋）是eureka的一作。dreureka: language model guided sim-to-real transfer，作者包括jason ma*, william liang*, hungju wang, sam wang, yuke zhu, linxi "jim" fan, osbert bastani, dinesh jayaraman，其中jason ma（马也骋）和william liang是dr eureka的共同一作。 以下为本文目录 👇 1. eureka的核心思想 2. dreureka的核心思想 3. eureka方法介绍 initial reward function generation environment as context rapid reward evaluation via massively parallel rl return reward reflection super human level reward function novel reward function 4. dreureka方法介绍 reward-aware physics prior 5. 一些问题 eureka和dreureka可以改进的地方 eureka与其他基于llm的机器人工作对比 目前模仿学习和真机操作数据更主流？ eureka可以成为解决sim+rl的方法吗？ eureka的应用情况 sim2real gap的渲染问题 正常怎么做domain randomization？ eureka效果仅局限在局部移动这类任务吗？ 仿真+rl在处理长程任务上的表现？ 仿真环境里的数据是怎么产生的？ 关于研究方向 vip简单介绍 6. 一些想法 众所周知，数据在机器人学习领域是最重要的问题之一，我们可以通过遥操作收集真实世界数据，也可以在仿真中收集数据。理论上，在仿真中我们可以扩展数据规模，然后将其转移到现实世界中。然而，使用仿真数据有一个非常重要且被低估的问题是必须由人来设计仿真环境，然后以某种方式验证仿真环境是否有效，或者说能否将其转移到现实中。否则即使你在仿真中收集到大量数据，不管用什么训练策略，如果数不可靠，这些方法也不会太有效。 那我们如何有效的为一个新任务或新机器人设计仿真环境？过去，这种仿真环境的搭建通常都需要人类完成，过程缓慢且需要大量专业知识。因此，在 eureka 的工作中，我们提出了一个设想：能否通过llm自动设计仿真环境，使我们能够在仿真中快速学习新技能，并迅速将其转移到现实世界中。这正是 eureka 工作的创新所在。 在仿真中，因为数据非常丰富，我们可以长时间运行仿真，探索不同的状态。因此在仿真中，流行的方法不是进行模仿学习，即人类使用键盘或游戏控制器提供示范，而是运行强化学习，让策略自己收集数据、观察反馈并逐步改进。这是为什么在仿真环境中机器人学习的常见方法是强化学习。但进行强化学习需要一个环境，而这就是问题所在。你需要设计一个奖励函数，这是一个数学函数，告诉策略哪些状态和动作有利于完成任务，哪些不利。这一直由人类设计，但过程缓慢且不直观。 阅读强化学习的论文时，你会发现人们并不会在主要论文中详细讨论奖励函数，通常只是一个简单的说明或在附录中提及，但实际上奖励函数的设计非常重要。如果奖励函数设计得当，强化学习通常可以找到解决方案。否则，效果会非常不理想。 eureka 使用大型语言模型（llm）来自动编写用于仿真机器人任务的奖励函数（reward function）。在仿真中，奖励函数就像仿真中的其他代码一样，是可以在计算机上运行的代码，而像 gpt-4 这样的llm非常擅长编写代码。因此，在 eureka 中，我们使用llm来自动编写奖励函数代码。但这还不是全部，我们还要求llm改进奖励函数代码。 具体操作是，llm会编写多个奖励函数代码，然后在仿真器中我们利用这些奖励函数来训练策略，并构建反馈，看看哪个效果更好，哪个效果更差。根据这些反馈以及策略实际表现，我们可以指导llm编写更好的奖励函数。由于llm非常擅长遵循指令，它们可以根据反馈生成更好的奖励函数。这就像一种自我改进的迭代过程，llm可以通过仿真反馈逐步编写出更好的奖励函数。这就是我们在论文中所称的进化算法（evolutionary algorithm），我们让大型语言模型进化这些奖励函数。你也可以把这看作是一种基于人工智能反馈的强化学习方法，即 rlaif (reinforcement learning from ai feedback)。最终目标是提出能够解决任务的策略，但在这个过程中，不仅策略在更新，环境的奖励函数也在更新，以便最终能提出最佳策略。这就是 eureka 的高层次工作原理。 最终结果是，使用相同的算法，不需要任何提示工程，我们可以直接解决 10 种不同机器人形态的 29 项任务。特别是，我们能够展示一些新颖的任务，比如让机器人第一次旋转铅笔。使用相同的理念，当eureka 的奖励生成能力与经典强化学习算法结合时，我们可以教机器人用多种方式旋转铅笔，效果非常好。 eureka 转笔 eureka转魔方 基于eureka，我们有了一种完全自动化的仿真环境奖励设计方法。理论上，我们可以在仿真中生成任何行为，因为现在有了能够生成高层次规划和行为生成奖励函数的语言模型。eureka 项目获得了很好的反馈，我在 neurips 2023 的多个研讨会上展示了它，并且它还被 iclr 2024 接受。但当我们第一次在各个研讨会上展示它时，最常被问到的问题是，这能在真实机器人上工作吗？你展示的一切都是在仿真中，这能在真实机器人上实现吗？为了回答这个关键问题，我们更进一步，开发了 dreureka，或者我称之为 doctor eureka。因为成为博士意味着你毕业了，所以让 eureka 从仿真到现实世界的转移就像是毕业典礼。为了实现从仿真到现实的强化学习，除了设计奖励函数，你还必须让仿真到现实的转移能够顺利进行。 通常，仿真环境和现实世界环境之间存在很多不匹配，特别是在物理模型方面。模拟器无法完美地模拟现实世界中的重力、摩擦力等。因此，现在很流行的一种做法是进行领域随机化（domain randomization），即在仿真中随机化物理参数。这样，策略就必须在更广泛的物理环境分布上进行学习。如果策略能够在更广泛的分布上进行学习，那么它可能更具鲁棒性，并且更有可能在现实世界中成功部署。因此，如今几乎所有的仿真到现实的强化学习方法都采用某种形式的领域随机化。 但在domain randomization的过程依然有一个问题，那就是人类必须手动涉及这个domain randomization的参数。以教机器狗行走为例：作为人类，我们凭直觉和常识知道摩擦力、重力、机器人质心等是需要随机化的重要物理参数。然而，这种设计需要大量领域知识。更重要的是，面对新任务时，我们可能需要重新设计整个随机化过程。 在dreureka中，除了自动编写奖励函数，我们还自动化了域随机化设计。具体做法如下：首先，我们向大型语言模型提供了一份可随机化的物理参数列表。在此基础上，基于具体任务，语言模型会自动决定应该随机化哪些参数，以及这些参数应该从模拟中的默认值随机化到什么程度。我们发现语言模型在进行超参数选择方面表现出色。其他研究已经证明，语言模型能为超参数生成产生相当好的样本，例如在线性回归任务中猜测数值。更令人兴奋的是，我们的研究表明，语言模型甚至能够零样本（即无需额外训练）生成相当好的域随机化参数。这种方法大大简化了域随机化的设计过程，减少了对人类专家知识的依赖，为自动化强化学习任务开辟了新的可能性。 现在，我们已经实现了奖励函数和域随机化的自动选择，我们可以部署在奖励函数分布和域随机化参数上表现最佳的策略。令人惊喜的是，我们发现将这些策略直接部署到现实世界中竟然是可行的。这意味着我们现在拥有了一个端到端的、完全自动化的仿真到现实世界的流程。整个过程完全由大型语言模型自动化完成，中间不需要任何人工干预。 这一突破性进展展示了大型语言模型在自动化强化学习任务中的强大潜力，从奖励函数的设计到域随机化的选择，再到最终策略的部署，全程无需人类专家参与。这不仅大大提高了效率，也为解决更复杂的现实世界问题开辟了新的可能性。 在dreureka中，我们展示了这个算法不仅可以教会机器人在手上旋转模仿，还可以教机器人如何向前行走。但我认为真正有趣的是，考虑到语言模型无法自动化所有事情，如果我们能教会机器人一项新任务会怎样？这就是我们让机器狗在瑜伽球上行走所做的，这个任务之前从未被演示过。我们在物理引擎模拟器中放置了一个机器狗在瑜伽球上，然后运行dreureka算法，任务目标是让机器人在球上行走，尽可能长时间地停留在球上。然后在没有任何人为监督的情况下，它能够提出奖励函数和域随机化参数。在现实世界部署中，也取得了不错的效果，当然有一个限制条件是人类要握着牵引绳。这主要是出于安全考虑，确保我们不会真的损坏机器人。但即使没有牵引绳，机器人也能在多种不同地形上站在球上超过5到10秒。 dreureka video 转魔方 狗走不同地形 这里值得特别提出的是，我们使用的模拟器isaacgym是刚体模拟器，它无法模拟可变形的表面。所以在仿真环境中，和机器狗配合的球实际上是一个刚体球，它没有形变。但在现实世界中，瑜伽球显然是可变形并且有弹性的。由于我们无法设计出一个尽可能接近真实世界的模拟器，这实际上迫使算法对模拟中的不准确性具有鲁棒性。换句话说，如果你的策略没有考虑到模拟中的不准确性，它在现实世界中可能无法工作。但llm能够自动生成一个有效的分布，使得现实世界的迁移成为可能。这展示了在未来使用llm自动处理模拟中的新任务并转移到现实世界的潜力。dreureka是展示未来实现这一目标的第一步。 设置模拟环境或奖励函数，无论你怎么做，最终它们都是代码。这些程序大多数是python程序，而llms（大型语言模型）如gpt-4非常擅长写python代码。所以在代码格式上，llms实际上非常擅长写这些代码，只要你正确提示它们。但是，为了让这些代码有用并控制llms的幻觉（因为llms可能生成一个环境代码，但这个环境可能很差，不太有用，这时反馈就很重要），你需要一种方法来判断奖励函数是好是坏。这时你可以在强化学习中训练策略，观察策略在模拟中的行为，总结这些行为，然后将这些作为反馈给llms，以生成更多的奖励函数。 eureka方法框架 这里有一个重要的注意事项：我们生成的密集奖励函数（dense reward function）实际上可以引导强化学习。另外，还需要一个独立于密集奖励函数的真实评价指标。否则，你会有一堆策略，它们做的事情都不一样，你无法判断哪个做得更好或更差。所以在eureka的工作中，我们假设可以访问一个表示成功与否的函数，该函数能够告诉我们某个策略是80%成功还是50%成功。通常，这会是一个指示函数（indicator function）。 举个例子，如果任务是开门，那么成功函数只会简单地告诉我们门是否打开了，这是一个是或否的问题。而密集奖励函数则需要捕捉诸如“机器人需要靠近门把手”，然后“旋转门把手并打开门”等步骤。这些对人类来说非常难以编写，编写成功检查器通常很简单。但是，成功检查器本身对于强化学习来说并不太有用，因为它的信号太稀疏。这时我们可以使用eureka来自动化生成密集奖励函数，获取反馈并不断改进。 在eureka中，除了成功函数外，我们还对eureka生成的奖励函数本身的策略统计进行了总结。每个奖励函数都是由不同的要点构成的。例如，一个奖励函数可能由要点a、要点b和要点c组成。要点a可能是靠近门把手，要点b是旋转门把手，等等。如果你还能总结这些单独组件的情况，那么这会给你非常详细的反馈，告诉你哪个项没有得到适当的优化。比如，你的策略可能会得到0%的成功率，因为它们从未靠近门把手。 如果我们对这些单独要点进行详细总结，并将其用作反馈给大型语言模型，那么在下一次迭代中，llm就会知道哪个要点需要更改或添加哪些新要点，以提供更好的密集奖励函数来改进策略。因此，eureka中的llm反馈部分实际上结合了真实成功函数和每个策略在eureka奖励函数中的各个单独要点的统计总结。这为llm提供了足够的信号，使其能够自主生成更好的奖励函数，并改进现有的函数。 zero-shot生成奖励函数非常重要，因为在数据稀缺的情况下，你需要一个奖励函数作为起点，但设计一个奖励函数通常非常困难。为新任务设计奖励函数时，通常很难找到合适的起点。然而，llm可以直接生成奖励函数，并通过自我改进来启动这一过程。这是llm在eureka工作中所需的关键能力之一，因为它能够在没有人工干预的情况下完成这项工作。 dreureka方法框架 llm可以生成一些人类想不到的奖励函数，可以从两个角度解释。首先，我们对比了人类编写的奖励函数和eureka生成的奖励函数，进行了相关性分析。我们把它们当作数学函数来看它们的相似度。这可以从数学层面上判断它们是否类似。有时，这两者的相关性很低，甚至是负相关，说明人类的奖励函数可能已经很优化，而我们生成的奖励函数可以做得更好。 randomization参数。这些参数有一个范围，而在物理仿真中，这个范围理论上可以从负无穷到正无穷。比如，视觉物理和重力参数可以在-100到100之间变化。但如果让llm在如此大的范围内搜索参数，得到的范围可能太宽泛且无用。因为如果范围太大，训练策略时可能会出现过多的变化，导致策略崩溃。 为了解决这个问题，我们采用了物理先验（physics prior）的概念。具体而言，我们先有一个初始的奖励函数和初始的默认物理值，然后逐渐增加或减少这些值，直到基于原始奖励函数训练的策略失效。这样就可以得到一个更小的、可用的参数范围。 通过这种方法，我们可以限制llm的搜索范围，使其得到一个有用的物理随机化分布。换句话说，我们需要知道奖励函数和策略仍然有效的上下限，然后在这个范围内进行搜索。否则，搜索空间太大，返回的结果可能无效且不实用。这种方式确保了domain randomization的有效性。 eureka和dreureka都没有考虑视觉输入，在这些工作中，机器人实际上无法看到环境，它仅仅依靠接收到的文字或代码输入来解决问题。然而，在现实世界中，特别是在操控任务中，机器人首先需要看到环境，以了解物体的位置以及如何与其互动。这两个工作都没有解决这一部分问题。但我们相信，借助现在的视觉语言模型，比如gpt4v、gpt4o、gemini等，我们可以利用视觉反馈来设计奖励函数，并从视觉输入中提供反馈。 robot-data-ep05-humanplus-mobile-aloha: ep5对话符梓鹏：humanplus和mobile aloha的数据故事——从合成数据到真实数据再到两者的结合 与符梓鹏讨论合成数据、真实数据、humanplus与mobile aloha。 robot data robot data专栏，我们围绕机器人训练数据采访一些具有代表性的学术论文作者。说到机器人训练数据相关的论文，斯坦福大学chelsea finn组里的mobile aloha可以说是2023年至今，在模仿学习和遥操作方面最知名的工作之一。斯坦福大学chelasea finn组陆续在2023年上半年发布aloha和act，2023年末发布mobile aloha，24年上半年发布humanplus，这一系列利用遥操作进行机器人训练的工作获得了学术界、产业界甚至各个科技媒体的高度关注。robot data第五期，我们很荣幸的邀请到了mobile aloha和humanplus的一作符梓鹏博士，聊一聊这两个工作背后的数据故事。 符梓鹏博士目前是斯坦福大学人工智能实验室的计算机科学博士生，由chelsea finn指导。此前，他在cmu ri获得硕士学位，由deepak pathak和jitendra malik指导。他在ucla完成了计算机科学和应用数学的学士学位，导师是朱松纯教授。符梓鹏博士的研究兴趣在机器人学、机器学习和计算机视觉的交叉领域，致力于在非结构化开放环境中实现稳健的机器人性能和可部署的机器人系统。 值得一提的是，符梓鹏博士在学术生涯的早期在机器狗locomotion方面有非常多优秀工作，近期的工作聚焦在通过遥操作和人类视频数据解决移动操作问题。可以说是学术界非常难得的横跨仿真数据、遥操数据、人类视频数据；纵跨locomotion和manipulation的优秀学者。我们这期文章借由humanplus这篇论文，来了解符梓鹏博士对机器人训练和数据的一些洞见。 以下为本文目录 👇 1. 从合成数据到真实数据再到两者结合 机器狗训练—合成数据 mobile aloha-遥操真机数据 humanplus—合成数据与遥操数据结合 2. humanplus：让人形机器人像人的影子一样 humanplus的数据来源 humanplus模型结构 3. 一些问题 怎么理解人形机器人和人体的影子结合 人形机器人控制路径对比 仿真环境中的真实度问题 更换硬件要怎么做？ 为什么用单个rgb摄像头 关于分层与端到端问题 4. 一些补充 我个人在机器人方向的研究最初是从机器狗的训练开始，利用仿真软件生成大量合成数据，通过强化学习训练机器人。这种路径在某些场景下确实非常有效，例如训练机器狗行走，把机械臂装在机器狗上协调控制、或者让机器狗跑酷等。虽然仿真数据可以大量的生成，可以做一些强化学习，比如告诉机器狗可以往前走、往前走的时候又不撞到任何东西、还要省力和节省电的损耗，这些告诉机器狗后它可以自己学出来。也不需要，或者说也没有真实世界的数据可以用，因为我不可能练一大堆宠物狗来收集数据。 但仿真数据加上强化学习也遇到了一个瓶颈，主要表现在它只擅长做一些偏向locomotion（局部移动）这类的动作，比如动动手动动脚，或者像in-hand orientation（手内物体重定向）这类动作，像openai也使用生成数据来训练灵巧手。然而，当任务涉及到需要更高层次决策和复杂规划时，机器人就需要更多的视觉信息。仿真软件现在没法很好的提供这些真实世界里的视觉信息，它更多的是提供物理碰撞和结构化信息，例如深度数据等。然而，要渲染出真实的颜色信息则相对困难。 到了mobile aloha的阶段，相当于我们完全没有用到任何仿真软件的信息，完全利用真实世界的数据来让机器人进行学习。收集机器人在真实世界中的数据，这些数据由人类通过遥操作方式采集，并通过高效的模仿学习用少量的数据进行训练；这时候可以获得更好的、比较真实的视觉信号，比如rgb数据，还有一些语义上的数据。 这种方法面临的一个挑战是，真实世界数据的收集速度较慢。所以，mobile aloha相当于是结合了一个高效的模仿学习算法，只需提供大约50次人类采数据的尝试，就可以让机器人学习并完成各种任务。这种方法高效地帮助人类采集数据，相比以往使用vr设备或3d鼠标键盘等工具采集数据，不仅速度快且易于上手。mobile aloha的主要作用在于快速让人们掌握如何操作机器人，以解决几乎所有真实世界中可能遇到的问题。 mobile aloha 在humanplus的阶段，我们尝试将合成数据和机器人遥操数据的特点融合：一种是海量的合成数据，虽然在仿真软件中的数据量大，但质量不高；另一种是高质量的真实世界数据，但采集速度慢，无法达到海量。因此，human plus的主要目标是能否结合这两者的优点，即在真实世界中收集高质量数据，同时利用海量的合成数据。 humanplus humanplus结合了两种数据来源：一边是机器人仿真数据，另一边是人类的运动数据。 关于机器人仿真数据，我们不能直接将人类的运动信息复制到机器人上，因为机器人的重量和关节结构与人类不同，直接复制可能会导致机器人失去平衡并倒下。因此，在最低层次的控制逻辑上，我们仍然使用强化学习在仿真环境中生成大量的仿真数据训练机器人。这意味着，当机器人接收到人类关节位置信号时，它会根据这些信号主动控制自己的动作，以模仿人类的动作，但同时也会考虑到自身的物理限制，以保持平衡。这种方法可以确保机器人既能够模仿人类动作，又不会因为不稳定而倒下。 关于人类的运动数据，虽然真实世界中没有大量的机器人，但有很多人的数据。例如，很多视频中会有人在跳舞或做饭。这些数据已经存在，而且非常大量。我们在想如何很好地利用这些人类数据，将它们有效地迁移到人形机器人上。人形机器人的最大优势就是能够很好地利用大量的人类数据。我们的工作就是让人形机器人通过这些数据进行精细控制。 大多数情况下，我们需要模仿视频中的人类动作。这些视频通常由摄像头记录人的生活，摄像头可能放在旁边或者安装在人的头上，例如运动相机。我们的工作重点是如何利用好一个rgb摄像头的限制来获取数据，通过摄像头捕捉到人的骨骼信号，包括身体骨骼、手部、手臂和腿部的关节数据。这些数据用于实时控制机器人，使其能够执行各种任务。 此外，我们还结合了类似mobile aloha这样的高效模仿学习，使机器人能够自主完成任务。机器人通过头上的rgb摄像头获取视觉信息，并根据这些信息完成任务。现在，机器人已经能够自主地完成一系列任务，比如自己坐在椅子上，把鞋穿到脚上，然后系鞋带，站起来走路。这些能力都是通过利用人类数据训练得以实现的。 通过模仿学习人类视频数据，我们可以将人类的运动模式转化为机器人控制策略。感觉就像是神经网络在控制一个人的动作，最终的神经网络输出可以直接映射到人形机器人上。由于人形机器人在形态上与人类相似，这种映射过程相对简单和直观。这使得我们可以更有效地利用人类数据来训练和控制机器人，使其能够执行类似人类的动作和任务。 humanplus的模型结构包括两部分，第一部分是在仿真环境中训练人形影子变换器（humamoid shadowing transformer），即通过仿真软件基于强化学习训练出一个可以让机器人既能像人的影子一样跟随动作又可以满足自身的物理特征做到平衡的低层控制器（上图左侧）；第二部分是通过人类数据进行模仿学习训练（humamoid imitation transformer，hit），将第一部分训练的低层控制器零样本部署到真实世界中的人形机器人上进行实时影子跟踪。 在shadowing部分，人类操作员站在人形机器人附近，将其全身实时动作像影子一样投射到人形机器人上，人类操作员通过视线观察环境和人形机器人的行为，确保系统的响应速度和灵活性，从而实现高效的遥操作。这部分的低层控制器的输入是仿人的本体感知和仿人的目标姿态，本体感知包括基准状态（滚动、俯仰和基部角速度）、关节位置、关节速度和上一次动作。本体感知观测值仅使用机载传感器测量，包括一个imu和关节编码器。仿人的目标姿态包括目标前进和侧向速度、目标滚动和俯仰、目标偏航速度和目标关节角度等。我们使用单个rgb摄像头实时估计人体和手部姿态，并将人体姿态重新定向为人形机器人的目标姿态。输出是19维的仿人身体关节位置设定点，这些设定点随后转换为力矩信号。 在autonomous skills部分，机器人通过模仿学习，自主学习到了一些人类技能并完成相应任务。人形机器人模仿学习框架（hit）要求机器人不仅仅是模仿而是能像影子一样跟随，并自主学习从自身观察中获取的信息，以发展出新的技能。机器人不仅需要本体感知信息，还需要处理左右眼的rgb图像。它的输入是两个第一人称视角的rgb摄像头采集的图像、本体感知和固定位置嵌入。输出是预测的目标位置，并将其发送给低层人形影子变换器，同时丢弃预测的未来图像特征标记。它相当于是学了一个左边底层控制器的输入，也就是我们希望这个机器人去什么样的目标姿势。 将人形机器人和人体做影子结合它不只是零重力结合。在零重力环境中，机器人不再受重力影响，因此不需要学习如何应对重力。例如，机器人漂浮在太空中时，它可以自由移动而不受重力约束，容易与人类动作相匹配。然而，重力在地面上的作用是一个挑战，比如人可以单脚站，但如果机器人也学人单脚站，很可能失衡或倒下。 首先，目前市面上的大多数机器人只能做基本的前后走动，甚至有些连站立都困难。它们缺乏多样性，例如无法像人类一样做手臂动作或者蹲下去拿取低处的物体，这些动作对于现有的大多数机器人来说是不可实现的。humanplus的一个特点是，上肢和下肢都是通过同一个神经网络来训练的，它的协调性很好。 仿真环境里的物体，无论多么真实，人眼实际上是可以分辨出来它是真的还是假的。一般人眼能看出来的东西，神经网络也可以。神经网络在区分物体时非常擅长注意到细微的差异，即使是小小的细节也能察觉到。当前的仿真器可能能够处理不同颜色和重量等方面的变化，但在处理软度、形变和复杂的视觉场景时，模拟效果会变得困难。 虽然训练过程是相似的，但更换人形机器人硬件需要重新训练算法，因为不同的机器人具有不同的关节长度和重量，这些因素会影响其运动控制能力和平衡性。 现在的想法是希望使用单个摄像头更好地模拟已有视频的采集方式。例如，如果我们使用vr或者全身外骨骼或动作捕捉系统，一方面这种做法非常贵，另一方面它也没有办法很好的匹配现有互联网上数据。现在的第一步是先确保整个数据处理流程顺利运行，而不是立即依赖互联网上的数据进行学习。第二步才是考虑如何利用互联网上的数据进行进一步的学习。 mobile aloha是一个端到端的模型，它没有传统意义上的规划阶段，因为传统方法通常需要先制定一个详细的计划然后执行。我们现在采用的是端到端的方法，从感知直接到执行。规划其实相当于直接融合到了神经网络的权重里去了。我更倾向于选择端到端的路线，而不是分层具身路线。如果数据来源相同，就无需进行分层处理。唯一可能需要分层处理的是人类数据，因为其中一部分数据来自仿真环境，另一部分来自真实世界的机器人和人类数据。但这个和感知-规划-执行的分层也不一样，它更多的是一种数据利用的分层。 4：mimicplay和dexcap则是结合了人类视频和动捕数据训练机器人对话王辰：mimicplay & dexcap——如何利用人类视频和人体动捕数据进行机器人训练感兴趣的朋友可以看之前的几期内容。 references： https://humanoid-ai.github.io/ https://mobile-aloha.github.io/ robot data ep05: zipeng fu on humanplus and mobile aloha—from synthetic data to real data, and combining the two zipeng fu discusses how humanplus and mobile aloha use simulation, human motion and real-world teleoperation data to train robots. in the robot data series, we interview authors of representative research papers about data for training robots. among these projects, mobile aloha from chelsea finn's group at stanford has been one of the best-known contributions to imitation learning and teleoperation since 2023. the group released aloha and act in the first half of 2023, mobile aloha toward the end of that year, and humanplus in the first half of 2024. these projects, which use teleoperation to train robots, have attracted considerable attention from academia, industry and technology media. for the fifth episode of robot data, we are delighted to welcome zipeng fu, a first author of mobile aloha and humanplus, to discuss the data stories behind both projects. at the time of this interview, zipeng fu is a computer science phd student at the stanford artificial intelligence laboratory, advised by chelsea finn. he previously earned a master's degree at carnegie mellon's robotics institute, working with deepak pathak and jitendra malik. he completed his undergraduate studies in computer science and applied mathematics at ucla, where he was advised by song-chun zhu. his research lies at the intersection of robotics, machine learning and computer vision, with the aim of achieving robust robot performance and deployable robotic systems in unstructured, open environments. biographical note: fu's official biography specifies a master's degree in cmu's machine learning department and research work in its robotics institute. earlier in his research career, fu produced a number of impressive projects on quadruped locomotion. his recent work focuses on solving mobile manipulation through teleoperation and human video data. he is an unusually versatile researcher, working across simulation data, teleoperation data and human video, as well as across locomotion and manipulation. in this article, we use humanplus as a starting point to explore his insights into robot training and data. contents 1. from synthetic data to real data, and combining the two training quadrupeds with synthetic data mobile aloha: real-world teleoperation data humanplus: combining synthetic and teleoperation data 2. humanplus: making a humanoid move like a human's shadow where humanplus gets its data the humanplus architecture 3. questions and discussion what does it mean for a humanoid to shadow a person? comparing approaches to humanoid control realism in simulation what happens when the hardware changes? why use a single rgb camera? hierarchical versus end-to-end approaches 4. additional notes my own robotics research began with training quadruped robots. we used simulation software to generate large amounts of synthetic data and trained the robots through reinforcement learning. this approach works very well in certain settings: teaching a quadruped to walk, coordinating a robotic arm mounted on a quadruped, or teaching a quadruped parkour, for example. simulation can generate data at scale. with reinforcement learning, we can tell the robot to move forward, avoid collisions while doing so, and minimize effort and energy consumption; it can then learn these behaviors for itself. we do not need real-world data—or, in a sense, there is no suitable real-world data available—because i cannot train a whole pack of pet dogs to collect it. but combining simulation data with reinforcement learning also reaches a bottleneck. it is particularly good at movements such as locomotion—moving the limbs—or in-hand object reorientation. openai, for example, also used generated data to train a dexterous hand. when a task requires higher-level decisions and complex planning, however, the robot needs more visual information. current simulation software cannot provide this real-world visual information particularly well. it is better at supplying physical collisions and structured information, such as depth data. rendering realistic color information is comparatively difficult. with mobile aloha, we moved to a setting that uses no information from simulation software at all. the robot learns entirely from real-world data. people collect this data by teleoperating the robot in the real world, and we use efficient imitation learning to train it with a small dataset. this gives us better, more realistic visual signals, including rgb data and semantic information. one challenge is that collecting real-world data is slow. mobile aloha therefore combines its data collection system with an efficient imitation learning algorithm: roughly 50 human demonstrations per task can enable a robot to learn and perform a range of tasks. the system helps people collect data efficiently. compared with earlier tools such as vr devices, 3d mice and keyboards, it is both faster and easier to learn. a central contribution of mobile aloha is helping people quickly learn how to operate a robot so that they can address almost any problem they might encounter in the real world. experimental note: the reported mobile aloha results also use co-training with existing static aloha data; this is not a claim of general-purpose competence from 50 demonstrations in total. mobile aloha with humanplus, we tried to combine the strengths of synthetic data and robot teleoperation data. on one side, simulation gives us enormous quantities of data, but the quality is limited. on the other, real-world data is high-quality, but collection is slow and cannot reach the same scale. the main question behind humanplus is whether we can combine the advantages of both: collect high-quality data in the real world while also making use of large amounts of synthetic data. humanplus combines two sources of data: robot simulation data and human motion data. for the simulation component, we cannot simply copy human motion onto a robot. a robot's weight and joint structure differ from a person's, so direct copying can cause it to lose its balance and fall. at the lowest level of control, we therefore still use reinforcement learning in simulation to generate large amounts of data and train the robot. when the robot receives signals specifying human joint positions, it actively controls its movements to imitate those signals while accounting for its own physical constraints and maintaining balance. this is intended to let it imitate human motion while avoiding instability and falls. as for human motion data, there are not many robots in the real world, but there is a great deal of data about people. many videos, for instance, show people dancing or cooking. this data already exists in enormous quantities. we are thinking about how to use it well and transfer it effectively to humanoid robots. a major advantage of the humanoid form is its potential to use abundant human data. our work uses this data to give humanoids fine-grained control. in most cases, we need to imitate the human movements shown in a video. these videos are typically recordings of everyday life made with a camera placed nearby or worn on the person's head, such as an action camera. we focus on making good use of the data obtainable within the limitations of a single rgb camera. from its images, we capture skeletal signals, including joint data for the body, hands, arms and legs. these signals control the robot in real time so that it can perform different tasks. we also combine this with efficient imitation learning, similar to mobile aloha, so that the robot can perform tasks autonomously. it obtains visual information from an rgb camera on its head and acts on that information. it can now autonomously perform sequences of tasks: sit on a chair, put a shoe on its foot, tie the laces, stand up and walk. these capabilities come from training with human data. verification note: the project page documents putting on a shoe, standing up and walking. tying the laces is retained here as an interview claim and is not separately established by that page. by learning to imitate human video data, we can turn human movement patterns into robot control policies. it is rather like having a neural network control a person's movements, with the network's final outputs mapped directly onto a humanoid robot. because a humanoid resembles a person in its physical form, this mapping is relatively straightforward and intuitive. that allows us to use human data more effectively to train and control robots that perform human-like movements and tasks. method note: in the demonstrated autonomous-skill pipeline, human shadowing is used to collect robot demonstrations, and behavior cloning learns from those robot observations and actions. this is distinct from directly training an autonomous skill policy on arbitrary internet videos. the humanplus architecture has two parts. first, we train a humanoid shadowing transformer in simulation: reinforcement learning produces a low-level controller that lets the robot follow a person's movements like a shadow while respecting its own physical properties and keeping its balance, as shown on the left of the diagram. second, we train through imitation learning with human data using the humanoid imitation transformer, or hit. the low-level controller trained in the first stage is deployed zero-shot on a real humanoid for real-time shadowing. in the shadowing stage, a human operator stands near the humanoid and projects their whole-body movements onto it in real time, as if the robot were their shadow. the operator observes the environment and the robot's behavior directly, ensuring a responsive and flexible system for efficient teleoperation. the low-level controller takes humanoid proprioception and target poses as its inputs. proprioception includes the base state—roll, pitch and base angular velocity—as well as joint positions, joint velocities and the previous action. these observations come only from onboard sensors: an imu and joint encoders. target poses include desired forward and lateral velocities, roll and pitch, yaw velocity and joint angles. we use a single rgb camera to estimate body and hand poses in real time, then retarget the human pose to the humanoid's target pose. the controller outputs 19-dimensional body joint position setpoints, which are subsequently converted into torque signals. in the autonomous-skills stage, the robot learns human skills through imitation learning and performs the corresponding tasks independently. the humanoid imitation learning framework, hit, requires more than simple imitation: the robot must shadow human movement and also learn from its own observations to develop skills. it needs proprioceptive information and must process rgb images from its left and right eyes. its inputs are images from two egocentric rgb cameras, proprioception and fixed positional embeddings. its outputs are predicted target positions, which are sent to the low-level humanoid shadowing transformer; predicted future image-feature tokens are discarded. in effect, it learns to produce the inputs for the low-level controller shown on the left—that is, the target poses we want the robot to reach. making a humanoid shadow a person's movements is not merely a matter of matching them in zero gravity. without gravity, the robot does not need to learn how to cope with it. a robot floating in space, for instance, can move freely without gravitational constraints and can more easily match human movements. on the ground, gravity is a challenge. a person can stand on one leg, but a robot trying to copy that pose may lose its balance or fall. speaking about the hardware landscape at the time of this july 2024 interview, at present, most robots on the market can only perform basic forward and backward walking, and some even struggle to stand. they lack a diverse movement repertoire: they cannot move their arms like a person or crouch to pick up an object near the ground. most existing robots cannot perform these actions. one feature of humanplus is that its upper and lower limbs are trained through the same neural network, giving it good coordination. however realistic an object in simulation looks, the human eye can generally tell whether it is real or synthetic. neural networks can usually detect the differences that people can see, too. they are particularly good at noticing subtle distinctions, even very small details. current simulators may handle variations in color and weight, but simulating softness, deformation and complex visual scenes becomes difficult. although the training process is similar, changing humanoid hardware requires retraining the algorithm. different robots have different limb lengths and weights, which affect their motion control and balance. the idea is to use a single camera to better match the way existing videos are recorded. vr equipment, full-body exoskeletons and motion capture systems are expensive, and they also do not match existing internet data particularly well. our first step is to make sure the entire data processing pipeline works smoothly, rather than immediately relying on internet data for learning. the second step is to consider how to use internet data for further learning. mobile aloha is an end-to-end model. it has no planning stage in the traditional sense, where a detailed plan is created and then executed. our approach goes directly from perception to action. planning is effectively integrated into the neural network's weights. i prefer the end-to-end route to a hierarchical approach to embodied intelligence. if the data comes from the same source, there is no need to divide the system into layers. human data is the one case where a hierarchy may be useful, because some data comes from simulation and some comes from real-world robots and people. but this is different from separating perception, planning and execution: it is more a hierarchy for making use of different data sources. the authors of humanplus: humanoid shadowing and imitation from humans are zipeng fu, qingqing zhao, qi wu, gordon wetzstein and chelsea finn. zipeng fu, qingqing zhao and qi wu are joint first authors. the authors of mobile aloha: learning bimanual mobile manipulation with low-cost whole-body teleoperation are zipeng fu, tony z. zhao and chelsea finn; zipeng fu and tony z. zhao are joint
