produce remarkable results. robotics is also becoming increasingly aware of the importance of data volume. whether you use reinforcement learning or imitation learning, enough data can produce very good performance. but there is a major problem: robot data is nowhere near as abundant as the text required by large language models. a robot foundation model may take observations of the environment, such as images, as input and output robot actions. these can be motor torques, changes in the coordinates of an arm's end effector, or rotation angles for individual motors—very fine-grained outputs. such data is difficult to obtain from the internet. how much robot data do prominent robotics papers currently use? at most, around 25,000 trajectories—far below the scale of language-model data. collecting it is difficult. it requires teleoperation devices such as gello or mobile aloha, motion capture gloves such as those in dexcap, or specialized approaches such as umi, which extracts control information using a gopro. omnih2o, for example, uses human keypoint detection to map human movements onto humanoids. their fundamental purpose is to record observations and actions together, then train an imitation learning model to control the robot. data-scale correction: the original interview gives 25,000 as a maximum, but this is not a global upper bound for robot datasets. larger datasets such as open x-embodiment already existed; the figure should not be used as a comprehensive dataset census. but why must we use complex teleoperation systems to obtain imitation learning data? human videos are an important and abundant source. youtube or douyin videos contain rich information about physics and behavior, making them valuable prior knowledge. we cannot yet use them effectively because they usually lack action labels and cannot directly support imitation learning. even when labels exist, different groups define and collect them differently. one may describe actions as end-effector displacement, another as rotation of each joint. inconsistent labels are also difficult to use for imitation learning. atm studies how to extract useful experience from video. many methods now pretrain on video, extracting knowledge in different ways from large datasets. one major approach is video prediction. a model trained on large-scale video receives a robot arm's current observation, such as an image, and predicts its future movement and changes to the object being manipulated. this provides a prediction of what happens next. learning those intermediate movements and changes makes it easier for the robot to acquire practical manipulation skills. if a generative model such as sora could provide perfect video generation, we could use it directly in robotics. for example, i give it the current image and specify that in the next image my arm moves a certain number of centimeters to the left. if it can predict the future correctly, very little data is needed to determine the action that moves the robot from the current state to the next. that simplifies the problem. the difficulty is that video prediction models are very hard to build. suppose an image calls for picking up an ear of corn, but the prediction shows only half of it being lifted. that is physically incorrect. sora's videos look beautiful, but some physical details are wrong. in one example, puppies are playing in the snow and an extra dog's head suddenly appears. training such models requires enormous data and compute. sora, for instance, might require thousands of gpus running for a month, which is impractical for a robotics task. the gpu count and duration here are an illustrative estimate from the interview, not a verified disclosure of sora's training compute. the main idea behind atm is that we do not want to predict video images. what future frames look like is not what matters for robot control. we only need to know how objects move, rather than how beautiful the image is. we care about motion. we took inspiration from earlier ways of modeling movement. in games and simulation engines, an object may be represented as many particles, with the scene modeled through collisions, compression and relative movement between them. this is especially effective for fluids, deformable objects and sand. if pixel-level video modeling is not a good representation, could we borrow that idea and turn a video into a collection of particles? modeling each particle's movement could capture the scene's physical regularities and support a control model. consider an arm picking up a bag and placing it on a table. a conventional representation models pixels changing over time, with values between 0 and 255. instead, we can model how individual points move. we select points on the bag and on the arm, then track their coordinates through the video. over time, the bag's points and the arm's points move differently, while points on the same object follow similar movement patterns. how did you arrive at this approach? i have been working on extracting control signals from video. after extensive thought and experimentation, we found that changes in pixels, lighting and texture are irrelevant to the arm's control task. we care about how objects move in space. the best approach is to explicitly separate motion from other visual information, such as color and texture. this is somewhat like a simulation engine: first model movement, then render color and texture. we do not need the rendering step, though. knowing the motion is enough to control the arm. we focus only on the moving component of video. we break it down into coordinate changes, ignoring color changes. existing computer vision tracking models can recover how those points change over time. in 2023, these models were already performing very well, with tracking errors below one pixel. we can use their outputs directly as training labels. the subpixel-error statement describes the performance being cited, not a guarantee for every point in an arbitrary video. our representation has several advantages. first, it respects physical continuity rather than producing implausible video events such as objects suddenly appearing or disappearing. every object's movement in our data is continuous, so the learned motion model naturally has that continuity, and the generated motion data remains continuous as well. another advantage is explicitly separating motion from lighting and texture. we focus on movement without interference from those other factors. technical note: point trajectories encourage object permanence and continuous motion, but the representation alone does not guarantee physically correct predictions or eliminate tracking and prediction errors. this diagram shows our architecture. video data enters at the upper left. a tracking model extracts the future trajectory of each point in each frame. the red, blue and green points indicate their trajectories across the video. with these trajectories, we train what we call a track transformer, a multimodal transformer model. it takes the current image, a language description and the coordinates of query points as input, and learns to predict those points' future trajectories. the track transformer's purpose is simple. give it the instruction to open a drawer and a current image showing that the arm has grasped the handle and pulled it halfway. it predicts that points on the arm should continue moving right, and points on the drawer should move right with them. the function is simple but effective. the predicted trajectories are supplied to our control model. instead of taking only an image and producing an action, as earlier policies did, the control model receives both the image and predicted tracks. this additional input makes control more accurate and effective. atm's perception module is a vit operating on 2d images; we do not use 3d perception here. 3d perception is important, but it need not take the form of a point cloud. with two cameras, for example, a model can learn three-dimensional information from the images. point-cloud approaches often perform less well in practice. a simulated point cloud may be perfect, but real depth cameras frequently produce missing or incomplete points, which hurts model performance. high-quality point clouds require more expensive capture hardware, such as lidar. our group has a project with a similar idea but 3d inputs, called general flow as foundation affordance for scalable robot learning. once we know a point's 3d coordinates, we can predict its future trajectory. opening a safe door, for example, can be learned through these future point tracks, and the same applies to new objects. one advantage of 3d points is that they allow direct zero-shot generalization. zero-shot generalization means we do not need extra training examples to train a new control model. we already know the end effector's movement in 3d and can predict its future path. solving the arm's kinematic equations gives the movement of each joint. this is more efficient and can work well in unseen settings. avoiding additional data for a new model improves both generalization and efficiency. atm primarily addresses planning, but unlike a typical planner, it operates at an intermediate rather than a very high level. i usually distinguish high-, middle- and low-level planning. vila is an example of high-level planning; see yang gao on the vila and copa embodied model framework. atm is middle-level planning. diffusion policy is an example of low-level planning; see diffusion policy: robot action generation with diffusion models. we tested on 130 language-conditioned simulation tasks, a larger evaluation than in many papers. atm is a multitask model: we did not train 130 separate models, which would defeat the point. we used five models: four handled ten tasks each, and the fifth handled ninety. a multitask model needs clear instructions for each task. language was commonly used before, but it is too coarse. our innovation uses trajectories to specify the task explicitly, making the problem more concrete and precise. for the real-robot experiments, we built a system in an actual environment. within the same setting, i described five different tasks with five language instructions, and the robot needed to complete all five. complex tasks still need more data. human video provides prior knowledge about the broad steps and movements involved. but mapping that knowledge into a robot arm's action space requires additional methods and data. our subsequent ideas include learning from human data and ultimately deploying on a robot. the final training step uses teleoperation, requiring only a very small amount of robot data. atm performs well on cloth manipulation atm also performs well on long-horizon manipulation atm can also reason about tool use our paper suggests that third-person views may be more useful. in first-person footage, such as videos of extreme sports filmed with a head-mounted gopro, the person's head moves involuntarily. this introduces substantial noise. much of that head movement is random and contributes little to robot control. third-person views may therefore be more important, and they also account for the largest share of human video online. another important point is that we support multiple views. we can produce good trajectory predictions from third-person videos, including reasonable predictions when the camera is mounted outside the robot arm. other representative approaches to learning from human video before our work, there were two main approaches. the first directly predicts video. unipi, from pieter abbeel's group at berkeley, is a representative example. given an initial frame and a task such as pouring water, it predicts how the video will change during the task. an inverse dynamics model then infers the arm's actions from those predicted frames. this is very end-to-end: videos train a video predictor, whose outputs train the model that recovers robot actions. it can use large amounts of data, but it is computationally expensive. generating a three- to five-second video may take ten or twenty minutes, half an hour or even longer. attribution note: unipi is a collaboration involving google research and academic researchers, including sherry yang and yilun du; it is not solely a berkeley lab project. the generation times cited above describe the interview's comparison and depend on implementation and hardware. the other approach is closer to ours: extract an intermediate representation of the action. we use keypoint trajectories. another family extracts the contact point on an object and its instantaneous movement direction. to open a drawer, for example, it identifies where to grasp the handle and that the drawer should be pulled outward along its surface normal. it simplifies motion into a contact point and direction. this is compact and concise, but cannot handle tasks that depend on the entire movement process, such as pouring water or folding a towel, where the required rotation and direction vary along the trajectory. it is better suited to articulated objects such as refrigerator doors and drawers, where you grasp a handle and pull in one direction. some work from deepak pathak's group at cmu represents this approach. what do you mean by a task that does not depend on the movement process? a simple example is warehouse sorting: grasp an object in one location and place it in another. work such as graspnet cares about the grasp location and target pose but does not specify how to reach that pose, assuming a conventional motion planner can handle the path. pouring water is different. you must hold the water and gradually tilt it at the cup's opening in appropriate directions. an ordinary motion planner might spill it. is atm fundamentally a form of imitation learning? it can be understood as imitation learning across embodiments, because human and robot bodies differ. fundamentally, it still learns to imitate human actions so that objects follow particular motion trajectories. but because of those physical differences, a model trained on human data still needs a small amount of robot teleoperation data before deployment to bridge the domain gap. how can 3d trajectories be extracted from 2d human videos? some neural networks estimate depth from rgb images, and this technology has been developing quickly. we can use it to add 3d labels to rgb videos and then extract 3d trajectories from that data. thank you to yang gao and chuan wen for taking the time to explain the paper, and to all the researchers and entrepreneurs i have previously interviewed or spoken with. these conversations have gradually shaped my understanding. i have worked in venture capital for eight years. from the beginning until now, my growth has been improvised and uneven, and my outlook has changed considerably. compared with entrepreneurs who enter the currents of their time and bravely take on risk and responsibility, most of us called investors are simply workers filtering, selecting, connecting, integrating and communicating information. whether a deal closes, a company succeeds or a fund makes money depends on many combinations of chance circumstances. so many external factors are involved. can we control the outcome? probably not. then why be anxious about it? at this moment, perhaps these words are the one thing i can control. stay humble, keep learning and move on. references

space），并用自回归预测下一个token，rfm-1利用其广泛的输入和输出模态来实现多样化的应用。例如，它可以执行图像到图像的学习，用于场景分析任务，如分割和识别。它可以将文本指令与图像观察结合起来，生成所需的抓取动作或运动序列。它可以将场景图像与目标抓取图像配对，以预测视频的结果或模拟沿途可能发生的数值传感器读数。关于any to any特性，我们在下文的专访中会特别解释。 any to any介绍（来源：covariant官网） 2. 陈曦（peter chen）个人简介 陈曦（peter chen）是covariant.ai的首席执行官兼联合创始人。covariant是一家领先的ai机器人初创公司，已经融资超过2亿美元。covariant正在构建用于机器人学的基础模型，使机器人可以对物理环境进行识别、推理和操作。在创办covariant之前，陈曦（peter chen）曾是openai的研究科学家，也是加州大学伯克利分校人工智能研究实验室（bair lab）的研究员，他专注于强化学习、元学习和无监督学习。他在领先的学术期刊上发表了30多篇论文，引用超过2万次。 2. 解密rfm-1 机器人基础模型是我们创立covariant时的一个核心想法。我们四位创始人中有三位来自openai，包括我自己、cto rocky duan和首席科学家pieter abbeel。我们创立covariant的一个主要原因是意识到要在机器人领域实现通用型智能，必须在现实世界中收集数据。因此，covariant从一开始就努力将真实的机器人部署到客户现场，并在实际环境中大规模收集数据。因此，从数据收集的角度来看，rfm-1的概念可以追溯到公司成立之初的思路。 谈到具体的模型框架transformer，以及any to any的multi-model model，这是我们过去一年多来的尝试。随着llm和多模态大模型的发展，我们最初的愿景变得更加可能。因此，rfm-1是我们六年来一直梦寐以求的东西，只是最近一年我们确定了使用何种模型框架和方法来具体实现这一想法。 这个问题的答案取决于对"chatgpt时刻"的定义。如果我们指的是在接下来机器人领域是否会有迅速的发展，那答案肯定是肯定的。另外，如果我们考虑到机器人的进步是否会借鉴和采用像chatgpt这样的技术和方法，我认为答案也是肯定的。 但是，如果问现阶段机器人智能是否已经像chatgpt那样通用，我认为还没有达到这个水平。不过，这种情况很快就会改变。 对于机器人大模型领域的竞争，我认为pi（physical intelligence，文章开头提过）的成立是一件令人激动的事情。机器人市场的潜力是非常巨大的，机器人大模型可以在数十亿级别的规模上应用，即有数十亿台机器人由机器人基础模型驱动。在这样庞大的市场中，有更多具备能力的公司在这个领域取得成功对所有人都是件好事。 然而，就目前而言，covariant拥有明显的领先优势。多场景和多硬件的适配能力对任何机器人大模型来说都是必不可少的。在covariant的实践中，我们已经积累了丰富的多硬件适配经验。举例来说，chelsea finn等人在离开google之前创建了一个名为openx的数据集（对应rtx项目的数据集），他们联合了全球20多个不同的机器人实验室，收集了大约一百万条数据，这些数据来自于22种不同的机器人硬件。而在实际的生产环境中，covariant已经部署了超过30种不同类型的机器人，这意味着我们一家的机器人种类已经超过了openx整个数据集中包含的机器人种类。 因此，对于rfm-1模型而言，它的训练数据不仅局限于一种硬件和一种场景。要想打造出真正优秀的机器人基础模型，它必须在不同的硬件、不同的任务和场景中适配，因此训练数据集也必须包含不同的硬件和场景。 简单来说，你可以将rfm-1视为一个大型语言模型，但它不仅仅预测语言的token。在rfm-1中，token不仅来自文本，还包括机器人的动作、传感器数据、图片、视频等多种模态。针对这些不同的模态，有相应的tokenizer将它们全部转换成token。最终，rfm-1实际上就是一个大型语言模型，但它的输入和输出预测不仅限于人类语言这一模态。这是对rfm-1在输入和输出预测方面的最简单理解。 rfm-1之所以如此强大的原因之一就在于any to any。传统的ai机器人通常是以图像作为输入，输出动作，或者以三维数据作为输入，输出动作，但这些模型存在着很大的局限性。rfm-1的一个重大突破是，它可以作为一个世界模型，预测未来会发生什么。对于这个模型来说，它最终都在进行下一个token的预测，而预测下一个动作、图像或视频只是不同的token而已。只要给出适当的提示，告诉它想要做什么，它就可以进行相关的预测。这也是rfm-1如此强大的原因之一，我们可以让它学习世界模型，从而理解物理世界，并基于这个理解做出更好的机器人动作。它对于物理世界的理解还可以用作模拟器，在模拟器中可以避免一些不良动作，进行规划，类似于alpha-go的规划方式。 你可以将rfm-1视为一个非常通用的模型，与传统的ai机器人模型不同，它不是单一用途的，因此我们引入了any to any的概念，因为有太多的可能性。如果是文本到文本，那就是传统的语言模型。如果是图像到机器人动作，那就比较容易理解，这是一种机器人策略。如果是文本到图像到策略，那就是人类通过语言与机器人沟通，机器人根据语言任务拆解和相关任务图像执行动作。甚至可以基于当前图像，告诉它目标图像，然后输出动作。any to any的核心意思是它可以适应各种输入模态和输出模态。 但确实，any to any是一个比较抽象的概念，因此我们在博客中提供了一些具体的例子来解释，而当我们将rfm-1实际应用到客户中时，我们将继续发布一些功能，让大家对any to any有更直观的理解！ rfm-1调用其他第三方语言模型吗 没有调用任何第三方的api，rfm-1它本身就是一个可以理解文本的多模态大模型，它也可以给出语言的反馈。甚至可以把它仅仅当成一个大语言模型来用，当然肯定没有chatgpt那么好用，因为很多参数要分散在理解机器人的事情上面。 作为机器人大模型，rfm-1不仅仅满足于输出动作，而是输出“any”多个模态，这是为了增强其通用性。 如果我们仅仅将rfm-1视为一个策略（policy），那它实际上是将不同的输入映射到动作上，例如给予自然语言指令、目标，甚至是一个展示某项任务的视频，让机器人学习并执行。作为通用模型，它应该能够理解视频中发生的事情，并且能够复现这些情景。没错，它的输出本质上都是动作，从这个角度来看，它并没有什么特别之处。 但如果我希望这个模型能够更好地理解视频，甚至学习到世界模型，一个非常好的方法就是给它视频的前半段，然后让它预测视频的后半段会发生什么。这就是所谓的“视频输入和视频输出”。只要进行大量的这种训练，这个模型将会具有对视频和物理世界更深入的理解，这个理解也可以在执行动作时加以利用。另外一个用途是将这种世界模型作为模拟器来使用。 rfm-1使用了互联网数据和covariant部署在全世界客户场景中的真实机器人数据。互联网的数据能够为模型提供文本或图片的常识性理解，但对于一个世界模型来说，互联网上的数据通常是不够的。因为互联网上的数据往往缺乏动作信息。例如，假设你观看一些公开的视频，通常视频中并没有包含动作信息，无论是人类行为还是机器人操作，你只是被动地观察，而不知道其中的具体动作。在这方面，真实的机器人数据起到了至关重要的作用，因为它包含了大量的机器人动作和结果的信息。在互联网上，你无法获取到这种关于动作的具体信息，因为互联网上的数据只提供了时间上的前后状态，而无法捕获其中的动作细节。 举例来说，尽管你可以通过观察一个人拿起物体来猜测他正在进行这个动作，但你无法知道他用了多大的力量、手指放在了什么位置、以及具体是如何抓取物体的。这些细节数据在互联网上是无法获取的。 因此，尽管互联网数据可以用于训练视频、图片或文本生成模型，但要学习一个完整的世界模型却非常困难，因为缺乏动作信息。covariant部署的机器人硬件提供了大量的传感器和关节数据，可用于模型训练。此外，我们还可以根据需要改变数据收集方式，因为我们可以控制硬件。例如，如果发现某种数据模态更有用，我们可以更新已有的机器人以收集相应的数据。 rfm-1和figure01的路径 背景信息：figure 01路径涉及接入像gpt4v这样的视觉语言模型，然后在此基础上添加机器人动作模型；而rfm-1是一个更加端到端的模型，直接将多模态输入映射到输出动作。 我认为最终的关键在于，无论采用何种技术路线，只要能够实现落地并产生效益，就是一条好路线。无论朝任何方向前进，都有可能取得成功。最终，机器人的成功与否取决于它是否能够在生产环境中为客户带来效益，并且该技术是否可扩展，能否在多个场景下成功推广。 对基于多模态大模型（比如gpt4v或gemini）接动作模型的路线，你会发现它们在进行demo时毫无问题，但是，要使机器人从实验室的demo变为可以在生产环境中使用的，其最大的差别在于稳定性和性能。就目前而言，市场上最优秀的多模态大模型gpt4v，其推理成本非常高，而且在可靠性方面存在问题。举个例子，在相对密集的场景中，比如将十个苹果放在一个篮子里或将3、4件衣服揉在一起，然后询问gpt4v统计图片中的物品数量，测试结果显示其成功率并不高。如果依赖gpt4v的上层决策出现错误，那么后续的底层控制将无法实现所需的稳定性。 首先，我们自身正在快速扩展规模，不仅仅是通过获取新客户，而且是通过我们已有客户的订单量增长。如果我们能够处理所有这些订单，我们的数据收集速度将提高一个数量级以上。 另一方面，随着rfm -1的成熟，我们计划将其开放给其他机器人公司，类似于openai的gpt api模式。通过向更多人开放这一模型，我们将能够加速数据收集的速度。 covariant将在不久的将来推出面向公众的rfm-1机器人大模型 api，传统机器人或新创公司都适用。在llm领域，当我想要进行自然语言处理时，我不会自己训练一个独立的模型，而是会使用openai的api。我可能对它进行prompting、fine-tuning，或者进行retrieval和generation，然后基于这些构建我的新自然语言处理应用程序。 对covariant来说，我们希望为未来数以百万计、数以千万计、数以亿计甚至数十亿的机器人提供大脑，它不仅仅是单一机器人应用，也不仅仅是硬件。未来将会有大量的机器人开发者和机器人公司，接我们的api，我们希望成为他们的gpt平台。他们可以依赖我们来解决大部分困难且数据密集的智能问题，但这并不意味着他们不需要做其他工作。他们仍然需要进行硬件开发、人机交互设计，并准确把握场景，我们希望能够为他们提供支持。 rfm-1是真正意义上的世界模型。sora具备成为世界模型的潜力，但它目前还不是，因为它没有动作数据。如果sora模型只是在游戏引擎中训练，而没有真实世界的视频数据，那么它学到的物理模型将会存在偏差，因为游戏引擎生成的视频中的物理规律通常与现实世界不一致。 如果sora只是在youtube上训练，而且只用了真实视频作为全部训练集，那它应该能够理解一部分物理世界的运行规律。但sora缺少的是什么？sora缺少的是中间的关键概念，即它没有对动作进行理解，它只是拥有一些视频，然后我用gpt为它生成了一个长长的说明，但实际上我无法指出视频中的具体行为者。 比如我们看到他用拳头砸向墙壁，但我们无法确定施加了多大的力。无论是他的拳头受伤了，还是墙壁被砸坏了，他只能描述事件的发生过程。他只能说拳头碰到了墙壁，然后墙壁坏了，但实际上他并不了解内在的动作过程。因此，sora虽然具备成为世界模型的能力，但它缺乏对动作的理解，这使得它很难学习到动作结果的因果关系，尽管它应该能够学到很多相关信息，但这些信息可能不够准确。 大模型在所有领域都一样的，就它最终应该只会有几家跑赢出来。因此，如果你觉得自己无法成为那几家大模型赢家之一，不论是在机器人领域还是其他领域，那就应该考虑去做应用层或工具链相关的事情，这方面是现在是投身到机器人非常好的时间。 随着机器学习大模型的迅速成熟，这个领域的发展速度也会加快。无论其他人的进展如何，在我们这里可以看到机器人大模型的进展非常非常快。另外，硬件技术的成熟速度都会非常快，例如，像figure这样的公司获得的投资以及国内对人形机器人、移动机器人和机械臂的投资都在增加，这也将促进硬件技术的发展。随着越来越多的产品推出和公关活动的开展，公众对机器人的接受度也将迅速提高。因此，现在是一个非常好的时代来从事机器人应用的开发，以及是在构建基础设施方面。将注意力放在这些领域都是非常明智的选择。 现在这个时间点，可能最值得关注的还是机器人大模型和工具链基础设施，但我觉得这种情况可能会在一年内迅速改变，一年之后可能会是机器人领域有很多机会的时间。 但从另外一个角度，如果现在能够投资一家应用型公司，并且相信他们能够度过最初一到两年的学习阶段，那可能是值得考虑的。因为我们可以看到，像language space这样的应用层面公司，比如character.ai和perplexity，他们在做应用层的时候都是在chatgpt推出之前。那个时候，底层的基础模型尚未完全成熟，他们快速迭代所，并获得了怎么基于不断演进的基础模型做应用的经验，使得他们可以很快跑出来。所以，如果我们能够放宽视野，从今年开始进行试错和学习，我认为并不会太早。但如果团队不能迅速取得商业上的成就，那可能会面临融资困难。不过，如果团队和市场都足够好，我认为从今年开始进行应用层面的尝试也是可行的。 经验的关键：机器人必须在真实世界中进行学习，它们必须与人类相互作用的无限范围的物体进行互动，并执行人类执行的无限数量的任务。 架构的关键：真实世界的数据比实验室的数据要多样性更高，我们需要建立根本性的新架构，以从这样的数据中进行学习。 因此，在2018年初，我们开始了一段旅程，让机器人接触真实世界，并研究能够吸纳这些经验的新型人工智能架构（远比典型实验室经验更丰富）。” references： modeling. source: covariant’s website. at the time of this march 2024 interview, peter chen was ceo and co-founder of covariant.ai, a leading ai robotics startup that had raised more than $200 million. covariant was building foundation models for robotics, enabling robots to perceive, reason about and manipulate their physical environment. before founding covariant, chen was a research scientist at openai and a researcher at uc berkeley’s bair lab, focusing on reinforcement learning, meta-learning and unsupervised learning. he had published more than 30 papers in leading academic venues, with over 20,000 citations. a robot foundation model was one of the central ideas behind founding covariant. three of our four co-founders came from openai: myself, our cto rocky duan and our chief scientist pieter abbeel. one of the main reasons we started the company was our realization that general-purpose intelligence in robotics requires collecting data in the real world. from the beginning, covariant therefore worked to deploy real robots at customer sites and collect data at scale in actual operating environments. from a data-collection perspective, the idea behind rfm-1 goes all the way back to our original thinking when we founded the company. the specific architecture—a transformer-based, any-to-any multimodal model—is something we have explored over the past year or so. as large language models and multimodal foundation models advanced, our original vision became increasingly achievable. rfm-1 is what we have been dreaming about for six years; it was only during the past year that we settled on the architecture and methods to make it concrete. that depends on how you define a chatgpt moment. if you mean whether robotics will develop rapidly in the coming period, the answer is definitely yes. if you mean whether progress in robotics will draw on and adopt technologies and methods like those behind chatgpt, i also think the answer is yes. but if you are asking whether robot intelligence today is already as general-purpose as chatgpt, i do not think we have reached that point. that situation will change quickly, though. i think the founding of physical intelligence, or pi, which you mentioned earlier, is exciting. the potential robotics market is enormous. robot foundation models could operate at a scale of billions: billions of robots powered by these models. in a market that large, it is good for everyone to have more capable companies succeed in the field. at this stage, however, covariant has a clear lead. the ability to adapt across settings and hardware is essential for any robot foundation model, and we have accumulated extensive experience doing that. for example, before leaving google, chelsea finn and others created open x-embodiment, the dataset associated with the rt-x project. they brought together more than 20 robotics laboratories around the world and collected roughly one million trajectories from 22 different robot embodiments. in actual production environments, covariant has already deployed more than 30 different types of robot. in other words, the range of robots deployed by our company alone exceeds the range represented across that entire dataset. rfm-1’s training data is therefore not restricted to one kind of hardware or one setting. a truly excellent robot foundation model needs to work across different hardware, tasks and environments, so its training dataset must also cover different hardware and settings. in simple terms, you can think of rfm-1 as a large language model, except it does not predict only language tokens. its tokens also represent robot actions, sensor data, images, video and other modalities. each modality has a corresponding tokenizer that converts it into tokens. ultimately, the model works much like an llm, but its inputs and predicted outputs are not limited to human language. that is the simplest way to understand its input and output structure. any-to-any is one of the reasons rfm-1 is so powerful. traditional ai robotics models usually take images as input and produce actions, or take 3d data as input and produce actions. those models have substantial limitations. a major advance with rfm-1 is that it can act as a world model and predict what will happen next. ultimately, everything it does is next-token prediction: the next action, image or video simply corresponds to a different kind of token. given the right prompt telling it what you want, it can make the corresponding prediction. we can train it to learn a world model, understand the physical world and use that understanding to produce better robot actions. its understanding of the physical world can also serve as a simulator, allowing us to avoid undesirable actions and plan within that simulator, in a way analogous to alphago’s planning. you can think of rfm-1 as a very general-purpose model. unlike conventional ai robotics models, it is not designed for a single use. we introduced the term any-to-any because there are so many possibilities. text-to-text is a conventional language model. image-to-robot-action is easier to grasp: that is a robot policy. text-to-image-to-policy means a person communicates with the robot through language, and the robot decomposes the language task and uses relevant task images to carry out the actions. you could even provide the current image and specify a target image, then have the model output actions. the essence of any-to-any is that it can accommodate different input and output modalities. it is admittedly an abstract concept, so we provided concrete examples in our blog to explain it. as we deploy rfm-1 with customers, we will keep releasing capabilities that make any-to-any easier to understand intuitively. it does not call any third-party apis. rfm-1 is itself a multimodal foundation model that understands text and can respond in language. you could even use it purely as a large language model. of course, it would not be as effective as chatgpt for that purpose, because much of its parameter capacity is devoted to understanding robotics. as a robot foundation model, rfm-1 is not satisfied with producing only actions. its ability to output multiple modalities—the any in any-to-any—is intended to make it more general-purpose. if we look at rfm-1 only as a policy, it maps different inputs to actions. you might give it a natural-language instruction, a goal, or even a video demonstrating a task, and ask the robot to learn and execute it. a general-purpose model should understand what happens in the video and be able to reproduce those situations. yes, its output is still actions. from that perspective, there is nothing especially unusual about it. but if i want the model to understand video better, or even learn a world model, a very effective approach is to give it the first half of a video and ask it to predict what happens in the second half. that is video input and video output. after extensive training of this kind, it develops a deeper understanding of video and the physical world, which it can also use when executing actions. another application is to use this world model as a simulator. rfm-1 uses internet data and real robot data from covariant deployments at customer sites around the world. internet data provides common-sense understanding of text and images, but it is generally insufficient for a world model because it tends to lack action information. when you watch publicly available videos, for example, the underlying action information is usually missing. whether the video shows human behavior or a robot operating, you are observing passively without knowing the specific actions involved. real robot data is crucial because it contains extensive information about robot actions and their outcomes. you cannot obtain that detailed action information from internet data, which shows states before and after an event but does not capture the action details in between. here, “action information” means recorded robot control commands and physical sensor quantities, not the absence of visibly observable movement in video. for example, watching someone pick up an object lets you infer that they are doing so, but it does not tell you how much force they applied, where their fingers were placed, or exactly how they grasped it. those details are not available in ordinary internet data. internet data can therefore train video, image and text generation models, but learning a complete world model from it is difficult because action information is missing. covariant’s deployed robot hardware provides large amounts of sensor and joint data for training. we can also change how we collect data when necessary, because we control the hardware. if we discover that a particular modality is more useful, for example, we can update the robots already deployed to collect it. background: the figure 01 approach connects a vision-language model such as gpt-4v to a robot action model. rfm-1 takes a more end-to-end approach, directly mapping multimodal inputs to action outputs. ultimately, i think the key is that any technical approach is a good one if it can be deployed and deliver value. success is possible in different directions. a robot’s success ultimately depends on whether it benefits customers in production environments and whether the technology can scale across multiple settings. with approaches that connect multimodal foundation models such as gpt-4v or gemini to action models, clothing together, and ask gpt-4v to count the objects in the image. our tests show that its success rate is not very high. if the higher-level decision made by gpt-4v is wrong, subsequent low-level 人类对世界的感知有六个维度，眼耳鼻舌身意，对应视觉、听觉、嗅觉、味觉、触觉、意识。我们假设机器人进化的终极能量来源还是电力，而不是食物，那么味觉和嗅觉对机器人来说似乎没什么用。剩下四个维度，视觉、听觉、触觉和意识在机器人领域的进展分别是什么样子？ 视觉，硬件以摄像头为主，融合激光雷达等传感器，过去几年自动驾驶和服务机器人的发展让视觉算法有很大发展；听觉，硬件以手机和智能音箱听筒和麦克风器件为主，近些年语音识别的算法也相对成熟；意识，chatgpt的出现让人们相信，也许ai很快会拥有自我意识。那么触觉呢，相比之下，不管是硬件还是算法目前都非常不成熟。 尽管近些年，学术界也有很多paper证明，加入触觉感知，机器人操作物体的准确性可以提高，但触觉感知依然没有完美的方案，甚至到目前为止都没有成熟的硬件平台。在和一些做操作相关的老师交流时，常常听到视触觉传感器，尤其是gelsight。这篇文章以gelsight学术进展为时间轴，呈现从提出到后面每个时期的关键进展。我们展示了大量的视频，以期用最直观的方式呈现什么是视触觉传感器以及它能做到什么。 触觉传感器模仿生物的皮肤触觉，检测外部物理环境引起的刺激。常见的触觉传感器类型包括压阻式、压电式、光学式、电容式、电磁式和视触觉传感器。我们今天这篇文章探讨的gelsight是视触觉传感器的典型代表，所谓视触觉传感器就是基于视觉的触觉传感器（vision-based tactile sensor，vbts）。 人类在操作物体的时候，手部的触觉信息包含两个维度：物体本身的状态和接触的状态；其中物体本身的状态信息包含表面纹理、物体形状、软硬度；接触状态信息包含法向力（垂直人手皮肤）、剪切力（平行人手皮肤）、相对滑动和物体的位姿。对上述触觉信息，大多数触觉传感器比如压阻式、压电式、电容式和电磁式大都只能感受法向力，而对其他信息无法采集或灵敏度很低。vbts和其他触觉方案相比，最大的优点就是可以高灵敏地感知上述全部信息，非常接近人手的触觉信息维度。 2. gelsight简介 基于荧光点的视触觉传感器早在2004年就由东京大学团队提出过（gelforce），但分辨率不高。gelsight是第一个超高分辨率的视触觉传感器，它于2009年由mit计算机科学与人工智能实验室（csail）的edward howard adelson（简称edward adelson）研究小组提出。gelsight是由“gel”和“sight”组成，gel（凝胶）是传感器弹性接触表面使用的材料；sight（视觉），传感机制是使用摄像头采集视觉图像。在gelsight触觉传感器接触物体时，内置的摄像头在led灯光的辅助下捕捉接触物体的凝胶产生的形变，通过计算机视觉的算法将凝胶形变信息与触觉信息进行映射。 gelsight触觉传感器结构 （gelsight 2017论文） 从2009年提出至今，edward adelson的小组经历了几代人持续十几年的努力，将视触传感器推到了机器人触觉感知领域的最前沿，获得了全球顶尖高校和科研机构的认可和跟随，ai机器人领域的顶级高校mit、stanford、cmu、ucb、uiuc、eth、牛津、清华、北大、上交、港科大、中科院等高校以及meta、tri（丰田）等大企业都推出过基于gelsight的各项工作。近些年，基于gelsight的论文也常常获得机器人领域顶会rss、icra、iros的best paper。接下来就让我们进入gelsight的历史长河，回顾它从诞生至今15年所经历的重要时刻。 3. gelsight科研时间轴 gelsight提出——gelsight @ mit 2009 提到gelsight视触觉传感器，就绕不开他的发明人mit教授edward adelson。edward adelson是一位美国神经科学家，目前是麻省理工学院john and dorothy wilson视觉科学教授，同时也美国国家科学院和美国艺术与科学学院的两院院士。他近些年的研究重点是机器人的人工触觉感知，他于2009年在cvpr首次提出gelsight视触觉感知技术（micah johnson and edward adelson, 2009）。 edward adelson 2009年的工作最初只是用于物体表面微观结构的观测，和机器人的触觉感知并没有关系。2009年的gelsight传感器由透明弹性体（一种凝胶状材料）和涂有颜色的外皮组成，可以测量触碰其表面的物体的纹理和几何形状。从背后观察，被按压到传感器上的物体呈现为一个具有均匀反射度的阴影表面。这些特性允许对物体表面进行三维重建。 gelsight 2009 #机器人触觉 #视触觉传感器（请在微信公众号原文观看） source：micah johnson et al. 2009 gelsight @ mit 2011 在2011年siggraph，edward adelson和团队对gelsight做了进一步优化，提出了一个用于捕捉微观表面几何的系统，将2009年的工作扩展到微观领域，展示了小至 2 微米的空间分辨率（micah johnson et al. and edward adelson, 2011）。该系统不受被测表面的光学特性的影响 - 无论物体是哑光的、光亮的还是透明的，它都能捕捉相同的几何形状。此外，硬件设计支持多种形式，包括手持设备，可用于在现场捕捉高分辨率表面几何。相较于 johnson 和 adelson 2009年提出的原始传感器，2011年的工作改进了传感器材料、照明设计和重建算法，也提出了在表面缺陷检测方面的应用可能。但至此，gelsight和机器人以及触觉依然没有什么关系。 gelsigh 2011 #机器人触觉 #视触觉 #gelsight（请在微信公众号原文观看） source：micah johnson et al. 2011 gelsight进化——gelsight @ mit 2013 在2013年的cvpr，edward adelson团队首次将gelsight与机器人触觉感知进行结合，构建了一个包含40个触觉纹理类别的数据库，使用了诸如织物、木材和砂纸等材料（rui li and edward adelson，2013）。这个系统可以正确分类来自该数据库的材料，表明 gelsight 传感器可以帮助机器人进行材料识别。 gelsight采集的40个物料材质图像 gelsight @mit 2014 在2014年iros，adelson团队首次提出了使用 gelsight触觉传感来进行机器人小零件的精确定位和操控（rui li et al. and edward adelson, 2014）。这也是全球第一个用于机器人的超高分辨率（10微米级别）指尖触觉传感器fingertip gelsight sensor，并首次将gelsight用于机器人插拔usb的任务，通过视觉和触觉结合实现类人的精细操作和闭环控制。至此，以gelsight为代表的视触觉用于机器人操作的学术研究正式拉开了帷幕。下图可以看到10年前第一款机器人指尖传感器的结构和外观设计和如今gelsight mini（后文会介绍）非常类似。 fingertip gelsight 这里值得一提的是，2009-2011年的gelsight设备比较大（最小的也有易拉罐大小）且不够实时，不适合用于机器人的操作。自2011年起，adelson团队将gelsight应用于机器人场景，在软硬件方面进行诸多改进，使得2014年提出的gelsight指尖触觉传感器同时具备小型化和超高分辨率的特性，且具备实时测量法向力、剪切力、相对滑动等能力。 带gelsight指尖传感器的baxter机器人插拔usb（source：rui li et al. 2014） 与基于压电、压阻、磁学等传统触觉传感器相比，gelsight指尖触觉传感器拥有超高分辨率、同时测量法向力和剪切力（很多操作需要剪切力）、软硬度测量（可用于抓取柔性物体），且不受环境磁场和温湿度影响。因此，用同一套gelsight软硬件，可以用于自适应抓取不同硬度、大小、形状的物体，如鸡蛋、薯片、草莓，甚至是树叶（见以下视频），可以根据多维力信息形成闭环控制，非常类似于人类操作物体的方式。这些性能对于通用机器人的通用和泛化操作显得尤为重要。 levine团队提出了omnitact，这是一种多方向高分辨率触觉传感器。omnitact使用多个摄像头，具有高分辨率和多方向的能力。下图左侧是gelsight 2017的指尖触觉传感器结构设计，右侧是omnitact触觉传感器的结构设计。 source：omnitact论文 9dtact @ 清华叉院 2023 9dtact是清华叉院许华哲团队提出的基于视觉的触觉传感器。在功能上，9dtact基于dtact的光学原理，并经过优化，以实现具有增强准确性和效率的3d形状重建。9dtact的硬件和软件均开源。 source：9dtact论文 insight @ max planck 2022 德国马普所提出了一种拇指大小的三维视触觉传感器，名为insight，它可以持续提供其整个圆锥形感知表面上的方向力分布图。该传感器围绕一个内部单目摄像头构建，只有一层弹性体覆盖在坚固的框架上。 source：insight论文 vitactip @ bristol 2023 vitactip是英国bristol大学nathan lepora团队的一款基于视觉的触觉传感器。vitactip上的嵌入式仿生尖端可以放大触摸运动。所得到的触觉图像在一个设备内提供了视觉和触觉信息的自然融合。该团队还开发了一种vitac传感器（没有仿生尖端）和一种tactip传感器（没有透明皮肤用于透明机制），用于进行比较研究。这里值得一提的是，nathan lepora的仿生触觉皮肤tactip对触觉的感知获得了很多大奖，但小编此时此刻脑袋有点转不动，关于bristol触觉感知的奥秘就留在以后的文章慢慢探索。 source：haoran li's website 6. vbts的机会与挑战 触觉作为人类与物理世界的重要感知系统，提供了独一无二的信息维度，甚至可以在没有视觉信息的情况下辅助人类生活（盲人）。以gelsight为代表的触觉传感在测量力的维度、物体的纹理和硬度以及分辨率等方面有非常强的优势，这也给于这类传感器很高的应用天花板。此外，因为gelsight的原理也是计算机视觉，采集的是图像信息，那么和机器人本身的视觉信息可以放到同一个模型中训练，真正做到视触融合的机器人操作控制。 但从未来广泛应用的角度，vbts依然面临很多问题，比如统一的硬件平台：需要低成本好用的统一vbts硬件平台，且需要搭载简单易用的调用接口来降低使用门槛；触觉数据集：作为本质是视觉信息的vbts，目前并没有类似imagenet这类触觉图像数据集；触觉大模型：在有了触觉数据集之后，也需要触觉大模型来进一步提升对物体物理层面的通用识别能力（参考了知乎水白关于gelsight的文章）；循环使用寿命的问题：gelsight表面的凝胶比较脆弱，用多了会发生磨损，如何提高核心器件的循环使用寿命也是非常重要的工程问题；算力需求：将触觉信息视觉化意味着需要相应的算力来进行图像处理；触觉感知面积：vbts的感知是基于摄像头，感知面有限，近些年很多工作（gelsight svelte等）都是针对提高感知面积和范围。 gelsight的本质是图像处理，它在近些年的加速发展与深度学习的发展密不可分。但目前，vbts的很多进展还局限在科研领域，产业化的道路非常迫切。目前大模型的进展正加速推进机器人产业的发展。那么回到开篇的问题，触觉是否必要？如果必要，哪种方案？ 我对这两个问题的回答是，对通用操作触觉感知是必要的，但哪种触觉方案可以被广泛使用要看场景。短期内的通用操作大概率是特定场景某类任务的通用操作，如果放触觉，要结合场景以及任务的需求来选择触觉方案。从长远来看，要实现通用操作，那么触觉方案也必须统一，而视触觉传感是我认为现有的触觉方案里最有潜力成为那个统一方案的，也或者有某种暂未发现的全新触觉方案会成为最终的触觉统一方案。通用操作以外，触觉传感器怎么样拓展现有机器人的场景和能力也值得期待。 2009 to robot fingertips, soft hands and commercial sensors: gelsight’s research history and the opportunities and challenges of camera-based touch. sensing & dexterous manipulation recently, i have often encountered discussions of tactile perception in robotics, especially the initially puzzling term “vision-based tactile sensor,” or vbts. i keep asking: is touch essential for general-purpose manipulation robots? without touch, could vision alone support a sufficiently broad range of manipulation tasks? one traditional framework describes six dimensions of human perception: eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body and mind, corresponding to sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch and consciousness. if robots ultimately run on electricity rather than food, taste and smell might seem of little use to robots. what progress has robotics made on the remaining four? [editor’s note: this is a philosophical framing, not an exhaustive scientific taxonomy. smell and chemical sensing can also be useful to robots, regardless of their energy source.] vision mainly uses cameras, often combined with lidar and other sensors; autonomous driving and service robotics have advanced visual algorithms considerably. hearing uses microphones and related components familiar from phones and smart speakers, with increasingly mature speech recognition. chatgpt led some people to speculate that ai might soon become self-aware, though its appearance does not establish consciousness. touch, by comparison, remains very immature in both hardware and algorithms, in my view at this article’s march 2024 publication. many papers show that tactile perception can improve manipulation accuracy, yet i do not think a perfect tactile solution, or even a mature hardware platform, has emerged. conversations with manipulation researchers often mention vbts, particularly gelsight. this article follows gelsight’s academic development, highlighting milestones from its introduction onward. the many videos aim to show intuitively what these sensors are and what they can do. contents an introduction to robot tactile sensing an introduction to gelsight gelsight’s research timeline commercializing gelsight other vision-based tactile sensors opportunities and challenges for vbts 1. an introduction to robot tactile sensing tactile sensors imitate aspects of skin, detecting stimuli from the physical environment. common approaches include piezoresistive, piezoelectric, optical, capacitive, electromagnetic and camera-based tactile sensing. gelsight is a representative vision-based tactile sensor: it uses visual images to measure touch. when humans manipulate objects, tactile information concerns both the object and the contact. object information includes texture, shape and softness; contact information includes normal force perpendicular to the skin, shear force parallel to it, relative slip and object pose. most piezoresistive, piezoelectric, capacitive and electromagnetic tactile sensors, in the comparison made in the original article, mainly sense normal force and cannot collect the other information or have low sensitivity to it. the greatest advantage of vbts in that comparison is its ability to sense all the dimensions above with high sensitivity, bringing it very close to the range of tactile information available to human hands. [editor’s note: this comparison is not universal: non-camera tactile sensors can also measure shear or other quantities, and recovering physical properties from vbts images requires appropriate models and calibration.] 2. an introduction to gelsight a university of tokyo team proposed fluorescent-marker-based optical tactile sensing, gelforce, in 2004, although its resolution was lower. in 2009, edward h. adelson’s group at mit’s computer science and artificial intelligence laboratory (csail) introduced gelsight, described in the original as the first ultra-high-resolution vision-based tactile sensor. its name combines “gel,” the compliant contact material, and “sight,” the camera-based sensing mechanism. when an object contacts it, leds illuminate the gel and an internal camera observes deformation. computer-vision algorithms map that deformation to tactile information. gelsight sensor structure, from the 2017 gelsight paper. since 2009, successive researchers in adelson’s group have spent more than a decade advancing this approach to the forefront of robotic touch. work based on gelsight has appeared at mit, stanford, cmu, uc berkeley, uiuc, eth zurich, oxford, tsinghua, peking university, shanghai jiao tong university, hkust and the chinese academy of sciences, as well as meta and toyota research institute. the original highlights the many best paper recognitions associated with this research at rss, icra and iros. specific wins and finalist selections are distinguished in the timeline below. let us revisit important moments in its first fifteen years, through march 2024. 3. gelsight’s research timeline introducing gelsight—mit, 2009 gelsight’s story begins with its inventor, mit professor edward adelson. he is a neuroscientist and the john and dorothy wilson professor of vision science at mit, and a member of the us national academy of sciences and american academy of arts and sciences. his recent research focuses on artificial touch for robotics. micah johnson and adelson introduced the sensing technique at cvpr 2009. the initial work observed microscopic surface structure rather than robot touch. the 2009 sensor used a transparent elastomer—a gel-like material—with a coated outer surface to measure the texture and geometry of an object pressed against it. viewed from behind, the contact surface appears with uniform reflectance, allowing its geometry to be reconstructed in 3d from illumination and shading. gelsight, 2009. #robottouch #visionbasedtactilesensors (watch in the original wechat article). source: micah johnson et al., 2009. gelsight—mit, 2011 at siggraph 2011, adelson’s team improved the system for microscopic surface geometry, demonstrating spatial resolution as fine as 2 micrometers (micah johnson et al., 2011). geometry capture did not depend on whether an object was matte, shiny or transparent. hardware could take various forms, including handheld devices for high-resolution measurements in the field. compared with 2009, the work improved materials, lighting and reconstruction, and suggested applications in surface-defect detection. its focus was still surface metrology rather than robot manipulation. gelsight, 2011. #robottouch #visionbasedtouch #gelsight (watch in the original wechat article). source: micah johnson et al., 2011. gelsight evolves—mit, 2013 at cvpr 2013, adelson’s group first connected gelsight to robotic tactile perception in the timeline presented here, building a database of 40 tactile texture classes including fabrics, wood and sandpaper (rui li and edward adelson, 2013). the system classified materials from that database, showing how the sensor could support robotic material recognition. tactile images of 40 material classes collected with gelsight. gelsight—mit, 2014 at iros 2014, the team demonstrated precise localization and manipulation of small parts using gelsight (rui li et al., 2014). its compact fingertip sensor achieved approximately 10-micrometer-scale spatial resolution and supported usb insertion and removal, combining vision and touch for fine manipulation and closed-loop control. this helped establish camera-based tactile sensing for robot manipulation. the design shown below resembles the later gelsight mini. [editor’s note: the original calls this the world’s first such sensor; that absolute priority claim is not independently established here.] fingertip gelsight sensor: design and structure for robot fingertips. source: rui li et al., 2014. the 2009–2011 devices were large—even the smallest roughly soda-can-sized—and insufficiently real-time for manipulation. from 2011, the team adapted the technology for robotics through hardware and software improvements. the 2014 fingertip version combined compactness and high resolution. the evolving platform subsequently supported normal force, shear and slip measurements; the explicit marker-based shear-and-slip work appears below in 2015. a baxter robot inserts and removes a usb connector using fingertip gelsight sensors. source: rui li et al., 2014. compared with many conventional piezoelectric, piezoresistive or magnetic sensors, gelsight offers high-resolution geometry, estimates of normal and shear forces, and softness estimation useful for compliant objects. its optical mechanism avoids some sensitivities associated with magnetic sensing. with the same basic hardware and software, robots can adapt their grasps to objects with different hardness, size and shape—eggs, chips, strawberries and even leaves, as the video shows. multidimensional contact information enables closed-loop control reminiscent of human manipulation, valuable for broader generalization. [editor’s note: optical tactile sensors are not completely immune to temperature, humidity, lighting or material aging; the original’s absolute immunity claim is too broad.] gelsight—mit, 2015 at icra 2015, the team introduced tracking markers into the fingertip system to measure shear, relative slip and torsional loading (wenzhen yuan et al., 2015). measuring normal force, shear and slip together became a widely recognized advantage in robot touch. the demonstration below shows this work. gelsight, 2015. #robottouch #visionbasedtouch #gelsight (watch in the original wechat article). source: wenzhen yuan et al., 2015. gelsight’s development accelerates—mit, 2017 the 2017 sensors paper gelsight: high-resolution robot tactile sensors for estimating geometry and force (wenzhen yuan et al.) played a major role in advancing its robotics applications. it reviews sensing principles, sensor and optical design, algorithms for shape, force and slip, and the design and manufacture of different hardware versions. it systematically addresses hardware and software issues and shows how high-resolution geometry and contact-force information support material perception and recognition. an iros 2017 paper presented an improved sensor for geometry and slip measurement (siyuan dong et al.). the core designs in that paper and the sensors review are illustrated below. together with the 2014 fingertip design, they became reference prototypes for many research laboratories. source: siyuan dong et al., 2017. across 2017–2018, the group published work on perceiving object and material properties through touch. two hardness-estimation projects, cited in the source as wenzhen yuan et al. and yuan with adelson, used fingertip gelsight without requiring precisely controlled contact conditions or known object shapes. deep convolutional and recurrent networks analyzed the data to estimate hardness across differently shaped objects. [editor’s note: one cited project, estimating object hardness with a gelsight touch sensor, was presented at iros 2016; the original reference labels it 2017.] gelsight hardness estimation, 2017. #robottouch #gelsight #visionbasedtactilesensors (watch in the original wechat article). source: wenzhen yuan et al., 2017. at cvpr 2017, the group studied 118 fabric samples, recording rgb and depth images of hanging fabrics and high-resolution tactile images (wenzhen yuan et al.). cnns trained across these three modalities related appearance to touch. each input produced an embedding representing physical properties, regardless of modality. comparing embeddings allowed the system to predict how a fabric would feel from an image, and vice versa. gelsight: look and feel, 2017. #robottouch #gelsight #visionbasedtouch (watch in the original wechat article). building on that work, the team developed a robot that actively perceived clothing properties (wenzhen yuan et al., 2019). guided by an external kinect sensor, it squeezed garments with gelsight and identified eleven attributes: physical properties such as thickness, fuzziness, softness and durability, and semantic attributes such as suitable season and preferred washing method. the dataset contained 153 garments, with cnns analyzing tactile data. gelsight grasping clothing. #robottouch #gelsight (watch in the original wechat article). and software are open-source. source: 9dtact paper. insight—max planck institute, 2022 researchers at germany’s max planck institute developed insight, a thumb-sized 3d optical tactile sensor that continuously estimates directional force distributions across its conical surface. it uses one internal camera and an elastomer layer over a supporting frame. source: insight paper. vitactip—university of bristol, 2023 nathan lepora’s team at bristol developed vitactip. its embedded biomimetic pins amplify tactile movements, and the resulting images naturally combine visual and tactile information in one device. for comparisons, the team also developed vitac without pins and tactip without transparent skin. lepora’s biomimetic tactile work has received many awards, but my mind is running out of steam right now; i will leave bristol’s tactile-sensing ideas for another article! source: haoran li’s website. 6. opportunities and challenges for vbts touch provides distinctive information about the physical world and supports activity even without vision, as blind people demonstrate. gelsight-like sensing offers rich force-related information, texture and hardness estimates, and high spatial resolution, creating substantial application potential. because it records images using computer-vision principles, tactile images and the robot’s external visual observations can train within a shared model, enabling genuinely integrated visual–tactile manipulation control. widespread use still faces challenges. a common hardware platform should be inexpensive, practical and offer simple interfaces. tactile datasets need scale and consistency comparable to what imagenet brought to vision; at this article’s publication, no similarly established general tactile-image benchmark existed in my assessment. after suitable datasets are available, tactile foundation models are also needed to improve general recognition of physical properties—an idea informed by shuibai’s zhihu discussion of gelsight. gel durability also matters, because contact wears its delicate surface. image processing requires computation. finally, camera-based sensing coverage is limited; recent designs such as gelsight svelte explicitly expand its area and reach. gelsight’s essence is image processing, and its accelerating development is closely tied to deep learning. much vbts progress remains research-oriented, making commercialization urgent. large models are accelerating robotics. returning to the opening questions: is touch necessary, and if so, which technology? my view is that general manipulation needs touch, but the technology depends on the setting. near-term “general” manipulation will likely mean varied tasks within a particular environment, so sensing should fit its tasks and requirements. over the longer term, i think tactile technology must also become unified. among existing options, camera-based touch seems most promising to me, although an undiscovered approach could ultimately emerge. beyond general manipulation, expanding existing robots’ applications and capabilities with touch is also exciting.
