policy。我非常好奇这个diffusion policy到底是什么？于是找了这篇论文的资料来看：应用了diffusion policy的机器人在任务过程中动作之丝滑，轨迹之连贯，对不同材质物体之广泛适用让我眼前一亮。不禁感慨，this is sota（state of the art）！ 那什么是diffusion policy？首先diffusion，它是一种生成方法，如今图像生成领域的成就基本都是基于diffusion方法，比如常听的stable diffusion和midjourney。其次policy，它是机器学习算法用来驱动机器人的核心组成部分，它的输入是各种感知信息（比如相机拍到的视频，还有机器人各个关节的位置），而输出的是机器人要执行的动作。所以简单理解，diffusion policy就是应用diffusion这种方法生成机器人动作的一种policy。 可能看到这里你并没有觉得这个方法有什么特别，虽然不敢夸大diffusion policy未来的影响，但我特别相信它会是通用机器人成为现实路上非常重要的工作！这篇关于diffusion policy的论文介绍和你以往看过的任何一篇论文介绍都不同，它不是生硬的学术介绍，也不是夸大的媒体pr，它是一篇可以让非学术背景的人看得懂的笔记。为了做到“看懂”，我非常荣幸的邀请到了“diffusion policy-visuomotor policy learning via action diffusion”这篇论文的一作迟宬博士做采访，也非常感谢他提供的清晰和生动的解释。 关于diffusion policy以及它可能带来的无限可能，请找20分钟左右的时间，坚持看到文末，以下，enjoy！ 以下为本文目录 👇 diffusion policy的效果 diffusion policy团队介绍 什么是diffusion policy 为什么用diffusion policy 采访中提到的其他问题 一些想法 1. diffusion policy的效果 在将机器人的手牵向人类的手：灵巧操作华人论文综述这篇文章里，我们提到了一个观点：机器人操作的执行（action）是木桶最短的板。在解决机器人灵巧操作执行方面，diffusion policy显示了非常好的效果和很大的潜力。作为非学术背景的人，看任何学术工作，最喜欢看视频，效果最直观。在介绍diffusion policy之前，我们直接看下它的效果。 摊披萨：在1x速度的情况下，摊披萨酱，机器人手部没有卡顿，尤其是在有人故意拖动披萨的情况下，摸酱的动作依然流畅。 摊披萨#diffusion policy（请在微信公众号原文观看） 扣杯子：不管你怎么扔杯子，机器人都可以精确地把它按照希望的角度和位置给扣过来。 扣杯子#diffusion policy（请在微信公众号原文观看） 对图：机器人将t精准对到图框里，和diffusion policy相比，其他方法在路径上没那么连贯，并且很容易出现在临近图框的位置卡死的情况。 对图#diffusionpolicy（请在微信公众号原文观看） mit教授兼丰田机器人研究院负责人russ tedrake在一个视频中详细的介绍了diffusion policy取得的惊人效果，他说每天醒来都期待着机器人能够完成新的技能。 diffusion policy #tri #russ tedrake（请在微信公众号原文观看） 根据论文摘要，作者在四个不同的机器人操纵基准的12项任务中对diffusion policy进行基准测试，发现它在性能上优于现有的最先进机器人学习方法，平均改进了46.9%。丰田机器人研究院（tri，oyota robotics institution）作为这篇论文的赞助商，也对diffusion policy给予了很高的评价：基于扩散策略的突破性生成式人工智能方法，可以快速而自信地教会机器人新的灵巧技能。这一进展显著提高了机器人的效用，是构建机器人“大行为模型（lbms）”迈出的一步，类似于最近彻底改变了对话人工智能的大型语言模型（llms）。 tri已经使用这种新方法教会机器人超过60种困难的灵巧技能，包括倒液体、使用工具和操纵可变形的物体。这些成就是在不写一行新代码的情况下实现的；唯一的变化是为机器人提供了新的数据。在这一成功的基础上，tri制定了一个雄心勃勃的目标，到今年年底教授数百项新技能，并在2024年底前教授1,000项新技能。 2. diffusion policy团队介绍 diffusion policy这篇工作是哥伦比亚大学宋舒然团队和mit教授russ tedrake带领的丰田机器人研究院共同创作。论文的一作迟宬目前是哥伦比亚大学的计算机科学博士生，在宋舒然的指导下做机器人操纵和感知相关的研究。 迟宬的研究兴趣在于计算机与物理世界的交互，他2019年本科毕业于密歇根大学。除了作为diffusion policy的一作，迟宬也是rss 2022 best paper “iterative residual policy for goal-conditioned dynamic manipulation of deformable objects”的一作；此外他也参与了roboninja（切牛油果）和dextairity（吹风叠衣服）两篇很有趣的操作工作（将机器人的手牵向人类的手：灵巧操作华人论文综述）。关于宋舒然我们在（ai+robotics华人图谱）文章中做过介绍。这篇论文的作者除了迟宬，还有哥伦比亚大学的zhenjia xu，mit yilun du，tri 的siyuan feng，eric cousineau和benjamin burchfiel。 3. 什么是diffusion policy？ diffusion policy是一种新型机器人行为生成方法（robot action generation），将机器人的视觉动作策略（visuomotor policy）表示为条件去噪扩散过程（conditional denoising diffusion process）。这是来自论文摘要里的一句介绍，但我想大多数和我一样非专业背景的人看到这段话应该是一脸懵，每个字都认识放在一起就不知道什么意思。 关于什么是diffusion policy，迟宬有一段很好的解释：diffusion policy其实解决的是一个机器人输出的问题，过往的很多工作大家都注重在解决输入的问题，但机器人最终要执行，我们的工作就在于解决机器人动作和输出的问题。更确切地说，我们的创新聚焦于机器人的动作端而非输入端，在输入端使用的是非常普通的东西。尽管输入端有很多可以提高的地方，但机器人学习方法必须注重输出端，先前的算法在输出端的表现都不够好。因此，无论输入端有多么创新，如果输出端表现不佳，就像"茶壶煮饺子倒不出"一样，将无法发挥潜力。 rss 2023宋舒然有一段对diffusion policy的讲解视频，也非常清晰。 diffusion policy和diffusion model的关系 diffusion policy可以理解为diffusion model在机器人领域的应用。大家都知道diffusion model在图像领域的应用产生了非常好的图像生成模型，比如stable diffusion这些，比gan这类图像生成模型的效果好很多。同样的，diffusion policy可以理解为这套diffusion model在机器人动作生成领域的应用，尤其是部署到物理机器人领域的动作生成。 4. 为什么用diffusion policy？ diffusion policy解决的核心问题 从最简单的形式来看，从演示中学习策略可以被表述为学习将观察映射到动作的监督回归任务。然而，在实践中，预测机器人动作有一系列挑战，比如存在多模态分布、时序相关性和训练稳定性的要求。 解决机器人multi-modal分布问题 机器人multi-modal的问题，简单理解，现实世界中解决某一特定任务的方式是多样的，而不是唯一的。但神经网络预测只能给出单一的方式，无法应对可能有多种方式的任务情况。 关于什么是机器人multi-moda问题，迟宬给了非常清晰的解释：假设我现在在开车，前面有一棵树。比如说，我雇佣了100个司机来解决这个问题。在这种情况下，有可能有50个司机选择往左拐，绕过树的左边，还有50个司机选择从树的右边绕过去。在这种情况下，往左绕和往右绕都是完全合理的。然而，当我们将所有这些解决方案合并为一个时，问题就变成了一个多模态分布，即我看到的相同场景有两种不同的选择。这对传统神经网络的预测来说并不友好，因为它通常使用均方误差（mse）损失进行训练，而这无法有效处理multi-modal情况。 前馈神经网络本质上是一个函数，即对于给定输入，只有一种输出。然而，在某些情况下，一个输入可能对应两种不同的输出。这导致了一个问题，即我想要神经网络执行的任务和它能够执行的任务存在冲突。强行让神经网络处理这种情况，通常是通过预测一个中间值，试图最小化与数据之间的距离。但这可能导致不符合预期的行为，例如直接往树上撞。为了解决这个问题，引入了概率分布，使得神经网络不再是一个输入一个输出的函数，而是一个输入可以有多个输出的函数。这种方法提供了更大的灵活性，可以表示各种概率分布，解决了原有方法的限制。 引入概率分布的方法提供了更大的灵活性，让机器人有机会在相同的情况下选择不同的行为，从而避免陷入不可预测的循环。这种非确定性的特性在实际应用中表现出很大的优势，可以防止算法陷入一成不变的状态。但这和传统机器人控制需要对机器人动作严格控制的思路相违背，每次只执行一项任务，整个机器人系统都被认为是受到严格控制的。这也是为什么大多数人没有把机器人动作生成表现为一个概率分布的原因。 但仔细想下人类在决策时也具有一定的非确定性，即在相同情境下可能做出不同选择。比如说，就像我刚才说的，正前方有棵树。你可能今天心情好，你就往右拐；今天心情不好，你就往左拐。这种非确定性对人类来说可能是一种优势，而不是劣势，对机器人同样如此。举例来说，假设我在机器人的算法里有个bug，就是看到一个锥筒，机器人就会绕着它打转。如果我的算法是确定性的，比如说你现在在这条路上开车，我往路上扔一个锥桶，你就开始绕着这个锥桶打转，可能一辈子也开不出来。然而，如果我的机器人预测不是单一模型，而是一个概率分布，有一定的概率它会绕着打转，有一定的概率它会往直走，这样它就能够突破这个无穷打转的情况，最终回到正常的状态。这个性质在实际应用中对提高算法的鲁棒性有很大的影响，它可以防止算法陷入在某些不太熟悉的情况下一直打转的困境。 action space scalability的问题 关于action space scalabiltiy或者sequential correlation问题，我简单理解就是机器人对未来动作的预测不应该只局限于眼前的一步两步动作，而应该更有前瞻性，可以往前预测数十步动作。 针对这个问题，迟宬给了非常清晰的解释：数据预测有两种方法：一是直接输出一个数值，另一种是将可能的数值分成几个区间，进行离散预测。在预测multi-modal action的时候，人们倾向于采用离散预测，将连续值问题转化为分类问题，但这样做涉及的算力成本很高，尤其在处理高维空间时。此外，针对机器人控制问题，如果采用分类方法，每一步都需要预测下一步要执行的动作，而实际需求是希望一次性预测多步动作，这就涉及到了连续控制中的动作一致性问题。解决这个问题的挑战在于平衡成本和对高维连续控制的需求。 假设我们仍然在进行驾驶操作。我们有选择往左或往右拐的能力，将这个过程比喻为方向盘的控制，这是唯一的控制维度。我们将这个控制维度划分成了100个段。接着，我通过神经网络让它在这100个段中选择我们要采取的方向。这种方法理论上是可行的，但问题在于实施的成本非常高昂。如果我们只有一个维度，例如方向盘，那么使用分类是可行的。但假设我要控制的是一个具有六个自由度的机械手，甚至考虑到夹爪开关，有七个自由度，这时如果我要对其进行分类，就不再是在一个维度上切分成100份，而是每个维度都要切分成1000份。然后，将所有这些切分的部分相乘，才能得到我们整个空间的方法。如果采用这种方法，成本将会非常非常高。随着维度的增加，成本会呈指数级增长。 我们再回到了之前提到的问题。假设我们在驾驶车辆，我们可以在下一步稍微往左偏一点，再下一步再进一步左偏。实际上，我们所绘制的行车轨迹有两种可行的选择。一种是持续向左开，从左侧绕过去，一直保持这种路径。另一种是持续向右开，从右侧绕过去。在预测这个动作时，我们可以逐步进行预测，即在每个时刻，预测下一步应该怎么走。然而，采用这种方式可能会导致问题，例如，如果我稍微向左偏了一点，我可能会左右摇摆；如果我稍微向右偏了一点，也有可能左右摇摆。这个问题被称为动作不一致（action inconsistent），即当我希望向左行驶时，神经网络的预测中仍然存在一定概率是向右的情况，这时候就会发现决策非常犹豫，时而向左，时而向右，这是一个问题。 在我刚刚提到的分类中，由于它们预测高维空间的成本非常高，因为它们只能预测一步，接下来的步骤是什么。如果再加上更多的步骤，维度就会变得越来越高，它们就无法胜任。然而，实际上我们现在追求的是具有以下特性的方法：不仅可以预测每一步，而且可以在高维连续控制中实现。对于我们来说，我们可以直接预测未来每一步，无论是接下来的20步还是100步，是向左还是向右，而不是在每一步预测之后再执行，再决定下一步该怎么走。 training stability问题 diffusion policy和其他使用生成式模型的策略比，他的最大特点是训练过程非常稳定。 关于训练稳定性，迟宬的进一步解释是：在robot learning领域，机器人动作执行主要有三种方法：包括直接回归、分类预测和生成式模型。第一类回归，即将神经网络视为一个函数，输入是图片，输出是一个动作。这是最常见的方法，绝大多数强化学习都采用这种方式。然而，这种方法存在一些问题，正如之前提到的。第二类分类预测，这种方法通过预测分类来生成动作，前文已经大致描述，不再详细赘述。第三类生成模型，理论上所有的生成模型都可以预测连续的多模态分布，但很多生成模型的问题是训练不稳定。 基于diffusion model的第三类方法具有一个重要的优势，即训练非常稳定。这也是为什么diffusion model当前在图像生成方面取得了成功，而当时的生成对抗网络（gan）并没有成功的原因。在当时，gan在学术界能够产生一些不错的效果，但当你真的将其应用于产品时，你会发现非常困难。要训练一个有效的gan，你需要疯狂地调整参数，然后才能训练出可用的生成器。 而diffusion方法的强大之处在于，它的性能不逊色于gan，但其训练过程非常稳定。基本上，你可以随便调整参数，生成器就能够输出结果，可能效果不是最优的，但基本上都能work。同时，这也解释了为什么像stable diffusion这样的方法，以及现在各种图像生成模型能够在如此庞大的数据集上进行训练，这是因为它们的训练非常稳定。如果你在如此大规模的数据上使用其他方法进行训练，可能会在训练一段时间后出现奇怪的问题，模型无法进一步优化。 5. 采访中提到的其他问题 diffusion policy和rl以及imitational learning是什么关系？ 在robot learning领域，机器人操作比较常用的两个路径是强化学习（reinforcement learning）和模仿学习（imitation learning），diffusion policy并不与强化学习和模仿学习冲突，它可以应用于两者。该方法是一种策略逻辑，适用于输入图像并输出相应动作的情境。在论文中，我们使用了模仿学习，即由人类遥控机器人执行动作，收集数据，并通过学习将其转化为策略。这种学习过程通过遥控机器人完成一系列动作开始，然后将其迁移到机器人身上。输入数据包括过去几帧的图像，而输出涉及对未来动作的预测。 很多强化学习的人，他们使用强化学习在模拟器中生成大量数据。在这个过程中，为了加速训练，rl policy的输入不是图片，而是一些低维度的底层状态信息。但是由于这些状态信息在现实环境里是无法获得的，因此这个rl policy不能直接用于驱动机器人。这个时候，他们会把rl policy生成的数据用于训练一个图片作为输入的模仿学习策略，这被称为蒸馏。在这种情况下，模仿的对象并非人类，而是一个强化学习“代理”（agent）。这也是这种方法的应用之一。 操作（manipulation）和移动（locomotion）的训练有什么不同？ rl在移动有更好的效果，sim2real gap的问题相对好解决；但在操作，rl存在最大的问题是sim2real gap没法很好的解决。对于操控而言，需要考虑的因素较多，其中一个关键区别是在机器人操作中除了需要考虑机器人本身的物理特性，同时还要适应复杂多变的环境和被操作物体。操控涉及与各种各样的物体进行交互，每个物体都具有独特的物理特性，如重心、摩擦力和动力学。这些在模拟器中难以准确模拟，即便能够模拟，精度通常较低，速度较慢。相比之下，对于locomotion，外界环境大多可以视为一个刚体，物理特性基本可以忽略。这使得可以花费更多时间来建立机器人本体的精确物理模型，以及设计更复杂的物理引擎。这是为什么rl更适合locomotion，而对有物理机器人部署manipulation没有那么好的效果。 diffusion policy目前会存在什么问题，未来有哪些工作？ 目前最大的问题不是policy本身，而是数据。训练数据对于机器人执行特定任务至关重要。尽管我们已经积累了一些关于遥控机器人执行任务的数据，但要将其部署到实际应用中，比如设计一个家用机器人来洗碗，就需要更大规模、更丰富多样的数据集，类似于chatgpt的规模。确保机器人能够在各种家庭环境中表现出足够的稳健性。目前，最大的挑战在于如何有效地收集大量、多样化的数据。这是下一步研究的关键，通过数据收集和训练，期望能够解决当前面临的问题，同时也认识到可能会有新的挑战随着数据规模的增加而浮现。 6. 一些想法 直接对话学者是我一直想尝试的一种输出方式，希望以一种更容易理解的方式，将最前沿的学术成果以及它们的可能性展现给更多人。因为担心我自己在一些基础知识上理解的不够深入，提出一些非常“业余”的问题，这个尝试迟迟没有展开。作为第一次尝试，我特别感谢迟博士非常耐心的回答我的很多“业余”问题，并对成文后的很多文字表述给予了非常细致的修改建议。我自己也在交流过程中收获很多。 最近一段时间，我将自己在robot learning领域学习的内容整理成笔记以公众号的形式分享出来，收到了很多读者的肯定。非常感谢所有读我文字的朋友！关于文字表达，我其实从小到大语文偏科，中文写作是我最讨厌的科目，没有之一。我可能做梦都没有想到我会写文字给别人看。有些投资人朋友问我，为什么我可以这么专注在一个领域，虽然有很多客观因素，但主观上我是真的好奇到底通用机器人是否会到来，什么时候到来，如何到来。以前看很多方向，会为了投成项目而去学习一些资料。但看robot learning是反过来的，我在试图从最前沿的学术里面找到一些答案的同时，顺带认识一些优秀的人，看到一些不错的创业项目。 最近在读吴军的《大学之路》，我觉得有一段话特别好分享出来：“教育是一辈子的事情，我们不必担心输在起跑线上，因为世界上大部分人跑到一半就不会再跑了，这就给了那些长跑者以机会。一个善于学习的人，随着年龄的增长，他会找到自己的兴趣点，而那时如果他还能够学习，就有目的性和针对性了。”投资这个行业最大的一个特点是，从业者必须保持持续学习的状态，这也推动了我不断学习。 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=whpk0hdtoj0&t=482s 宋舒然rss 2023报告： https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=heo2-ly5i0o diffusion policy: generating robot actions with diffusion models an interview with cheng chi explaining diffusion policy, multimodal action distributions, coherent action sequences and the data needed for general-purpose robots. robot learning & foundation models a few days ago, i listened to the corl debate can large models enable general-purpose robots? russ tedrake, someone strongly associated with model-based methods, was unexpectedly sitting on the learning side and repeatedly mentioning diffusion policy. curious about what it was, i looked up the paper. the robots’ fluid movements, coherent trajectories and ability to handle objects made of different materials immediately caught my attention. my reaction was simple: this is state of the art. what is diffusion policy? first, diffusion is a generative method behind many achievements in image generation, including familiar systems such as stable diffusion and midjourney. a policy, meanwhile, is the component of a machine-learning system that drives a robot. it takes perceptual information—camera images or video, for example, and robot joint positions—as input and outputs the actions the robot should execute. put simply, diffusion policy uses diffusion to generate robot actions. that description alone may not sound especially remarkable. i do not want to exaggerate its future impact, but i strongly believe this could be an important contribution on the road to general-purpose robots. this article aims to explain the paper differently from a conventional academic introduction or a promotional media story: it is a set of notes that readers without an academic background can understand. to make that possible, i was fortunate to interview cheng chi, first author of diffusion policy: visuomotor policy learning via action diffusion. i am grateful for his clear and vivid explanations. set aside about 20 minutes and stay with me to the end as we explore diffusion policy and the possibilities it may open up. enjoy! contents what diffusion policy can do the team behind diffusion policy what is diffusion policy? why use diffusion policy? other questions from the interview some reflections 1. what diffusion policy can do in bringing robot hands closer to human hands: a review of dexterous manipulation research, we discussed a view that action execution is the weakest link in robot manipulation. diffusion policy has demonstrated impressive results and considerable potential in addressing that problem. as someone outside academia, i particularly like watching research videos: they make the results immediately tangible. before discussing the method, let us look at what it can do. spreading pizza sauce: at normal playback speed, the robot spreads the sauce without hesitation or jerky motion. even when someone deliberately moves the pizza underneath it, the spreading action remains fluid. spreading pizza sauce with diffusion policy. watch the video in the original wechat article. flipping a mug: even when the mug is tossed into a different position, the robot can turn it over precisely to the desired position and orientation. flipping a mug with diffusion policy. watch the video in the original wechat article. push-t: the robot precisely pushes a t-shaped block into the target outline. compared with diffusion policy, other methods produce less coherent trajectories and can easily get stuck near the target. push-t with diffusion policy. watch the video in the original wechat article. in a video, mit professor and toyota research institute robotics leader russ tedrake describes the remarkable results achieved with diffusion policy. he says that every morning he looks forward to discovering new skills the robots can perform. diffusion policy at tri, presented by russ tedrake. watch the video in the original wechat article. according to the paper’s abstract, the authors evaluated diffusion policy on 12 tasks across four robot manipulation benchmarks. it outperformed existing state-of-the-art robot learning methods, with an average improvement of 46.9%. toyota research institute, or tri, which supported the research, also praised the approach. it described diffusion-based generative ai as a breakthrough for teaching robots new dexterous skills quickly and confidently, significantly increasing their utility and moving toward large behavior models, or lbms, analogous to the large language models that had recently transformed conversational ai. at the time of the announcement, tri had used the method to teach robots more than 60 challenging dexterous skills, including pouring liquids, using tools and manipulating deformable objects. these results required no new lines of code: the only change was the data given to the robot. building on that success, tri set the ambitious goal of teaching hundreds of additional skills by the end of 2023 and 1,000 by the end of 2024. 2. the team behind diffusion policy diffusion policy was a collaboration between shuran song’s group at columbia university and toyota research institute, with mit professor russ tedrake. at the time of this interview, first author cheng chi was a computer science phd student at columbia, studying robot manipulation and perception under song’s supervision. chi’s research interests center on interactions between computers and the physical world. he graduated from the university of michigan in 2019. besides being first author of diffusion policy, he was first author of the rss 2022 best paper, iterative residual policy for goal-conditioned dynamic manipulation of deformable objects. he also contributed to two intriguing manipulation projects: roboninja, which cuts avocados, and dextairity, which uses airflow to fold clothing. both appear in bringing robot hands closer to human hands: a review of dexterous manipulation research. i previously introduced shuran song in my map of chinese researchers in ai and robotics. other authors of the diffusion policy paper include zhenjia xu at columbia, yilun du at mit, and siyuan feng, eric cousineau and benjamin burchfiel at tri. 3. what is diffusion policy? diffusion policy is a new method for generating robot behavior that represents a visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising diffusion process. that is how the abstract introduces it. for many readers without a specialist background, including me, the individual words may be familiar while the sentence as a whole remains bewildering. chi offered a helpful explanation: diffusion policy addresses the robot’s output. much previous work has focused on inputs, but eventually the robot must act, and our work focuses on actions and outputs. more specifically, our innovation lies on the action side rather than the input side, where we use fairly ordinary components. inputs can certainly be improved, but robot learning must also address outputs, where earlier algorithms did not perform well enough. however innovative the input processing, poor outputs prevent the system from realizing its potential. it is like cooking dumplings in a teapot: they are inside, but you cannot get them out through the spout. shuran song also gave a very clear explanation of diffusion policy in her rss 2023 presentation. how are diffusion policy and diffusion models related? you can understand diffusion policy as an application of diffusion models to robotics. in image generation, diffusion models have produced excellent systems such as stable diffusion, with results much better than those of many gan-based generators. diffusion policy applies the same family of methods to generating robot actions, particularly actions executed on physical robots. 4. why use diffusion policy? the core problems it addresses in its simplest form, learning a policy from demonstrations can be formulated as supervised regression: learning to map observations to actions. in practice, however, action prediction brings several challenges, including multimodal distributions, temporal correlations and training stability. handling multimodal action distributions here, multimodal means that a real-world task may have several valid solutions rather than just one. a conventional neural-network predictor may output only a single solution, making it difficult to handle tasks with multiple valid ways of acting. chi explained this clearly: imagine driving toward a tree. suppose i hire 100 drivers to deal with it. fifty might turn left and go around the tree on that side, while fifty might go around the right. both are perfectly reasonable. combining these demonstrations produces a multimodal distribution: the same observed situation has two distinct valid choices. that is challenging for conventional neural-network prediction, which is often trained with mean squared error, or mse, and cannot handle this situation effectively. a conventional deterministic feedforward network is a function: a given input produces one output. but here, one input may correspond to two different outputs. the task we want it to perform conflicts with what that formulation can express. forcing it to fit the data usually makes it predict an intermediate value that minimizes distance to the demonstrations. that can yield undesirable behavior, such as driving straight into the tree. modeling a probability distribution instead allows a given observation to correspond to multiple possible outputs. this adds the flexibility to represent different distributions and overcomes the original limitation. that flexibility lets a robot choose different actions in the same situation, helping it avoid getting trapped in repetitive loops. in practice, this nondeterministic property can be highly useful because the algorithm need not remain stuck in one unchanging behavior. it does depart from the traditional robotics view that actions should be tightly controlled, with each execution treated as fully deterministic. that is one reason many people have not represented robot action generation as a probability distribution. humans also show some nondeterminism in their decisions: we may choose differently in the same situation. with a tree ahead, perhaps you turn right when you are in a good mood and left when you are in a bad one. that variability can be an advantage for humans and robots alike. suppose a bug causes a robot to circle a traffic cone. with a deterministic algorithm, throwing a cone onto the road might make it circle forever. with a probabilistic prediction, it may sometimes circle and sometimes go straight, giving it a chance to escape the loop and return to normal behavior. this property can substantially improve robustness in practice, preventing endless repetition in unfamiliar situations. action-space scalability and temporal correlation my simple understanding of action-space scalability and sequential correlation is that a robot’s prediction should not stop at the next one or two actions. it should look farther ahead, potentially predicting dozens of future steps. chi explained that there are two broad approaches to numerical prediction: directly output a value, or divide possible values into bins and predict a discrete category. for multimodal actions, researchers often favor discretization, turning a continuous-valued problem into classification. but the computational cost can be very high, especially in high-dimensional spaces. classification-based control often predicts just the next action, whereas we would prefer to predict several steps together. that introduces the need for consistency across a continuous action sequence. the challenge is to balance computational cost with high-dimensional continuous control. return to the driving example. we can turn left or right, which we can think of as controlling the steering wheel—a single control dimension. divide that dimension into 100 bins and ask a neural network to choose one. in principle, that works, and classification is manageable for one dimension. but consider a robot manipulator with six degrees of freedom, or seven including the gripper opening. if each dimension is discretized into, say, 1,000 bins, the total number of combinations is the product across all dimensions. the cost becomes enormous and grows exponentially with dimensionality. technical note: this exponential cost refers to explicitly enumerating joint combinations across dimensions. factorized or autoregressive classification can avoid that full enumeration; not all discrete-action methods have the same cost. there is also the earlier consistency problem. a viable driving trajectory goes continuously left around the tree, or continuously right around it. we can predict one step at a time, but that may cause oscillation: after moving a little left, the next prediction might favor right, then left again. this is action inconsistency. even when we intend to commit to turning left, the network retains some probability of choosing right, making its decisions hesitant and alternating. because joint classification over high-dimensional spaces is expensive, such approaches may be limited to predicting one step. adding more future steps increases the dimensionality further until the method becomes impractical. what we want is a method that can predict whole sequences in high-dimensional continuous control. we can directly predict the next 20 or 100 steps, committing to left or right, rather than predicting a step, executing it, and only then deciding what comes next. in the paper's receding-horizon controller, only part of the predicted sequence is executed before new observations are used to generate another sequence; the robot is not committed to running the entire prediction open-loop. training stability compared with policies based on other generative models, a particularly important feature of diffusion policy is its very stable training process. chi elaborated: robot action generation broadly uses three types of methods—direct regression, classification and generative models. regression treats the neural network as a function that takes an image and outputs an action. it is the most common approach and is used by most reinforcement-learning systems, but it has the problems we discussed earlier. classification generates actions by predicting categories, as described above. generative models can, in principle, predict continuous multimodal distributions, but many are unstable to train. diffusion-based methods have an important advantage: training is very stable. that helps explain their success in image generation compared with gans at the time. gans produced some good academic results, but turning them into products was difficult. training an effective gan often required extensive hyperparameter tuning before you could obtain a usable generator. diffusion methods can achieve performance comparable to gans while being much more stable to train. across a fairly wide range of parameter choices, the generator will usually produce results. they may not be optimal, but the method generally works. that stability also helps explain why stable diffusion and other image generators can be trained on enormous datasets. with less stable methods at that scale, unusual problems may emerge partway through training and prevent further optimization. 5. other questions from the interview how does diffusion policy relate to reinforcement learning and imitation learning? two common approaches to robot manipulation are reinforcement learning and imitation learning. diffusion policy does not conflict with either; it can be used in both. it is a policy formulation for mapping inputs such as images to corresponding actions. in our paper, we use imitation learning: humans teleoperate the robot, we collect demonstrations and learn a policy from them. the process begins with people remotely controlling a sequence of actions, which is then transferred to autonomous robot execution. inputs include images from the past few frames, while outputs predict future actions. many reinforcement-learning researchers generate large amounts of data in simulation. to accelerate training, the rl policy often takes low-dimensional underlying state information rather than images as input. those states may not be available in the real world, so the policy cannot directly drive the deployed robot. researchers can then use the rl policy’s demonstrations to train an image-based imitation policy, a process called distillation. here, the expert being imitated is an rl agent rather than a human. that is another possible application. how does training differ between manipulation and locomotion? reinforcement learning tends to work better for locomotion, where the sim-to-real gap is relatively easier to address. for manipulation, a major difficulty is closing that gap. manipulation requires modeling not only the robot’s own physics, but also complex environments and the objects it handles. those objects have different centers of mass, friction and dynamics. accurately simulating all of them is difficult, and available simulations may be imprecise or slow. for locomotion, much of the external environment can be treated as rigid, so some of its physical details are less important. researchers can devote more effort to an accurate model of the robot itself and more sophisticated physics engines. that helps explain why rl has been more successful in locomotion than in manipulation deployed on physical robots. what are the current limitations and future directions? the largest problem today is not the policy itself but the data. training data is crucial for executing a particular task. we have accumulated some teleoperated demonstrations, but deploying a practical application—for example, a home robot that washes dishes—requires a much larger and more diverse dataset, on a scale closer to chatgpt’s, to ensure robustness across different homes. the biggest challenge is collecting large amounts of diverse data efficiently. that is the key next research step. we hope that collection and training at greater scale will address current problems, while recognizing that new challenges may emerge as the dataset grows. 6. some reflections direct conversations with researchers are a format i have long wanted to try, hoping to make frontier research and its possibilities understandable to more people. i put it off because i worried that my grasp of the fundamentals was not deep enough and that i would ask very amateur questions. for this first attempt, i am especially grateful to chi for patiently answering so many of those questions and offering detailed suggestions on the wording of the finished article. i learned a great deal from our conversation. recently, i have organized what i have learned about robot learning into notes and shared them through my wechat account, receiving encouraging responses from readers. thank you to everyone who reads my work. writing never came naturally to me: chinese language was my weak subject at school, and composition was the subject i disliked most. i never imagined that i would write for other people. some investor friends ask how i can stay so focused on one field. there are many external reasons, but personally i am curious about whether general-purpose robots will arrive, when they will arrive and how. when studying other sectors, i often learned in order to make an investment. with robot learning, the order is reversed: i seek answers in frontier research, and along the way meet excellent people and discover promising startups. i have recently been reading wu jun’s the road to university. one passage particularly resonates with me: “education is a lifelong undertaking. we need not worry about losing at the starting line, because most people stop running halfway through, leaving opportunities for those who keep going. a person who knows how to learn will discover their interests as they grow older. if they can still keep learning then, their learning will become purposeful and focused.” one defining feature of investing is the need to keep learning continuously, and that also pushes me to continue. the enthusiasm around robotics startups and investment has cooled somewhat recently, and may cool further in 2024, the year following this article. but for someone truly interested in the field, how much does the market’s temperature matter? references diffusion policy project page: cheng chi’s website: russ scaling solve robotics?: perspectives from corl 2023”（通过在非常大的数据集上训练大型神经网络是否是解决机器人问题的可行途径？）直击我的一系列问题，我也迫不及待地将这篇文章翻译出来分享给大家。 这篇文章的主要内容来自于corl2023一个workshop：deployable@corl2023的一个辩论环节。辩论参与者都是robot learning和机器人控制领域的大佬（有的要称为巨佬）。这个辩论的议题是：is scaling enough to deploy general-purpose robots?（大模型方法是否适用于机器人行业？）正方辩手：sergey levine@ucb，chealse finn@stanford，russ tedrake@mit；反方辩手：stefan schaal，scott suindersma@bd以及emo todorov@uw。主持人：王小龙。 考虑到易读性的问题，在听了两遍视频内容的基础上，我对nishanth j. kumar的原文做了一些再编辑，感兴趣的读者可以在reference部分找到辩论的youtube视频和b站视频以及nishanth j. kumar的文章链接。 以下为本文目录 👇 1.辩论参与者的简介 2.正方观点 3.反方观点 4.其他相关论点 5.一些想法 1. 辩论参与者简介 认为大模型方法可以在机器人领域奏效的正方辩手都是robot learning领域的大佬： sergey levine目前是uc berkeley电气工程与计算机科学系的副教授，同时是rail(robotic ai&learning lab@bair)实验室主任。除了在berkeley的教职，levine也是google brain的研究员，他也参与了google知名的机器人大模型palm-e，rt1和rt2。他在uc berkely完成了计算机科学博士学位，师从pieter abbeel。 chelsea finn是stanford计算机科学与电气工程系的助理教授。她的实验室iris通过大规模的机器人互动研究智能，并与sail（斯坦福人工智能实验室）和ml group（机器学习团队）有合作关系。他还在谷歌的google brain团队工作。她对机器人和其他智能体通过学习和互动来发展广泛智能行为的能力感兴趣。他在uc berkely完成了计算机科学博士学位，师从sergey levine，本科毕业于mit。 russ tedrake是麻省理工学院（mit）的电气工程与计算机科学、航空航天学以及机械工程的教授，是计算机科学与人工智能实验室（csail）机器人中心的主任，也是mit团队参与darpa机器人挑战的领导者，是mit robot locomotion group的负责人。russ还担任toyota research institute (tri) 副总裁。russ于1999年在密歇根大学安娜堡分校获得计算机工程学士学位，并于2004年在mit获得电气工程和计算机科学博士学位，师从sebastian seung。russ tedrake在控制领域有很多工作，近些年，他的主要研究兴趣在于把系统理论的方法应用到操控机器人上。 认为大模型方法无法直接应用于机器人领域的辩手大多是机器人控制理论和基于模型控制领域的大佬： scott kuindersma是波士顿动力公司的研究科学家，也是atlas团队的负责人。此前，他曾是哈佛大学的工程与计算机科学助理教授，是harvard agile robotics lab的主任。他曾在mit的robot locomotion group进行博士后研究。他的工作重点是利用最优控制算法在移动机器人中实现高性能的行为。 stefan todorov是uw运动控制实验室的副教授兼主任，他引入了最优控制作为生物运动的正式解释框架。他是mujoco物理引擎的主要开发者。emo todorov在mit完成了他的博士学位，曾在ucl的盖茨比计算神经科学单位做博士后研究，他是2004年斯隆神经科学奖学金的获得者。重点是开发更强大的最优控制方法，并将其应用于更难的问题。他的研究重点是对动物和机器人的复杂运动控制，开发更强大的最优控制方法。 2. 通过在非常大的数据集上训练大型神经网络可以解决机器人问题（正方观点） scaling在cv和nlp领域被验证有非常好的效果，那么在机器人领域也同样可以取得好的效果：chelsea finn指出，最近，通过在极大的数据语料库上训练大型模型，取得了前所未有的惊人效果以及“涌现”能力，gpt4-v和sam这样最新模型的效果有目共睹。训练大型模型的基本方法是通用的，它并不是针对nlp或cv领域独有的，既然它被证明在一些领域有效，那么它理应对其他领域（比如机器人）也有效。 目前已经有很多进展可以证明scaling在机器人领域很可能会有效：chelsea finn提出deepmind近期的rt-2工作，可以证明单一模型在大量机器人数据上训练可以得到泛化能力；russ tedrkake指出最近的diffusion policies论文也显示了令人惊讶的能力；sergey levine指出他的团队在构建和部署导航用途的机器人通用基础模型方面取得了不错的进展。虽然这些工作都比较初期，使用相对较小的模型和相对较少的数据进行训练（和gpt4比），但似乎有些苗头是扩大这些模型和数据集会指向更好的机器人学习结果。 数据、算力和基础模型的进展是机器人行业应该抓住的浪潮：这里的主要思想来自rich sutton的一篇很有影响里的论文：ai研究的历史表明，相对简单、能够随着数据规模扩大的算法总是胜过那些复杂却无法随数据规模扩大的算法。karol hausman在早期的职业演讲中提出的一个很好的类比是，对数据和算力的改进就像一场浪潮，这是技术进步的结果。无论人们是否喜欢，都会有更多的数据和更好的算力。人们可以选择顺应这场浪潮，也可以选择忽略它。对机器人行业，顺应这场浪潮意味着利用在nlp和cv领域已经取得成功的大规模预训练这套方法用于机器人任务。 大型模型是机器人获得“常识”能力的最佳途径，而这种能力贯穿整个机器人学：russ tedrake还提到了一个观点，“常识”几乎贯穿了所有的机器人任务。以一个例子来说，想象一下一个机器人的任务是将一个杯子放到桌子上。即使忽略寻找和定位杯子的困难，这个任务本身也充满了许多微妙之处。如果桌子上一团糟，机器人必须先移动其他物体以腾出空间。如果杯子掉到地板上，机器人需要捡起它、重新定位，并将其放回桌子上。如果杯子里有液体，机器人还必须小心，以免它洒出来。这些看似小问题实际上经常发生，而且它们通常是任务成功与失败之间的关键因素。通过在大量数据上训练大型模型，我们可以使机器人具备这种“常识”推理的能力，从而更好地完成各种任务。 3. 通过在非常大的数据集上训练大型神经网络无法解决机器人问题（反方观点） 虽然关于将scaling作为解决机器人问题的实际方案的争论有很多。有趣的是，几乎没有人直接否认将这种方法应用在机器人领域，理论上可能奏效。相反，大多数论点可归结为以下两种情况之一：（1）认为这种方法在实践中简直是不切实际的，以及（2）认为即使它确实有点奏效，也不会真正‘解决’机器人学。 （1）认为这种方法在实践中简直是不切实际的 目前没有大规模的机器人数据，而且也没有明确的获得途径：数据问题几乎是每个大规模机器人学研究中的最大问题。互联网上有大量的cv和nlp数据，但完全没有任何机器人数据。快速收集庞大的机器人数据集需要时间、金钱和合作，即使能做到也无法与互联网上拥有的海量cv和nlp数据量相比。cv和nlp之所以能获得如此多的数据，是因为它们有一个令人难以置信的‘数据飞轮’：几十亿人连接并使用互联网。收集一个非常大的机器人学数据集相当困难，无法获得大数据集可能会使这种扩展方法在机器人领域的应用变得无望。 机器人有不同的实体：收集非常大的机器人学数据集的另一个挑战是，机器人有各种各样的形状、大小和形态。发送给波士顿动力spot机器人的输出控制动作与发送给kuka iiwa机械臂的动作完全不同。机器人实体的多样性意味着可能需要针对机器人的类型来收集数据，这使得上述数据收集问题变得更加困难。 机器人面对的人类环境变化极大：要使机器人真正‘通用’，它必须能够在任何人类可能希望将其置于其中的实际环境中操作。这意味着在可能出现的任何家庭、工厂或办公楼中操作。收集到所有人类生活空间的数据集似乎是不切实际的。目前的做法是只收集一部分空间的数据，其余的将由泛化来处理。然而，我们并不知道这种泛化能力需要多少数据才能启动，而且它可能也是不切实际的庞大。 在如此大规模的机器人数据集上训练模型可能会消耗大量算力：毫无疑问，训练大型基础模型是昂贵的，无论是从金钱还是能源消耗的角度。gpt-4v，openai目前最大的基础模型，据称耗资超过1亿美元，消耗了5000万千瓦时的电力。这远远超出任何学术实验室目前能够承受的预算和资源，而机器人大模型训练需要消耗的算力、能源和资金可能会再次激增一个或更多数量级。谁又能最终承担的起呢？ （2）即使它在cv/nlp中效果一样，也不能解决机器人学问题 99.x%可靠性问题：google robotics的vincent vanhoucke提出了一个断言：大多数机器人学习方法无法用于任何实际任务，原因是现实世界的工业和家庭应用通常需要99.x%以上的准确性和可靠性。机器人学习算法目前尚未达到这一水平。大多数学术论文中呈现的结果最多达到80%的成功率，这和99.x%的门槛看似接近但有本质区别：从99%往100%需要的努力是呈指数级增长的，这可能需要scaling以外一整套全新的技术。 即使在cv和nlp领域，现有的大型模型也无法达到99.x%，但这并不妨碍这两个领域已经可以有很好的应用，chatgpt偶尔一本正经胡说八道并不会产生很大的负面影响。但对机器人行业，即使scaling套路可以让机器人行业达到nlp行业现有成就，也不意味着机器人可以被实际部署到人类环境中。纯软件应用和涉及硬件应用对可靠性和准确性的要求有本质区别，硬件系统单次失效成本远高于软件系统，意味着对硬件系统的可靠性要求远高于软件系统。 自动驾驶行业的经验：自动驾驶汽车公司尝试过这种方法，但尚未完全成功。许多自动驾驶汽车公司，比如特斯拉，尝试通过在大量数据上训练这样一个端到端的大模型来实现5级自动驾驶，他们拥有训练模型所需的资源，资金和数据。特别是特斯拉在实际部署的10几万辆汽车中，不断收集并注释数据。尽管如此，特斯拉迄今尚未能生产出5级自动驾驶系统。这并不是说他们的方法根本不起作用，它能够处理大量驾驶情况，然而，它远未达到99.x%的可靠性。 此外，数据似乎表明特斯拉的方法比waymo或cruise表现得差得多，后者都使用更模块化的系统。这或许证明了大规模机器学习方法很难克服99.x%问题。此外，考虑到自动驾驶是通用机器人学的一个特殊案例，特斯拉的案例应该让我们对大规模模型方法作为机器人学的完整解决方案产生怀疑，特别是在中期。 机器人任务long-horizon的问题：机器人的很多任务都需要经历一系列正确的动作，而这些任务通常都是长期的（long-horizon）。比如，想要用一个机器人制作一杯茶，需要依次进行很多步骤，如烧水、倒热水、放茶包等。如果我们训练一个模型，让它根据图像输出电机扭矩指令，那么在这个简单的任务中，我们可能需要以每秒40次的频率发送扭矩指令给7个电机。假设这个泡茶的任务需要5分钟，那就需要发送 7*40*60*5=84000 次正确的扭矩指令。这还仅仅是针对一个静止的机械臂的情况，如果机器人是移动的，或者有多个机械臂，问题就更加复杂了。对于大多数任务来说，随着时间的推移，误差往往会逐渐累积，这就是为什么即使是能够生成长篇文本的大型语言模型（llms），也无法完全创作连贯的小说或故事的原因之一：对真实预测的微小偏差会随时间累积，最终导致在长时间尺度上出现极大的偏差。因此，即使是性能相当不错的模型，也可能在解决这些长期任务方面面临很大的挑战。 4. 其他相关论点 稳健地部署基于学习的方法 机器人领域反对基于学习的方法的一个常见论点是缺乏理论保证和可解释性。人类目前对神经网络理论知之甚少，他的运行原理是黑盒，我们不太清楚它们为什么学得好，更重要的是，我们对它们在不同情况下会输出什么值没有任何保证。另一方面，在机器人学中广泛使用的大多数经典控制和规划方法都内置了各种理论保证。在确保系统安全性方面，这些通常非常有用。 针对这一点，sergey levine指出，大多数控制的保证对机器人面临的任务并不是那么有用。正如他所说：“self-driving car companies aren’t worried about controlling the car to drive in a straight line, but rather about a situation in which someone paints a sky onto the back of a truck and drives in front of the car”，从而混淆了感知系统。sergey levine的观点是：参考自动驾驶的经验，费劲的不是车辆的controller，而是应付现实世界的复杂性。 此外，波士顿动力的scott kuindersma谈到了他们如何在他们的机器人上部署基于强化学习的控制器，并通过严格的模拟和实际测试获得他们所需的信心和保证。总的来说，虽然人们认为理论保证和可解释性是重要的，并鼓励研究人员继续努力研究它们，但他们并不认为学习系统缺乏保证就意味着它们不能被稳健地部署。 部署人机协同系统 emo todorov指出，现有成功的机器学习系统，如codex和chatgpt，之所以表现良好，仅因为人类与其交互并清理其输出。以使用codex进行编码为例：它的目的不是直接生成可运行、无错误的代码，而是作为程序员的智能自动完成，从而使整个人机团队比单独操作更高效。因此，这些模型不必达到99.x%的性能阈值，因为在部署过程中人类可以帮助纠正任何问题。正如emo所说：“人类是宽容的，物理则不是”。 chelsea finn对此表示基本认同，强调所有成功部署和有用的机器学习系统都需要人类参与，这可能是已部署的机器人学习系统需要采取的操作方式。在机器人领域也是类似，让人类参与机器人操作并非像在其他领域那样简单，但这可以解决机器人行业面临的99.x%的问题。 不需要收集那么多真实世界的数据来进行扩展 关于如何克服真实世界数据的瓶颈，无需实际收集更多真实世界数据的问题，其中一些人认为快速、逼真的模拟器可能在这里非常关键，在模拟环境中训练机器人策略，然后将其转移到真实世界（sim2real）。另一组人认为，人们可以利用现有的视觉、语言和视频数据，然后只需“撒入”一些机器人数据。谷歌最近的rt-2模型展示了如何使用在互联网规模的视觉和语言数据上训练的大型模型，然后仅在较小的机器人数据集上进行微调，可以在机器人任务上产生不错的性能。 将基于模型的控制和基于学习的方法结合起来 波士顿动力的scott kuindersma提到：基于模型的控制有助于学习（反之亦然）。他坚信在短期到中期内，实现可靠的现实世界系统的最佳途径涉及将学习与经典方法结合起来。一些论文探讨了经典控制和规划与基于学习的方法结合使用如何使能比任何系统单独更多的功能。总体而言，大多数人似乎认为这种“中间道路”非常有前途，特别是在短期到中期内，但在长期内，纯学习或某种暂未发现的全新方法可能是终极答案。 通过大规模数据集来扩大学习的方向 尽管有关大模型能否完全解决机器人学的各种争论，大多数人似乎都同意在机器人学习中进行大模型尝试是一个值得探讨的有前途的方向。即使它不能完全解决机器人学，它仍然可能在一些我们一直陷入困境的难题上取得重大进展。此外，正如russ tedrake所指出的，小心谨慎地追求这个方向可能会为我们提供有关通用机器人问题以及当前学习算法以及它们为何效果如此良好的有用见解。 不要忽视经典控制等其他方向 即使是扩展方法的最热心支持者也明确表示他们不认为每个人都应该在此工作。在同一个篮子里放入整个机器人学习社区的所有鸡蛋可能是个坏主意，特别是考虑到有很多理由相信扩展不能完全解决机器人学。经典机器人技术已经取得了相当大的进展，并导致了许多成功和可靠的部署：推动它们前进或将它们与学习技术结合使用可能是正确的方式，特别是在短期到中期。 更加关注移动操作和易于使用的系统 vincent vanhoucke提出了这样一个观察，即今年corl的大多数论文都局限于桌面操作。虽然桌面上有很多困难的问题，但当机器人移动时，事情通常会变得更加复杂，尤其是其相机视野。另外，sergey levine观察到llm之所以如此令人兴奋并得到广泛采用，很大程度上是因为它们非常易于使用：特别是对于非专业人士来说。人们不必了解训练llm的细节，也不必进行任何繁琐的设置，就可以提示和使用这些模型进行自己的任务。大多数机器人学习方法目前远未达到这一点。它们通常需要对其内部运作有相当深入的了解才能使用，并涉及非常重要的设置。也许思考如何使机器人学习系统更易于使用和广泛适用，可能有助于提高这些方法的采用和潜在的可扩展性。 更加坦率地对待那些不起作用的事情 许多机器人学习方法并未充分报告负面结果，这导致了许多不必要的重复努力。此外，也许从期望其有效但实际上效果不佳的事物的持续失败中可能会出现模式，这可能会为学习算法提供新的见解。目前没有足够的激励让研究人员在论文中报告这样的负面结果，但大多数人似乎都赞成设计出一种。 应该尝试做一些全新的东西 有一些人指出当前的所有方法，无论是基于学习的还是经典控制论，在许多方面都是不令人满意的。每种方法似乎都有一些缺点，很可能有一套完全不同的方法最终解决了机器人学，需要学界继续探索。 5. 一些感想 最近大半年，中国创投圈、机器人产业圈、学术圈都处于主动或被动亢奋状态。投资人圈：在2023年仅有的几个赛道里，具身智能无疑是最热门的赛道。曾经的文娱、消费、web3投资人争相出手，火急火燎贴上具身智能标签，各种所谓“水下”项目流窜在投资人的微信和短会里；机器人产业圈：一个2022年还在谷底的行业，到了2023年坐过山车一样来到了风口浪尖，一些反应快的，已经迅速华丽转身具身智能或人形机器公司。学术圈：要说这波风口里，最“遭殃”可能是清华、北大、上交的助理教授们，听说有投资人在清华门口某咖啡馆，冲了5万块的会员卡，专门约教授；甚至远在北美的robot learning领域的学者也时不时被国内投资人轮番约聊，当然，我也是其中之一 [表情] 。 当然，不同背景和知识体系的人相互交流是件好事，信息和知识的流通可以让大家对通用机器人可行性和可能性的认知进一步对齐。但在这有点浮躁的现阶段，早期投资的模糊正确要怎么寻找？看的好的团队，估值都很高；谈到落地场景，又是一声叹息；当然还有推项目内部会遇到的各种问题。在连着一个月每周出差，当天来回式的出差之后，身心俱疲的投资人还是决定做回公众号主理人。 在看待通用机器人这个大方向，我有一个非常坚定的观点是，学术界和大企业可以不对终端产品的交付负责，但作为创业公司，如果没有机器人终端交付的思维，是无法生存的。机器人本质上是一个蓝领，他的价值来自于他对特定任务的完成。如果一个创业公司，一味描绘他在算法上有多牛，而忽视硬件和系统整合能力，缺乏产品交付视角，那注定无法在机器人行业成功。 在达到通用机器人的道路上，还有诸多科学问题没有解决，它并不是个两三年内可以看到的东西。我们梦想的那个robot在成为现实之前，首先它得先是个机器人，然后才有可能成为一个通用机器人。什么意思，具身智能决策-感知-执行，三个环节现在最大的短板不是决策和感知，而是执行，涉及到机器人执行，得去一个个场景的啃，没有细节的交付能力没有客户愿意为产品买单。硬件在场景解决上的容错率很低，这个可能是涉及硬件的ai和纯软件ai最大的区别。 这波机器人的浪潮，所有人的目标都是通用机器人（通用机器人不等于通用人形机器人），但这个目标更像是一个北极星，如果一味仰望星空，注定成为炮灰。机器人作为蓝领，他的创造者既要脚踏实地，又要仰望星空。作为这个赛道的投资人或创业者，期待我们都能在仰望星空和脚踏实地之间，寻找一个立足点。 references： 文章链接： foundation models bring us general-purpose robots? a full account of the corl 2023 scaling debate: data, embodiment, reliability, long-horizon control, human intervention and an investor’s reflections. robot learning & foundation models after the unprecedented achievements of chatgpt and other foundation models in natural language processing and computer vision, robot foundation models became a major topic in 2023. building a general-purpose robot—one that can competently and robustly perform many useful tasks in any home or office—is perhaps a shared ultimate goal of ai and robotics. given the success of large models in language and vision, could the same paradigm help us reach that goal in robotics? recently, as i have evaluated startups, promoted projects, convinced myself and then tried to convince others, a series of questions has kept circling in my head. what is driving the growing excitement around embodied intelligence in 2023? has there been an algorithmic breakthrough? why have so many computer vision researchers moved into robot learning? will collecting ever more data really work in robotics? llms and vlms mainly advance perception and decision-making, but seem to have less impact on physical execution. how do we make execution reliable? robotics has to confront shortcomings in actuation and demanding reliability requirements. can the paradigm that succeeded in vision and language really transfer to this field? a few days ago, while browsing twitter, i found nishanth j. kumar's article, will scaling solve robotics? perspectives from corl 2023. it asks whether training large neural networks on very large datasets is a viable route to solving robotics, and directly addresses many of my questions. i wanted to translate and share it immediately. much of this article draws on the debate at deployable@corl2023. the participants are leading researchers in robot learning and control. the question was: 'is scaling enough to deploy general-purpose robots?' arguing the affirmative were sergey levine of uc berkeley, chelsea finn of stanford and russ tedrake of mit. arguing the negative were stefan schaal, scott kuindersma of boston dynamics and emo todorov of the university of washington. xiaolong wang moderated. these are their debate roles, not an assertion that their research belongs exclusively to one camp. to make the discussion easier to read, i edited kumar's account after listening to the debate video twice. the references include the youtube and bilibili recordings, along with his original article. the following is my chinese article rendered into english, including my framing and reflections, rather than a substitute for kumar's own original text. contents ↓ 1. introducing the participants 2. arguments for scaling 3. arguments against scaling as a complete solution 4. other points of discussion 5. some reflections the affirmative participants are prominent figures in robot learning. in this 2023 account, sergey levine is an associate professor in uc berkeley's department of electrical engineering and computer sciences and leads the robotic artificial intelligence and learning lab, rail, within bair. the original introduction also identifies him as a google brain researcher and notes his participation in palm-e, rt-1 and rt-2. editorial correction: the chinese original says he earned his phd at berkeley under pieter abbeel. his official biography states that he earned his computer science phd at stanford in 2014, not berkeley. chelsea finn is an assistant professor of computer science and electrical engineering at stanford. her iris lab studies intelligence through robotic interaction at scale and is affiliated with the stanford ai lab, sail, and the machine learning group. she has also worked with google brain. she is interested in how robots and other agents develop broadly intelligent behavior through learning and interaction. she earned her computer science phd at uc berkeley, working with sergey levine, and her undergraduate degree at mit. the positions described here provide the background to the 2023 debate. russ tedrake is a professor of electrical engineering and computer science, aeronautics and astronautics, and mechanical engineering at mit. he leads the robot locomotion group and led mit's entry in the darpa robotics challenge. the original introduction also describes his directorship of the csail center for robotics and his vice-presidential role at toyota research institute. he earned his bachelor's degree in computer engineering at the university of michigan, ann arbor, in 1999, and his eecs phd at mit in 2004 under sebastian seung. his work spans control, with a growing emphasis on applying systems-theoretic methods to robotic manipulation. this describes his role around the time of the debate, not a current employment update. the negative participants bring extensive experience in control theory and model-based robotics. scott kuindersma is introduced here as a research scientist at boston dynamics and a leader of the atlas team. previously, he was an assistant professor of engineering and computer science at harvard, where he directed the harvard agile robotics lab, and a postdoctoral researcher in mit's robot locomotion group. his work uses optimal control to produce high-performance behavior in mobile robots. stefan schaal is a german-american computer scientist working in robotics, machine learning, autonomous systems and computational neuroscience. he has been a professor at the university of southern california in computer science, neuroscience and biomedical engineering, and a founding director of the max planck institute for intelligent systems. his work on dynamic movement primitives, or dmps, has been influential in robot learning. he is a towering figure in model-based control as well as an influential researcher in learning. emo todorov is introduced in the original as an associate professor and director of the movement control laboratory at the university of washington. he helped establish optimal control as a framework for explaining biological movement and is a principal developer of mujoco. he earned his phd at mit, did postdoctoral work at ucl's gatsby computational neuroscience unit, and received a sloan research fellowship in neuroscience in 2004. his research develops powerful optimal-control methods for complex movement in animals and robots. this is the historical background presented for the debate; the lab's current page is an archive rather than a current faculty listing. 2. arguments for solving robotics by training large networks on large datasets scaling has worked remarkably well in vision and language, so it should also work well in robotics. chelsea finn points to unprecedented progress and emergent capabilities from models trained on enormous corpora, including gpt-4v and sam. the basic training approach is general rather than unique to nlp or computer vision. since it has proved effective in those areas, finn’s argument is that it should work in other areas, such as robotics, too. there are already signs that scaling could help robotics. finn cites rt-2 as evidence that a single model trained with substantial robot data can generalize. tedrake points to the surprising capabilities of diffusion policies. levine discusses progress in building and deploying general-purpose navigation models. these are early results, with far smaller models and datasets than gpt-4, but they suggest that increasing scale may yield better robot learning. robotics should take advantage of the wave of data, compute and foundation models. the central idea is drawn from rich sutton’s influential essay, the bitter lesson: ai’s history shows relatively simple algorithms that scale with data always beating complex algorithms that do not scale. editorial clarification: this is the article’s formulation; sutton’s essay emphasizes computation and general methods such as search and learning, rather than a universal theorem about every dataset or algorithm. karol hausman's analogy is a technological wave. whether we like it or not, more data and better compute will arrive. we can ride that wave or ignore it. for robotics, riding it means exploring large-scale pretraining for physical tasks, building on what succeeded in language and vision. large models are the best route we have to the common sense needed throughout robotics. tedrake gives the example of putting a cup on a table. even setting aside the difficulty of finding and localizing the cup, the task contains subtleties. a cluttered table may require clearing space. a dropped cup must be retrieved and repositioned. a cup containing liquid must be handled without spilling. such details occur frequently and can determine success or failure. the affirmative argument is that training on large quantities of experience could help robots reason through these situations. 3. arguments against scaling as a complete solution to robotics interestingly, few participants reject the theoretical possibility that scaling could work in robotics. most objections fall into two categories: first, that it is simply impractical; second, that even if it works to some extent, it may not truly solve robotics. (1) the approach is simply impractical we do not have robot data at internet scale, nor a clear way to obtain it. this is the central problem in discussions of large-scale robot learning. the original puts this bluntly: the internet has enormous amounts of vision and language data, but no robot data at all. vision and language benefit from an incredible data flywheel: billions of people connecting to and using the internet. collecting an enormous robot dataset requires time, money and collaboration, and may still fall far short of those corpora. since important capabilities in other domains emerged only at scale, insufficient data could make this scaling approach hopeless in robotics. editorial clarification: the original says there is no robot data on the internet at all. public robot datasets existed in 2023; the issue is their scale, diversity and action coverage compared with web image and text data. robots have different embodiments. a command sent to boston dynamics' spot differs from a command sent to a kuka iiwa arm. robots vary in shape, size and morphology, so data may need to be collected or adapted for different robot types, making the collection problem harder. human environments vary enormously. a truly general-purpose robot must operate in the homes, factories and offices where people want to use it. collecting data from every possible space is impractical. we can sample some environments and rely on generalization for the rest, but we do not know how much data is needed for that generalization to emerge. the required amount may itself be impractically large. training on such a dataset could also demand enormous compute. foundation-model training is expensive in money and energy. the original article cites reported estimates of more than us$100 million and 50 million kilowatt-hours for gpt-4-related training, and asks whether robot models might require another order of magnitude or more. these figures are not independently verified official measurements, and should not be treated as established costs for gpt-4v specifically. the underlying question remains: such resources are beyond an academic lab's budget—who can afford the required scale? (2) even matching the success of vision and language may not solve robotics the 99.x% reliability problem. google robotics researcher vincent vanhoucke makes a provocative assertion: most robot learning methods cannot be deployed for any practical task, because real industrial and household applications typically demand reliability above 99.x%, beyond what most learned robot systems demonstrate. the discussion contrasts that requirement with most academic results topping out at 80% success. the remaining gap is qualitatively difficult: the effort required to go from 99% toward 100% increases exponentially, and may require an entirely new set of techniques beyond scaling. the assertion of exponentially increasing effort expresses the difficulty, rather than a proven universal scaling law or a success-rate figure applicable to every paper. existing vision and language models also fall short of such reliability, but can still be useful. the article argues that chatgpt’s occasional confident nonsense does not have a large negative impact, while hardware failures cost far more than software failures and thus demand much higher reliability. therefore, even reaching the present achievements of nlp would not automatically make a robot deployable. the relevant reliability requirement depends on the task; software errors can also have serious consequences, so the point is about the physical setting and its failure costs rather than all software being harmless. autonomous driving offers a cautionary example. companies such as tesla have tried to achieve level 5 autonomy by training an end-to-end large model on huge datasets, with the necessary money, compute and data from deployed cars. the original discussion describes data collection from more than 100,000 vehicles. yet in 2023, that had not produced level 5 autonomy. the approach could handle many situations, but was still far from 99.x% reliability, in the article’s assessment. this is a historical argument about deployment limits, not a current fleet-size report. the discussion also suggests that tesla's approach performed much worse than the more modular systems of waymo or cruise, raising doubts about whether scale alone overcomes the reliability problem. that is an argument made in the 2023 discussion, not a controlled comparison of equivalent deployments or a current assessment of those companies. autonomous driving is one particular physical application, so its experience gives reason to question scaling as a complete robotics solution, especially over the medium term. long-horizon tasks compound the challenge. making tea involves a sequence of operations, such as boiling water, pouring and adding a tea bag. imagine a policy sending torque commands to seven motors at 40 hz for five minutes. that is 7 × 40 × 60 × 5 = 84,000 individual motor commands. add mobility or more arms and the system becomes more complex. errors can accumulate over time, as they can in an llm generating a long story. the original argues that even llms able to produce long passages cannot yet write entirely coherent novels or stories, because small prediction deviations accumulate into large departures over long timescales, so even a capable local predictor may struggle with a lengthy task. the arithmetic illustrates how many outputs are involved; it does not imply that the commands are independent trials or that every tiny deviation necessarily causes failure. feedback and replanning matter. deploying learned systems robustly a common objection to learned robotics is the lack of theoretical guarantees and interpretability. neural networks remain difficult to understand completely, and their outputs under unfamiliar conditions are hard to guarantee. classical planning and control methods often offer guarantees under explicit assumptions, which can be valuable for safety. levine responds that many conventional control guarantees do not address the failures that matter most in real applications. his example is a truck with a sky painted on its rear, confusing an autonomous vehicle's perception—not the comparatively straightforward task of controlling the car along a straight line. the challenge is dealing with the world's complexity, not only stabilizing the low-level controller. kuindersma describes deploying rl-based controllers on boston dynamics robots and building confidence through rigorous simulation and real-world testing. the participants value theoretical guarantees and interpretability, and encourage further research, but do not conclude that their absence makes robust deployment impossible. testing-based confidence and formal guarantees are different forms of evidence. deploying human–machine teams todorov points out that successful systems such as codex and chatgpt work well only because people interact with them and clean up their outputs. in his example, codex is intended as intelligent autocomplete for a programmer, rather than a way to generate runnable, error-free code directly; the human–machine team is more efficient than either working alone. these models need not meet the 99.x% threshold because people can correct problems during use. human correction changes the performance requirement on the model itself. his point is that people can tolerate and fix some mistakes, whereas physical processes do not forgive an incorrect command in the same way. finn broadly agrees that all successfully deployed and useful machine learning systems require human participation and could also be part of deployed robot learning. human involvement is harder to arrange in robotics than in some software applications, but she argues it can solve robotics’ 99.x% problem. it does not automatically guarantee 99.x% reliability without an effective intervention mechanism. scaling may not require collecting all the data in the real world there are ways to address the real-data bottleneck. fast, realistic simulators might let us train policies in simulation and transfer them to reality. existing visual, language and video data might also provide much of the prior knowledge, with a relatively small amount of robot experience added. rt-2 illustrates how internet-scale vision–language pretraining combined with robot action training can support robot tasks. the original summarizes this as fine-tuning on a smaller robot dataset; rt-2's published method co-fine-tunes web and robot data. combining model-based control and learning kuindersma argues that model-based control can help learning, and vice versa. he firmly believes combining learning with classical techniques is the best route to reliable real-world systems over the short to medium term. research has shown that such combinations can enable capabilities neither approach provides alone. many participants see this middle route as promising. over the longer term, pure learning—or an approach not yet discovered—might turn out to be the answer. pursuing large-scale learning despite disagreement about whether scaling can solve everything, most participants see it as a promising research direction. even an incomplete solution could advance problems that have long resisted progress. tedrake also notes that pursuing it carefully may teach us about general-purpose robotics, current learning algorithms and why they work as well as they do. do not neglect classical control and other approaches even strong supporters of scaling do not think everyone should work on it. putting the entire robot learning community's effort into one approach would be risky, particularly when there are reasons to doubt its completeness. classical robotics has already enabled substantial, reliable deployments. advancing those methods or combining them with learning may be the right route, especially in the short to medium term. pay more attention to mobile manipulation and usable systems vanhoucke observes that most corl 2023 papers stay within tabletop manipulation. there are difficult problems there, but mobility adds complexity, particularly when the camera view changes. levine also observes that much of the excitement and adoption around llms comes from ease of use. nonexperts can prompt them without understanding training details or performing elaborate setup. robot learning methods are far from that experience: using them often requires extensive knowledge of their internals and significant setup. making them easier to use and more broadly applicable could improve adoption and help scaling. be more candid about what does not work robot learning papers often underreport negative results, causing needless repetition of failed efforts. patterns in repeated failures could also provide new insight into algorithms. researchers currently have little incentive to report such outcomes, but many participants support creating better incentives. try something entirely new some participants note that current approaches, whether learned or classical, remain unsatisfactory in several ways. a quite different family of methods might eventually solve the problem. continued exploration beyond today's familiar alternatives is therefore important. over the past six months of 2023, china's investment, robotics and academic communities have been swept up in enthusiasm, willingly or otherwise. for investors, embodied intelligence is unquestionably the hottest of the few remaining investment themes in 2023. people from entertainment, consumer and web3 investing are rushing in, adopting the label as supposedly undiscovered startups circulate through wechat and brief meetings. the robotics industry, still near a low point in 2022, has suddenly found itself riding a wave; some quick-moving companies have recast themselves as embodied ai or humanoid businesses. in academia, the assistant professors at tsinghua, peking university and shanghai jiao tong may feel the pressure most. i have heard of an investor putting rmb50,000 onto a cafe membership near tsinghua just to meet professors. even robot learning researchers in north america are repeatedly approached by chinese investors. of course, i am one of those investors too [watermelon reaction emoji: watching the spectacle] . dialogue between people with different backgrounds is valuable. sharing information and knowledge can help us understand what general-purpose robots might make possible. but in this restless moment, how do we find the approximately right early-stage investment? strong teams command high valuations; discussion of real deployment brings sighs; promoting a project internally raises its own problems. after a month of weekly trips, often out and back on the same day, this exhausted investor decided to return to being the author of a public account. i hold one firm view about general-purpose robotics. academic groups and large companies may explore without being responsible for delivering a final product. a startup cannot survive without thinking about delivery. a robot is fundamentally a blue-collar worker: its value comes from completing particular tasks. a startup that talks only about brilliant algorithms, neglecting hardware, system integration and the ability to deliver a product, is destined to fail in robotics. many scientific problems remain on the road to general-purpose robots. in my view at the time of writing, this is not something we will see fully realized in two or three years. before our imagined general-purpose robot can exist, it first has to be a functioning robot. what do i mean? among decision-making, perception and execution, i see execution as the largest bottleneck. it requires working through individual applications in detail. customers will not pay without that practical delivery capability. physical products allow little tolerance for failures in the task, which may be the biggest difference between embodied ai and software-only ai. everyone in this wave seems to be aiming for a general-purpose robot—which does not necessarily mean a general-purpose humanoid. but that goal is more like a north star. anyone who only gazes at the stars is destined to become cannon fodder. the people building robots need to remain grounded while keeping the distant goal in sight. as investors and founders in this field, i hope we can find a place to stand between those two perspectives. references original article https://nishanthjkumar.com/will-scaling-solve-robotics-perspectives-from-corl-2023/

dexterous-manipulation-research-review: 将机器人的手牵向人类的手：灵巧操作华人论文综述 梳理灵巧操作研究，从机械手、刚体与可变形物体操作到模仿学习和遥操作。 感知与灵巧操作 在智人的发展历史中，聪明的大脑和灵巧的双手起到了至关重要的作用，人类灵巧的五指手可以操作工具，让世界变得丰富多彩。在通用机器人成为可能的路上，除了大脑，我认为最大的制约是机器人能否拥有一双和人类一样灵巧的手。那么公元2023年，机器人的双手到底可以完成什么样的任务呢？ 带着好奇，我浏览了上百篇近两三年关于机器人手部操作（hand-based manipulation）（夹爪或多指）的论文，梳理了在这个细分领域有较多工作华人学者，也将呈现在一些常见任务上机器人手部能达到的最好成果。 在手部操作上，本文重点探讨偏灵巧操作的robot learning，比如利用强化学习在模拟器中训练策略，然后迁移到物理机器人上，相较传统方法有更强的通用性。尽管非常希望覆盖全面，但不免遗漏一些优秀的工作和学者，也欢迎读者留言指教。 灵巧操纵一直以来都是机器人领域的挑战。虽然机器学习技术在模拟环境中显示出一些潜力，但结果大多仅限于模拟，这主要归因于缺乏合适的硬件。机器人手部常用的选择是两指（夹爪）和多指灵巧手，我们这里简单介绍一下高校科研常用的末端执行器选择。 夹爪：在进行一些基本的直线操作，夹爪是常用的末端执行器，硬件门槛不高。 多指灵巧手：科研界常用的多指灵巧手有三指d'claw，四指allegro和五指shandow hand。 除了上面常用的多指灵巧手，一些实验室也会自己搭建硬件系统。比如cmu的助理教授deepak pathak团队的leap hand。其成本仅为allegro hand的1/8，他们还研发了软体灵巧手dash hand，成本均在2000美金以内。 其他可能选择的灵巧手有德国宇航的dlr hand，医疗级假肢bebionic hand，schunk svh hand, vincent hand。 国内做灵巧手的代表有哈工大刘宏教授团队，中科院自动化所王鹏团队，因时科技等。 3. 刚体操作 从物体的分类层面，常见的操作对象可以分为刚体（比如乐高、易拉罐等）、可行变物体（比如面团，布料等）和液体。因为刚体相对容易操作，所以很多涉及刚体的工作可以部署到物理机器人上。针对刚体的操作，学术界的一些研究方向包括手中物体重定位（简单理解就是按照特定方向拿东西）、非抓握操作（不用手拿而是用推或戳）、外部灵巧性操作（比如利用墙壁把箱子竖起来）、长时间（long horizon）灵巧操作（多动作连续操作完成一项任务）。所有这些学术名词对人类来说都是不值一提的手部动作，下面我们逐一看下机器人做到了什么程度。 手中物体重定向：手中物体的重新定向对于执行许多灵巧操纵任务是必要的，chen tao等人提出了一个在模拟中使用强化学习进行训练并在现实世界中进行评估的通用物体重新定向控制器。该控制器具有对未在训练中使用的新物体进行泛化的能力。由下向上的手持状态下重新定向悬浮的物体，手必须在重新定向过程中抵消重力。论文中使用的硬件是成本不到5000美元的开源组件。 "visual dexterity: in-hand dexterous manipulation from depth", by tao chen, megha tippur, siyang wu, vikash kumar, edward adelson, pulkit agrawal chen tao和jie xu的另一个工作提出了一个简单的无模型框架，在模拟器中学习在手朝上和手朝下的情况下重新定向物体，并展示了这些策略在两种情况下都能够重新定向超过2000个几何不同的物体。这些学习的策略在新物体上表现出强大的零次迁移性能。但这个工作仅在模拟器中实现，并未应用到物理世界的机器手上。这篇论文获得了2021 corl best paper。 “a system for general in-hand object re-orientation” bytao chen, jie xu, pulkit agrawal，corl 2021 (best paper award) 最近，英伟达联合宾大、加州理工和ut austin联合发布的eureka结合了大型语言模型和强化学习的研究成果，用gpt4来完善奖励函数，用强化学习来训练机器人控制器，实现了在虚拟器中五指手转笔、盘核桃等复杂的灵巧操作。 eureka: human-level reward design via coding large language models, by jason ma, et al，https://eureka-research.github.io/ 非抓握操作和外部灵巧性操作：当物体处于难以抓取的姿势时，例如书籍或其他大型平面物体水平放在桌子上时，进行抓取是一项具有挑战性的任务。针对这个问题，有两个方向的工作是非抓握操作和外部灵巧性操作。其中非抓握操作指在不需要抓取的情况下操作物体，比如用戳或者推的方式；外部灵巧性指利用外部环境帮助夹爪操作物体，比如将一个躺着的长方形的盒子推到墙边竖起来，再夹住窄边，夹爪学会利用墙壁将物体竖起来。david held团队的wenxuan zhou的很多工作涉及以夹爪为主的非抓握操作和外部灵巧性操作。清华大学的孙富春团队与德国洪堡大学张建伟团队在也有这个方面的工作，具体论文可以参看reference部分。这里我们展示wenxuan zhou一篇文章的视频来直观展示飞抓握操作和外部灵巧性操作。 “learning to grasp the ungraspable with emergent extrinsic dexterity” by wenxuan zhou, david held, corl 2022 对刚体的长时间灵巧操作（long-horizon） 你扔我接：你扔我接对人类很常见，但对机器人来说充满挑战：机器人需要以高速进行这些动态动作，精确协作，并与各种不同的物体互动。这个工作用机械臂和五指手作为硬件系统，使用多智能体强化学习在模拟环境中训练该系统，并进行sim2real转移以在真实机器人上部署。为了克服sim2real的差距，作者提供了多种新颖的算法设计，包括学习物体的轨迹预测模型。这样的模型可以帮助机器人捕手实时估计物体的运动轨迹，然后相应地做出反应。论文的一作binghao huang和yuanpei chen在灵巧操作方面有非常多出色的工作。 “dynamic handover: throw and catch with bimanual hands”， binghao huang*, yuanpei chen*, tianyu wang, yuzhe qin, yaodong yang, nikolay atanasov, xiaolong wang, corl 2023 拼乐高：灵巧手在拼乐高任务上面临着高维动作空间和长期任务的复杂组合动力学的挑战。stanford karen liu团队提出了一种基于强化学习（rl）的通用系统，它通过链接多个灵巧策略来实现长期任务目标。这个工作也有非常好的sim2real的迁移能力。 “sequential dexterity: chaining dexterous policies for long-horizon manipulation” by yuanpei chen, chen wang, li fei-fei, c. karen liu, corl 2023 在长时间（long-horizon）灵巧操作方面，腾讯roboticsx黄碧丹团队也有非常多优秀的工作，他们在2023年4月推出的机械臂搭配3指灵巧手演示的调酒工作非常惊艳。ut austin的朱玉可带领他的学生做了一个有趣的工作是煮泡面机器人，这个机器人的手用的是夹爪。这两个工作的相关视频在ai+robotics华人图谱可以找到。 4. 可行变物体操作 可形变物体的操作在我们的日常生活中有许多应用，例如捏面团和叠衣服。但对机器人来说，可行变物体的操作特别具有挑战：面团这类弹塑性物体，因为缺乏紧凑的状态表示，需要丰富的接触互动；布料因为褶皱，涉及很多遮挡问题的处理。在末端执行器的选择上，相比刚性物体，可行变物体的物理操作更多是以夹爪的形式进行，多指对面团这类物体的操作更多的是在仿真环境中进行的。下面我们挑几个典型的工作来看看机器人对可行变物体的操作上已经达到了什么程度。 穿衣服：3d空间对可变形布料进行复杂操纵对机器人来说是一个具有挑战的任务。过往的方法涉及大量假设，需要固定的服装和手臂姿势，泛化能力差。cmu david held团队的yufei wang在布料操作上有不少工作，他2023年的一篇工作可以对不同手臂姿势和不同服装的参与者穿衣服。 “one policy to dress them all: learning to dress people with diverse poses and garments” by yufei wang, zhanyi sun, zackory erickson*, david held*, rss 2023，https://sites.google.com/view/one-policy-dress 对可行变布料进行触觉推理：yufei wang的另一个工作使用视觉和机器人运动观测进行触觉推理（施加力的位置和大小）。 “visual haptic reasoning: estimating contact forces by observing deformable object interactions” by yufei wang, david held, zackory erickson, iros 2022 布料展开：如果我有一个机器人保姆，我最需要它做的家务就是套被套 [表情] ，在看了十几篇关于布料操作的论文后，我觉得十年内套被套这件事情，人类还是无法解放自己。哥伦比亚大学shuran song团队介绍了一种双机械臂协同可移动电吹风的方案，是目前我看到的叠衣服效率比较高的。dextairity是一个自监督学习框架，通过一系列抓取或基于气流的吹气动作来学习有效执行目标任务。通过使用封闭回路的吹气方案，系统根据视觉反馈不断调整吹气方向，以适应高度随机的动力学。这篇工作的一作 zhenjia xu本科毕业于上海交通大学，目前在shuran song团队读博，他也是后文会介绍的切牛油果文章roboninja的一作。 “dextairity: deformable manipulation can be a breeze” by zhenjia xu, cheng chi, benjamin burchifiel, eric cousineau, siyuan feng, shuran song, rss 2022, https://dextairity.cs.columbia.edu/ 面团操作 出于对面食的热爱，很多学者都在尝试用机器人揉面，切面，甚至包饺子。在物理世界中，面团操作大多是夹爪配合多工具组合，也有一些学者在仿真世界中用多指手对面团进行操作。到目前为止，机器人针对面团进行最复杂的操作是包饺子，饺子下锅之后会怎么样就不知道了 。 压面团：从rgb-d图像将一块面团铺展成特定形状的任务，对人类来说非常简单，但对机器人来说，如果没有固定的外部环境和编程好的运动轨迹，将一个面团压成一个面饼是非常难的任务。cmu david held团队的xingyu lin非常热衷于处理面团，有很多这个方面的工作，2022年的一篇工作以部分点云作为输入，可以轻松从仿真转移到现实世界，在不给定外部环境和没有事先轨迹编程的情况下，将现实世界中将一团面团铺展成目标形状。 "learning closed-loop dough manipulation using a differentiable reset module" by carl qi, xingyu lin, david held, iros 2022 (https://sites.google.com/view/dough-manipulation) 长时间操作可变形物体：xingyu lin的另外一篇工作展示了结合多个工具使用技能，如使用刀具切割、使用推杆推动和使用滚轴展开面团。 “planning with spatial-temporal abstraction from point clouds for deformable object manipulation” by xingyu lin*, carl qi*, yunchu zhang, zhiao huang, katerina fragkiadaki, yunzhu li, chuang gan, david held, corl 2022 （https://sites.google.com/view/pasta-plan ） 包饺子：stanford svl吴佳俊团队的haochen shi、许华哲（现清华叉院助理教授）、zhiao huang和yunzhu li（现uiuc助理教授）合作了robocraft和robocook两个工作，展示了机器人用多工具组合对面团进行长时间连续操作（long-horizon）的可能性。robocraft仅假定可以获得原始rgbd视觉观察，将传感数据转化为粒子，并使用图神经网络（gnns）学习基于粒子的动力学模型，以捕获底层系统的结构。学到的模型与基于模型预测控制（mpc）的算法相耦合，来规划机器人的行为。仅仅使用10分钟的真实机器人交互数据，机器人就能够学习一个能够合成控制信号将弹塑性物体变形成各种目标形状的动力学模型，包括机器人以前从未遇到过的形状，有很好的泛化能力。 “robocraft: learning to see, simulate, and shape elasto-plastic objects with graph networks” by haochen shi*, huazhe xu*, zhiao huang, yunzhu li, jiajun wu，rss 2022 五指灵巧手捏面团：umass amherst教授chuang gan团队的dexdeform通过人类示范来抽象多指手对可形变物体的熟练操作技能。参与这个工作的还有来自mit的sizhe li 和ucsd的zhiao huang，他们都有很多工作是在虚拟环境中处理类似橡皮泥这类可行变物体。dexdeform这篇论文的两个导师chuang gan和ucsd的苏昊在3d模拟有很多工作。 “dexdeform: dexterous deformable object manipulation with human demonstrations and differentiable physics” by sizhe li, zhiao huang, tao chen, tao du, hao su, joshua b. tenenbaum, chuang gan， iclr 2023 切割多材料物体：shuran song和chuang gan团队的roboninja，是一个用于多材料物体（例如，软外皮中带有刚性内核的物体，如鳄梨或芒果）的学习型切割系统。不同于切割单一材料物体（例如，切黄瓜），roboninja的目标是去除物体的软部分，同时保留刚性内核，从而最大化产量。 “roboninja: learning an adaptive cutting policy for multi-material objects” by zhenjia xu, zhou xian, xingyu lin, cheng chi, zhiao huang, chuang gan, shuran song，rss 2022 模仿学习是在灵巧操作领域常用的方法。正如人类幼崽和大人模仿各种动作、表情和语言一样，让机器人模仿人类在特定任务中的行为是一种被广泛应用的方法。在手部细节操作上，有以下几个工作可以直观展示灵巧操作模仿学习。 灵巧操作模仿学习（无物理部署）：ucsd王小龙团队提出的dexmv包括一个用于进行复杂灵巧操纵任务的多指机器人手的仿真系统，以及一个用于记录人手进行相同任务的大规模演示的计算机视觉系统。通过模仿学习算法，将人类动作转化为机器人演示，可以大幅改善机器人的学习，并解决了仅仅使用强化学习无法解决的复杂任务。 "dexmv: imitation learning for dexterous manipulation from human videos." by yuzhe qin*, yueh-hua wu*, shaowei liu, hanwen jiang, ruihan yang, yang fu, xiaolong wang, eccv 2022. 灵巧操纵模仿学习（有物理部署）：通过单摄像头遥控系统，在只使用一个ipad和一台计算机的情况下高效地收集人手3d演示。该系统的一个关键贡献是，在物理模拟器中为每个用户构建了一个自定义的机器人手，该机器人手的运动学结构和形状与操作者的手相似。这不仅避免了在数据收集过程中不稳定的人机手重定位，还为不同用户提供了更直观和个性化的界面。作者首先在模拟环境中使用自定义的手进行远程操作示范，然后通过重新定位（retargeting）将示范转化为allegro手，最后使用转化后的示范来训练策略，并部署到真实机器人上。这篇工作来自ucsd的yuzhe qin。 “from one hand to multiple hands: imitation learning for dexterous manipulation from single-camera teleoperation.” by yuzhe qin, hao su*, xiaolong wang*, iros 2022. 遥操作（teleoperation）顾名思义，人手远程操作机器手，远程操作的方式可以是基于视觉，力控和触觉传感等。遥操作在灵巧操作领域是常用的方法，接下来让我们看一下最近在遥操作方面比较有代表性的工作。 基于视觉的遥操作：当前的基于视觉的远程操作系统是针对特定的机器人模型和部署环境进行设计的，随着机器人模型数量的增加和操作环境的多样化，系统扩展性较差。anyteleop，是一个统一的通用远程操作系统，支持在单个系统内使用多个不同的机械臂、手、现实环境和摄像头配置。anyteleop是英伟达ai实验室dieter fox、yu-wei 关于灵巧操作和灵巧手相关的文章酝酿了将近三个月，一直没有找到好的角度去梳理。在经历了这大半年具身热和人形热之后，我觉得是时候冷静下来，重新思考究竟这波热潮的终点会是大家脑海中想象的通用机器人吗？除了大模型和tesla的擎天柱，到底这波热潮的底层驱动力是什么？是软件或硬件技术上有什么实质性的突破吗？ imitation learning, teleoperation and multimodal sensing, with research demonstrations. sensing & dexterous manipulation in human development, intelligent brains and dexterous hands have been crucial. our five-fingered hands use tools and help make the world richer. on the path toward general-purpose robots, i think the biggest limitation beyond intelligence is whether robots can acquire hands as dexterous as ours. what can robotic hands actually do in 2023? curious about that question, i reviewed more than a hundred papers from the preceding two or three years on hand-based manipulation with grippers or multi-fingered hands. i organized the work of chinese researchers active in this area and selected the best results i could find on familiar tasks. the focus is robot learning for dexterous manipulation, such as training an rl policy in simulation and transferring it to a physical robot, offering broader generalization in the comparison i am making than traditional methods. i hoped for comprehensive coverage, but inevitably missed excellent work and researchers. corrections and suggestions are welcome. this review is a snapshot as of october 2023. special thanks to yuanpei chen, binghao huang, yixuan wang and man xie for their expert suggestions. contents 1. a map of chinese researchers in dexterous manipulation 2. robot hands 3. rigid-object manipulation 4. deformable-object manipulation 5. imitation learning 6. teleoperation 7. multimodal sensing 8. reflections this article builds on a map of chinese researchers in ai and robotics, focusing more closely [editor’s note: the source incorrectly names humboldt university for jianwei zhang; his tams group is at the university of hamburg. affiliations are presented in the original review’s historical context.] dexterous manipulation has long challenged robotics. machine learning shows promise in simulation, but many results remain simulated, mainly because suitable hardware is lacking. common end effectors are two-finger grippers and multi-fingered dexterous hands. here is a brief introduction to research hardware. grippers: common end effectors for basic manipulation, including simple linear motions, with a relatively low hardware barrier. multi-fingered hands: common research choices include the three-finger d’claw, four-finger allegro and five-finger shadow hand. “shandow” in the source is a spelling error. some laboratories build their own systems. deepak pathak’s cmu group introduced leap hand, reported at roughly one-eighth the cost of allegro, and the compliant dash hand. the source reports costs under us$2,000 for these low-cost designs; these are historical hardware estimates, not current quotations. other options include dlr hand from the german aerospace center, the bebionic prosthetic hand, schunk svh and vincent hands. chinese examples include hong liu’s team at harbin institute of technology, peng wang’s team at the chinese academy of sciences’ institute of automation, and inspire robots. common objects include rigid items such as lego and cans, deformable materials such as dough and cloth, and liquids. rigid objects are relatively easier, so many results can run on physical robots. research areas include in-hand reorientation, non-prehensile manipulation through pushing or poking, extrinsic dexterity using the environment—for example, a wall to stand a box upright—and long-horizon manipulation that chains movements to complete a task. these academic terms describe everyday human actions. let us see what robots can achieve. in-hand reorientation is necessary for many dexterous tasks. tao chen and colleagues developed a general controller trained with rl in simulation and evaluated on new objects in the real world. it generalizes to object shapes absent from training and handles objects suspended in the air, counteracting gravity while reorienting them. the hardware uses open-source components costing under us$5,000. [editor’s note: the source describes the hand as facing upward; the especially challenging demonstrated setup uses a downward-facing hand.] “visual dexterity: in-hand dexterous manipulation from depth,” by tao chen, megha tippur, siyang wu, vikash kumar, edward adelson and pulkit agrawal. the published science robotics title is “visual dexterity: in-hand reorientation of novel and complex object shapes.” another project by tao chen and jie xu uses a simple model-free framework to learn reorientation with upward- and downward-facing hands in simulation. the policies reorient more than 2,000 geometrically varied objects and transfer zero-shot to new ones. this work remained in simulation rather than physical deployment and received the corl 2021 best paper award. “a system for general in-hand object re-orientation,” by tao chen, jie xu and pulkit agrawal, corl 2021, best paper award. recently, nvidia, the university of pennsylvania, caltech and ut austin introduced eureka, combining llms and rl. gpt-4 improves reward functions, and rl trains controllers. in simulation, this supports complex five-fingered skills such as pen spinning and rotating objects in the hand, likened in the source to rolling walnuts. “eureka: human-level reward design via coding large language models,” by jason ma et al. https://eureka-research.github.io/ non-prehensile manipulation and extrinsic dexterity address objects difficult to grasp, such as a book or a large flat object lying on a table. non-prehensile manipulation moves objects without grasping, for example by pushing or poking. extrinsic dexterity uses the environment: push a flat box against a wall to stand it upright, then grasp its narrow edge. wenxuan zhou in david held’s group has extensive gripper-based work in both areas. fuchun sun’s tsinghua group and jianwei zhang’s hamburg group also study them; see the references. zhou’s video below illustrates the ideas. “learning to grasp the ungraspable with emergent extrinsic dexterity,” by wenxuan zhou and david held, corl 2022. long-horizon dexterous manipulation of rigid objects throwing and catching is familiar to humans but challenging for robots, requiring high-speed movement, coordination and varied object interactions. this project uses arms and five-fingered hands, training through multi-agent rl in simulation and transferring to real robots. to overcome the sim-to-real gap, it introduces several algorithmic designs, including an object-trajectory predictor that helps the catching robot estimate motion and respond in real time. co-first authors binghao huang and yuanpei chen have extensive dexterous-manipulation work. “dynamic handover: throw and catch with bimanual hands,” by binghao huang*, yuanpei chen*, tianyu wang, yuzhe qin, yaodong yang, nikolay atanasov and xiaolong wang, corl 2023. *equal contribution. assembling lego: dexterous hands face high-dimensional actions and complex compositional dynamics over long tasks. c. karen liu’s stanford group developed an rl system that chains dexterous policies to achieve longer-term goals, with strong sim-to-real transfer. “sequential dexterity: chaining dexterous policies for long-horizon manipulation,” by yuanpei chen, chen wang, fei-fei li and c. karen liu, corl 2023. bidan huang’s tencent robotics x team also has excellent long-horizon work. its april 2023 demonstration of cocktail preparation using an arm and three-fingered hand was striking. yuke zhu’s ut austin group built an interesting instant-noodle-making robot using grippers. videos of both appear in a map of chinese researchers in ai and robotics. manipulating deformable objects has many everyday applications, such as kneading dough and folding clothes, but is particularly difficult for robots. elasto-plastic dough lacks a compact state representation and requires rich contact; folds in cloth create occlusion. physical demonstrations more often use grippers than multi-fingered hands, while much multi-fingered dough work remains simulated. here are representative results. dressing: manipulating cloth in 3d is difficult. earlier approaches made strong assumptions about fixed garments or arm poses and generalized poorly. yufei wang in david held’s cmu group studies cloth manipulation. a 2023 project dresses participants with varied arm poses and garments. “one policy to dress them all: learning to dress people with diverse poses and garments,” by yufei wang, zhanyi sun, zackory erickson* and david held*, rss 2023. https://sites.google.com/view/one-policy-dress visual haptic reasoning for deformable cloth: another yufei wang project infers where forces act and their magnitude from visual observations and robot movement. “visual haptic reasoning: estimating contact forces by observing deformable object interactions,” by yufei wang, david held and zackory erickson, iros 2022. unfolding cloth: if i had a robot housekeeper, the chore i would most want it to handle is putting a duvet inside its cover. [emoji] after reading more than ten cloth-manipulation papers, i doubt we will escape doing that ourselves within ten years—a personal prediction made in 2023. shuran song’s columbia group proposed two robot arms working with a movable air blower, one of the most efficient clothes-folding approaches i have seen. dextairity is a self-supervised framework that learns to perform tasks through grasping and airflow-based actions. closed-loop blowing continuously adjusts direction from visual feedback, handling highly stochastic dynamics. first author zhenjia xu earned his undergraduate degree at shanghai jiao tong university and was then a phd student with song. he also led roboninja, the avocado-cutting project discussed below. “dextairity: deformable manipulation can be a breeze,” by zhenjia xu, cheng chi, benjamin burchfiel, eric cousineau, siyuan feng and shuran song, rss 2022. https://dextairity.cs.columbia.edu/ dough manipulation perhaps out of a love for flour-based food, many researchers try robotic kneading, cutting noodles and even making dumplings. physical systems usually combine grippers with multiple tools, while some simulated systems use multi-fingered hands. the most elaborate dough demonstration i had seen was making dumplings. what happens after they go into the pot, i cannot say! wang’s uc san diego group introduced dexmv, combining a simulated multi-fingered hand for complex tasks with a computer-vision system recording large-scale human demonstrations of those tasks.
